Security teams now ask language models to help sort a flood of threat reports, but the reports themselves mislead. Yuqiao Meng and 6 co-authors study how LLM help in cyber threat intelligence goes wrong. They argue the core problem is the landscape: evidence is tangled, crowdsourced, and quick to change. A human-in-the-loop scheme labels failure modes across the threat intelligence life cycle.

Three domain-specific failures stand out: false links from surface metadata, clashing facts from conflicting sources, and weak reach toward new threats. Causal interventions confirm these causes, and targeted defenses cut failure rates a lot. The team offers the results as a roadmap for sturdier threat intelligence agents.
arxiv-2509-23873:
Fine-tuning data can be pruned by dropping whole examples or by trimming tokens, but doing only one wastes the other. Shaobo Wang and 11 co-authors unify both in Q-Tuning. Their diagnostic, the Error-Uncertainty plane, maps the value of training data across samples and tokens at once. Rich examples can still hold redundant tokens, while token pruning can cut vital corrective signals.

Q-Tuning first keeps examples rich in informative misconceptions or calibration value. It then trims weak tokens only from the misconception examples, leaving calibration ones whole. On one small model it beat full-data training by a wide margin while using an eighth of the data, a first for dynamic pruning.
arxiv-2509-23973:
Planets around old, fast-moving stars may have been stirred harder than planets in the calm thin disk. Sheila Sagear and 6 co-authors compare orbital eccentricities of Kepler planets by their hosts' galactic disk membership. The photoeccentric effect constrains each orbit's shape. Gaia astrometry and chemically calibrated criteria then sort host stars, probabilistically, into the kinematic thin and thick disks.

Among single-transiting systems, thick-disk planets run more eccentric than thin-disk ones. Multi-transiting systems show no such gap. The authors check that metallicity or giant planet rates alone do not explain the split. They call for fuller analyses to untangle age and other star-planet links.
arxiv-2509-24073:
Adnan Abbas and 5 co-authors watched how people live with a chat agent that speaks first. For two weeks, twelve volunteers used an agent that checked in to help plan the day and reflect on it. The agent acted as a coach, not a clerk that waits for orders.

People took up tips, pushed back on them, or haggled over terms. Over time, some built a shared sense of how the agent thinks. Others drifted away or resisted. The agent also misstepped: it could be rigid, cut in too soon, and promise more than it could do. The authors draw design lessons for agents that aim to change habits.
arxiv-2509-24173:
Some data are sensitive and some are not, and privacy rules can treat them apart. Sun-Moon Yoon and 3 co-authors study distribution estimation under utility-optimized local differential privacy. Each person randomizes their own data before sharing, with strict protection for sensitive values and looser handling for the rest.

The team characterizes the exact trade-off between privacy and accuracy in this setting. Their proof uses a generalized variance bound, a reduction to a new class of extreme mechanisms, and a way to split distributions into parts. They also give schemes that reach the limit, built from a block design known to be optimal under standard local privacy.
arxiv-2509-24573:
Design problems tied to physics equations are slow to solve, since each design choice changes the state the equations describe. Yusuf Guven and 2 co-authors built a learning framework with two networks to speed that up. One network predicts how the system evolves over time. The other predicts near-best decisions for the design.

Together they give real-time strategies while keeping the link between decisions and physics clear. On test tasks built on Burgers' equation, the heat equation, and voltage control, solution quality matched classic control methods. Speed improved by up to ten thousandfold in the best case.
arxiv-2510-00173:
Alfredo Gamboa, Juan Limaco, and Luis Yapu wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on steering a heat-like equation to rest. The equation is parabolic and semilinear, and its diffusion fades to zero at one boundary point. The domain itself changes shape over time, which makes control harder. The authors use a game-like Stackelberg-Nash strategy, with one leader control and follower controls chasing Nash balance.

First they handle the linearized system with a Carleman inequality built for degenerate, time-varying cases. That estimate gives local controllability for the linearized problem. A classical inverse function theorem then lifts the result to the full nonlinear equation. The conclusion is local null controllability: nearby starting states can be driven exactly to zero. Results like this extend control theory toward realistic settings where domains move and materials degenerate.
arxiv-2510-00573:
Yen-Ling Tai and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on robots that scoop food without spilling it. Scooping sounds simple, but foods shift, slump, and scatter unpredictably. Demonstration-trained policies often fail on new dishes and portion sizes. Their system, GRITS, wraps a diffusion policy in guidance from a dedicated spillage predictor.

The predictor learns from simulated spills involving spheres, cubes, cones, and cylinders of varied mass and friction. At run time it scores candidate motion rollouts and steers sampling toward safer paths. Training covered six food categories on a real robotic platform. Testing then threw ten unseen categories with different shapes and quantities at the robot. The system succeeded in about eighty-two percent of trials overall. Spillage dropped to about four percent, over forty percent below unguided baselines.
arxiv-2510-00673:
Luciano examines a modified cosmology built on a generalized mass-to-horizon entropy relation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Entropic cosmology explains the universe's faster expansion through forces tied to the cosmic horizon. Earlier work showed that simple versions collapse back to the standard entropy formula and inherit its limits. A generalized relation with two free parameters opens a genuinely different model.

Luciano tests what that model implies for the early universe. Using a spherical top-hat model, he shows the growth of matter clumps changes clearly under the modified expansion history. He also studies primordial gravitational waves, the faint ripples born in the universe's first moments. In parts of the parameter space, the model boosts their expected abundance. Upcoming detectors sensitive below a thousand hertz could therefore test the idea directly.
arxiv-2510-00973:
Constantinou, Shorttle, and Rimmer constrain lightning on Venus through atmospheric chemistry in this 2025 arXiv paper. Whether Venus has lightning at all is still disputed, since flashes, radio signals, and plasma waves have given conflicting answers. The authors take an indirect route through nitric oxide, a gas that only lightning produces in Venus's lower atmosphere. If the reported nitric oxide abundance is real, some lightning rate must sustain it against chemical destruction.

Their photochemical-kinetic modelling asks how much lightning power that balance requires. Matching the reported abundance demands at least three times the total lightning power released on Earth, by their headline calculation. That could mean more frequent strikes, stronger strikes, or both. The rarity of optical flashes hints the strikes may sit deep below the clouds, perhaps from volcanic or wind-driven charging near the surface.
arxiv-2510-01373:
Sakai and a large Thai-led collaboration detect hydroxyl maser emission from a famous returning comet with a national radio telescope. Comet 12P/Pons-Brooks swings by every seventy-one years, and its recent return drew global attention. Water breakdown products produce the hydroxyl signal, a tracer of the comet's activity.

The forty-meter Thai National Radio Telescope made the detection during the apparition. Maser emission signals active outgassing as sunlight warms the nucleus. Such measurements calibrate how much water the comet sheds compared with its dust and gas displays. A regional facility thereby joined the worldwide watch on a historic visitor. Hydroxyl radicals are water's fingerprint after sunlight splits the molecule. Dozens of Thai institutions share the author list. Outburst-prone 12P drew crowds during its bright 2024 approach. Maser amplification makes the faint line detectable at all. Radio eyes complement the optical show.
arxiv-2510-01473:
Halstead and co-authors ask researchers whether they would actually trust language models to find datasets for them. Keyword matching forces searchers to guess the exact words earlier researchers used, and relevant data hides. Semantic search promises relief, but acceptance by working researchers was unmeasured.

Focus groups with twenty-seven researchers fed a conceptual model of adoption. Benefits alone do not persuade researchers to switch tools. Barriers around trust dominate, while transparency features offer the route past them. Developers get a co-design mandate: build with users, or watch the tool sit unused. Natural language questions replace brittle keyword strings in the vision. Missing relevant data is the quiet cost of vocabulary mismatch. Human-centered design frames the whole inquiry methodologically. Reporting limitations openly counts as a transparency feature users wanted. Discovery quietly shapes what science gets done downstream.
arxiv-2510-01573:
Liu, Zhou, and Loureiro show that a common plasma instability can freeze the growth of magnetic fields. In many plasmas, small magnetic tangles merge into larger ones, moving energy upscale. That inverse transfer helps explain how weak seed fields could grow into cosmic magnetism.

Simulations of decaying collisionless plasma reveal the firehose instability spoiling the mergers. By canceling magnetic tension, it stops islands from coalescing and leaves them stretched thin. A strong guide field, or larger starting structures, restores the merging. The result warns that seed fields from early-universe processes may often fail to grow. The structures stall near the particle Larmor scale, far below cosmic sizes. First-principles simulation catches the kinetic effects that fluid models miss. Magnetization level becomes the switch that decides whether growth proceeds. Astrophysical seed theories must now check this kinetic gate. Elongated shapes are the visible scar.
arxiv-2510-01873:
Fabian, Kąkol, and Leiderman clarify a differentiability property for spaces of continuous functions in this 2025 mathematics paper. The Asplund property is well understood for Banach spaces, where it ties to where functions can be differentiated. Extending it to function spaces with the compact-open topology produced clashing definitions in the literature. The authors set out to unify that scattered picture.

Their treatment covers the space of continuous functions on any Tychonoff space, far beyond the Banach setting. They establish a characterization of when that function space holds the Asplund property. Classical results enter along the way, including the Namioka-Phelps theorem and what it implies here. Every proof is presented in self-contained form using standard techniques. The paper thus serves as both a correction and a reference. Functional analysts get one consistent language for Asplund behavior in general function spaces.
arxiv-2510-01973:
Øvereng, Baggaley, and Angheluta simulate collisions between vortices and waves in quantum fluids in this 2025 physics paper. Their system is a two-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate, governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation. Vortex collisions drive the decay of quantum turbulence in such fluids. What happens to the energy during each collision type was only partly understood.

When vortex-antivortex dipoles collide, kinetic energy moves from swirling flow into sound-like modes. Below a critical separation, annihilation events release quantum energy that mediates the transfer. Above that threshold, plain vortex acceleration does the job instead. Wave-vortex collisions look different again. An incoming solitary wave splits into two transient phase slips at the vortex. One slip helps annihilate the vortex, while the other grows a stable core and replaces it. Trajectory and spectrum analysis backs each of these mechanisms. The results sharpen the picture of how quantum turbulence spends its energy.
arxiv-2510-02073:
Behrmann and ten co-authors read tissue properties from wearable light signals with a physics-based model in this 2025 paper. Optical sensors in smartwatches use light pulses to yield heart rate and blood oxygen. The waveforms hold richer body information, but deep learning reads it through opaque features. Clinicians cannot interpret those features, and sensor designers cannot use them.

Their model, PPGen, ties the signal to readable physical and optical parameters of the tissue. On top of it, hybrid amortized inference estimates those values quickly and robustly. Simulation-trained inference keeps the speed of deep learning while restoring physical meaning. Validation used synthetic datasets generated by the model itself. The approach promises wearables that report tissue properties, not just pulse statistics. It also gives sensor designers a principled way to test hardware choices in simulation.
arxiv-2510-02473:
Sawczuk and Gnang give two fresh proofs of a classic graph polynomial identity. Their 2025 mathematics paper concerns the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial. That polynomial lists every cycle visiting all vertices once. It also connects to two famous matrix polynomials. The determinant and permanent sit at the heart of algebra. The identity ties the cycle polynomial to both of them. The first proof uses a direct counting argument. It stays accessible to readers with basic combinatorics. The second proof treats monomials as lists of graphs. Algebra and combinatorics meet in that viewpoint.

A matching identity for Hamiltonian paths follows the same route. Hamiltonicity testing is a landmark hard problem in computing. Polynomial identities give theorists new handles on it. Two proofs illuminate different faces of one truth. Students gain an entry point through the simpler proof. Researchers gain a flexible method for related identities.
arxiv-2510-02773:
Al Rahat and co-authors fix security bugs in OpenID Connect programs with a counterexample guided repair engine. Their 2025 software security paper presents a tool called AuthFix. Single sign-on bugs have caused breaches and heavy losses. Hand patching such flaws is slow and error prone. AuthFix chains three stages together. Fault localization finds where the flow breaks. A language model synthesizes candidate patches. A Petri net model checker verifies each patch. Counterexamples steer the next repair attempt when checks fail.

A dataset of known OpenID bugs graded the tool. It produced correct patches for seventeen of twenty three bugs. Many patches matched developer fixes in meaning. The verifier keeps plausible but wrong patches out. Authentication code guards nearly every online account. Automated, verified repair scales where audits cannot. The model checker is the trust anchor of the design.
arxiv-2510-04273:
Strang and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on learning better branching decisions while a mixed-integer programming solver works through a stream of problems. Branch-and-bound solvers depend heavily on which variable they branch on, yet expert heuristics are tuned for broad average performance. Industrial users often solve many similar instances whose matrices, right-hand sides, bounds, or objectives change slightly. The authors exploit that repetition with an online learning method built around a graph-based heuristic called influence branching.

The heuristic uses graph representations of an instance's structure during the early branch-and-bound iterations. Thompson sampling ranks representations by the speedup they deliver over SCIP, updating choices as more instances arrive. Competition experiments achieved performance comparable to leading online learning approaches. The authors report evidence that the method transfers to online settings with changes in several parts of an instance and more samples for learning.
arxiv-2510-04373:
Hadi Nekoei and coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on helping AI agents learn new tasks. Agents do well on familiar work but often fail in new settings. Fixing them with training runs is costly, and it can make them forget older skills. Past work sessions hold useful lessons, but the records are long and noisy. The team built a system that turns those old records into short hints.

The system is called JEF Hinter, and it zooms in on key steps inside long work records. It learns from failed runs as well as good ones, which most older methods cannot do. At run time, it picks the hints that fit the current task and shows them to the agent. Tests on three task suites beat strong baselines, including hints written by people. The gains held on new goals and new tasks, at only a small added cost.
arxiv-2510-04573:
Haoqiang Kang and six coauthors at the University of California, San Diego wrote this 2025 paper on better reasoning in language models. Models reason by writing a chain of thought, one token after the next. That order locks early words in place, so the model cannot go back and revise them. The team moved reasoning into a latent space where whole blocks can be reworked.

An autoencoder first compresses text reasoning steps into blocks of latent thought tokens. A diffusion model in that space then denoises a block at once, with attention running both ways inside the block. Longer horizons and repeated refinement become cheap in that setup. Many diverse reasoning paths can grow in parallel for one question. On math and planning tests, the system beat rival methods. It won on accuracy, on diversity of solutions, and on how readable the reasoning stayed. The authors call the system LaDiR.
arxiv-2510-04673:
Chan Hee Song and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on teaching computer agents from videos of people. Agents that use software need demonstrations of real tasks, but labeled demonstrations are scarce and costly. The web, meanwhile, overflows with screen recordings of people doing tasks in real programs. Their framework, Watch and Learn, mines those videos for training material. It turns footage into action traces an agent can replay.

The key move is an inverse dynamics task: guess the action that links two screen states in a row. That puzzle is easier to learn than generation and needs little hand engineering. A retrieval step first gathers videos that match a task family. The pipeline produced more than fifty three thousand high quality traces from videos. Those traces helped agents both as examples inside the prompt and as training data. Gains showed up on an operating system benchmark, for leading frameworks alike.
arxiv-2510-04973:
Arjan Cornelissen extends a young framework for building quantum algorithms in this 2025 arXiv paper. In the framework, an algorithm is drawn as a hypergraph. The edges act like switches that route inputs to the output the algorithm computes. Until now, the framework handled only yes-or-no style problems.

Cornelissen generalizes it to problems with many possible answers. The wider framework turns out to contain three older approaches as special cases. They are quantum divide and conquer, decision trees, and unified quantum walk search. For walk search, his methods let subroutine costs be shared across runs. That change simplifies the algorithm and removes log factors from its query cost.
arxiv-2510-05073:
Watwood and twenty-three colleagues probe the inner structure of a silicon isotope in this 2025 arXiv paper. They study silicon-32, whose protons and neutrons occupy a shell called 1s-0d. Knowing which orbitals sit empty reveals how the nucleus arranges itself. The team fired helium-3 at silicon-32 in inverse kinematics to add a proton.

The reaction produced phosphorus-33 states up to about 4.5 MeV of excitation. From the measured rates, the authors extracted spectroscopic factors for each orbital. Combined with neutron data, these gave the proton vacancies in the silicon-32 ground state. The 1s orbital proved consistent with being completely empty, in both silicon-32 and silicon-34. Shell-model calculations matched the measured distributions well.
arxiv-2510-05373:
Utkarsh Saxena and Kaushik Roy squeeze the memory cache of large language models to two bits in this 2025 arXiv paper. The key-value cache grows with every token and dominates GPU memory at long contexts. Quantizing it aggressively introduces errors that corrupt attention. Generation quality then degrades noticeably.

Their framework, KVLinC, attacks the two error sources separately. A Hadamard rotation reduces quantization error in the stored values. Lightweight linear correction adapters then compensate for errors in the quantized keys. Across LLaMA, Qwen2.5, and Qwen3 models, KVLinC matched or beat strong baselines at higher compression. A custom attention kernel ran up to about 2.55 times faster than FlashAttention.
arxiv-2510-05473:
Yánez-Parreño and colleagues grew aluminum films in deep cold and watched the metal change. Aluminum is the workhorse material of superconducting quantum circuits. The team deposited thin films on sapphire in vacuum at six kelvin, far below room temperature. Their 2025 paper compares those cold-grown films with normal ones across structure, optics, and electrical behavior.

Cold growth made the films grainy and more disordered than usual. Thicker cold films even turned yellow instead of mirror bright. The smaller grains strengthened superconductivity, raising the temperature and field the films could withstand. The method offers a clean way to tune disorder without adding chemical impurities. The team then built microwave resonators from both kinds of film. Both kinds showed similar quality, limited by the same surface loss process. Cold films also carried higher kinetic inductance, a trait prized in sensitive detectors.
arxiv-2510-05773:
Haisch settles a dispute over tiny hadronic effects in a flagship Higgs decay. The Higgs decay into two photons runs through W boson and top quark loops. Recent studies reported puzzling, contradictory sizes for non-perturbative hadronic contributions. His 2025 dispersive analysis computes them systematically at last.

Dispersion relations respecting low-energy QCD symmetries organize the calculation. Hadronic effects enter through form factors of intermediate hadronic states. The result shifts the decay width by only about zero point zero zero four percent. That is negligible even for future high-precision collider measurements. The finding matches the naive expectation that perturbative loops dominate completely. The channel thus stays among the cleanest for precision Higgs studies. The Standard Model prediction's accuracy now rests on perturbative corrections alone. Percent-level branching ratios at the high-luminosity LHC motivated the check. Haisch also estimates hadronic effects in gluon-fusion Higgs production.
arxiv-2510-05973:
Smagin and colleagues extend the Fourier modal method to bi-anisotropic gratings. The method is a fast, exact workhorse for layered optical stacks. Standard versions cannot treat matter that couples electric and magnetic fields. Their 2025 version admits any magneto-electric tensor for such chiral matter.

Fourier tensors of the matter values are derived for two schemes. One scheme applies Lifeng Li's factor rules, and the other omits them. Without magneto-electric coupling, both fall back to the standard forms. With coupling, the factor-rule scheme gains speed much faster. The gain holds even when the chirality strength is large. Circular dichroism and optical activity are the effects behind the advance. Chiral molecules, lacking mirror symmetry, cause both effects at root. The scope is layered stacks periodic in two directions. Non-reciprocal and chiral stacks can now be modeled exactly with the standard toolkit.
arxiv-2510-06273:
Srivastava and Niedzielski classify transient noise in LIGO data with a vision transformer in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Short glitches contaminate the detector stream and hinder gravitational wave detection. Gravity Spy sorts these noise events into classes, and the O3 run added two classes older models never saw.

They fine-tuned a pretrained Vision Transformer, ViT-B/32, on a combined dataset. Training merged the original classes with two additional O3a classes, twenty-four in total. The model reached classification efficiency near ninety-two percent. Sorting glitches reliably helps analysts veto noise and protect real signals. It feeds detector characterization, since glitch families guide hardware fixes. Image transformers transfer well to spectrogram-like detector data. Vision transformers join the toolkit for keeping gravitational wave searches clean as new noise types appear.
arxiv-2510-06573:
Xinyun Cao and four colleagues build tools that help blind and low-vision people use virtual 3D worlds. Their 2025 paper presents RAVEN, a system for real-time access to virtual scenes. Blind users often struggle with spatial awareness, navigation, and interaction in these spaces. Older aids add sound or touch cues, but those aids are fixed in advance.

RAVEN lets users ask questions and request changes in plain language while a scene runs. The system understands the scene and generates code to modify it on the spot. Eight blind or low-vision participants tested the system in a study. They found it intuitive, flexible, and empowering to use. The team also reports real limits around reliability and clear error reporting. Their work moves accessibility from a static feature toward a conversation that users control themselves.
arxiv-2510-06973:
Zhantao Yang leads a team tackling a failure in captions for long videos. Their 2025 paper studies the ID-Matching problem, where a caption must recognize the same person across different frames. Getting identities wrong makes captions confusing and hurts text-to-video generation. Prior fixes relied on point-wise matching and generalized poorly.

The team built a benchmark to measure identity matching in captions. Probing GPT-4o with it revealed two levers that help. Captions improve when the model uses image information more fully, and when each person's description carries more detail. Their method, RICE, builds on those insights inside vision-language models. It tracks individuals through a long video. On GPT-4o, identity precision jumped from fifty percent to ninety percent. Recall leapt from fifteen percent to eighty percent. RICE beat the previous best system, ShareGPT4Video, on every benchmark tried. Consistent identities make long captions more trustworthy.
arxiv-2510-07173:
Khondaker, Harrington, and Shehata introduce NurseLLM, which they call the first language model built just for nursing. Their 2025 paper notes that medical models mostly serve doctors' tasks. Nursing has its own knowledge, exams, and daily decisions. The team set out to build both training data and tests for that field. Their model targets multiple-choice questions across a wide range of nursing topics.

A multi-stage pipeline generated a large set of nursing questions for training. New benchmarks were built to grade models fairly on nursing knowledge. In tests, NurseLLM beat general and medical models of similar size. The authors also probed step-by-step reasoning and teams of cooperating models. Both showed promise for harder nursing tasks. Specialized models like this could support nurse training and exam practice. The work argues that each health profession may need its own tailored model.
arxiv-2510-07373:
Lesser and co-authors teach a machine to predict which materials will superconduct, and at what heat limit. Their 2025 paper mixes chemistry-aware inputs with learning whose logic can be inspected. Their inputs sum up local bonding patterns through graphlet histograms and symmetry counts drawn from crystal structures. A custom kernel feeds those inputs into Gaussian-process models. The models both estimate the limit and sort likely superconductors, reporting doubt alongside each call. Training data came from a checked database of three-dimensional superconductors.

The heat predictor explained most of the spread in measured values. A test of which inputs mattered then found that just four local bonding inputs nearly matched the full model's power. One overlooked input stood out: the gap in electron affinity between neighboring atoms. Bonding-related values proved surprisingly strong across compounds. Readable predictors like this guide lab synthesis toward promising candidates.
arxiv-2510-07573:
Willcox and a large team argue that black hole masses come in two families, and the gravitational wave data now show it. Their 2025 paper uses the latest LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA catalog, which nearly doubles the known merging binary black holes. Below thirty solar masses, the distribution of chirp masses, the combination detectors measure best, shows three peaks. Recent stellar evolution models independently predict two families of newborn black hole masses, stamped by structure in the collapsing star's core. Folded through binary pairing, two black hole families naturally produce three chirp-mass peaks.

The trimodality survives every variation, emerging as a robust fingerprint of the new remnant-mass prescription. Traditional formation models without the bimodal spectrum cannot reproduce it. The updated models also predict merger rates a few times lower, closer to what the detectors observe.
arxiv-2510-07673:
Nguyen and a large collaboration wrote this 2025 cosmology paper on supernovae and cosmic structure. Type Ia supernovae explode with nearly standard brightness, so small brightness changes carry information. Their host galaxies drift with the growth of large-scale structure. Those drifts should leave matching patterns in galaxy maps and supernova brightness. The team searched for that cross-pattern using survey data. Their sample covered only the nearby universe, within redshift one tenth.

They combined the DESI Bright Galaxy Survey release with the Pantheon+ supernova collection at low redshift. The cross-correlation signal was detected between galaxy positions and supernova brightness. Fitting the signal gave a growth rate of structure that matches the standard cosmological model's prediction. Mock catalogs from large simulations confirmed the method recovers the true value. The authors argue that supernova brightness patterns can become a new tool for measuring how cosmic structure grows.
arxiv-2510-08473:
Lynn Engelberts and co-authors speed up a quantum attack on lattice cryptography in a 2025 arXiv paper. Finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, the problem called SVP, underpins post-quantum cryptosystems. The fastest heuristic attacks use sieving, which repeatedly combines lattice vectors into shorter ones. Taking triples instead of pairs in each step saves memory but was slower in quantum time.

Their improved 3-tuple sieving cuts the quantum time exponent from 0.3098 to 0.2846 in the dimension, a meaningful drop for exponential algorithms. A preprocessing step links each vector to nearby center points, focusing the search on promising neighborhoods. Two-level amplitude amplification, a quantum search booster, does the rest of the work. Memory use matches the improved time budget in their accounting. They call it the fastest known quantum algorithm for this problem under that memory limit.
arxiv-2510-08873:
Jin and co-authors design custom AI chips by snapping together a small set of reusable blocks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Modern accelerators are usually built as one uniform design, yet each operation inside a neural network has its own pattern of work and memory needs. Custom chips fit those patterns better but cost a fortune to design from scratch. Chiplets, small prefabricated pieces of silicon, promise reuse, if designers can tell which pieces are truly needed.

Their framework, Mozart, breaks networks down operation by operation and explores mixes of chiplets and memory types. Eight well-chosen chiplets sufficed to build composite chips that cut energy use by more than forty percent against uniform rivals. Performance stayed within a few percent of designs with no reuse limits. For data center language model serving, energy fell by roughly a sixth, and speculative decoding ran much faster while using far less power.
arxiv-2510-08973:
Patra, Kolte, and Bandyopadhyay solve a geometry problem with practical uses in simulation and robotics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Given a point in space and a quadric surface, a bowl- or saddle-shaped surface with a central axis of symmetry, how close is the point to the surface? The answer feeds collision checks, where a physics engine must know the gap to a curved wall.

The team first classifies general quadrics to recognize the axisymmetric ones. Symmetry then lets them flatten the three-dimensional problem into a two-dimensional one about conics, the classic curves of plane geometry. Their method works directly with conic properties such as eccentricity and the sub-normal. Cases split by where the point sits: two sub-cases for parabolas and three for ellipses and hyperbolas. Implemented in the C language, the solver ran faster than the widely used Bullet physics library.
arxiv-2510-09573:
Siphiwe Shandu, Thabiso Moropa, and Alain Ndjiongue explore a new way to connect underground mines in a 2025 arXiv letter. Mines need wireless links deep below ground, and laying new infrastructure is costly. Their idea, contactless power line communication, sends signals through the radiation of existing power cables, treating the wires as long-wire antennas rather than plugging into them directly.

The authors build a system-level model that cascades a radio channel with the power line channel. It accounts for multipath propagation, frequency-dependent weakening, and Rician fading, a standard model of signal fluctuation. Simulations between one and twenty gigahertz show the wire's length strongly shapes its radiation pattern, directivity, and input impedance. The findings suggest the approach transmits waves without direct electrical contact. The team presents it as a robust, low-cost option that fits existing mining power infrastructure and reduces maintenance.
arxiv-2510-09673:
Simone Fischer-Hübner, Leonardo Martucci, Lejla Islami, Ala Sarah Alaqra, and Farzaneh Karegar survey cybersecurity readiness in Swedish organisations in a 2025 arXiv paper. Threats and incidents keep growing, and organisations in Värmland, a region of Inner Scandinavia, must raise their defences. The authors ask what competence those organisations have and what education they still need.

The study combines interviews with key leaders from firms and public sector bodies and an earlier survey of the same population. It examines current readiness and the demand for training and skills growth. The authors then discuss how far the findings generalise beyond Värmland and Sweden, and which parts may be specific to the local context. They conclude by proposing concrete efforts to strengthen cybersecurity competence across Inner Scandinavia, aimed at both firms and public bodies.
arxiv-2510-09873:
Chan, Pantangi, Razafimahatratra, and Peter Sin study state transfer in oriented Cayley graphs in this 2025 arXiv paper in quantum information. Perfect state transfer means a quantum state placed at one vertex arrives intact at another after a fixed time. Oriented Cayley graphs are directed networks built from a group's structure.

The authors construct examples of perfect and multiple state transfer across a wide range of groups. Their examples span abelian groups, where operations commute, up to nonsolvable groups with far richer structure. They also prove general restrictions and nonexistence results, marking where transfer cannot happen. The results map the border between groups that support faithful quantum communication and those that do not.
arxiv-2510-10073:
Ying and co-authors present SecureWebArena in this 2025 arXiv paper on the security of web agents. Agents built on large vision-language models can automate complex online tasks. In real deployments they face serious security risks, from malicious pages to deceptive prompts.

SecureWebArena is a holistic benchmark for those risks. It evaluates how agents behave when the web environment itself turns hostile, rather than only whether they finish a benign task. A shared security benchmark lets developers compare defenses on equal footing. The authors motivate the work by the gap between agent capability and agent safety: automation that books, buys, and clicks must also resist manipulation while doing so.
arxiv-2510-10173:
Haimes introduces Chord Colourizer in this 2025 arXiv paper on music visualization. The system finds the musical key of an audio signal in near real time and shows it visually. Notes are assigned colors from Isaac Newton's original color wheel, keeping the historic link between pitch and hue.

A graphical interface displays the key as the music plays. The system also drives an Arduino-controlled LED display with 3D-printed star-shaped diffusers, giving a physical ambient representation in the room. The design joins music analysis with synesthetic display, where one sense is rendered as another. Such tools can support teaching, performance, and accessible music experiences for listeners who benefit from visual cues.
arxiv-2510-10373:
Salas studies boundary behavior of analytic functions on Banach spaces in this 2025 arXiv paper in functional analysis. The spaces considered hold analytic functions on the unit disc, with polynomials dense inside them and point evaluations continuous. The question is how wildly a typical function's values can grow near the boundary circle.

Salas proves that if such a space contains one function whose modulus has limit superior infinity almost everywhere on the circle, then the same holds for a residual set of functions. Residual means topologically generic: wild boundary behavior is the rule, not the exception. The result extends classical facts about Hardy-type spaces to a broad abstract setting.
arxiv-2510-10673:
Filippo Calderoni and Adam Clay measure how hard it is to classify a class of ordered groups, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The groups are finitely generated and bi-orderable, meaning their elements can be lined up in an order respected by multiplication from both sides. The question is the isomorphism problem: how complex is it to tell whether two such groups are really the same? The authors approach the problem through descriptive set theory, which grades classification problems by difficulty.

They analyze the standard Borel space of left orderable groups that are finitely generated, and its subspace of bi-orderable ones, using spaces of relative cones to encode the orders. With this setup, they show the isomorphism relation on these groups is weakly universal. That is a strong complexity statement, ruling out any simple complete invariant for them.
arxiv-2510-10973:
Sanchit Sinha and four co-authors train vision language models to reason about charts reliably and explainably, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These models ace many visual tasks but falter on unfamiliar chart data, and asking them to show their reasoning often makes answers worse. Their Chart-RVR framework fine tunes models with reinforcement learning driven by automatically verifiable rewards. Three rewards are combined: correct chart type classification, faithful reconstruction of the chart's data table, and conformity to a sound reasoning process.

Applied to models with three billion parameters, Chart-RVR consistently beat standard supervised fine tuning on both familiar and out of distribution chart datasets. It closed much of the out of distribution gap while improving the fidelity of the reasoning traces. The resulting models set state of the art results on six chart reasoning benchmarks among models of comparable size.
arxiv-2510-11173:
Segmenting the object described by a sentence, such as the drone trailing another and partly hidden by trees, requires reasoning before drawing a mask. Zhenyu Lu and co-authors present CoPRS in this 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Their model connects language reasoning to segmentation through a positional prior, a heatmap that marks where the described object likely sits.

CoPRS makes the reasoning explicit with a multimodal chain of thought, then turns it into a dense, differentiable heatmap through a learnable concentration token that aggregates image and text features. A lightweight decoder converts the heatmap into precise masks. On the RefCOCO benchmark series and on ReasonSeg, CoPRS matches or surpasses the best reported results on each standard split. Experiments also show that heatmap quality strongly drives mask quality, confirming the consistent link between reasoning output and the final segmentation in these tests.
arxiv-2510-11273:
A result is directionally replicable when several independent studies find the effect pointing the same way, not just present. Vera Djordjilović, Tamar Sofer, and Jonathan M. Dreyfuss study the statistics of that claim in this 2025 arXiv paper. When the expected direction is not fixed in advance, standard practice tests both directions with one-sided p-values and then doubles the smaller combined value to correct for multiple testing.

The authors show that this doubling correction is not always necessary. They give conditions under which the factor of two can be safely omitted while keeping the test valid. Dropping an unneeded correction matters in practice, because it restores statistical power that the conservative doubling throws away. The work sits in the partial conjunction framework for replicability analysis and sharpens how strong a directional claim the combined evidence can support.
arxiv-2510-11573:
Cryptographic code must run in constant time to avoid leaking secrets through timing, and Spectre attacks demand the stronger property of speculative constant time, where even the processor's wrong guesses cannot leak. Santiago Arranz-Olmos and co-authors build the missing formal bridge between the two verification worlds in this 2025 arXiv computer security paper. Speculative tools had grown as informal liftings, seldom made precise.

The authors introduce Speculation-Passing Style, a program transformation that instruments code with an extra input representing attacker-controlled predictions and rewrites the program to follow them. The transformation is sound and complete: a program is speculatively constant-time exactly when its transformed version is constant-time in the ordinary sense. They demonstrate the idea with three tools, EasyCrypt, Binsec/Rel, and CTGrind, covering proofs via non-interference, assertion safety, and dynamic taint analysis, evaluated on Kocher's Spectre-v1 benchmarks, .
arxiv-2510-11673:
Nihar Gargava, Vlad Serban, Maryna Viazovska, and Ilaria Viglino count special matrices in this 2025 arXiv paper. The matrices have entries drawn from the integers of a number field, which is a finite extension of the rational numbers. Each matrix has a fixed rank, and its entries stay below a chosen size bound. Earlier work by Katznelson settled the counting problem over the ordinary integers.

The team proves an asymptotic formula for the count over any number field, giving the main growth term as the bound grows. They then apply the formula to lattices built from algebraic codes, deriving an approximate Rogers integral formula for these module lattices. As a payoff, earlier moment estimates about short vectors in random lattices carry over to these code-based lattices when the sets are large enough. Short vectors govern how secure and efficient such lattices are.
arxiv-2510-11773:
Matteo Robbiati and fourteen colleagues present Qiboml, a free software library for hybrid quantum-classical machine learning. Their 2025 arXiv paper describes a toolkit for building models that mix ordinary neural networks with quantum circuits. It builds on the Qibo quantum computing framework and plugs into TensorFlow and PyTorch, the two most popular machine learning libraries. The aim is to let researchers build hybrid models without rewriting plumbing for each machine.

Qiboml models can run almost anywhere. Simulations execute on multi-threaded processors, graphics cards, or multi-GPU systems, using either statevector or tensor network methods. The same models can also run on real quantum processors, whether installed locally or reached through cloud providers. The library supports noise-aware simulation, which imitates the errors of real hardware. It also performs error mitigation and calibration in real time. The authors showcase these features as steps toward practical quantum learning workflows.
arxiv-2510-11973:
Emilia Del Bono, Angus Holford, and Tommaso Sartori ask whether a child's rank in class echoes forty years later. Grades alone might not capture it: being near the top of one's class could build confidence independent of raw scores. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses records for every child in Aberdeen's primary schools in 1962. Quasi-random differences in classmate composition let them separate rank itself from ability.

A higher rank improved performance on the high-stakes eleven-plus exam. It also strengthened internalizing skills, traits tied to self-concept and confidence, which the authors identify as the main channel. A follow-up survey forty years on finds lasting effects. Rank raised educational attainment, especially for girls. Long-run income gains, however, appeared only among boys. The authors read that gap as a fingerprint of the era. In the nineteen sixties, women's access to higher education and skilled jobs was sharply constrained.
arxiv-2510-12773:
Heakl and colleagues address wasted computation in large language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such models push every word through every layer of their network, even for easy questions, yet hard questions may need extra passes. Earlier fixes often needed costly searches, design changes, or full retraining, and they tended to lose accuracy.

The authors built Dr.LLM, which adds small router modules to a pretrained model so each layer can be skipped, used once, or repeated for a given input. They trained the routers on layer plans found by tree search, which explores many options before choosing. On logic and math benchmarks the method raised accuracy while saving about five layers per example on average, and it kept most of that gain on unseen tasks.
arxiv-2510-13173:
Zhemchugov describes the BUTTON-30 detector in this 2025 arXiv paper, a thirty-tonne technology demonstrator built deep underground at the Boulby lab in England. Neutrino detection at a few million electron volts is very hard because interaction rates are tiny and radioactive backgrounds are large. Hybrid detectors promise to help by recording both Cherenkov and scintillation light from the same event.

BUTTON-30 tests that hybrid approach using water-based liquid scintillator doped with gadolinium. The liquid raises light yield while prompt Cherenkov photons preserve position resolution. It captures neutrons from neutrino interactions, tagging them through a follow-up gamma cascade. Placing it more than a kilometer down cuts cosmic ray interference. That lets the team evaluate it in a realistic low-background environment. The paper details its design and construction for future experiments.
arxiv-2510-13273:
Zhao, Thoma, Hertwig, and Wulff map the gender attrition gap in academic psychology in this 2025 arXiv paper. More women than men enter the social sciences, yet senior ranks remain male-dominated, a leaky pipeline whose leak points were unclear. The authors studied career trajectories of more than seventy-eight thousand psychology researchers.

Women made up over sixty percent of the researchers but left academia at higher rates than men, most in the first years after their first publication. Academic performance, above all first-authored publications, predicted early retention more strongly than collaboration networks or institutional setting. Even with publication, collaboration, and institutional differences counted, women still left at higher rates in early career. This points to persistent barriers beyond productivity alone. The authors conclude the core problem is retention rather than recruitment, calling for targeted early-career interventions.
arxiv-2510-13473:
Tariq and co-authors test whether quantum reservoir computing can resist adversarial attacks better than classical models. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a reservoir from strongly interacting Rydberg atoms. The atoms evolve under a fixed Hamiltonian, producing rich high-dimensional embeddings of input data. Only a small classical readout layer needs training on top.

The study is the first systematic check of adversarial robustness for this kind of model. The team attacked the hybrid system in a white-box setting, where attackers know the model fully. Tests ran on three balanced image datasets: MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and Kuzushiji-MNIST. Across every perturbation strength tried, the hybrid beat purely classical models on accuracy. The authors frame this as a fresh source of quantum advantage. They also draw guidance for deploying learning systems safely on near-term quantum hardware.
arxiv-2510-13573:
Li, Tang, Hovland, and Liu present NCF, a compiler that cuts the T-gate cost of Hamiltonian simulation. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets fault-tolerant quantum computers, where T gates are far pricier than Clifford gates. Simulating a Hamiltonian means decomposing it into Pauli strings, each needing rotation gates. Synthesizing those rotations produces long Clifford and T sequences.

NCF groups Pauli strings so each group can be reshaped to act on few qubits. Whole groups are then synthesized at once instead of string by string. Experiments show an average T-gate count reduction of 57.4 percent against the best prior method, with T-depth and Clifford counts falling by about half as well in the same comparisons. The savings matter because T gates rely on costly magic state distillation. Cheaper synthesis brings large simulations closer to practical fault-tolerant hardware.
arxiv-2510-14173:
Zhuo Chen simulates the plunge-in phase of common envelope evolution, when one star swallows its companion and the envelope is expelled, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These events shine as red novae, and whether the envelope escapes depends on physics, including radiation pressure and the energy released as hydrogen recombines.

Using radiation hydrodynamic simulations with the code Guangqi, Chen surveys how settings affect the unbound mass fraction and the light curves. He varies the radiation-to-gas energy ratio, the envelope's energy against its gravitational binding, and the mass injection rate, across subsonic and supersonic expansion. Three findings stand out. Radiation pressure dominates mass ejection just below the recombination front in opaque regions. The unbound fraction depends nonlinearly on the energy ratio, modulated by injection rate and gravity. Hydrogen atoms joining into molecules release latent heat that sustains a plateau in the light curve.
arxiv-2510-14373:
Van Chien Le and Karel Van Bockstal build the foundations for heat-like equations posed on a domain with a moving region inside, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such problems model phase change, growing tumors, and moving reaction fronts. A coefficient in the time-derivative term jumps across an interface that evolves with time, breaking the theory.

The authors introduce function spaces for the variational solution. These extend the Sobolev-Bochner spaces to accommodate the discontinuous coefficient. They prove smooth functions are dense in these spaces by extending mollification, a smoothing technique, and the Reynolds transport theorem. They establish the embedding theory and an integration-by-parts formula. These are the tools every later argument needs. Using the Banach-Necas-Babuska theorem, a criterion for variational problems, they prove the variational formulation is well-posed in its setting. Solutions exist, are unique, and depend stably on the data.
arxiv-2510-14773:
Jo and co-authors show, in a 2025 arXiv paper, that how you read a reasoning model's answer can matter as much as the answer itself. Benchmarks usually score a model by the probability of its final choice. Reasoning models, though, produce long chains of thought, and the algorithm that extracts the final answer from that text can swing the measured performance and even the distribution of answers.

The authors propose Answer Regeneration, a deliberately simple fix. Run the model once more, feeding back its own input and output, prefaced by the prompt Answer. Then take the final answer from this cleaner second pass. The method makes no assumptions about the extraction rule. Applied to general math problems and open-ended question answering, it improved measured performance and made results more robust. The broader lesson is that evaluation pipelines deserve the same scrutiny as the models they grade.
arxiv-2510-14973:
Nguyen-Tri, Ranjan, and Shen find, in a 2025 arXiv paper, redundancy inside diffusion language models and a cache policy to exploit it. These models refine an answer over denoising steps, and decoders recompute key-value caches for every token, step, and layer. Yet the caches barely change across steps, especially in shallow layers, so the recomputation is waste.

Three observations shape their fix. Distant masked tokens act as a length bias. They can be cached in blocks outside the active window. Cache dynamics grow with depth, so refreshing from a chosen deeper layer onward suffices. And the most-attended token drifts least, a safe gauge of cache change. Their Elastic-Cache uses an attention-aware drift test on that token to decide when to refresh, and a depth-aware schedule to decide where. The strategy needs no training, fits any architecture, and adapts rather than following a fixed period.
arxiv-2510-15073:
Kwietniak and Wierzbowski give, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a simpler proof about chaos on spaces containing an interval. The setting: continuous maps on spaces with a free arc, an open piece shaped like an interval. A 2013 theorem of Dirbák, Snoha, and Špitalský covers every continuous, transitive, but non-minimal map of such a space. Each is relatively mixing and non-invertible. Each has positive topological entropy and dense periodic points. It is a bouquet of chaotic traits from modest assumptions.

The proof rests on two short facts. First, every weakly mixing map of a space with a free interval must be mixing, and must have positive entropy. Second, a transitive but non-minimal map of such a space has dense periodic points and is non-invertible. Combining the two yields the theorem with less machinery than the first route, a streamlining for dynamicists who cite it often.
arxiv-2510-15273:
Liner Xiang, Jiayi Wang, and Hengrui Cai study online decisions where treating one person changes what happens to others. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses contextual bandits, algorithms that learn which action pays best for each arriving case while balancing trials against safe choices. Standard versions assume no interference between cases, an assumption that fails in settings like hotel pricing or public health.

Their method, FRONT, weighs the long-term effect of today's decision on later cases linked through an interference network, instead of grabbing the best immediate reward. It alternates exploratory and exploitative phases to keep estimates sound while regret, the loss versus an ideal policy, stays sublinear under two definitions of that loss. The team proves error bounds for its online estimator and works out the long-run distribution of its parameters. Simulations and a real study of urban hotel profits back the method's effectiveness.
arxiv-2510-15373:
Pranay Agarwal and D. Manjunath model a money dispute at the heart of the modern internet, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Internet providers want content providers, such as streaming and social platforms, to help pay for upgrading access networks. A content provider can instead invest privately in its own infrastructure. The paper asks how a provider should split its spending between the two routes.

The answer depends on how providers interact. The authors compare four setups, namely centralized allocation, a cooperative game, a non-cooperative game, and a bargaining game. Numerical results show the bargaining setup can draw out more public investment than either the non-cooperative or the centralized model. That benefit shrinks when providers are rewarded for building private infrastructure instead. Agarwal and Manjunath frame the findings as guidance for the running policy fight over who funds internet capacity.
arxiv-2510-15473:
Petra Berenbrink and six colleagues settle how evenly a network can share work when neighbors only compare loads pairwise. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies discrete iterative load balancing on arbitrary graphs, where each node starts with some tokens and matched pairs average their loads each round. An odd leftover token goes to one side at random, which makes the discrete problem thornier than its continuous cousin.

Their main result shows the process reaches a discrepancy of just three tokens between the most and least loaded nodes. It gets there in a number of rounds matching the best possible spectral bound for continuous balancing with fractional loads. Earlier work reached only large, unspecified discrepancies and often needed regular graphs. The scheme covers random matchings, fixed periodic matching schedules, and asynchronous edge choices under one analysis. The authors conclude that, in this general model, discrete balancing is no harder than continuous balancing.
arxiv-2510-15773:
Qihao Peng, Tierui Gong, Zihang Song, and Qu Luo analyse a satellite design in a 2025 paper. The satellite receives radio signals with Rydberg atoms. These are highly excited atoms. They act as sensitive quantum antennas. The satellite uses many antennas at once. It serves direct ground-to-space uplinks. The authors derive exact formulas for channel estimation error.

From the estimated channels, they derive rate bounds. These are lower bounds on achievable data rates. Two standard combining schemes are covered. The atomic receiver beat conventional radio equipment. This held under both fading models tested. The atomic system has its own noise quirks. Even so, the result supports quantum receivers for future satellite networks.
arxiv-2510-15873:
Hengyuan Chang, Xiaoxuan Xie, Syuhei Sato, and Haoran Xie present a poster paper in 2025. It turns an artist's sketch into animated smoke. The method has two stages. Smoke adds expressive motion to illustrations. Making it normally means running physics fluid simulations. Illustrators cannot easily art-direct those simulations.

Their pipeline first converts the sketch into a stream function. That is a mathematical description of flowing motion. Diffusion-based generators then produce a velocity field. The field guides a smoke simulation as a driving force. The smoke follows the sketched shape. It still moves like real smoke. Artists gain control with far less technical overhead.
arxiv-2510-16073:
A. Golebiewska, S. Rybicki, and P. Stefaniak study when symmetric Newtonian systems hold whole connected sets of periodic solutions. The systems are autonomous and symmetric under circle actions. The solutions sought are non-stationary and repeat after one full period. An energy-like parameter ranges over positive values for each family.

The three authors state necessary conditions for such closed connected sets to exist. They also state sufficient conditions for the same sets. Closed means the family has no loose ends in the space of periodic paths. Their main tool is the degree for equivariant gradient maps. That tool counts solutions while respecting the symmetry of the system. The result gives a two-way checklist for researchers. It says when symmetric mechanical systems must carry continua of periodic motions, not just isolated ones.
arxiv-2510-16173:
Aria Pessianzadeh and five co-authors measure how much the public trusts generative AI, using years of Reddit talk. Trust shapes whether people adopt these tools and how they should be governed, yet it is rarely tracked at scale over time. Their data covers thirty-nine Reddit forums and more than two hundred thirty thousand posts from 2022 to 2025.

Human labels on a sample trained sorting models that scored the full set. Trust and distrust came out nearly even, with trust a bit ahead, and both swung when big new models launched. Talk focused most on how well the tools work and how easy they feel to use. Personal stories were the most common reason people gave for their stance. The study offers a reusable way to watch public trust shift as AI spreads.
arxiv-2510-16273:
Jingyue Huang and six co-authors present MuseTok, a way to chop written music into tokens that AI models can learn from. Tokenizing worked well for images, speech, and text, but music has its own symbols and structure. MuseTok cuts scores bar by bar and squeezes each bar into a short code with a trained autoencoder.

The codes rebuild the music faithfully and also carry music theory sense. Models using them beat older methods at reading tasks like pulling out the melody, naming chords, and spotting the mood. At writing new music, they match the best older methods. Probes of the codes show they capture real musical ideas from big collections. A shared token scheme like this could let one model both write and understand music.
arxiv-2510-16373:
Federico Ravenda and three co-authors steer a language model toward mental health work by nudging its inner states. Small models often stumble on specialist tasks, and full retraining is costly. Their method applies a simple linear shift to the activity of one layer. Steering vectors guide the shift toward the desired behavior.

Two tasks test the trick on Reddit posts. One asks whether a post helps detect signs of depression. The other completes a standard depression screening questionnaire from a user's post history. With only the cheap nudge, the model improves on both tasks, with no heavy training runs. The results suggest steering hidden states is an untapped, low-cost way to adapt models for sensitive fields like mental health.
arxiv-2510-16473:
Dario A. Bini, Massimiliano Fasi, and Bruno Iannazzo study a matrix task in their 2025 paper. A matrix is a grid of numbers that can stretch or turn vectors. Their task takes a function of a paired matrix set, called a pencil. One grid is firm and sure, and one is mirror-even in form. Such tasks show up in control, waves, and sound work.

They first gauge how touchy the task is to small input shifts. Then they give methods that split the pencil with a clean split step. Some use a matrix square root, and some use a Cholesky split. Tests show the Cholesky forms win on speed and on exactness. Their cost counts help users pick the right method per task.
arxiv-2510-16673:
Yuki Ohnishi and three co-authors estimate causal mechanisms inside cluster-randomized trials, where whole groups, not single people, get a treatment. Mediation analysis asks how much of an effect flows through an in-between variable. Trials of this kind add interference between units, confounders that appear after treatment, and layered covariates.

Their Bayesian nonparametric framework handles all three problems at once. A Gaussian copula with one dependence parameter replaces a strict cross-world independence assumption, which builds in a sensitivity check. A nested prior shares information across clusters while adjusting for covariates without disturbing the outcome model. The authors derive the prior's partition structure and convergence guarantees to support the method.
arxiv-2510-17373:
Parkinson disease often flattens the face, a symptom called the masked face, and Yintao Zhou with four co-authors uses that clue to grade how severe the disease is. Judging severity matters for catching patients early and tailoring care. Older methods leaned on a single facial expression, which can mislead, and they struggled when some disease stages had far fewer examples than others.

Zhou and his co-authors merge several kinds of expression features through an attention based fusion step, which learns which features deserve more weight. A balancing method then adjusts how much each training example counts, based on how common its class is and how hard it proves to classify. Their tests show promising grading accuracy.
arxiv-2510-17473:
Dark matter remains unseen directly, yet the hunt for it is changing fast on every front, Milena Crnogorčević reports in a conference summary. Direct searches, which wait for a dark matter particle to strike a detector, have entered an era where ordinary solar neutrinos now form a limiting background. Indirect searches, which look for products of dark matter meeting itself, have become genuinely combined efforts across gamma rays, neutrinos, cosmic rays, and radio data.

Crnogorčević also notes that candidates beyond the classic heavy particle idea are moving to centre stage, including axions, very light particles, primordial black holes, and larger relic objects. Progress, the report argues, now depends as much on shared data and common analysis methods as on new hardware. The summary distils how assumptions have shifted since the previous conference and where decisive steps may come next.
arxiv-2510-17773:
Enamul Atiq and Shaikh Anowarul Fattah build a skin cancer classifier that explains itself. Early detection greatly improves patient outcomes in skin cancer. Sorting lesions from microscope-style skin images is hard and error prone. Many deep learning tools act as black boxes, which limits clinical trust.

Their system first outlines each lesion with a custom segmentation network. Two encoders then read the full image and the outlined lesion separately. An attention step fuses both views, focusing on the diseased region. Patient details like age, sex, and lesion site join the prediction. Heat maps confirm the model looks at lesions, not background.
arxiv-2510-17873:
Tadesse K Bahiru and three co-authors audit the data behind gender classification systems and find a shared flaw. All five widely used data sets they checked leave out many mixed groups of age, race, and gender. Models trained on the two most balanced sets still erred more on female faces and skewed by race.

To fix the data, the team built BalancedFace from real, unedited photos drawn from several sources. It evens out shares across many age, race, and gender groups. A plain classifier trained on it cut the largest racial gap in correct rates by over half in their tests.
arxiv-2510-17973:
Michael Unger, writing alone, reports measurements that help track how cosmic rays spread through our galaxy. When cosmic rays smash into gas, they break into lighter pieces, and the rates of that breakup shape what detectors see. The NA61/SHINE setup at CERN is well placed to measure those rates at high energy.

New results cover carbon breaking into two boron forms and one carbon form. They come from a pilot run and feed into reading the boron-to-carbon ratio in space data. A much larger 2024 campaign, spanning many light nuclei, promises the full reaction network that transport models need.
arxiv-2510-18173:
Ritam Upadhyay and four co-authors test how well language models turn long sports tables into faithful written summaries. Common recipes lean on heavy prompt tricks, pipeline splits, or entity scaffolding, all costly and opaque. Their SporTabSet benchmark spans two sports and demands tracking many players while adding numbers under each sport's own rules.

Splitting the task into parts raised accuracy and number fidelity a lot. The gains came mostly from untangling multi-entity interference, not from better arithmetic. Shuffled and stressed inputs also exposed fragility. Data-to-text researchers get a clear diagnosis of where long-context summarizers wobble.
arxiv-2510-18273:
Mohammadreza Doostmohammadian and Sergio Pequito design resilient resource sharing algorithms in a 2025 paper. Distributed resource allocation means many linked devices divide a shared supply without one central boss. Real networks drop links, delay messages, and distort signals, which breaks many older methods.

Their algorithm keeps total supply and demand balanced at every moment, even if work stops early. It still converges when links carry nonlinear distortions like quantization, meaning rounding of values, and saturation. It also needs only uniform connectivity, meaning the network must reconnect over time, not stay linked always. Simulations show optimal results despite delays and heavy link failures.
arxiv-2510-18473:
Yuya Sasaki, writing alone, benchmarks methods meant to keep graph neural networks fair when they learn from knowledge graphs. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked entities and power tools such as recommender systems, yet no earlier study had tested fairness-aware versions of these networks on them. Sasaki built new test graphs from three large public sources, YAGO, DBpedia, and Wikidata, each far bigger than the graphs used in past fairness work.

The study compared fixes applied before training and during training, across several network designs and stopping rules. Knowledge graphs behaved differently from older test data: the trade-off between accuracy and fairness showed up more clearly. Results depended not only on the fairness method but also on the network design and on when training stopped. Early data fixes often improved fairness, while in-training fixes tended to protect accuracy.
arxiv-2510-18673:
Sungtae Cho and Su Houng Lee compute charm-strange meson production. The setting is nuclei colliding at nearly light speed at the Large Hadron Collider. Matter melts into a quark-gluon plasma there. As it cools, quarks recombine into particles. Each meson in their study pairs a heavy charm quark with a strange quark. Several excited versions are included.

First they pinned down the momentum spread of charm and strange quarks. Measured phi and D-zero mesons served as guides. Their recombination math then matched both the momentum pattern and the yield of the basic meson well. They studied a ratio comparing charm-strange output with D-zero output. It shows how light and strange quarks shape charmed output. They also computed an exotic candidate two ways, as a four-quark state and as a two-quark state.
arxiv-2510-18773:
Jannis Fleckenstein and his five co-authors apply a geospatial foundation model to the urban heat island problem, where cities run hotter than their surroundings. Planning shade and green space requires detailed temperature maps, but conventional models trained on scarce local data often predict poorly, especially in underserved neighborhoods. Foundation models, pretrained on global data, promise strong general performance with only a little local fine-tuning.

The team first built an empirical picture of real heat patterns by measuring how much green spaces cool their surroundings, and checked the model's predictions against it. They then fine-tuned the model to predict land surface temperatures under future climate scenarios. A simulated inpainting exercise, where a changed landscape is painted into the data, showed how planners could test mitigation ideas before spending on them. The authors argue such models are a powerful tool for data-scarce regions aiming at climate-resilient cities.
arxiv-2510-18873:
Ziang Zhang and his seven co-authors benchmark how well vision models understand scenes where both the camera and the objects are moving. Static and two-dimensional skills do not guarantee a model can track dynamic three-dimensional relationships. Their benchmark, DSI-Bench, contains nearly one thousand dynamic videos and more than one thousand seven hundred hand-annotated questions, organized around nine separated motion patterns for observers and objects.

Symmetric designs in space and time reduce biases and let evaluators isolate reasoning about self-motion from reasoning about object motion. Testing fourteen vision-language and specialist models exposed recurring failures: models confuse the observer's motion with the object's, fall back on semantic expectations, and misjudge relative relationships in moving scenes. The authors offer the benchmark as a diagnostic for building models with genuine dynamic spatial intelligence.
arxiv-2510-19073:
Sebastian Nagies and eight co-authors test whether dynamical decoupling can protect quantum annealing from local field noise. Annealing offers a route to hard optimization problems on quantum hardware, yet noise in real devices steadily degrades the quality of the answers it returns.

Periodic pulses that flip all spins together suppress that noise in their scheme. Test problems include small object-tracking and cutting-stock cases built for industry-style use, plus a classic spin glass model where the method stays robust across size and structure. The results point toward annealing protocols that survive contact with real machines.
arxiv-2510-19273:
Zhang Nengbo and Ho Hann Woei present MobiAct, a lightweight system for recognizing the actions of micro air vehicles from video. Drone swarms need fast motion recognition on tiny platforms, but accurate models are usually too heavy, forcing a trade between recognition quality and speed.

MobiAct uses a compact MobileNetV4 network as its backbone and adds a stage-wise distillation strategy that transfers motion features from a larger teacher network into the small student. Contrastive learning further sharpens the features. The result aims for high accuracy at low cost, so small drones can perceive and coordinate in real time.
arxiv-2510-19373:
Basavasagar Patil and four co-authors propose temperature sampling to fix a hidden imbalance in robot training data. Robot datasets keep growing, yet many differently named tasks share nearly the same physical motions, so common actions dominate while rare actions are scarce, and policies trained on such data generalize poorly.

Sampling with a temperature rule rebalances which examples the policy sees during training. The change takes only a few lines of code in existing systems. The authors test it both when pretraining small models and when fine-tuning large foundation models, finding better generalization in each case from the same collected data.
arxiv-2510-19673:
Julen Expósito-Márquez and four co-authors test whether a neural network recovers galaxy mass profiles better when it can see both gas and star motions. Astronomers weigh galaxies by watching how their material orbits, but combining two kinds of kinematic maps is hard for traditional methods. The team trained a probabilistic convolutional network on mock maps from several cosmological simulation suites.

Models were trained on gas-only, stars-only, and combined maps so the comparison is direct. The combined input cut the scatter in recovered mass profiles by up to a factor of about one and a half. The network clearly extracts complementary information from the two tracers, though performance dropped when a model trained on one simulation suite was applied to another.
arxiv-2510-19873:
Junfeng Gong and four co-authors help small language models write optimized GPU code like large ones, without sending code to the cloud. Big models generate good CUDA, but cloud APIs risk leaking code and local deployment is costly; small models run privately yet reason too weakly for complex optimization. Their framework, ReGraphT, needs no additional training.

ReGraphT stores recorded optimization sessions as a reasoning graph, where combined optimizations become transitions between states, and searches that graph with Monte Carlo methods to guide the small model. A tiered CUDA benchmark supports the evaluation. On two benchmark suites the method averaged a speedup of about two and a third times, beating fine-tuned specialist models and other retrieval approaches and bringing small models close to large-model quality.
arxiv-2510-19973:
Hatim Chergui and three co-authors write a tutorial on cognitive biases in the AI agents proposed to run future 6G networks. Language-model agents that negotiate across network domains inherit human-like biases from their design and training. Those biases can distort decisions. The tutorial catalogs well-known biases with their mathematical forms, how they emerge in telecom systems, and tailored countermeasures.

Two case studies validate the ideas. In inter-slice resource negotiation, a randomized starting anchor replaced a fixed one. Agents then used contract slack intelligently, and energy savings doubled, peaking at twenty-five percent. A small local model kept decisions fast enough for near-real-time use. In cross-domain negotiation, a debiased collective memory cut latency fivefold. It also raised energy savings by roughly forty percent over memoryless agents.
arxiv-2510-20073:
Swaroop Hegde proves an inverse and stability result for Ruzsa inequality on triple sumsets in additive combinatorics. The inequality bounds the size of a triple sumset by a power of the size of the double sumset for any finite set in a commutative group. Ruzsa own examples show the bound is nearly sharp, which raises the question of what near-extremal sets look like.

Hegde shows that if a set comes close to the bound, within a factor set by a parameter, then it must resemble the sets in Ruzsa construction. New families of examples suggest that description is likely best possible in qualitative terms. The method extends to higher sumsets, with an almost exact stability version included.
arxiv-2510-20373:
Gabriele Riccio and eleven co-authors present FAST-SBF, an automatic Python pipeline for measuring galaxy distances with the Surface Brightness Fluctuation method. That method is among the most reliable and efficient distance tools for galaxies within one hundred megaparsecs, and it still works on ground-based data when seeing is sharp and fields are wide. Upcoming surveys will offer thousands of suitable galaxies.

The pipeline is built for automation with minimal user intervention and aims at large datasets from surveys such as LSST, Euclid, and Roman. The authors validate it on high-quality Hyper Suprime-Cam imaging of luminous early-type galaxies and fainter dwarfs. Their measurements agree excellently with recent Virgo cluster results and with stellar population synthesis models, supporting its readiness for survey-scale use.
arxiv-2510-20573:
Amartya Chakrabortty, Georges Griso, and Julia Orlik run three limit steps at once on a mixed plate in bend: grain growth, flat cut, and line fit. The plate sits in non-linear bend with load on it, and its full bend power scales by a set law of two small marks. Part one runs all three steps at once with no link set on the pair of small marks.
