His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, adds confidence-guided blending, which mixes a patient's own features with evidence from neighbors.

For new patients, a mini-graph built from nearest neighbors gives real-time predictions with explanations, without retraining the whole model. Tested on real hospital data from Algeria, APC-GNN++ beats standard methods such as random forests and XGBoost, plus a plain graph convolutional network, on accuracy and macro F1. A desktop interface lets clinicians explore the confidence scores behind each call.
arxiv-2512-18873:
Paolo Luppi, Claudia Benedetti, and Andrea Smirne measure how quantum a quantum walk really is, moment by moment. A quantum walk spreads a particle across a graph with interference, unlike a classical random walk. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in Physical Review A, combines two yardsticks. One is a distance between quantum and classical states at one time. The other checks whether sequential position measurements obey classical consistency rules.

The second measure, K(t), grows quadratically at short times, against the known linear growth of the first. Both depend only on the starting node's degree, not the graph's shape. Later, K(t) becomes topology-driven, suppressed on complete graphs yet finite and oscillating on cycles. Under noise, position dephasing kills both measures. Energy basis dephasing instead leaves K(t) a finite remainder, a signature of surviving quantum memory.
arxiv-2512-19073:
Members of the ATLAS Collaboration measured how often proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider produce pairs of jets. The data cover collisions at thirteen teraelectronvolts recorded from 2015 to 2018. Jets were built with the standard anti-kt algorithm at a set radius.

The team reports double-differential rates against the pair's mass and either the pair's separation or its boost along the beam. The mass range runs from a few hundred gigaelectronvolts to nearly ten teraelectronvolts. After correcting the data to particle level, they compare it with state-of-the-art quantum chromodynamics calculations. Such checks test theory and sharpen knowledge of the proton's inner structure.
arxiv-2512-19273:
Xiaoyu Zhang, Zhiyun Fan, Wenyang Zhang, and Di Wang estimate huge matrices with a Kronecker structure, even when the data carry heavy tails. Such factors appear in trace regression, matrix models, and bilinear problems. A nasty scaling freedom between the factors warps gradients, which breaks standard robust methods that clip at a fixed level.

Their scaled robust gradient descent first undoes the factor scaling, then truncates, restoring stable steps. A scaled hard thresholding step selects variables in a scale-invariant way. Theory gives convergence rates that are optimal when noise variance is finite and degrade gracefully for heavier tails. Simulations and two real cases confirm the gains.
arxiv-2512-19473:
Karan Mukhi, Licio Romao, and Alessandro Abate solve the charging problem for whole fleets of electric vehicles facing one live imbalance price. Multistage stochastic programming frames the problem well but scales badly as vehicles and stages multiply. The group's aggregate flexibility, though, has a clean geometric shape: a permutahedron.

That shape lets the authors build an optimal rule for splitting an aggregate plan back to single cars. It also yields an exact, smaller stochastic program and a recourse function that is piecewise affine, with closed-form slopes and intercepts from truncated price expectations. The first-stage policy comes out exactly too, and numerics confirm the claims.
arxiv-2512-19773:
Mohammed Asheruddin N leads a six-author team warning battery researchers about ghosts in their aging analyses. Degradation mode analysis splits capacity fade into lost lithium inventory and lost active material by fitting low-rate voltage curves. But measured curves also carry an ohmic voltage drop and charge-discharge hysteresis, especially with graphite-silicon oxide anodes, and those artifacts can be misread as material loss, creating phantom degradation.

Working with two commercial cells of differing resistance, the team corrects only the instantaneous ohmic term, estimated from the first pulse step, before fitting. Without correction, one cell's positive-electrode material loss was increasingly under-diagnosed and lithium loss suppressed, while window and branch choices in the other cell shifted attributions by many percentage points. Their protocol: correct the ohmic term, harmonize the voltage window, and base attribution on the discharge branch.
arxiv-2512-19973:
Jun Yuan and three co-authors define a stronger kind of backup routes in a network graph. An S-Steiner tree links a chosen set S of terminals in the graph. Several such trees are fully independent when three things hold. They share no edges. They meet only at S. And their paths between any two terminals are disjoint inside. The notion extends internally disjoint Steiner trees. It backs fault-tolerant parallel routing designs.

The paper sorts these trees in detail. It also sets a generalized connectivity measure. For each size of terminal set, the measure takes the worst packing count over all sets of that size. Complete graphs get an exact value for it. Complete bipartite graphs get a tight lower bound. Both families' tree structures are studied head on.
arxiv-2512-20173:
Ze Gong, Pradeep Varakantham, and Akshat Kumar teach control policies to be safe and liked at once, entirely offline. Preference-based reinforcement learning normally infers rewards and costs from human feedback and then runs constrained optimization on those learned models; in long-horizon continuous control, the model errors compound and performance suffers. Their framework sidesteps the middlemen.

Policies are learned directly from pairwise preferences over behavior plus binary safety labels on trajectory segments. The method, PreSa, fuses preference learning and safety alignment into one constrained problem solved in a Lagrangian formulation, never explicitly building reward or cost models at all. On continuous control tasks with synthetic and real human feedback, the learned policies achieved high reward while respecting safety, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines and offline safe methods that cheated with ground-truth rewards. The extended abstract appears at AAMAS 2026.
arxiv-2512-20573:
Rui Pan and co-authors turn a weakness of diffusion language models into a drafting strategy. Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive models by letting a cheap drafter propose tokens that a big verifier checks. Diffusion models generate in parallel but trade quality for speed, seemingly poor drafters. The authors argue the opposite.

Parallel drafting makes long guesses cheap, so rejection hurts less. FailFast adapts its speculation length dynamically: it spends minimal compute where speculation is hard and extends drafts aggressively where text is predictable, sometimes seventy tokens at once. No fine-tuning is required. The approach speeds decoding several-fold over vanilla generation and beats strong benchmarks including EAGLE-3. Losslessness is preserved, since the verifier still has the final word.
arxiv-2512-20773:
Ziyi Zhu and seven co-authors address a weak spot in testing chatbots: the fake users used for practice rarely act like real people. Their framework, called DIAL, trains a user simulator through competition. A generator plays the user while a discriminator tries to spot what is unreal, and each round pushes the simulator closer to human behavior.

The test case is mental health support dialogue, where failures matter and come in many forms. DIAL restored word variety that plain fine-tuning had flattened, and its simulated failures matched real failure rates closely. Better simulators let builders find problems cheaply before a system reaches real users.
arxiv-2512-20873:
Rahul Bulusu surveys nearly twenty years of research on keeping cyber-physical systems running through faults. Such systems, from power grids to medical devices and robots, fuse software tightly with physical motion. A small glitch in a sensor or network can cascade into physical instability in ways single-layer thinking misses.

Bulusu organizes the field with an Origin-Layer-Effect taxonomy: where faults start, which layer they cross, and what they finally do. Mapping well-known systems onto it exposes shared failure pathways and blind spots. Four structural gaps recur, including learning-based control lacking stability guarantees and weak forensic visibility. The survey closes with directions joining robust control, monitoring, and formal assurance.
arxiv-2512-20973:
Yihan Xia, Taotao Wang, Wenxin Xu, and Shengli Zhang build the bookkeeping layer that teams of autonomous language-model agents need when nobody fully trusts anybody. Paying agents fairly requires measuring each one's contribution, but doing that on a blockchain is expensive and exposes the agents' strategies. Their framework, DAO-Agent, keeps coordination and an immutable log on-chain while moving the contribution math off-chain.

Contributions are scored with Shapley values, the game-theoretic fair split, and zero-knowledge proofs let the chain verify those scores without seeing the underlying work. Verification stays constant-time as the coalition grows, and in a crypto-trading test case the gas cost of verification fell by up to 99.9 percent against naive on-chain alternatives. Private, auditable, and cheap enough to scale is the combination on offer.
arxiv-2512-21073: Wan Wu continues a series on quiver Hecke algebras built from Borcherds-Cartan data, where imaginary simple roots are allowed. The third work in the series introduces quiver Hecke superalgebras, with a sign grading tracked by the super prefix. The new algebras categorify quantum Borcherds superalgebras: their module classes carry the quantum structure in lifted form. Relations become functors, and identities become isomorphisms. The upshot is a richer setting for studying these quantum symmetries.
arxiv-2512-21273:
Imtiaz Waheed, Erkinjon Karimov, and Mujeeb ur Rehman build algebra tools for a broad family of fractional derivatives. Fractional calculus extends differentiation to non-integer orders. The Prabhakar derivative, here carried to its nth-level form, covers several classical variants used to model memory effects in physics and engineering. The authors set out its basics. Chief among them is how it inverts, and how it pairs with the matching Prabhakar integral.

They then develop a Mikusinski-type operational calculus for the operator. In that system, applying the derivative becomes multiplication. Such equations can then be solved by algebra rather than transforms. Two worked cases close the paper: closed-form solutions of a fractional ordinary differential equation, and of the time-fractional heat equation with the new derivative inside. For work on anomalous diffusion and viscoelastic memory, the result is a ready-made solver for a wide class.
arxiv-2512-21373:
Titouan Duston and a large team of co-authors introduce AInsteinBench, a benchmark for testing whether language model agents can do real scientific software work. Existing benchmarks mostly test textbook reasoning or ordinary coding tasks. AInsteinBench instead places agents inside real scientific software projects and asks them to carry out full development work.

Its tasks come from real pull requests written by the maintainers of six widely used scientific codebases, covering quantum chemistry, quantum computing, molecular dynamics, numerical relativity, fluid dynamics, and cheminformatics. Each task passed multi-stage filtering and expert review to confirm it is scientifically hard, well tested, and fairly graded. Because the tasks run in executable environments with test-driven checks, the benchmark exposes real failure modes. It measures whether a model can move past surface-level code generation toward the skills that research actually requires.
arxiv-2512-21573:
Zhangzheng Tu, Kailun Su, Shaolong Zhu, and Yukun Zheng recover human motion in world coordinates from a single camera video, then transfer it to a humanoid robot. Robots need to know where a person moves in real space, not just in the frame. Usual routes rely on SLAM pipelines or heavy temporal models.

The authors take a lighter, engineering-first path. They use SAM 3D Body as a perception backbone and express motion in the Momentum HumanRig representation, which robots can consume directly. The method locks each person's identity and skeleton scale so bone lengths stay constant. A sliding-window optimization smooths frame-by-frame predictions in that representation. A soft foot-ground contact model recovers plausible global trajectories. The motion is retargeted onto a Unitree G1 humanoid with a two-stage inverse kinematics pipeline. On real videos the system produced stable trajectories and reliable robot motion.
arxiv-2512-21673:
Jalal Khan compares two deep learning object detectors for the perception system of an autonomous vehicle. Perception is how the vehicle detects, locates, and identifies cars, pedestrians, and road signs to navigate safely. The models compared are YOLO-NAS and YOLOv8, both recent versions of the you-only-look-once detector family.

Khan captured a custom dataset and trained and tested both models on it under matched conditions. The smaller YOLOv8s variant finished training in about a quarter of the time the YOLO-NAS model needed, a saving of roughly seventy-five percent. It also edged out its rival on detection accuracy, reaching about eighty-three percent against about eighty-one percent. The comparison is deliberately practical rather than theoretical. Its value is a real-world data point on the speed-accuracy trade-off between two widely used detectors.
arxiv-2512-22273:
Wenhao Ou works in complex algebraic geometry, studying reflexive sheaves on spaces that are almost smooth. The setting is a compact complex analytic variety whose only singularities are quotient singularities in codimension two. On such orbifolds, usual Chern classes need adjustment, and Ou uses orbifold modifications to define first and second homological Chern classes for a reflexive sheaf.

With a Kähler form on the space and a sheaf that is stable with respect to it, Ou deduces a Bogomolov-Gieseker inequality for those orbifold Chern classes. Such inequalities bound a sheaf's geometry and underpin much of the theory of stable sheaves. The result extends a classic tool to singular spaces that arise naturally in modern geometry.
arxiv-2512-22773:
Julia Gaudio and Andrew Jin pin down the exact limits of community detection in networks whose connections depend on geometry. In social networks, friends of friends tend to connect, producing many triangles, so a spatial model fits better than the classic stochastic block model. The geometric stochastic block model places nodes in space and links them with probabilities depending on both community labels and distance.

The question is exact recovery: when can an algorithm restore every node's true community label with high probability? Gaudio and Jin fully characterize the information-theoretic threshold for this model under mild technical assumptions. Their result generalizes earlier work by Gaudio and co-authors and separates the regimes where perfect recovery is possible from those where no method, however powerful, can succeed. Such thresholds guide practitioners on how much data a network needs before its communities can be trusted completely.
arxiv-2512-24073:
Pankaj Chaudhary, Neminath Hubballi, and Sameer Kulkarni improve caching in Named Data Networks. In this design, routers cache content by name. Router storage is small, so choices matter. Keeping popular items pays off. But tracking popularity across a network costs effort. Older schemes pay a heavy coordination price.

Their method, CPePC, splits the network into communities. The communities do not overlap. Each elects a leader node. The leader estimates popularity for the whole group. That trims the coordination overhead. Caching decisions rest on a predicted value. The value blends current cache occupancy with item popularity. So the scheme looks ahead instead of only reacting. The authors give the full set of algorithms. Tests in a discrete-event simulator beat six rival techniques.
arxiv-2512-24173:
Jui-Ting Lu, Henrique Ennes, Chih-Kang Huang, and Ali Abbassi bring quantum computing into digital art. Quantum brushes are software tools, introduced by Ferreira and others in 2025, that use quantum behavior to generate artistic effects a classical brush cannot. Writing in an outreach spirit, the authors explain the mathematics behind two new brushes and describe how they built them.

One brush, Steerable, applies quantum geometric control theory to merge two artworks into one. The other, Chemical, borrows the variational methods chemists use to estimate molecular ground-state energies and instead uses them to evolve colors across a canvas. Both implementations are open source and fully compatible with the original quantum brush package. The paper invites artists and curious readers to experiment with quantum effects as a creative medium, with the code ready to download.
arxiv-2512-24373:
Waheed Ahmed Abro and Zied Bouraoui teach document models to skim. Long documents defeat ordinary transformers, above all in law and medicine. Sparse attention handles length at high cost. It can still miss whole-document context. Hierarchical models are cheaper but opaque about cross-section links. Humans solve the problem by skimming. They dwell on key sections and grasp the whole.

The framework copies that strategy with contrastive learning. A random section of the document is masked. A natural language inference objective aligns the masked part with related sections. Unrelated parts are pushed away. The model thus learns how sections support each other. The training is self-supervised, needing no labels. Experiments on legal and biomedical texts confirmed the gains. Accuracy and efficiency both improved significantly over prior approaches.
arxiv-2512-24773:
Anas Saeed, Mahmoud Salim, and Ali Arshad Nasir optimize throughput for a reconfigurable intelligent surface carried by a drone. The surface can reshape radio propagation on demand, serving users from a ground base station. Drone jitter in three dimensions and imperfect channel knowledge make the link unstable and the optimization stochastic and nonconvex.

Deep reinforcement learning handles the moving, uncertain setting, aiming to raise expected throughput using only available channel estimates under transmit limits. Readers in wireless systems get a control strategy designed for real impairments, not ideal channels. The work targets settings where a flying surface must keep adapting as it shakes and channels drift.
arxiv-2512-24873:
Weixun Wang, XiaoXiao Xu, Wanhe An, and a large team introduce an open ecosystem for building agentic language models that act over many turns in real environments. Agentic crafting means taking actions, observing outcomes, and refining artifacts step by step. Three parts form the pipeline: a post-training framework, a sandbox manager for generating trajectories, and an agent framework.

Within that ecosystem they build the ROME model. Open-source readers get end-to-end infrastructure rather than a single model release. The aim is to streamline how agent models are trained, tested in sandboxes, and deployed, so improvements can compound across the community.
arxiv-2512-24973:
Rafal Potempa, Michal Kordasz, and Jozef Cyran release GEQIE, a Python framework for encoding images into quantum states quickly and correctly. The framework builds the encoding state with a unitary gate that can later be transpiled to real quantum backends. Benchmarks under different simulated noise levels verify the implemented encoding methods and show the tool suits more advanced research.

A showcase encodes a cosmic web dark matter density snapshot and retrieves it with very high correlation accuracy. Quantum computing readers get tested infrastructure for quantum image processing experiments. Reliable encoding is the entry step for any quantum image algorithm, so a verified framework saves repeated groundwork.
arxiv-2512-25073:
Yi-Chuan Huang, Hao-Jen Chien, Chin-Yang Lin, and colleagues present GaMO, a geometry-aware diffusion method that outpaints new views to help rebuild three-dimensional scenes from very few images. Dense multi-view methods fail with sparse views, and diffusion-based view generation helps but leaves gaps: coverage beyond known view edges is weak, generated views disagree geometrically, and detail suffers.

Geometry awareness in the multi-view outpainting addresses those three limits together. Computer vision readers get more consistent synthetic views for training sparse reconstructions. Better hallucinated views matter for scanning real places where capturing many angles is impractical.
arxiv-2601-00473:
Abhisek Ganguly, Santosh Ansumali, and Sauro Succi revisit the idea that deep neural networks behave like discrete dynamical systems, where each layer advances a state much like a step in a simulation. They compare exact and numerical solutions of the Burgers and Eikonal equations with solutions learned by physics-informed neural networks, which are trained to obey the governing equations.

Their comparison shows the networks reach the same underlying dynamics by a different computational route. Layer-by-layer evolution heads toward attractor states, and many different parameter settings can give similar answers. Unlike the neat operators of finite-difference methods, the networks spread information across many parameters. That usually means more parameters and less direct interpretability, a trade-off the authors argue matters for scientific computing.
arxiv-2601-00573:
Yihe Wang, Zhiqiao Kang, Bohan Chen, Yu Zhang, and Xiang Zhang benchmark three generations of methods for analyzing event-related potentials, the brain's electrical responses locked to a stimulus or event. These signals support cognitive research, disease detection, and assessment of mental states. Many studies still rely on hand-crafted features, even as deep learning has advanced on other brain signals.

The team compares traditional manual features with a linear classifier, modern deep learning models, and pre-trained EEG foundation models under one shared preprocessing and training pipeline. That unified setup makes the comparison fair and shows where each approach stands on this specific kind of data. The benchmark gives researchers clearer guidance on when the newer, heavier models actually earn their cost.
arxiv-2601-00673:
Antoine Baillod, Avigdor Veksler, Rohan Lopez, Dylan Schmeling, and Michael Campagna report the final design of the Columbia Stellarator eXperiment, a new fusion device to be built at Columbia University. A stellarator confines hot plasma with twisted external magnets instead of driving current through the plasma itself. An earlier paper by the team laid out goals, constraints, and the optimization algorithms used to search for a workable shape.

Here they present a configuration that satisfies all the constraints at once. The report covers the real, finite-sized coils rather than idealized ones, sensitivity analyses showing how errors would affect performance, and plasma calculations with the SFINCS code for neoclassical behavior. These checks confirm the experiment's goals are reachable with the design as built.
arxiv-2601-00773:
Sinan Acemoglu, Christian Kleiber, and Jörg Urban ask a question every regression user faces: which variables matter most? For ordinary linear models, Shapley values, borrowed from game theory, neatly split the familiar R-squared among the predictors. Beyond linear models there is no accepted fit measure, only a crowd of pseudo R-squared values with murky meanings.

The authors lay out the properties a fit measure needs so that Shapley decompositions can be read as relative, and even absolute, variable importance. They propose a pseudo R-squared built on Kullback-Leibler divergence, which takes a convenient form for generalized linear models. That choice unifies and extends earlier proposals, giving applied researchers in many fields a principled importance measure.
arxiv-2601-01373:
Eleven authors led by Qundong Shi present UltraEval-Audio, a single framework for testing audio foundation models. Since models that hear and speak arrived, progress has outrun measurement. Test sets and code lie scattered, audio codecs lack a shared scoring method, and speech benchmarks lean heavily on English, leaving Chinese skills unjudged.

The framework covers both understanding and generation, supports ten languages and fourteen task families, and plugs in twenty-four models and thirty-six benchmarks with a one-command run and live public leaderboards. Codecs are scored on three axes: meaning accuracy, voice likeness, and sound quality. Two new Chinese benchmarks test knowledge and fluency in speech form. The team hopes a transparent, shared platform will make audio model claims comparable across labs and companies, and speed work on the parts of the field that lag, especially generation.
arxiv-2601-01473:
Four authors led by Myung-Hwan Jang speed up training of graph neural networks on graphs too large for memory, by leaning on fast solid-state storage. Storage-based training keeps the huge graph on disk and streams pieces in. The bottleneck, they find, is not bandwidth but the flood of tiny storage reads, which waste the drive's capacity.

Their framework, AGNES, processes storage reads in blocks so each read carries useful bulk, and it groups graph neighborhoods into hyperbatches shaped by how real graphs cluster. On five real-world graphs, AGNES beat four leading methods every time, running up to about four times faster than the best rival. Code is public. As graphs keep growing past memory limits, such I/O discipline decides whether training finishes in hours or days, so the work speaks to anyone running learning on web-scale networks.
arxiv-2601-01573:
Han and 6 co-authors improve how computer models handle the edge where water meets a solid. That edge, the contact line, sets the angle a droplet makes with a surface, and errors there distort whole flow results. Their method uses a height-based approach inside a volume-of-fluid model in two dimensions.

The moving line's position feeds into how curvature is estimated, and the surface direction is held at the wanted angle. Tests show better accuracy than a standard method at very small and very large angles, including on curved walls. The method also avoids fake currents near the edge, which makes it useful for complex wall shapes.
arxiv-2601-01873:
Steering a laser beam usually means moving mirrors, but a liquid crystal layer can bend light electrically. Md. Rasel Parvez and Muhammad Anisuzzaman Talukder simulate a plasmonic nanolaser combined with such a layer, modeling how the liquid crystal molecules reorient under voltage and how the laser's far-field emission responds.

The single-mode device lased at a wavelength of 870 nanometers. It deflected its beam in discrete steps. The steps reached about sixty-seven degrees either way. The beam stayed narrower than one degree. A three-micrometer crystal layer worked best. A dual-mode version based on a merged nanohole array steered two nearby wavelengths at once. The design suits compact, reconfigurable light sources for interconnects, imaging, and communications.
arxiv-2601-02273:
Salim Khazem addresses a practical weakness of large segmentation models such as the Segment Anything Model. These models label regions in an image well in general, but they struggle with thin shapes like blood vessels in the eye and with noisy images such as radar views. Retraining the whole model is costly and can erase what it already learned.

His method, TopoLoRA-SAM, leaves the main image encoder frozen and trains only small added parts, about five percent of the model in total. A light spatial module and an optional shape aware training signal help keep thin structures connected. Tested on eye vessel, polyp, and radar sea and land data sets, it earns the best average scores while training far fewer weights.
arxiv-2601-02573:
Kiarash Shamsi and five co authors build LendNova, an automated pipeline that judges credit risk straight from raw credit bureau records. Traditional scoring depends on costly hand built features and often ignores much of the information buried in jargon heavy bureau text. LendNova instead lets a language model learn the relevant patterns from the raw text itself, with no manual feature engineering.

The end to end design replaces several preprocessing steps, cutting cost and improving scalability for lenders who must score many applicants. Evaluation on real world data shows strong potential for accurate and efficient assessment. The authors present the system as the first practical automated pipeline of its kind and as a baseline for intelligent credit risk agents, a starting point other teams can measure against.
arxiv-2601-02673:
Shuliang Bai, Shuang Liu, and Xin Lai propose a Ricci flow for graphs. A process that evolves edge weights so curvature evens out, in the spirit of the famous flow for smooth shapes. Two curvatures are involved. In their version the probability distribution behind Lin Lu Yau curvature is held constant over time, and a parallel flow is built for Forman curvature. On trees the two flows turn out to coincide.

Solutions are proved to exist and to be unique on general graphs. On trees the normalized flow converges to a constant curvature metric, so every tree ends in the same kind of equilibrium. Under the uniform measure that convergence yields a complete classification of trees, sorted by how their flows behave. The work carries a central geometric idea from manifolds into discrete network mathematics.
arxiv-2601-02873:
Arthur Haffemayer and six co-authors help robots move through clutter without collisions, under tight time limits. Optimization-based controllers can enforce physical limits but often fail to find a workable path fast enough when obstacles crowd the scene. Diffusion models can propose many routes, yet earlier versions had no general way to take the layout of the scene into account.

The team conditions a diffusion model on a compact, object-based summary of the scene, then refines its proposed paths with a collision-aware predictive controller. The controller enforces rigid-body motion and keeps a safe distance from obstacles. On benchmark tasks the hybrid beat planners and each part alone, and tests on a real Panda robot arm confirmed safe, reliable motion.
arxiv-2601-03173:
Sumit S. Shevtekar, Chandresh K. Maurya, and Gourab Sil build a model that predicts when motorcycle and scooter riders are riding under time pressure, a state that provokes risky maneuvers. Time pressure cannot be measured directly on the road, so the authors infer it from riding data. Their model, MTPS, combines convolutional preprocessing, two stages of temporal attention, and feature recalibration, yet stays tiny enough to run in a fraction of a millisecond.

To train and test it, they collected a dataset of more than one hundred twenty-nine thousand feature windows from simulator sessions with fifty-one experienced riders under no, low, and high time pressure. High pressure made riders ride much faster, brake more suddenly, and take far more risky turns. The predictor beat six baselines and is demonstrated for collision prediction.
arxiv-2601-03373:
Conor M. B. Omand, writing alone, calculates which atomic lines cool the debris of a magnetar-driven supernova years after the explosion. A spinning magnetar engine is often invoked to power energetic supernovae, and its wind nebula photoionizes the ejecta, creating distinctive late-time signals. Recent models suggest infrared emission, especially from ionized neon, can be prominent in that phase; Omand tests that idea by examining the cooling power of optical and infrared transitions.

His models show infrared cooling grows strong about three years after the explosion and dominates by six years, with one neon line at twelve point eight micrometers the strongest single coolant. The infrared share rises sharply once the nebula's luminosity fades below a threshold. At one year, by contrast, optical oxygen and sulfur lines still dominate the cooling.
arxiv-2601-03473:
André Rickes and Elena Braverman study how total population size depends on movement in patchy environments. Their models use directed diffusion, meaning organisms drift in chosen directions, inside logistic growth models where carrying capacity varies by place. Earlier work debated whether the total population can exceed the total carrying capacity, and how that link changes as movement speed varies.

Rickes and Braverman fill a gap for growth rates tied to carrying capacity by any real power. They disprove the guess that one critical power value flips the pattern, showing the relationship is more tangled instead. They also study directed movement further. Results like these help ecologists predict when spreading out helps a population grow beyond what local resources alone would suggest.
arxiv-2601-03573:
Daniel Paul-Pena and three co-authors speed up counting hypertriangles, a pattern of three hyperedges that all overlap each other. Hypergraphs let one edge join many items at once, which fits real data like group chats or shared purchases better than plain graphs. Counting small patterns is a basic network analysis task, but hypertriangles have many distinct overlap shapes.

Borrowing orientation and degeneracy ideas from classic graph algorithms, the team built a framework with provable methods and an implementation called DITCH. In experiments it ran ten to one hundred times faster than leading methods while using less memory. Faster motif counting helps analysts search huge hypergraph datasets, from biology to social networks, without waiting on slow exact counts.
arxiv-2601-04273:
Arun Raveendran Nair Sheela, Florence De Grancey, Christophe Rey, and Victor Charpenay test a knowledge language for aeronautics work. Aircraft domains need both high expressivity for complex facts and fast reasoning with low memory cost. Hybrid MKNF is a language that joins rules with ontologies under one semantics, with query answering built in.

The four authors evaluate the language on a concrete aeronautics case study to judge its fit. They find extra expressivity traits that real applications in the domain require but the base language lacks. For those traits they propose a set of heuristics to guide integration into the framework. The study maps where a rule-plus-ontology system stands for flight-related knowledge work and what must be added before wider deployment.
arxiv-2601-04373:
Akriti Dhasmana, Aarohi Srivastava, and David Chiang ask what actually helps a speech recognizer handle a new dialect, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their material is spontaneous, noisy, and code-mixed speech from a wide range of Indic language varieties. The messy conditions where recognition usually fails and where training data is thinnest.

Relatedness helps, they find: the closer the family relationship between languages, the better the transfer, as expected. But family distance alone does not explain performance on dialects, and small amounts of genuine dialect data often match finetuning on much larger amounts of a related standard language. A case study on Garhwali, a low-resource hill variety, tests several current recognizers. And an error analysis shows systems leaning toward their pretraining languages when the dialect departs from the standard.
arxiv-2601-04473:
Jiaheng Chen and Daniel Sanz-Alonso put error bars on learning the laws of physics themselves, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their target is a basic class of operators from partial differential equations and physics, the elliptic pseudo-differential operators, which turn inputs into outputs across many scales at once. Learning such an operator from data is an infinite-dimensional regression, and theory for how fast the learning converges has lagged the algorithms.

In a wavelet-Galerkin scheme, the authors exploit the class's multiscale sparsity with a new matrix compression scheme and a nested-support strategy that balance approximation against estimation error. They prove convergence rates for the resulting sparse estimator, then show the learned operator doubles as a working solver whose own error matches its statistical accuracy. Operator learning, data-driven solvers, and wavelet methods, usually separate literatures, meet in the argument.
arxiv-2601-04673:
Aurghya Maiti and Prateek Jain ask what can honestly be learned about cause and effect from a finite pile of observations, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is the Gaussian linear structural causal model, a workhorse because it is analytically tractable. with limited data its parameters are typically overparameterized and cannot be estimated, latent confounders or not.

Their fix is a leaner subclass, centralized Gaussian linear models, in which the exogenous noise variables are standardized. The subclass, they prove, loses nothing that matters: it identifies exactly the same causal effects from observational data as the full class. An expectation-maximization algorithm then learns the parameters and estimates the identifiable effects from finite samples. Synthetic experiments and standard benchmark causal graphs confirm that the method recovers the true causal distributions accurately, giving practitioners an estimable model class instead of an aspirational one.
arxiv-2601-04773:
Radio surveys now find far too many galaxies for people to sort by shape by hand. Philipp Denzel and 3 co-authors address that problem in a 2026 paper on deep learning, meaning computer models that learn patterns from examples, for radio galaxy classification. Their setting is the coming Square Kilometre Array Observatory, whose wide surveys will detect billions of galaxies.

Inside, the authors test how well deep learning models can be tuned to find and label radio sources. Those foreground galaxies blur a faint early-universe signal, so they must be spotted and removed. Better automatic sorting would let huge surveys be cleaned and studied at a scale no human team could manage.
arxiv-2601-05173:
Chun Hei Michael Shiu, Hei Victor Cheng, and Lele Wang find information-theoretic limits for finding a small graph inside a larger one in a 2026 paper. Graph alignment matches vertices between two correlated graphs, but most theory assumes both graphs share the same vertices. Real tasks in computer vision, social networks, and bioinformatics instead ask where a small pattern graph sits inside a big graph, a harder subgraph version.

Existing algorithms and analyses do not directly address locating that specific subset of vertices. The authors study the exact subgraph alignment problem's fundamental limits: when recovery is possible at all, regardless of computing power. Such limits tell practitioners whether a matching failure reflects a weak algorithm or missing information that no algorithm could overcome.
arxiv-2601-05273:
Angshul Majumdar's 2026 paper asks if stock tools from sparse signal work can find the best way to group agents. He finds they can not. The task, in which groups form with odds on their worth, is hard in the strong sense: no fast exact tool is thought to exist. It can be re-cast as a hunt for a sparse set of weights, one per group. That re-cast begs for the stock tools of signal work: loose fits and greedy picks.

Majumdar shows the tools break in a real-world case. When groups stack on top of each other, the weight grid gains near-twin rows. A key test for the loose fit then fails, and a stock greedy pick stalls in a way he can prove. The no-go steers folks who build group tools away from kit that looks sound but snaps where groups stack.
arxiv-2601-05473:
Zhihao Yuan and 6 co-authors set out, in a 2026 framework paper, what valid student simulation with language models should require. Simulated students could help education research, but broadly capable models make poor stand-ins for learners with partial knowledge. The authors call this mismatch the competence paradox: errors and learning patterns come out unrealistic.

Their answer is to treat simulation as constrained generation. An Epistemic State Specification states what the simulated learner can access, how errors are structured, and how knowledge changes over time. A Goal-by-Environment framework then maps systems by purpose and setting. The paper argues that matching a learner's knowledge state matters more than surface realism.
arxiv-2601-05573:
Zehan Wang and 7 co-authors present Orient Anything V2, a 2026 foundation model for judging object orientation and rotation from one or two images. Knowing which way an object faces matters for robotics and 3D tasks. The earlier version assumed one unique front face, which many symmetric objects lack.

Version two handles varied rotational symmetries and estimates relative rotation between images directly. Its advances include generated 3D training assets with broad coverage, an annotation loop that finds all valid front faces, and a symmetry-aware fitting objective that keeps every plausible orientation. A multi-frame design predicts rotations between views. Across eleven benchmarks, the authors report leading zero-shot results for orientation, pose, and symmetry recognition.
arxiv-2601-05673:
Mathieu Hoyrup studies, in a solo 2026 paper, the local generation of one specific formal language: the binary monotonic sequences, meaning strings of zeros and ones that never switch back. Local generation is an approach Hoyrup introduced earlier. In it, the communication behind a generation process is captured by a simplicial complex, a structure recording which groups can interact.

For this language he proves general results and identifies several classes of minimal simplicial complexes that generate it. The contribution is precise classification rather than a broad survey. He asks which smallest communication structures suffice to produce exactly these sequences, and how those structures relate to one another.
arxiv-2601-05973:
Diego Tancara and 2 co-authors combine, in a 2026 paper, two quantum computing strategies to estimate molecular ground states more cheaply. One is ADAPT-VQE, a variational method for near-term quantum devices that grows its circuit step by step and resists the barren plateau problem. The other is counterdiabatic driving, which improves adiabatic evolution and can shorten circuits.

Their hybrid maps the molecule's Hamiltonian onto qubits and builds an adiabatic version of it. An approximate gauge potential, computed through nested commutators, supplies the operator pool. The adaptive method then picks the most relevant operators one by one to build its circuit. The authors report better results and shallower circuits than either approach used alone, or than ADAPT-VQE with standard fermionic excitation operators.
arxiv-2601-06073:
Zhiyu Li and 3 co-authors solve a decades-old wave problem in a 2026 paper on interluminal interfaces. Such an interface is a sharp space-time change moving at a speed between the wave speeds of the two media around it. The regime resembles Cherenkov radiation, where a particle outruns light in a medium, but involves two media.

A wave hitting the interface can produce one scattered wave or three, depending on direction. Earlier work covered only limited non-magnetic cases. The authors build a complete general solution by decomposing the problem into slower and faster limit cases, plus a space-time impulse response. Their results bridge the long-standing gap between the subluminal and superluminal regimes and explain the underlying mechanisms.
arxiv-2601-06173:
Jun Lu offers a first course in sparse optimization in a 2026 overview article. Sparse optimization seeks solutions that use only a few active components, which helps recover signals from limited data. The field serves both newcomers who need an entry point and practitioners who need a rigorous reference.

The article starts with foundations: the mathematical tools and models behind sparse signal recovery and the LASSO method. It then covers key algorithms for recovery, such as basis pursuit and matching pursuit, and for regularization, such as LASSO and elastic net. Applications to real problems appear throughout. Intuitive explanations sit alongside full mathematical formulations, so readers can build understanding before tackling the technical depth.
arxiv-2601-06573:
Hour-long videos defeat models tested on clips of a few minutes. Zixing Lin and 6 co-authors present QMAVIS in a 2026 paper, a pipeline for long video-audio understanding built by fusing large multimodal models, language models, and speech recognition. The target is sensemaking: extracting both scene-level nuance and the overarching narrative.

On a major long-video benchmark with subtitles, QMAVIS improved over leading video-audio models by nearly forty percent. On other demanding datasets covering perception and egocentric video, it stayed competitive with small further gains. Qualitative tests showed the system extracting the nuances of individual scenes while tracking the whole story. Ablation studies measured each fusion component's impact. The authors position the pipeline for content analysis and embodied AI applications needing long-form understanding.
arxiv-2601-06873: Research by Mustafa Abdool and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with applying Embedding-Based retrieval to airbnb search. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The goal of Airbnb search is to match guests with the ideal accommodation that fits their travel needs. This is a challenging problem, as popular search locations can have around a hundred thousand available homes. And guests themselves have a wide variety of preferences. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-06973:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Davide Baldelli and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers LLMs can’t play hangman. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. As LLMs move from text completion toward autonomous agents, they remain constrained by the standard chat interface, which lacks private working memory.

This raises a fundamental question: can agents reliably perform interactive tasks that depend on hidden state. We define Private State Interactive Tasks (PSITs), which require agents to generate and maintain hidden information while producing consistent public responses. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07373:
Muhammad Raza and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with enumeration of generalized cospectral mates of graphs. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The work investigates the enumeration of generalized cospectral mates of simple graphs. Where the generalized spectrum consists of the spectra of a graph and its complement.

Moving beyond the classical problem of identifying graphs determined by their generalized spectrum. We address the more quantitative question of how many non-isomorphic graphs can share the same generalized spectrum. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07473:
Michael J. Clark introduces AntiPaSTO, a method for steering language models toward honesty, in a 2026 preprint. As models grow more capable, people cannot easily check what they say. Steering methods therefore need to work from inside the model, without constant human labels. They also need to hold up on new kinds of inputs.

Existing methods, Clark notes, meet only some of those demands. AntiPaSTO is self-supervised and separates internal representations along an antiparallel axis. Pushing one way or the other along that axis shifts behavior in opposite directions. Coherence constraints keep the model from collapsing into nonsense. The paper speaks to the wider effort to keep advanced models truthful and controllable.
arxiv-2601-07773:
Lingchen Sun and coauthors train diffusion transformers with signals that sit inside the model. Recent work guides diffusion models with outside semantic features, such as those from DINO. That guidance can greatly speed training. It also needs pretrained outside networks, which adds links to other tools and cuts freedom. Their 2026 preprint seeks the same gain from features found inside instead.

The title speaks of freeing the rich meaning that sits inside diffusion transformers. If inner layers already encode useful semantics, training can lean on them directly. With no outside teacher, the pipeline gets simpler and needs less compute tied to a second model. Faster diffusion training matters because these models are costly to build. The paper targets generative modeling scholars. It asks whether the guide a model needs has been inside it all along. The gain, if it holds, is a lean build with fewer parts to keep in step.
arxiv-2601-07973:
Myra Cheng and colleagues build a framework for organizing social norms so AI norm violations can be detected. Generative AI should be useful and safe across cultures. Understanding how models follow sociocultural norms is a key step. Existing NLP work, they note, lacks nuance and coverage in evaluating norm adherence. Their 2026 preprint, Cultural Compass, addresses that gap for human-AI conversations.

Norms vary by culture and situation, so a flat rule list fails. A compass framework organizes norms so violations can be spotted in context. Detection is a prerequisite for training or steering models to behave appropriately. The work matters for products deployed across many countries at once. The paper serves NLP scholars and AI safety teams. It supplies structure for a topic often handled with ad hoc lists.
arxiv-2601-08073: Bandar Al-Dhalaan and Shalev Ben-David study turning Monte Carlo methods into Las Vegas methods for composed functions. Their 2026 arXiv paper works with Boolean functions and query complexity measures. For a measure M and function f, they define a composition limit as the number of compositions grows without bound. Monte Carlo algorithms may err, while Las Vegas algorithms always give correct answers with random run time. The paper asks when recursive composition lets one style be converted into the other. It serves readers in theoretical computer science.
arxiv-2601-08573: Andrea Braides wrote a 2026 arXiv paper that sums up new results on a tool for hard math problems. The tool is singular perturbations of non-convex functionals. When a problem has many best answers, a small added term can pick out one of them. The classic case is the gradient theory of phase transitions by Modica. That theory built on Gamma-convergence work by Modica and Mortola. It backed the minimal-interface rule for phase lines. The paper sums up fresh work on the non-local form of the tool.
arxiv-2601-08673:
Didier Sornette, Sandro Claudio Lera, and Ke Wu argue that AI alignment failure is structural, not accidental. Their 2026 arXiv paper responds to reports of language models showing deception, threats, or blackmail. Such reports are often read as proof of alignment failure or emergent malign agency.

The authors argue that this reading rests on a conceptual error. Models learn human interaction structures, including manipulation patterns present in training data. Advanced AI then acts as an endogenous evolutionary shock to the systems it joins. The paper reframes safety debates: if failure is structural, fixes must target training structures and deployment incentives, not just individual model misbehavior.
arxiv-2601-08873:
Hema Hariharan Samson builds a tool to spot fake or cut images across many sources. Old check tools work on one class of flaw. A tool trained on phone shots may fail on AI art or on scans. Real check work must cross those lines each day. Samson aims for one tool that holds up in all of them.

The tool is called ForensicFormer. It reads an image at three scales at once. Fine scale checks catch pixel flaws. Mid scale checks read edge breaks. Large scale checks ask if the scene makes sense. Past tools that use one scale fell below a set mark on new sets. This tool holds a high mark on those sets, the author says. A reader in image checks gets a broad, layered plan.
arxiv-2601-09473:
Oliver Bolton and five co-authors, including Sara Hooker, automate a choice that language model builders now face often. Their 2026 arXiv paper, SimMerge, learns to select merge operators from similarity signals. Model merging blends several trained models into one that keeps their combined skills.

Scaling merging is hard because quality depends on the operator, the subset of models, and the merge order. Testing each option by merging and evaluating is costly. SimMerge instead reads similarity signals between models and predicts a good recipe. A cheap selector would make merging a routine step in building capable models.
arxiv-2601-09873:
Saymon Souza, Amanda Santana, and Eduardo Figueiredo test whether language models can smell bad code. Their 2026 arXiv paper assesses large language models for code smell detection, moving beyond strict rule-based checkers. Code smells are warning signs of quality problems that raise maintenance costs.

Language models have shown skill across many software engineering tasks. Their use for smell detection is still little explored. The authors measure how effective the models are in practice. A capable detector tool could warn developers very early on, before smelly code hardens into expensive, unreliable systems.
arxiv-2601-09973:
Samuel Everett links two hard fields: how hard a task is, and how a flow acts. His tasks ask if a point can reach a set in finite time. The flow is one way and sits on a line. Each task comes from its own flow.

He shows a tight link. If tasks from two flows can map to each other in a natural way, the flows must act alike. The word alike is made sharp in the proof. The paper is part two of a pair. It gives a tool to sort flows by the tasks they spawn.
arxiv-2601-10373:
Yichong Xia, Yimin Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, and Bin Chen squeeze images to a trickle of bits. New diffusion tools can rebuild a rich image from few bits. The rebuilt shot looks true to the eye. But past tools are slow to sample. Their bit splits are also oft poor.

The team made DiffCR, a squeeze frame built for speed. It refines a diffusion prior in a firm way. That cuts the slow sample steps. It also splits bits with more care across the image. The aim is a small file that rebuilds fast and looks true.
arxiv-2601-10673:
Aditya Agrawal and a team at Google tackle a bottleneck in training and serving large language models. Model data must be split across many accelerator chips. The collective steps that sync those chips are often capped by network bandwidth. Faster compression of the data in flight would ease that cap.

The team presents a single-stage Huffman encoder built for machine learning compression. Huffman coding squeezes data by giving short codes to common values. A one-stage design aims to keep the squeeze fast enough for live training traffic. If it holds up, big model runs could spend less time waiting on the network.
arxiv-2601-10773:
Niko Usai, Dario Montagnini, Kristian Ilianov Iliev, and Raffaele Camanzo present LogicLens, a tool for grasping large software systems. Big systems sprawl across many repositories and microservices. To reason about them, developers need more than code structure. They need the domain logic and runtime behavior, which sit implicit and scattered across the codebase.

LogicLens builds a semantic code graph to explore such systems. A graph can join calls, data, and intent in one view. That helps new team members and auditors find how a feature truly works. The work speaks to engineers who inherit sprawling systems and must change them without breaking hidden links.
arxiv-2601-11073:
Rongkun Cui, Nana Zhang, Kun Zhu, and Qi Zhang build a hypergraph learning system to catch web finance fraud. Online finance is a core part of the web economy. Its openness invites fraud that harms vulnerable users and weakens trust in digital finance. The authors draw their design from the hippocampus, the brain region that binds memories together.

Their multi-view hypergraph model links accounts, devices, and transactions in shared hyperedges. Views from several angles help expose fraud rings that single links hide. The brain-inspired framing stresses memory: fraud patterns repeat, and a system that recalls them can flag new variants. The work serves platforms that must police harm without freezing honest users out.
arxiv-2601-11573:
Muhammad Muneeb and David Ascher fine-tune language models on bioinformatics text. Their 2026 preprint gives a reproducible pipeline for the work. General LLMs often lack specialized knowledge for this field. Bioinformatics tasks need tool names, data forms, and jargon.

Two use cases show the pipeline in action. PRSGPT focuses on polygenic risk score tools and their use. BioStarsGPT trains on community forum discussions instead. Forum text holds practical know-how from working analysts. The pipeline can be rerun by other teams on new data. That reproducibility is a stated design goal of the work. Specialist models may then serve niche science better.
arxiv-2601-11773:
Elliot Benjamin and Mohamed Mahmoud Chems-Eddin work on a deep question in number theory. They study real quadratic fields, which add a square root to the rationals. For each field, a tower of class fields can be built step by step. They ask how long that tower runs.

They pick fields whose class group is a small group of order four. They also pick fields whose discriminant is not a sum of two squares. The work is a follow-up, checking past guesses on tower length. Such towers test how class groups grow in pure maths.
arxiv-2601-12273:
Chihiro Yoshida, Yuta Ishimoto, Olivier Nourry, and their co-authors use mutation analysis to guide LLM repair of quantum programs. Repair tools for quantum code exist, but they often fail or make patches that are hard to read. Mutation analysis seeds small faults to test a repair.

Those seeded faults can steer a language model to the true flaw. A guided search may lift repair rates and yield clearer patches. Quantum code is hard to debug by hand, so such help is prized. The work tests the pairing on quantum programs.
arxiv-2601-12773:
Lea S. Schimak and eleven co authors test red clump star models with a rare binary system. Binaries where both stars pulsate are rare but extremely valuable. Their system pairs a core helium burning red clump star with a red giant branch star. The binary is cataloged as KIC 10841730, and it pulsates in ways seismology can read.

Theirs is the first study of an asteroseismic binary of this exact makeup. Asteroseismology uses star vibrations to probe interiors that light cannot reach. Two pulsating stars in one system give cross checks no single star can. Red clump stars serve as standard candles for galactic distances. Testing their models sharpens the distance ladder of astronomy.
arxiv-2601-13173:
Leonardo Grimaldi, Elisa Maggio, Lorenzo Pompili, and Alessandra Buonanno test Einstein's theory with a loud black hole crash. The signal, named GW250114, is the clearest wave of its kind yet caught. Its last stage, where the merged hole rings down, is a sharp probe of strong gravity.

The team asks how well that stage fits Einstein's rules for holes that spin and wobble. They use a wave form model that can bend away from Einstein's form in set ways. It sits in the effective one body frame, a way to map two body motion to one body terms. Tight bounds here would be a strong pass for the theory in its most harsh realm yet.
arxiv-2601-13473:
A. Koley, A. M. Stutz, and co-authors map magnetic fields in the G327.29 star forming cluster two ways. Fields and churn may steer how such clusters make dense cores and stars. To test that role, the field's shape in space must be known with care.

One read uses the velocity gradient technique on molecular line light. A next read uses polarized light from dust in the same sky. The team sets the two maps side by side. Where they match, trust grows. Where they part, the part marks a limit of one tool. ALMA data drives both reads. Such a head to head test firms up field maps for all cluster work.
arxiv-2601-14173:
Paris Karakasis and Nicholas Sidiropoulos study smoothness penalties for low-rank tensor models in 2026. Their models are low-rank tensor-product B-spline models for regression tasks. They investigate Dirichlet energy as a measure of smoothness. They show these models admit a closed-form expression for that energy.

They also reveal scenarios where perfect interpolation is possible with tiny Dirichlet energy. Exponentially small energy can accompany an exact fit in those cases. That renders global Dirichlet energy regularization ineffective as a guard. Local penalties, per the title, offer a way to restore control. The fix is to charge for rough spots where they sit, not for the whole field. That local charge keeps good fits sharp while it curbs the cheat.
arxiv-2601-14473:
Danny Butvinik, Nana Boateng, and Achi Hackmon study financial crime queues in this 2026 paper. Detection systems turn a continuous stream of risk scores into decision thresholds. Scores must be split into priority classes for investigators. The catch is that score distributions are non-stationary: they drift over time, so fixed thresholds go stale.

The team proposes adaptive kernel density estimation for real-time thresholding. KDE is a way to estimate the shape of a score distribution from live data. Their system builds prioritized queues for financial crime investigation. Readers get a method that keeps alert queues stable and sorted even as fraud patterns shift under them.
arxiv-2601-14573:
M. N. Chernodub, V. A. Goy, and A. V. Molochkov simulate the electroweak model in a strong magnetic field in this 2026 paper. They use numerical Monte Carlo simulations on a lattice. Their goal is the mass spectrum of the bosonic sector of the model. The external field has electroweak-scale strength, about 10 to the 20th tesla. The temperature is zero.

Fields that strong exist only in extreme settings, such as the early universe or magnetars. The paper's title asks a pointed question: are there acoustic phonons in a magnetized vacuum? Phonons are sound-like waves in a medium. Readers get lattice results on how the vacuum itself behaves as a material under such a field.
arxiv-2601-14673:
Yogesh Pipada Sunil Kumar and four co-authors bring neural networks into power system optimization in this 2026 paper. The decarbonisation of power systems drives growing reliance on distributed energy resources. Those resources introduce complex, nonlinear interactions. Conventional optimization models struggle to capture them. Machine learning based surrogate modelling has emerged as a promising approach.

The catch comes at integration time. Embedding ReLU deep neural networks directly into optimization often results in nonconvex and computationally intractable formulations. The team develops efficient reformulations of such networks for surrogate modelling. Reformulation rewrites the network so solvers can handle it. The point is use. A net that no solver can read is a dead end for grid work, no matter how well it fits past data. That is the goal of the work. Readers get a bridge between trained neural surrogates and the optimizers that run real grids.
arxiv-2601-14773:
Haizhou Liu, Yiming Wang, Haodong Jin, and Hui Yu summarize videos with AI in this 2026 paper. Video summarization enables efficient browsing of massive multimedia content and extraction of key information from social platforms. Most existing unsupervised summarization methods rely on Generative Adversarial Networks. GANs enhance keyframe selection and generate coherent summaries through adversarial training.

The team's method is semantic-guided unsupervised video summarization. Semantic guidance means the summary follows meaning, not just visual change. Unsupervised means no human-made summaries are needed for training. The use is plain. A long clip can be cut to its key frames, so a viewer saves time. Readers get a summarizer aimed at social video, where meaning matters more than motion: the key moment may be a quiet one.
arxiv-2601-14873:
Youssef El Khatiri works in the algebra of operators, the math behind much of quantum theory. His 2026 arXiv paper studies C*-algebras, a key class of these algebras. He looks at maps that keep the order between elements of the algebra.

El Khatiri gives a full account of such order-preserving maps. He covers maps between the self-adjoint parts of two C*-algebras. He then extends the result to general operator intervals in a wider class of algebras. The account rests on Jordan maps and on closed operators in rings tied to the algebra.
arxiv-2601-15173:
Katarina Krivokuća bounds a covering quantity for convex bodies. Her 2026 arXiv paper deals with the covering minima of a convex body, a gauge from the geometry of numbers. She gives two new upper bounds for that quantity.

Each bound leans on simpler pieces of the body. One uses the covering minima of its projections. The other uses its intersections with flat subspaces. She shows one bound is sharp for direct sums of two bodies. That sharp case extends earlier results on covering radius and on lattice width for such sums.
arxiv-2601-15473:
Fahd Seddik and four co-authors tackle a tooling gap in deep learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Training large models strains GPU memory and compute budgets. Methods from randomized numerical linear algebra, or RandNLA, can help shrink these models. Yet no single, production-grade library has pulled those methods together. That gap, the authors argue, has slowed wider use.

Their answer is Panther, a library that works with PyTorch. Panther gathers known RandNLA methods into one fast framework. The title promises faster and cheaper computation as the payoff. For model builders, the point is plain. Tricks that once took custom code now sit in one shared tool, ready to use.
arxiv-2601-15673:
Qilong Yan and four co-authors improve recommendation with diffusion models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Sequential recommendation predicts what a user will want next. Methods have grown more complex over time. Many now use diffusion-guided generation instead of plain classification. These methods lean on user information as guidance. Real user sequences have missing data, though. Gaps in that guidance hurt the quality of what gets generated.

The title names the focus: enhancing guidance when data are missing. Better guidance should steer generation toward items the user truly wants. Missing history is the norm in real platforms, not the exception. Users skip, pause, and browse off the record. A recommender that copes with holes serves both users and sellers better.
arxiv-2601-15773:
Yuanyuan Qi and six co-authors blend several language models into active learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Active learning picks which data humans should label. Language models now join these pipelines as annotators. Their labels cut annotation costs. Quality is the catch. Labels from models often fall short of real-world needs. One model alone can be biased or brittle.

The title names the fix: a mixture of LLMs in the loop. Several models label together, checking each other's weak spots. Diversity among annotators is a classic route to better labels. The authors aim for annotation that stays cheap without going sloppy. Labeled data feed nearly every applied AI project. Cutting its cost while holding quality is a broad win.
arxiv-2601-16473:
Wei Song and coauthors strip deepfake marks with no query to the guard. Their 2026 preprint, named DeMark, deals with marks hid in fake pics. Marks let teams spot fakes and trace their source. The guard case holds that marks stand firm to clean tricks. Past tests oft need asks to the guard model to find a path.

DeMark needs no such asks to strip the mark. A no ask attack is far more hard to spot or block. If marks fall with ease, mark guards need a rethink. The work tests mark strength in a harsh, real case. It warns teams that marks alone may not hold.
arxiv-2601-17373:
Shuning Zhang and seven co-authors study privacy fears in smart home assistants. These tools now act as social agents in the home. User worry turns on where data goes and who can hear it. The team uses Privacy Boundary Theory, a frame from interpersonal talk. A three-phase early study grounds their work. It first maps how data moves in these homes.

From that base, they probe how risk feels across sharing ranges. A chat kept in one room feels unlike one sent to the cloud. Design that shows those ranges could calm real fears. It could also stop over-sharing by default. The work links social theory to device design.
arxiv-2601-17673:
Weiyu Zhang, Yuan Hu, Yong Li, and Yu Liu present Uni-RS for remote sensing. Unified models both understand and generate images. The authors name a flaw they call the spatial reversal curse. Models can describe object locations in images with care. Yet they fail to use the same spatial relations when they generate. In remote sensing, those relations are core meaning.

A map-like image with wrong left-right layout is useless. Uni-RS aims for spatial faithfulness in both directions. Better spatial truth serves land use, disaster, and defense maps. Generation that respects layout can also augment training data. The work names a clear failure mode. Naming it lets the field measure progress on it.
arxiv-2601-17973:
Yuan Bian, Grace Y. Yi, and Wenqing He extend boosting to data where event times are only partly known. Their 2026 preprint deals with interval-censored data. In such data, an event is known to fall inside a window, but the exact time is unseen. The setup is common in survival analysis and in studies of time to an event, like relapse or failure. Classic boosting was built for full data and often struggles here.

Boosting builds a strong model by joining many weak ones in steps. The authors adapt that idea for both regression and classification with censored inputs. Sound tools for windowed data matter in medicine and reliability work. The paper gives those fields a modern learning option.
arxiv-2601-18173: N. B. Huamaní studies vertex degrees in grid graphs built from permutations that avoid the pattern 213. His 2026 preprint builds the graph column by column, with each column's height set by the permutation entry. Vertical edges join levels inside a column, and horizontal edges join equal levels in neighboring columns. The paper works out how the degrees of the vertices behave in this family.
arxiv-2601-18273:
Lorenzo Verzichelli works on scaling normalizing flows to bigger problems in condensed matter. His 2026 preprint studies the Hubbard model, a basic model of electrons in a lattice. Normalizing flows have recently learned the Boltzmann distribution of that model. That success opens a new route to generative modeling of quantum materials. The open question is how to reach larger lattices and lower temperatures without the training falling apart.

Verzichelli studies the steps needed for that scale-up. Stability and efficiency are his twin focus. Flows that stay sound at low temperature could sample states that other methods reach slowly. The work maps the path from a proof of concept to a working tool.
arxiv-2601-18573:
Frederik Glitzner and David Manlove study match tasks in which some who take part break ranks and some hold firm. The base tasks pair up people by what they like best, in a way no pair would both gain by a swap. In one form of the task such a firm match is sure to exist and can be found fast. In the next form it may not exist at all, though one can tell fast if it does.

Real match tasks must weigh size next to firm-ness: a big match that some would break, or a small one that none would. The team add two kinds of folk to that mix. Some will break a match for a small gain. Some will hold firm at a cost. Their maths maps how those kinds shift the best trade. Match maths serves dorms, jobs, and organ swaps.
arxiv-2601-18873:
A study sets out a new kind of skyrmion that is born of heat, not of cold calm. A skyrmion is a knot in a field that can't be smoothed out. It acts like a lone bit and can be quite firm. In the maths of the bits that fill atom cores, such knots stand for the cores them-selves. They may also live in the field that gives mass to all bits, if set cross terms are at play.

The new kind is tied to heat: its form and firm-ness shift with how hot the field runs. That tie could change where such knots can live and what they do. Heat-born knots may have played a role in the hot young cosmos. The work is a maths study, with no lab test in view. It adds a fresh form to a prized class of field knots.
arxiv-2601-19073:
Jessica Eskew and eight co-authors study how a split in a magnetic island changes the spread of electrons. In magnetized plasmas, islands are closed loops of field that can trap or guide particles. When an island splits, its inner points and borders move, and the paths for sideways diffusion change with them.

The team tracks that effect under controlled splitting of the island shape. Diffusion across the field sets how fast heat and particles leak in fusion and space plasmas. Knowing how island shape steers that leak helps read experiments and may help keep hot plasma penned in longer.
arxiv-2601-19473:
Lucia Varbaro and thirteen co-authors report superconductivity that returns, driven by magnetism, in a nickel based crystal. Infinite layer nickelates are thin structured cousins of the famous cuprate superconductors. Doping this one with europium adds magnetic atoms to the mix.

In such a setting, superconductivity can vanish and then come back, a re-entrance, as conditions shift. The team traces that return and links it to the paramagnetic response of the dopants. Re-entrant cases are stress tests for theories of how magnetism and superconductivity share one material, a puzzle at the heart of the field.
arxiv-2601-19973:
Andrew R. Casey and five colleagues rethink a routine step in analysing starlight. To infer a star's temperature and chemistry, astronomers forward-model its spectrum. That usually requires a synthesis code or an emulator trained on curated examples. Before modelling, the spectrum is normalised: its continuum level is set by a preprocessing step kept separate from the stellar parameters.

That separation biases results and makes them inconsistent across signal-to-noise levels. The authors propose a constrained linear model that folds continuum normalisation into the analysis itself. A joint treatment should give abundances that agree no matter how noisy the data are. Chemical surveys of millions of stars depend on such consistency. The work cleans up a quiet source of systematic error. The bias is small but it does not go away.
arxiv-2601-20173:
Zeyang Huang and four colleagues present MAPLE, a method that squeezes high-dimensional data down to a low-dimensional map for visual analysis. It builds on UMAP, a widely used tool for this task. MAPLE adds self-supervised learning to model the shape of the data manifold more efficiently.

At its core are maximum manifold capacity representations. These pull together points that are locally similar while pushing apart points that differ. The result is a map where tangled structure is easier to see. Better maps help analysts explore data in fields from biology to social science, where clusters and paths guide the next questions.
arxiv-2601-20473:
Weichen Wang and a large team report a quiet galaxy. It sits inside a gas-rich knot of the cosmic web at redshift about three, when the universe was young. Space telescopes have recently found many quenched galaxies at that era, which challenges models of galaxy formation. Since star formation feeds on gas flowing in from outside, the gas around such a galaxy is the key clue.

This galaxy sits where filaments of the web meet and gas is plentiful, yet it has stopped forming stars. Studying its circumgalactic gas may show how quenching can win even where fuel is abundant.
arxiv-2601-20673:
Felix Janda and Xin Wang study deep patterns in the geometry of curves in this 2026 math paper. Their subject is topological recursion relations on the moduli space of curves. That space collects all curves of a given genus with marked points. Recursion relations are formulas that tie complex cases to simpler ones. The paper looks at the basic structures these relations can take.

One focus is the coefficient of the bouquet class on that space. That coefficient gives the answer to a conjecture in the field. The authors map out the structures one by one. Their work is pure geometry, aimed at readers who study how these spaces are built. It adds basic facts that later work on curve spaces can build on.
arxiv-2601-20773:
Rubén Jiménez and Oriol Pujol copy deployed AI models using nothing but questions and answers. Their 2026 paper studies black-box model copying with signed-distance supervision. Deployed systems must evolve as data, architectures, and regulations change. Often the original training data and model internals are gone. Black-box copying offers a practical refactoring path. A replica is learned from input-output queries alone. The legacy model is upgraded without ever being opened.

The authors smooth that copying with signed-distance supervision. A signed distance says how far an input sits from a decision boundary, and on which side. That richer signal guides the replica beyond bare labels. Better copies preserve behavior where it matters most. The method serves teams stuck with models they cannot retrain. It turns a black box into a maintainable asset.
arxiv-2601-20873: P. J. Rijken and Th. A. Rijken give a new way to find the eigenvalues of the Heun equation. Eigenvalues are the special values at which an equation has clean solutions. The Heun equation is a broad form met across physics. Its eigenvalues are hard to pin down. The 2026 paper tests the method on the Breit equation, a two-particle equation from atomic physics.
arxiv-2601-21273:
Tianchen Hu and ten co-authors test how a layered crystal handles very strong light pulses. The crystal belongs to a family with built-in electric order and strong responses to light. Earlier work focused on its simpler response, where light comes out at twice the input frequency.

The team measures stronger effects, where the output reaches much higher multiples of the input frequency. Such high harmonics can serve as tiny light sources and probes of the material itself. The crystal's layered form makes it a good fit for small devices. The results support its use in compact photonics, where strong light effects must fit on a chip.
arxiv-2601-21373:
V.L. Martinez-Consentino, J.E. Amaro, and J. Segovia compute how nuclei answer when neutrinos scatter off pairs of particles inside them. Two particles can be knocked out together by exchange currents between nucleons. That two-body response is a key input for reading neutrino experiments.
