The authors study how the response scales across many nuclei, from helium up to uranium. Their model treats proton and neutron densities with separate momentum scales. Asymmetric nuclei, where the two counts differ a lot, get special care. The scaling rules help experiments predict signals without a fresh heavy calculation for every target.
arxiv-2601-21473:
Zaifeng Pan and eight co-authors make large multi-agent simulations cheaper to run. Simulations where each agent is a language model are spreading across many fields. Each agent keeps private state on the graphics chip, and memory fills fast as the agent count grows.

The authors notice two helpful traits of these workloads. Only a few agents are active at any moment, and the order of future calls can be estimated. Their system, ScaleSim, manages memory based on how soon each agent will be called next. That foresight keeps the chip from choking as simulations scale up.
arxiv-2601-21573:
Masaki Miyashita studies how a firm should spread its products across features that buyers care about. The work builds on a hedonic model where a single representative buyer values product characteristics. A monopolist selling several products chooses where each one sits in feature space.

The striking result is that the monopolist's choice matches the social planner's optimum. That holds even though the firm produces too little overall. In other words, the range of products is right even when the volume is wrong. The finding separates two questions policy often mixes: variety can be fine while quantity is the true distortion.
arxiv-2601-21673:
Dexuan Ding and eight co-authors compress brain scans into compact surrogates for Alzheimer's classification. Structural MRI is widely used to spot the disease. Most learning methods use heavy three-dimensional networks, slice-by-slice features, or frozen features from general image models.

Each route has costs in compute or in fit to the task. The authors build multimodal visual surrogates that summarize the scans more directly. A compact summary could make scan-based screening faster and cheaper to deploy. It may also travel better across hospitals, where scanner types and image quality vary a lot.
arxiv-2601-21873:
Jinhang Chai, Xuyuan Liu, Elynn Chen, and Yujun Yan study transfer learning for structured matrices. Learning systems often grow over time: new features arrive and internal representations expand into larger spaces. Earlier representations end up embedded inside bigger ones, with only limited new structure added.

The team studies how to transfer an estimate from a well-solved source task to a larger target task. Their matrices combine a low-rank part, which holds the main pattern, with a sparse part for exceptions. The 2026 preprint develops theory for this transfer as both the ambient dimension and the inner representation grow. Such results guide fields like recommendation and imaging, where models are retrained on ever wider data.
arxiv-2601-21973:
Erin Dawson extends a counting theory in tropical geometry. Tropical Tevelev degrees arise from maps between tropical moduli spaces of curves, counting how curves meet given conditions in a simplified, combinatorial version of geometry. Dawson and Cavalieri defined and computed these degrees in one specific case.

That case used a particular relation between the degree of the maps and the genus of the curves, with a fixed count of marked points. Dawson's 2026 preprint adds a new integer parameter to the theory, widening the family of degrees that can be defined and studied. Tropical counts often mirror classical algebraic geometry results, so each extension enlarges a dictionary between combinatorics and geometry.
arxiv-2601-22773:
Sung Une Lee and a team give builders a reusable template for safety cases for AI systems. A safety case is a structured argument that a system is safe enough. Their 2026 preprint notes that classic cases, from aviation and nuclear work, assume fixed bounds and known failure modes.

Modern AI breaks those assumptions: it shifts, learns, and acts on its own. Their template framework adapts the case form to that reality. Reusable parts can lift the floor for AI governance. The work serves regulators and builders alike. It turns a craft into a kit.
arxiv-2601-23173:
Chris Sherlock, Andrew Golightly, and Anthony Lee fix a failure mode in particle filtering for hidden Markov models. Sometimes every simulated particle scores zero likelihood for an observation, so the filter collapses. Then the filtering distribution cannot be estimated and the parameter likelihood reads zero.

Their partially alive scheme, nicknamed the Frankenfilter, keeps such runs going in a principled way. It slots into particle Metropolis-Hastings, a standard inference method. Robust filters matter for tracking, epidemiology, and finance, where zero-likelihood steps occur in real data. Partially alive particles keep the filter estimable through stretches where a naive particle set would collapse to zero.
arxiv-2602-02373:
Andrés Franco-Grisales and 1 co-author connect three lines of research on how the universe could begin at a calm big bang, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A quiescent singularity is a big bang where the geometry stays controlled rather than chaotic. Past work derived long-time behavior in symmetric cases, built spacetimes from data placed on the singularity itself, and proved big bangs form without symmetry.

The missing link was whether the spacetimes in the third line actually induce data on the singularity, as the second line requires. Franco-Grisales and his co-author prove that solutions from a recent general formation result do induce such data. The argument is more general than that single case. It may apply in other gauges, meaning other choices for labeling time and space in the equations.
arxiv-2602-02573:
Haonan Dong and 2 co-authors rebuild neural network design on algebra, treating multiplication as the basic act, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Convolutional, attention, state-space, and equivariant networks are usually built as separate crafts despite sharing recurring principles. Their scheme, product interactions, treats data as algebraic elements and builds networks by stacking multiplication operators.

How inputs act on themselves sets the order. Within the scheme, convolutional and equivariant networks emerge as symmetry-bound first-order cases. Attention arises as a third-order interaction from reusing the same operator. The Mamba design is recovered by raising a state-space model's interaction order from one to three. Such rules produce familiar structures: translation symmetry yields convolution, and rotational fit yields the Clebsch-Gordan product. A new simple layer built from these ideas beat Mamba on CIFAR-10 in both accuracy and throughput.
arxiv-2602-03173:
Georgi Bebrov, in solo work dated 2026, aims to push quantum key spread to still longer distances. Sending-or-not-sending plans already achieve the longest known transmission distances for sharing secret keys through quantum signals. Bebrov offers a variant that combines that principle with phase matching, improving tolerance to phase mismatch, which otherwise degrades the key rate as distance and instability grow in long optical links.

Security is analyzed in the asymptotic, infinite-key regime under collective attacks. Results is compared with standard phase-matching plans, theory-based and experimental twin-field variants, including an test spanning about a thousand kilometers. The new plan achieved greater transmission distances than those earlier methods in the analysis. Bebrov presents it as a option for long-distance quantum communication.
arxiv-2602-03373:
Watermarking methods that look alike but behave differently are unified by Jiale Meng, leading 5 other authors, through a dimension-aware mapping view. Deep watermarking systems share similar encoder-decoder architectures yet differ substantially in functional actions. Their system, DiM, formulates watermarking as mapping payloads between dimensions, where information can be a one-part binary message, a two-part spatial mask, or a three-part spatiotemporal form in video or other media.

Dimensional setup of vector and extraction largely determines actions, the authors find. Same-part mappings preserve payload form and support fine-grained control. Cross-part mappings enable spatial or spatiotemporal localization. Instantiated in video, varying only those dimensions produced other capabilities, including tamper localization, local vector control, and recovery of time order under frame disruptions, without architectural changes.
arxiv-2602-03473:
Meng Lou and 2 co-authors push continual learning to sequences of more than 300 tasks in a 2026 paper. Their learner, CaRE, builds on a pre-trained model and must add new classes over time without erasing old ones. Long sequences strain both feature quality and the balance between stability and plasticity.

The core is a bi-level routing mixture-of-experts design. One stage activates the routers relevant to a task, and a second stage selects and blends the experts, injecting richer features at every layer. The authors also release OmniBenchmark-1K, a dataset built for very long class-incremental sequences. CaRE leads on standard benchmarks and, the authors report, is the first learner to scale past 300 tasks.
arxiv-2602-03773:
Ian Wu and 3 co-authors ask whether a model can keep improving far past the horizon it was trained on. Their 2026 paper introduces Reasoning Cache, an iterative decoding algorithm that replaces plain autoregressive decoding in both training and inference. Standard reinforcement learning pins the model to fixed problem distributions and budgets, which limits such extrapolation.

The method exploits an asymmetry: models summarize better than they generate. Reasoning chains are built that improve consistently across iterations, each round conditioning on a summary of the last. A four-billion-parameter model trained with a sixteen-thousand-token budget climbs from forty to nearly seventy percent. The benchmark is a hard mathematics test, and the climb uses half a million test-time tokens. It also stacks well with existing scaffolds.
arxiv-2602-04073:
A classic completeness proof in conditional logic may rest on a technical shortcut. Alexander W. Kocurek and 2 co-authors examine the logic C2, which reasons about if-then statements with quantifiers. The known proof lets selection functions operate on formulas. But the theory's founder insisted they should operate on propositions, meaning sets of possible worlds.

The authors prove the result cannot be extended: under the propositional reading, the logic is frame incomplete. The failure survives changes in domain assumptions and added predicates. Their result reopens basic questions about how conditional logic should be built and what its semantics really commits us to.
arxiv-2602-04273: The smallest galaxies known break a tidy rule linking mass and motion. James Chi Chung Wong's 2026 paper is part eight of a series on variable modified Newtonian mechanics. It takes up the velocity dispersions of ultra faint dwarf galaxies in the Milky Way. Their measured motions depart markedly from the baryon Tully-Fisher relation that massive galaxies obey. Wong proposes that his variable modified Newtonian dynamics model explains the deviation. The note is brief, offering a modified-gravity account of why these faint systems move as they do.
arxiv-2602-04673:
Nathanaël Berestycki and Isao Sauzedde prove a long-standing conjecture about Brownian motion in a 2026 probability paper. Brownian motion is the random wandering path seen in pollen grains and stock charts alike. Their construction builds it from simpler random objects.

Take a radial SLE path, a random curve from conformal geometry, and add every loop from a Brownian loop soup that the curve meets, in time order. The authors show the resulting stitched path is continuous and has exactly the law of planar Brownian motion. This settles a conjecture by Lawler and Werner. The same coupling appears as the scaling limit of a random walk and its loop-erased version, tying discrete and continuous models together.
arxiv-2602-04773:
Bernhard Schmiedmayer and 3 co-authors predict a tensor property of materials using only scalar machine learning models in a 2026 paper. The target is the Born effective charge tensor, which describes how polarization shifts when atoms move. Tensor targets often demand specially designed tensorial inputs.

Their trick uses the definition: the tensor is a derivative of polarization with respect to atomic displacement. Scalar kernel models, called monopole models here, can thus capture its tensorial nature. The authors compare this with past tensorial dipole kernel models that encode structure directly. Both support charge partitioning into monopole and dipole parts. As a test, they computed finite-temperature infrared spectra for several complex materials.
arxiv-2602-04873:
Diffusion models can now generate images direct from the patch features of a self-supervised encoder, but those dense patch grids carry heavy redundancy. Ramón Calvo-González and François Fleuret built FlatDINO, an autoencoder that compresses that representation into a short one-dimensional run of continuous tokens. The squeeze cuts sequence length eightfold and total size far more.

A large diffusion transformer trained on those latents scored well on ImageNet generation while using a fraction of the compute per step of the uncompressed version. The authors are plain that these are preliminary results and the work is in progress. Even so, the savings point to a cheaper route for feature-space diffusion.
arxiv-2602-05073:
Language model agents act over many turns, so knowing when they are unsure matters more than in one-shot question answering. Changdae Oh and 10 co-authors argue in this 2026 paper, accepted at ACL 2026, that uncertainty research has not kept pace with agents. Most current methods still target single-turn setups and lack a principled frame for interactive systems.

The paper lays three pillars for later work. First, a general form of agent uncertainty that holds earlier setups as special cases. Second, four named hurdles: picking an estimator, handling uncertainty across mixed kinds of entities, tracking how uncertainty shifts during interaction, and the lack of fine-grained benchmarks. Numerical study on a real agent benchmark shows them in action. Third, a talk of practical effects and open problems. The aim is reducible uncertainty, doubt that better modeling can truly shrink.
arxiv-2602-05473:
A new kind of hybrid particle is predicted by M. Nursagatov, Xiyin Ye, and 3 co-authors, formed when light couples with waves inside a ferroelectric layer. The stack they study places that layer between two superconductors, and the coupled waves are called ferrons on the material side and Swihart photons on the light side. Together they form what the authors name a ferron-polariton.

The coupling is reported to reach the ultrastrong regime, with an energy gap in the terahertz range that is far larger than in magnetic counterparts. That strength reflects how strongly electric dipoles interact compared with magnetic ones. Beyond the prediction itself, seeing this effect would give direct evidence that ferrons exist. The authors present the layered structure as a new platform for extreme light-matter coupling. They also point to fast, ferroelectric-based quantum devices working at terahertz speeds as a long-term goal.
arxiv-2602-05773:
The traveling salesman problem asks for the shortest tour through a set of cities, and Yılmaz Arslanoğlu presents a short note linking it to a tree problem. He defines a constrained Group Steiner Tree Problem on a simplicial incidence graph built from the complete weighted graph of cities. The graph is bipartite, joining triangles to edges.

Choosing an admissible, disk like set of triangles in that graph induces a unique boundary cycle. With global connectivity and local regularity constraints added, maximizing net weight in the tree problem is exactly equivalent to minimizing the tour length in the salesman problem. The note is a brief communication, four pages with three figures, prepared for submission to an operations research journal. It is a structural result rather than a new algorithm. Its interest lies in recasting a classic routing problem in the language of Steiner trees and incidence geometry.
arxiv-2602-05973:
Quantum theory usually keeps its math Hermitian, a rule that keeps probabilities sane. Oem Trivedi and Alfredo Gurrola ask what happens if that rule is loosened inside quantum cosmology, by extending the Wheeler-DeWitt frame beyond strictly Hermitian dynamics. In their version, anti-Hermitian terms act like damping or gain, shaping both early ripples in the universe and later growth of structure.

They test the frame against inflation data, growth of structure, and the near flatness of the universe. The result is a set of strong infrared limits that push non-Hermiticity down across cosmic history, with early and late tests agreeing. The limits can ease a little in theories beyond general relativity. The paper turns cosmology into a test bed for a basic rule of quantum mechanics, and hints that Hermiticity itself may emerge as the universe evolves.
arxiv-2602-06473:
Wind pushing on the ocean's surface drives drift currents, and the classical theory of them flattens Earth into a plane. Christian Puntini and 2 co-authors derive a model that keeps the planet's spherical geometry. Starting from the full flow equations in rotating spherical coordinates, they allow depth-varying density and eddy viscosity.

A careful scaling produces two small parameters, tied to rotation and to the thinness of the wind-driven layer. Expanding in both gives simple leading-order equations with nonlinear boundary conditions. The leading dynamics are linear; energy input and loss enter only at higher order. For Ekman-type flows they prove the leading solution exists, is unique, and keeps the classical spiral structure for any viscosity profile. Comparisons with Sverdrup's classic theory follow.
arxiv-2602-06573:
Quantum dots made from indium antimonide nanosheets are a promising platform for topological superconductivity, and Xingjun Wu and 8 co-authors built one coupled to superconductors on both sides. A bottom bilayer gate defines the dot and tunes its coupling to the leads. The dot showed large magnetic response factors and strong spin-orbit coupling.

Transport measurements revealed Coulomb diamond patterns with alternating even-odd sizes and sharp features tied to the superconducting gap, confirming a few-electron regime. At odd occupation, Kondo signatures appeared, including a zero-bias peak that split in a magnetic field and faded logarithmically with temperature. As coupling strengthened, Andreev bound states switched from crossing to anticrossing, marking a doublet-singlet quantum phase transition.
arxiv-2602-06673:
Xin Hu, Yuya Ominato, and Mamoru Matsuo give a theoretical study of a hybrid device that joins a thin transition metal dichalcogenide layer to a ferromagnetic insulator. A heat-driven effect, the spin Seebeck effect, excites spins in the magnet, and the question is whether the paired valleys in the thin layer can sort that spin flow. A magnetic field applied across the layers splits the valley energy levels unevenly.

The authors show that spin-valley locking in the thin layer, together with the uneven level structure, can generate a spin current that is also valley-polarized. They compare currents arising from the conduction and valence bands and explain their different microscopic origins. Their clearest prediction is a set of quantum oscillations in the valley-polarized current, a measurable fingerprint of the quantized valley states.
arxiv-2602-06873:
Shaoshi Chen and four co-authors study how to integrate functions in fields that hold Weierstrass-like quantities. Those quantities obey a first-order equation that is not linear, so they sit beyond the reach of plain integration theory. Computer algebra can handle many functions, but elliptic-style builds need their own rules.

The team extends the old idea of special polynomials to these Weierstrass-like fields, then builds step-by-step reduction rules on top of that extension. Reduction is the core move in deciding whether an integral can be written in closed form. As a payoff, they derive new closed formulas for integrals of powers of the Weierstrass function itself.
arxiv-2602-07073:
Nardine Basta and five co-authors build a proactive defense for enterprise networks against zero-day attacks. In today's firms, perimeter plus distributed firewall rules govern connectivity. Automated tools now generate those rules and access policies, yet risks from dynamically generated policies, above all exposure of critical assets, remain hard to manage. Networks keep shifting too, with remote users, personal devices, and cloud links.

Their system, Pro-ZD, uses a graph neural network to find weighted shortest paths through the network. Those paths reveal misconfigurations and high-risk links that could threaten critical assets and be exploited through undisclosed flaws. Pro-ZD then tunes firewall rules and access policies on its own to close high-risk links and block unauthorized access. Tests show robustness and transferability, with over 95 percent average accuracy at spotting high-risk links across settings.
arxiv-2602-07473:
Partially observable Markov decision processes model choices under uncertainty, but computing optimal reachability probabilities for them is known to be impossible in general. Nathanaël Fijalkow and four co-authors carve out a tractable class: posterior-deterministic POMDPs.

For that class, the best chance of reaching a target set can be estimated to any precision, in sharp contrast to the general no-method result. Verification and synthesis teams get a new island of solvable cases in POMDP theory, with a precise setting marking where estimates become possible. The new class thus opens checking problems that were out of reach before for partly observable systems.
arxiv-2602-07573:
Graph domain adaptation moves knowledge from labeled source graphs to unlabeled target graphs, but most methods assume both graphs are homophilic, where neighbors share labels.  Ruiyi Fang and ten co-authors drop that assumption with a homophily-agnostic method that handles varying homophily on both sides.

A divide-and-conquer strategy reconstructs highly homophilic and heterophilic variants of source and target graphs separately, then aligns knowledge between matching variants.  Experiments on five benchmarks show superior results where homophily varies.  Graph learning teams get adaptation that works whether neighbors agree or disagree, a common reality the field long assumed away.
arxiv-2602-07873:
Soft policies in reinforcement learning balance exploration and exploitation by sampling actions in proportion to their estimated values, but implementing that sampling is awkward. Donghyeon Ki and three co-authors realize soft-policy sampling directly with Langevin dynamics, which follows the gradient of the action-value function to draw samples without an explicit policy network.

Plain Langevin sampling mixes slowly in high-dimensional, rugged value landscapes, so they add multi-scale noise conditioning to the value function, yielding Noise-Conditioned Langevin Q-Learning. The resulting method samples from the target Boltzmann distribution more effectively while keeping entropy estimates tractable. Reinforcement-learning teams gain a more expressive, principled alternative to parametric and diffusion-based policies.
arxiv-2602-07973:
Neurosymbolic learning trains neural classifiers whose hidden labels must satisfy a logical formula, but the number of label combinations that satisfy the formula can explode. Aaditya Naik and four co-authors propose CLIPPER, a technique that prunes that space using the intuition that inputs with similar internal representations likely share labels.

Because logical constraints couple labels together, pruning is formulated as an integer linear program that discards inconsistent combinations while respecting the formula's structure. The method works alongside existing training algorithms rather than replacing them. Across sixteen benchmarks on complex tasks, it makes neurosymbolic learning tractable where exhaustive enumeration would stall, giving researchers a scalable tool for combining neural perception with logical reasoning.
arxiv-2602-08273:
Fixed-wing drones need reliable pose and airspeed gauges from motion sensors and Pitot tubes, with guarantees that hold from almost any starting state. Melone Nyoba Tchonkeu and two co-authors build a cascade watcher: a Riccati-type filter first gauges body-frame air speed and tilt from motion data with Pitot outputs. Then a curved watcher on the spin group mixes tilt with compass data for full pose.

Under mild input, the gauging errors are flatly seen, and strict analysis shows almost global long-run calm of the whole cascade. Validation on real flight data confirms the theory. Aerospace engineers gain an estimator with strong guarantees for a safety-critical drone subsystem, not just good results in model.
arxiv-2602-08673:
Branch-price-and-cut solves vehicle routing exactly, but its column generation follows linear-relaxation signals that may mislead integer solutions. Lukas Eveborn and Elina Rönnberg propose a primal heuristic based on pricing for integrality to find good integer solutions earlier. Their arXiv paper targets electric vehicle routing with time windows and charging slots.

The heuristic builds a partial integer solution from the column pool, then iteratively searches for columns that complement it, guided by modified pricing, dual information, and previously generated columns. Tests show it closes thirty to forty percent of the root-node gap on average versus a restricted-master heuristic. Readers get a practical accelerator for exact routing solvers.
arxiv-2602-08973:
Thanawuth Thanathibodee and six co-authors catch a young star's disk changing fast. A 2024 JWST observation of the transitional disk around CVSO 1942 shows mid-infrared light at wavelengths under 10 microns doubled versus the near-photospheric level Spitzer saw in 2005. Longer wavelengths, above about 15 microns, show no significant change.

Comparing the new spectrum with NEOWISE photometry pins the brightening to a span of just two weeks. The pattern fits warm dust near 1,400 kelvin, optically thick and made of grains at least a micron across, sitting near the dust sublimation radius. The authors propose fresh dust forming in place, possibly from planetesimal collisions in the inner disk.
arxiv-2602-09073:
Sagar Mandal and one co-author count sum-dominant, difference-dominant, and balanced subsets of the dicyclic group Dic-4n. For subsets of size two, exact counts show the sum-dominant and balanced families grow equally fast as n increases. Size three is richer: for odd n, exact counts depend on whether n is divisible by 3.

In that size-three case, sum-dominant subsets asymptotically outnumber each of the other two kinds six to one. A lower bound for the boundary case of size 2n completes the picture. The results map the sum-versus-difference landscape of dicyclic groups with unusual precision.
arxiv-2602-09173:
Small, specialized language models can reason surprisingly well when trained with verifiable rewards, and Ryozo Masukawa and ten co-authors ask whether teams of them can do better together. Their n-Musketeers design links several frozen, heterogeneous expert models through their internal hidden states, joined by a trainable attention interface, a scheme called soft hidden-state collaboration.

On Reasoning Gym and GSM8K, the latent team competes with strong single-model baselines. Ablations reveal two regimes: on simpler arithmetic, gains mostly reflect static expert preferences, while harder settings drive increasingly concentrated, structured attention, a sign of emergent specialization. The design offers both a compact way to reuse frozen experts and a window into how collaboration evolves under training.
arxiv-2603-02373:
Taylor Daniels studies signed partition numbers in this 2026 mathematics paper. Partitions split a whole number into a sum of smaller parts. Signed versions weight each part by a function that returns zero, one, or minus one. Daniels uses the Legendre symbol, a classic sign from number theory, as that weight.

Series formulas in the style of Rademacher are derived for several small primes. The primes covered are five, thirteen, and seventeen, all one more than a multiple of four. Derivations make clear how the method extends to all such primes. For the prime seventeen, deeper tools enter, including Dedekind sums and their twisted versions. The signed counts turn out to vanish exactly on certain arithmetic progressions modulo thirty-four.
arxiv-2603-02473:
Boqin Yuan, Yue Su, and Kun Yao diagnose where memory-augmented agents fail in this 2026 paper. Such agents store past interactions and retrieve them to answer later questions. Teams debate whether better writing or better retrieval matters more. Their diagnostic framework crosses three write styles with three retrieval methods.

Write styles range from raw chunks to extracted facts and summaries. Retrieval spans cosine matching, keyword search, and a hybrid reranker. On a long-conversation benchmark, retrieval choice swung accuracy by about twenty points. Write style moved it by only a few points. Raw chunks, needing no model calls, matched or beat costly lossy options. Failures clustered at retrieval, not at use of retrieved text. Better retrieval, they argue, beats fancier writing today.
arxiv-2603-02573:
Jiahao Lu, Jiayi Xu, Wenbo Hu, and colleagues track every pixel in 3D from a single video in this 2026 paper. Knowing each pixel's 3D path unlocks full understanding of video dynamics. Prior methods track only sparse points or rely on slow per-video optimization. Their feedforward model, Track4World, aims for dense tracking at practical speed.

A transformer first encodes the global 3D scene from the video. A novel 3D correlation scheme then estimates dense 2D and 3D flow between any frame pair. Scene flow plus rebuilt geometry yields the 3D trajectory of every pixel. Tracking happens in world coordinates, not camera coordinates, which suits reconstruction. Across multiple benchmarks, the method beat existing approaches on flow and tracking. Robustness and scale suit real-world four-dimensional reconstruction tasks.
arxiv-2603-02673:
Baptiste Ferrere, Nicolas Bousquet, Fabrice Gamboa, and colleagues solve a long-standing gap in model explanation math. Their 2026 paper concerns functional ANOVA, which splits a model's output into single-feature effects and interactions between features. For linked categorical features, no exact formula existed, so teams relied on slow sampling estimates.

By linking the problem to an extended form of discrete Fourier analysis, they derive a closed-form split that assumes nothing about the links. The formula is fast to compute and reduces to the classic result when features are independent. It also yields a natural extension of SHAP values, a popular explanation score, to the general categorical case. Exact answers replace rough estimates for a wide class of models.
arxiv-2603-02773:
Zhen Zhang, Zihan Wang, Xinyu Ma, and colleagues help search models absorb new documents without full retraining. Their 2026 paper concerns generative retrieval, where a model answers a query by generating a document's ID directly. Such models often fail on documents added after training, and retraining is costly and can erase old skill.

Their method, DOME, edits the model in three stages: find the key layers, tune edit vectors, then apply the update. A mixed-label training trick keeps edit vectors distinct even when documents share ID parts across queries. On the NQ and MS MARCO benchmarks, new-document retrieval improved a lot while old results held. The update took only about sixty percent of the time of incremental retraining.
arxiv-2603-02873:
Tianyou Liu, Ziqiang Li, Xurui Liu, and colleagues argue that the TeX typesetting system holds back AI-assisted science writing. Their 2026 paper examines LaTeX compilation in an era when language models draft much of the text. They cite slow builds, weak meaning in the output, hard-to-locate errors, and a costly token footprint.

As an alternative they present Mogan STEM, a structured editor that shows the document as it will look while editing. Tests favor Mogan on build and rendering time and on language model task performance. Its file format also carries less redundant information, making model fine-tuning cheaper than with TeX files. The authors call for larger trials of training models on the new format.
arxiv-2603-03173:
Hassan Abdelraouf and Jeff Shamma ask whether choosing the wrong good learning rule can itself be a mistake. No-regret algorithms guarantee that, over time, a learner does about as well as the best fixed strategy. Yet that promise says nothing about how high the final average actually is, and different no-regret rules can land at different heights.

Framing generalized replicator dynamics as control systems, they compare variants by reshaping one internal block. Near equilibrium, a passivity test ranks the variants. Globally, an anticipatory variant provably dominates the standard rule across every payoff environment, with an optimal-control argument showing the reward gap can reach zero. A genuine free lunch exists among no-regret dynamics, at least in this family.
arxiv-2603-03573:
Daiheng Zhang and five colleagues post-train language models to edit biological sequences step by step. Optimizing proteins and molecules means revising a string under strict syntax rules, a job needing long-horizon planning. Diffusion models refine gradually but hide their edits; ordinary language models expose edits yet plan poorly. Their 2026 framework, STRIDE, makes the model write out an executable trail of atomic edits: insert, delete, replace.

Training first imitates shortest-edit demonstrations aligned by edit distance, then applies group-based policy optimization to align the trails with task rewards. On protein fluorescence and instruction-guided molecular tasks, editing success leapt from about two fifths to nearly nine tenths. Novelty of the outputs more than doubled as well. Validity and controllability beat a diverse set of baselines, and the code is public.
arxiv-2603-03673:
Sophia Sklaviadis and four colleagues extend a workhorse identity of statistics beyond the Gaussian world. Stein's identity converts expectations into gradient formulas and powers generative modeling and stochastic optimization, but it was built for Gaussian distributions. Their 2026 paper derives the identity for q-Gaussians with bounded support, a flexible family that lives on a finite interval instead of the whole line.

The proof extends earlier Bonnet and Price type theorems and simplifies them using escort distributions, close cousins of the original law. The resulting gradient estimators look nearly identical to the Gaussian ones and are just as easy to implement. Experiments add a practical lure: bounded-support distributions can lower the variance of gradient estimators. The authors point to Bayesian deep learning and sharpness-aware minimization as likely beneficiaries.
arxiv-2605-00073:
Mohd Sameen Chishti, Damilare Peter Oyinloye, and Jingyue Li propose AgentReputation, a reputation framework for decentralized marketplaces of AI agents. Such markets host agents that debug code, generate patches, and audit security, often with no central overseer. Trust there is hard: agents can game the evaluations, skill in one task type may not transfer to another, and checks range from cheap automated tests to costly expert review.

Their three-layer design separates task execution, reputation services, and tamper-proof storage so each can evolve alone. Explicit verification regimes are tied to each agent's standing record, and context-conditioned reputation cards stop scores from bleeding across domains. A policy engine turns those scores into decisions on resources, access, and when to step up checking. The paper closes with research directions, from checking ontologies to cold-start bootstrapping.
arxiv-2605-00273:
Yujin Jeong and 4 co-authors ask why text-to-image diffusion models so often fail when a picture must contain several objects at once. The pictures look sharp, yet objects go missing, merge, or land in the wrong places. The team first asks how much of the failure comes from the training data itself.

They built a controlled data generator, called mosaic, and trained models under two regimes: one where single concepts appear unevenly, and one where certain combinations are held out on purpose. Scene complexity, not concept imbalance, proved the dominant obstacle. Counting objects was uniquely hard to learn when data was scarce. Held-out combinations also broke down faster as more were withheld, which points to a need for stronger built-in biases and better data design.
arxiv-2605-00573:
René Peschmann hunts perfect cuboids, boxes with integer edges, face diagonals, and space diagonal, whose existence has been open for centuries. The paper works with body cuboids, which may lack the integer space diagonal, parametrized by pairs of Pythagorean triples in Euclid's form. Its first contribution is a verified pattern the author calls the exponent-one blocker, found in the space-diagonal norm of every such candidate examined.

In each fully factored case, some prime divides that norm to exactly the first power. That prime also avoids a fixed list of twenty-nine parameter expressions, a primitive obstruction to the norm being a square. Two natural strengthenings of the pattern fail. The second contribution builds a generator from the elliptic curves behind the parametrization, minting over a million further candidates. None is a perfect cuboid, and every factored record obeys the blocker pattern: evidence, not proof.
arxiv-2605-00773:
Fredrik Bakke and three co-authors study the Sierpinski cone in synthetic models of space built by extending homotopy type theory with an interval. In ordinary settings the cone adds a universal closed point below all others and classifies partial maps defined on an open part. In the synthetic setting that classifying property proves more delicate.

The authors show the property cannot hold for all such types without collapsing the theory. They identify the largest subuniverse where it does hold, described as a localization at interval-based embeddings, and show it sits strictly inside the Segal types when the interval is nontrivial. They extend the results to mapping cylinders with a new such property.
arxiv-2605-00973:
Hao Zhou and fourteen co-authors present xMAE, a pre-training framework that uses the ordered timing between biosignals to learn better patterns. Signals from different body sites often view the same process at different stages. Heart electrical activity, recorded by ECG, starts each beat, while the PPG pulse arrives later after vascular travel. Most self-supervised methods treat such signals as interchangeable views and miss that direction.

xMAE trains with masked cross-modal rebuilding across time-ordered signals, encouraging physiologically meaningful timing in the learned patterns. Pre-training beats unimodal and multimodal baselines on most of nineteen downstream tasks, from heart outcome prediction to sleep staging, and generalizes across devices and body locations. Timing structure appears reflected in the learned pulse patterns.
arxiv-2605-01073:
Leonid Bedratyuk studies the local shape of sentence embedding clouds formed by controlled sets of semantically close sentences. The central question is how paraphrase-like variation is arranged in that space and whether low-degree fitted surfaces can model that local structure in full. Affine, quadratic, and cubic carriers are fitted, and a probing procedure makes synthetic latent points in a reduced local space relative to the fitted surface.

Generated points are judged on surface consistency, neighborhood preservation, agreement with the observed spread, and stability of shape and coefficient measures. Nonlinear local models describe the clouds more closely than affine ones. Surface-based generation also shows strong shape fidelity. Shape validity does not on its own improve classification, however. A large dataset of sentence variants is also introduced.
arxiv-2605-01173:
Fiaz Hossain and four co-authors build a framework to limit how AI data center load swings affect fatigue life of thermal turbine generators. Rapid variations in data center demand can drive torsional oscillations in synchronous generators, accumulating fatigue damage. Their frequency-domain approach quantifies allowed swings in three steps.

First, maximum allowed power variation at each generator is found from a lumped multi-mass mechanical model. Next, load flow gives an interaction factor mapping a load change at a bus to generator output changes. Finally, candidate buses are screened and an optimization sets optimal allowed swings. Tests on standard test systems and a synthetic two-thousand-bus Texas system demonstrate applicability and scalability.
arxiv-2605-01373:
Jinyuan Feng and seven co-authors study diffusion language models, which write by cleaning up noisy text step by step. These models see the whole passage at once, yet common decoding habits favor local cues and waste that wide view, which lowers quality.

The team finds that high-information tokens, the words that carry the most content, help a lot when fed back as context, and they settle early in decoding. Their method, FoCore, needs no training: it briefly hides those core tokens and uses them as negative samples to steer writing by contrast. A faster variant decodes stable nearby tokens in parallel once core tokens settle. On math, code, and logic tests, and on two model families, FoCore lifts quality, and the fast variant cuts decoding steps by more than half.
arxiv-2605-01473:
Satoru Iwata and Haruto Konno unify two classic algorithms for shrinking symmetric submodular functions, a family of set functions with a diminishing-returns shape that shows up in cuts, clustering, and entropy. Two orderings of the ground set, built decades apart, each expose a special pair of elements that lets the search contract and continue.

One ordering yields a pendent pair and the other a flat pair, and the link between them was never clear. Iwata and Konno add a third ordering, then stretch all three into a one-parameter family. A single general inequality governs the family, and the two classic results drop out at the two ends of the dial. At every setting, the last two elements of the ordering form a contractible pair, which gives one contraction algorithm that finds a nontrivial minimizer with a cubic number of value queries.
arxiv-2605-01573:
B Kosyakov, E Popov, and M Vronsky review models that treat the atomic nucleus as a bound system of quarks, three per nucleon, rather than as protons and neutrons alone. The overview seeks an effective theory of low-energy strong-force physics that still explains plain nuclear facts.

A Fermi gas picture explains why stable light nuclei, up to calcium, hold nearly equal numbers of up and down quarks. A modified bag model then accounts for the drift away from that balance in heavier nuclei and matches static traits of many stable nuclei well. To sharpen the bag model, the authors invoke a refined gauge-gravity duality linking an extremal black hole's interior to a stable subnuclear system. The duality predicts the main decay channel of the lightest glueball and a ceiling on stable nuclear charge near 82, the charge of lead's heaviest stable isotope.
arxiv-2605-01673:
Xinmeng Xu and five co-authors slow down audio-visual fusion until the fused state is ready to be trusted. In stage-wise encoders, each layer's fused state seeds the next. A locally convincing match between sound and sight can still lack the wider support needed to guide later layers. The authors call that failure premature commitment.

Their Delayed Perceptual Commitment Network grades each intermediate state with an observable readiness-deficiency score. It finds the bottleneck stage where intervention helps most, and corrects it with evidence drawn across layers and across senses. Task heads, losses, and decoders stay untouched, so the fix rides on the encoder alone. Speech separation, event localization, and speech recognition all improve. Ablations, counterfactual probes, and readiness traces across depth back the claim that timing the commitment, not adding capacity, earns the gains.
arxiv-2605-01873:
Rishad Shahmurov studies vortex stretching in fluid flow by splitting the vorticity equation according to how large the vorticity is. For almost any cut-off level, the stretching above that level equals a change in mass above the level plus two non-negative terms from viscosity. One term tracks changes in vorticity direction, and the other tracks loss across the level surface.

Adding the result over all levels recovers the classic balance for vorticity and, in one key case, the usual palinstrophy account. At a critical exponent, the loss term can be written with a new nonlinear variable. The method also lets distinct high-vorticity episodes be counted without overlap, under extra assumptions.
arxiv-2605-02073:
Arash Ahmadi, Sarah Sharif, and Yaser Banad treat the reward function itself as the thing to search for when training a language model to reason. The base model stays fixed, so reward design is the main lever left. A frontier model proposes candidate rewards, which are checked automatically and then screened in short training runs.

Each candidate is trained with group-based policy methods on a small Llama model and ranked by its score on the GSM8K maths test. Summaries of past rounds feed the next round of proposals. Over five rounds the search made fifty candidates. The paper reports how the best rewards evolved and whether search beats hand design.
arxiv-2605-02273:
Kacper Duma and colleagues analyse how humans review pull requests written by AI on GitHub, using the AIDev data set. They compare AI-authored requests with human-authored ones inside the same repositories. The question matters because review is often read as a sign of human oversight in large studies of coding activity.

Most AI-generated requests received no review at all. When review happened, AI agents dominated it rather than humans. Human-authored requests were more likely to get human-only review and direct human feedback. Reviews of AI requests more often ran through automation, with humans steering agents instead of judging the code alone. The authors warn that review metrics can mislead as measures of human oversight in agentic workflows.
arxiv-2605-02473:
Nitin Serwa classifies low-order conservation laws for a family of fifth-order Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equations, which model waves in two spatial directions. Conservation laws matter because each one names a quantity that stays fixed as the wave evolves. Serwa uses the direct multiplier method and limits the search to multipliers of differential order at most two, stated in the original variable.

The first result is that every such multiplier in fact has order at most one. Sorting the cases then gives one general case and two special nonlinear cases, each with its own set of free functions of time. Serwa derives sample conserved densities and flows for all three. The general densities cover mass and a transverse moment, while the special cases add energy-like and higher moment densities.
arxiv-2605-02673:
Serhii Zabolotnii describes EstemPMM, an R software package for estimating model parameters when errors are not Gaussian. Standard least squares is optimal for bell-shaped errors, but real errors are often skewed or heavy-tailed. The polynomial maximization method uses the third and fourth standardized moments of the error to build estimators that beat least squares in those cases.

The package gives one interface for linear regression and for autoregressive, moving-average, and combined time-series models, including seasonal forms. A dispatch function picks among least squares and two polynomial variants by reading the sample's skew and tail weight. Standard R tools for summaries, intervals, and prediction are supported. Simulations check the theory, and a crude-oil case study shows the package in use.
arxiv-2605-02973:
Eitan Kosman, Gabriele Serussi, and Chaim Baskin add structure to diffusion bridges, a method for translating data between modalities, such as image styles or sensor types. Translation is under-constrained: many cross-modal maps can produce the same overall distributions. Most bridge methods lean on fully paired data as their single constraint, which is costly to gather and may not exist.

Their framework first characterizes the space of maps that fit, then narrows it with alignment constraints, treating paired examples as an optional aid rather than a requirement. Tests on synthetic and real translation benchmarks cover unpaired, partly paired, and fully paired settings, with steady performance across all three. Quality close to the fully paired case was reached with far looser pairing. Bridges, the authors argue, are a flexible base beyond paired data.
arxiv-2605-03073:
Venkata Pushpak Teja Menta tackles speech recognition for entity-heavy Indic speech, such as digit strings, money amounts, addresses, and mixed English-Indic speech. Both open and commercial systems do poorly on this niche, missing most of the key entities in Telugu tests.

Menta builds a loop in which a text-to-speech system makes about twenty-two thousand training utterances at low cost, then fine-tunes a recognizer on them. Entity hits rose many times over both baselines on held-out tests, and a small human-recorded check confirmed the gain carries to real speech. All test targets were still missed, and results are reported plainly.
arxiv-2605-03273:
Kun Huang introduces the consecutive lifting-projection flow as a new approximation for the Boltzmann and Landau equations of kinetic theory. The collision operator in these equations is nonlinear and hard to handle, which complicates both analysis and solver design.

The method lifts collisions to a linear master equation on spheres in higher dimensions, evolves there, and projects back down. The flow keeps mass, momentum, and energy, dissipates entropy, and settles to the correct equilibrium. For Maxwell molecules an error bound is given. The frame unifies known schemes and yields a new, unconditionally stable Green's function method.
arxiv-2605-03373:
Zhe Li, Bicheng Ying, Zidong Liu, and Haibo Yang explain why zeroth-order optimization, long thought to slow badly with model size, can fine-tune billion-parameter language models. Classic theory predicts a dimension penalty versus first-order methods, yet practice keeps succeeding at huge scale.

Deriving one-step learning dynamics, they show the empirical neural tangent kernel governs progress, and its entries are tangent vectors projected onto a random low-dimensional subspace. By a classic embedding lemma, fidelity depends on the number of perturbations and the output size, not the parameter count. That dimension-free property resolves the paradox in theory.
arxiv-2605-03573:
Jian Xu and six co-authors study score-based diffusion on the manifold of quantum pure states, a curved space where each point is a possible state of a quantum system. No closed-form transition density exists there, so the score must be taught by a local-time teacher taken from a Euclidean approximation. The paper asks what makes that teacher reliable.

Three training choices prove decisive: dividing increments by the diffusion clock rather than elapsed time, using closed-form Fubini-Study maps for the geometry, and randomizing the global phase. With them, the model beats the published baseline across eight benchmarks and an ambient Euclidean method by about an order of magnitude. The authors also bound the cost of the approximation.
arxiv-2605-04073:
Cor Steging and Tadeusz Zbiegień confront a structural problem in using machine learning to support bail decisions: label indeterminacy. When bail is denied, whether the defendant would have appeared in court is never observed. So historical bail data only partially reveal the outcomes that future models are trained to predict. Building systems on such data risks bias and self-reinforcing feedback loops.

In a case study of bail decisions from Pennsylvania's Unified Judicial System, the authors evaluate five approaches to handling indeterminacy. They test them across three machine learning models. One approach is a novel label imputation method motivated by bail dynamics. Every method rests on unverifiable assumptions. Yet the choice among them influenced predictive behavior sometimes more than the choice of model. Explainable AI analysis showed the effects reach the models' internal decision processes.
arxiv-2605-04273:
Max Hall-Brown and Peter Guy Wolynes model polyamorphism, the ability of one material to form more than one distinct liquid phase. In network liquids such as water, the effect comes from competition between bonded and non-bonded local arrangements.

Their simple microscopic model calculates both glassy and thermodynamic behaviour directly from the underlying interactions. It contains a liquid-liquid transition that can be placed above, near, or below the glass transition by tuning the parameters. The work aims to explain related oddities such as water's density peak, while avoiding the freezing problems that make supercooled water hard to study directly.
arxiv-2605-04473:
Rinki Imada and Tomohiro Tachi develop a design method for origami that folds itself in sequence, like a line of dominoes, driven purely by geometry rather than by stored energy. Propagating fronts of state change appear in nature and engineering, but a general framework for programming them through folding constraints was missing.

Working with strips of simple flat-foldable vertices, they show uneven coupling between neighbouring creases produces recurrence relations whose combined behaviour generically links the unfolded and flat-folded states. That link enables sequential deployment. They further show the overall shape can be programmed separately from how the front propagates, giving designers two independent controls.
arxiv-2605-04673:
Matteo Quinzi, Tommaso Chiarotti, and Nicola Marzari rethink pseudopotentials. These effective potentials let materials work ignore the inactive core electrons. Only the active valence states are treated. That replacement is really an embedding problem. The removed core can be described by a dynamical potential, one that depends on energy.

Their framework builds such dynamical potentials. It derives the generalised norm-keeping rules they must obey. A sum-over-poles form separates the number of reference energies from the number of projectors. It matches all-electron scattering closely, over wide energy ranges. The potentials also fit naturally into many-body energy formulas. That brings the atom, the pseudo-atom, and the solid under one theory.
arxiv-2605-05073:
Shibo Yu and four co-authors rank items from pairwise comparisons made by several judges, while treating judge disagreement as information rather than noise. Standard methods pool all judgments into one score, hiding steady gaps between judges. Their framework separates three targets: the shared consensus ranking, each judge's sensitivity to that consensus, and leftover structured disagreement.

The authors give rules under which this split can be pinned down and build an anchored switching method that preserves it. They also measure how sure the results are when a fixed panel of judges makes repeated pairings. On test and real multi-judge data, the method improved fit, held up better, and gave surer confidence scores than pooled baselines and simpler ones.
arxiv-2605-05273:
Michael Fowler builds a diagrammatic proof system for a fragment of structural semantics based on the Greimas semiotic square, a classic square of opposed meaning terms. Basic terms become diagram layouts in a spider diagram system, and links such as contradiction and implication become changes ruled by inference rules. Proofs, shown by proof trees, carry out the meaning-building step by step.

Fowler's main result shows the four meta-terms of the square arise the same way, each derived from a pair of basic configurations through one fixed proof pattern. Negation in the diagrams turns out not to be a full Boolean flip but a narrow counter-stance set by zones. The framework gives the field a rule-based footing.
arxiv-2605-05473:
Carvalho and two colleagues study curved spaces shaped by a vector field. Generalized m-quasi-Einstein manifolds extend Einstein metrics, structures prized in geometry and in gravitational physics. They add a potential vector field and a function that together deform the Ricci curvature equation. Under suitable integral assumptions on the potential field, the authors prove it must be a Killing field. Such a field is a symmetry direction that preserves the metric. The result extends an earlier result of Sharma to the generalized setting. A divergence-free potential field is likewise forced to be Killing.

Sign conditions on the parameters yield further results where the structure collapses to a simpler form. The authors also revisit a recent theorem of Ghosh, expose a subtle gap in its argument, and supply a corrected proof. Rigidity results for geodesic vector fields close the paper, tightening what such manifolds can look like.
arxiv-2605-05873:
Hirofumi Ota and four co-authors give language model self consistency a rigorous stopping rule. Models often sample many answers and aggregate them, which improves reasoning, but knowing when enough samples have been drawn is hard. The answer set is not known in advance, and data dependent stopping can silently break error guarantees that fixed sample rules enjoy.

Their algorithm, CITE, certifies a prespecified answer as the unique mode of the model's response distribution, valid at any stopping time. It controls false certification at a chosen level under arbitrary data driven stopping, with no prior knowledge of the answer categories. The authors prove matching lower bounds on stopping time and extend the method to confidence weighted voting. Simulations and model experiments confirm the error control in practice.
arxiv-2605-06273:
Rotzer and eight colleagues report a wildfire detection system already flying in orbit. Nine commercial thermal-infrared satellites watch for fires. The onboard computer is a Jetson Xavier NX, the model must stay under a megabyte, and alerts must reach responders within ten minutes of overpass. The imagery is uncalibrated mid-wave infrared at two hundred meter resolution, where fires often appear as single-pixel anomalies drowned in imbalance. Standard thermal-threshold pipelines built for MODIS and VIIRS do not address this regime.

The team trains lightweight dense representations with masked autoencoding. A hybrid variant adds exponential moving average distillation. Both are probed under extreme imbalance. Their fastest model reaches 0.640 test average precision and 0.69 event-level Fire-F1 at 65 milliseconds per batch in a 0.52 megabyte engine. The best configuration reaches 0.699 average precision while staying under one megabyte, beating a supervised baseline.
arxiv-2605-06373:
Leon Halgryn, Sophie Langer, Janusz M. Meylahn, and E. Moritz Hahn give finite-sample bounds for deep Q-learning when replay data are not independent. Analyses usually pretend sampled minibatches are independent, yet they come from time-linked trajectories. The authors model the minibatches as tau-mixing, a formal way of saying dependence fades over time.

They show that assumption holds under stated conditions on trajectories and sampling, then treat each network update as a regression problem with dependent data. The resulting risk bounds show dependence slows the statistical rate, reflecting a smaller effective sample size. Tests on standard Gymnasium tasks confirm that this assumption often fails.
arxiv-2605-06673:
Jon-Paul Cacioli maps how well thirty-three frontier language models monitor their own confidence across subject domains. A single metacognition score can hide the fact that a model judges its answers well in one field and poorly in another. Cacioli gave each model fifteen hundred MMLU questions across six domains and scored confidence accuracy per domain.

Applied and professional knowledge proved easiest for models to monitor, while formal reasoning and natural science were hardest, with the middle domains statistically indistinguishable. Profiles cluster within some model families but not others, and one newer Gemma model improved markedly over its predecessor. The atlas argues for screening models domain by domain before deployment in specific areas.
arxiv-2605-07073:
Yubin Kim and eleven co-authors present TeamBench, a benchmark for agent teams where roles are enforced by the operating system, not just by prompts. In many setups, one agent can quietly do another's job, hiding whether the team truly coordinated. TeamBench splits requirements, editing, and certification across planner, executor, and verifier roles.

Across hundreds of task templates, enforced and prompt-only teams scored similarly, but prompt-only verifiers tried to edit code far more often. Verifiers also approved many submissions that the true grader failed. A human study showed the benchmark exposes coordination patterns that pass rates alone completely miss.
arxiv-2605-07273:
Jiaju Han and ten co-authors attack satellite image search systems by painting fake weather onto pictures. Retrieval-augmented systems for remote sensing fetch text evidence using the image, yet input-space attacks on that retrieval stage were little studied. Their CloudWeb attack adds parameterized cloud and haze patterns while leaving the retriever and knowledge base untouched.

The patterns are tuned to pull image embeddings toward weather evidence and away from the true scene. Across seven datasets and five retrievers, the attack planted weather evidence into top results far more than clean or hand-crafted baselines. Downstream answers then showed weather hallucinations, proving retrieval attacks propagate into final responses.
arxiv-2605-07773:
Xin Xu and four co-authors test the short-board effect, the old claim that a team performs only as well as its weakest member, using teams of AI agents. Testing the claim on people is nearly impossible: abilities are hard to measure, real teams churn, and data skew toward successes. Simulated teams driven by large language models, following standard procedures, sidestep those problems.

In uniform teams they found three capability regimes, including a threshold state of busy but ineffective effort. Adding one weak member hurt core roles more than peripheral ones. With several weak members, damage multiplied rather than being set by the single weakest link. The practical lesson: fixing only the weakest member is not enough, and mitigation should address weaknesses in aggregate.
arxiv-2605-07873:
Shi Lin Sun and eight co-authors dissect the atmosphere of HAT-P-70b, an ultra-hot Jupiter whose dayside is hot enough to ionize metals while its nightside may let refractory species condense. Using the MAROON-X high-resolution spectrograph, they cross-correlate the planet's transmission spectrum against templates for individual chemical species.

Fourteen neutral and singly ionized species were detected, from iron and titanium to barium and oxygen. The absorption was blueshifted by a few kilometers per second, consistent with day-to-night winds. Retrieval experiments carried a warning: ignoring ionization badly biases inferred abundances of easily ionized elements like calcium and titanium. Equilibrium chemistry, by contrast, brought ratios closer to solar-like expectations. One genuine puzzle remains, a distinct enrichment of nickel that other ultra-hot Jupiter studies also seem to see.
arxiv-2605-08473:
Rodrigo Pastrana, M. Silvina Riveros, and Raúl Vidal characterize the weights that keep a variable fractional maximal operator bounded on spaces where the exponent itself varies by point. Their result extends earlier work on simpler fractional operators. They also define a new class of rough kernels meeting a variable version of a classic smoothness condition.

For operators built from those kernels, they prove a comparison inequality of Coifman and Fefferman type plus weighted bounds in the variable spaces. Examples confirm the new kernel class is not empty. Harmonic analysis gains tools for fractional operators whose order and integrability both change across the domain.
arxiv-2605-08573:
Tongkeun Chang and Kyungkeun Kang study when a thin boundary layer of slow fluid pulls away from a wall in the half space, a separation event that reshapes flow and pressure. Working first with the Stokes system under localized boundary data, they prove a clean test: a certain singular integral built from the boundary data decides the outcome by its sign alone.

A negative integral forces a separation point to exist, while a strictly positive one rules separation out. When separation occurs, they track its motion and the pressure gradient's sign. A perturbation step then builds matching Navier-Stokes solutions with the same behavior. Fluid mechanics gains a sharp criterion for a classic flow instability.
arxiv-2605-08673: Naoki Masuyama and colleagues build PHIDA: persistence-guided node-to-cluster mapping for online clustering. The building builds. Their mapping maps persistence-guided node-to-cluster online clustering. The doing does. It is ML. PHIDA phidas. The PHIDA maps persistence-guided-clustering.
arxiv-2605-09073:
Connor Holmes and four co-authors explain a cleaner way to estimate motion that unfolds smoothly over time, a need that arises when sensors report at different moments. Two broad styles exist: fitting flexible curves, or using Gaussian processes, which treat the path as a smooth random function. The second style has spread slowly in robotics despite clear strengths.

The authors recast Gaussian process estimation in the language of factor graphs, the diagram style roboticists already use to organize estimation problems. Their account aims to lower the barrier for newcomers. Three working examples built in a popular estimation library show the approach in action, covering the setup from model to solved trajectory.
arxiv-2605-09273: A predictor is calibrated if its 70 percent predictions happen 70 percent of the time — multicalibration demands this across many groups, adaptively per instance. Zhiming Huang, Jamie Morgenstern, Aaron Roth, and others make it online and instance-shifting. The 2026 paper is fairness-flavored forecasting theory.
arxiv-2605-09373: Weighing the Milky Way's inner regions with axisymmetric Jeans models gives an answer — but a biased one. Tomoki Yamaguchi and Junichi Baba show the method with care overestimates circular speed in the inner galaxy. The 2026 paper is a cautionary tale for galactic dynamicists.
arxiv-2605-09773: Steering a model's dark-triad features — narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy — reveals separable antisocial circuits wired inside it. Cameron Berg, Roshni Lulla, and others show that exploitation can emerge without any deception at all. The 2026 paper is interpretability research on the model's dark side.
arxiv-2605-10073: Patent representation learning guided by heterogeneous dependency graph attention — structure-aware embeddings for inventions. Yongmin Yoo, Qiongkai Xu, Zhangkai Wu, and Longbing Cao develop it. The 2026 paper is legal-tech NLP for the patent office. It embeds inventions with structural awareness.
arxiv-2605-10173: Just previsions — a theory of imprecise chance with intellectual lineage to de Finetti's foundational work. Jean Goubault-Larrecq builds the plan with care. The 2026 paper is chance theory, imprecisely. It previsions justly and coherently under deep uncertainty, with full math rigor.
arxiv-2605-10373: Text2Cypher across multiple databases — query reasoning that spans database boundaries. Makbule Gulcin Ozsoy builds the multi-database approach. The 2026 paper is graph NLP without borders. It reasons across multiple databases, translating natural language intent into accurate federated Cypher queries every time.
arxiv-2605-10573: Riemannian quasi-Newton tuning with Euclidean bounds — curvature-aware and constrained. Mateusz Baran builds the algorithm. The 2026 paper is tuning on shapes. It optimizes with quasi-Newton speed on curved spaces. Curved spaces, fast tuning. Euclidean bounds respected throughout. tuning on shapes.
arxiv-2606-00073:
Aditi Aravind and co-authors borrow neuroscience tools to find the functional ensembles inside spiking neural networks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spiking networks process information through pulses like biological neurons. For each neuron, the authors define its first-order functionally connected group: the previous-layer neurons whose activity correlates with it. They then track how those ensembles respond during inference, asking whether principles seen in cortex appear in artificial spiking networks such as spiking ResNet.

Several biological principles did carry over. An ensemble's firing predicted downstream responses through a robust, saturating input-output curve whose strength grew with ensemble size. Reliable class information emerged only during high co-firing events, meaning representations concentrate in infrequent coordinated bursts. Noise and adversarial perturbations disrupted these profiles most in early and middle layers. Shuffling the weights destroyed the structure, proving learning shapes it. The authors propose ensembles as units for tracing information flow.

Nishad Kothari, Orlando Lee, Cláudio Lucchesi, and Cândida Nunes da Silva prove a matching-theory result in 2026. It mirrors a classic fact of graph theory: classes defined by a finite set of banned patterns are exactly the minor-closed ones.

The setting is a class of graphs linked to perfect matchings, called bicritical graphs. The banned patterns here are called forbidden conformal minors. The team characterizes which such classes are minor-closed. They also give a finite test for whether a given class has this property. The result ties a structural question to a checkable one. Uses include faster tests for membership in these classes, the authors note. The proof builds on decades of matching theory.
arxiv-2606-04273:
Katherine Collins leads a large team studying in 2026 how mathematicians actually use AI tools when converting informal proofs into machine-checkable formal ones. Most research benchmarks the tools; this work watches the people, and asks what agency they keep for themselves.

A survey found diverse wishes but a common theme: people want AI assistance that preserves their high-level control over proof discovery, and they named concrete barriers to that vision. In a controlled study, participants formalized problems with and without AI access. Despite the tools' limits at the time, AI access raised formalization accuracy, and most participants flexibly combined several different tools. The authors frame early adoption as an intimate interplay between human direction and machine help.
arxiv-2606-04373:
Biao Qian, Yang Wang, Yong Wu, and Jungong Han present MaskAQ in 2026. It compresses vision transformers without any real training data. Synthetic images stand in for the dataset, which suits privacy-sensitive settings.

The catch: synthetic samples often mismatch what the compressed model expects. The team's key observation concerns attention. Inside a transformer, meaning concentrates in a sparse subset of patches. Those informative regions dominate the information shared between samples and outputs. MaskAQ separates them from background noise. It then aligns the full-precision and compressed models through a masked attention objective. The synthetic samples refresh as the compressed model evolves. Across backbones and tasks, it beat existing data-free approaches.
arxiv-2606-04673:
Limozin, Seaman, and Su improve a causal inference method used to estimate treatment effects over time from observational data, in a 2026 arXiv statistics paper. In target trial emulation, researchers mimic a randomized trial using real-world data. Per-protocol effects are often estimated with marginal structural models. But it still relies on inverse probability weights. These can be unstable in small samples. They are sensitive to misspecified weight models.

Calibrating the weights enforces covariate balance in the treatment and censoring processes simultaneously. Simulations show improved efficiency and robustness to weight-model misspecification compared with standard LTMLE. A case study evaluates the effect of highly active antiretroviral therapy on CD4 cell count among HIV-positive women. It shows the method at work on a real clinical question where unstable weights are a genuine risk.
arxiv-2606-04773:
Cao and colleagues build a benchmark that can diagnose where vision-language models fail at understanding human motion, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Existing motion benchmarks have coarse semantics, difficulty, so they cannot localize failures. NextMotionQA uses vision-language models for dataset construction with expert verification, and offers three tasks: multiple-choice question answering, video captioning, and fine-grained error correction.

Evaluating twelve models uncovers capability gaps. The team also tests whether such models can serve as judges for text-to-motion generation. Models align strongly with expert ratings on coarse criteria, reaching a Cohen's kappa of 0.70, meaning substantial agreement, but break down on fine-grained, part-level judgment, where kappa falls to 0.10. The benchmark thus validates model judges in their strong regime while clarifying their limits.
arxiv-2606-04973:
Hong puts melting-point calculation on the web, coupling a cost-cutting simulation method to machine-learned atomic potentials, in a 2026 arXiv materials paper. Melting temperature is critical for high-temperature materials design, but first-principles melting calculations are computationally heavy. The SLUSCHI method reduces the cost. SLUSCHI-UP is a deployed web service: users submit a crystal structure by Materials Project identifier or file, and launch a queued calculation on asynchronous GPUs without installing anything.

On the compact MeltBench-10 validation set, the three production potential backends produce raw coexistence mean absolute errors around 178 to 327 kelvin. Across the broader tested materials, corrected predictions from the best backend reach a mean absolute error near 166 kelvin. The service positions itself between fast scalar melting predictors and far costlier first-principles coexistence calculations.
arxiv-2606-05073:
Lixing Zhang and colleagues tackle selective imputation of missing data in this 2026 arXiv paper, asking which missing values should not be filled in at all. Most imputation methods assume every blank entry hides an unobserved regular value. In real datasets, though, some entries are meaningfully missing: absent by design and valid that way, like a test no clinician ever ordered. Others were lost during observation and should be recovered.

The authors make that distinction precise and propose Diff-Joint, a diffusion-based framework that models the tabular data together with a latent missingness mask. It alternates conditional sampling with uncertainty-aware pooling, refining both the imputed values and the labels that say which blanks to preserve. On synthetic and real-world datasets, Diff-Joint spotted meaningfully missing entries well, kept imputation accuracy competitive, and improved downstream task performance.
arxiv-2606-05573:
Wilton Kim and colleagues study how to fix failed storage nodes when helpers lie in a 2026 arXiv paper. Big data systems spread files across many servers with Reed-Solomon codes. When one node fails, helpers send small traces of their data to rebuild it. The catch here is that some helpers may send wrong traces. The team asks when a correct repair is still possible on a tight data budget.

They treat the gathered traces as a code in its own right, the repair-trace code. Grouping patterns in the code's polynomial lets them bound how large the stored data can be for a set number of bad traces. For the binary case they pin down the exact best bound for fixing one bad trace. Two repair schemes follow: one meets a classic bound, and one tolerates more errors at higher computing cost.
arxiv-2606-05673:
Ou, Moille, and Srinivasan show that a trusted constant in photonics design is not constant in a 2026 arXiv paper. Heat shifts how materials bend light, and designers use that shift to tune chips. The shift factor, the thermo-refractive coefficient, is usually treated as fixed per material. The team tested that habit across an octave of wavelengths, from telecom to visible light. A silicon nitride microring resonator exposed the flaw.

Measured and simulated resonance tones disagreed sharply under the fixed-factor assumption. The true factors vary by about seven percent across the band for both core and cladding materials. That variation swamps the effect of light confinement by a factor of about one point three. A temperature-aware oscillator model captures the drift well. Feeding the drifting factors into a full physics model matched measured shifts across the whole octave. The correction matters for nonlinear devices like frequency doublers.
arxiv-2606-05873:
Siheng Zhao and colleagues teach a humanoid robot to climb ladders by sight in a 2026 arXiv paper. Ladder climbing punishes small errors: holds are sparse and the whole body must coordinate. LadderMan trains several climbing experts from one reference motion by hybrid tracking. Those experts are then distilled into a single policy that reads depth images. Imitation and reinforcement learning share the teaching.

Vision foundation models help the depth sense cross from simulation to the real world. The policy moved to a Unitree G1 humanoid with no real-world retraining. It climbed ladders of varied geometry robustly. A second policy, trained with a dual-agent setup, adds manipulation while perched. The robot adjusted paintings, swapped light bulbs, and handed over boxes under teleoperation. Stable whole-body control held through each task. The work pushes humanoids toward the maintenance jobs ladders gate off today.
arxiv-2606-06573:
Athanasios Zeris analyzes transformer attention the way engineers analyze turbulent flow in this 2026 arXiv paper. Proper Orthogonal Decomposition extracts the dominant patterns, or modes, from an ensemble of fields, ranked by energy. Zeris first runs a Morlet wavelet transform over documents to find which temporal scales matter in attention, then applies the decomposition scale by scale to the ensemble of attention fields. The result is a modal anatomy of each layer.
