Clear organization emerged. Early layers emphasize fine scales, later layers shift toward coarser ones. From how fast the mode energies decay he defines a concentration index, a single number for a layer's attention complexity. The modes are also provably optimal reconstructions, so each layer gets a data driven effective rank, a principled guide to how many attention heads it needs. No model changes or text annotations are required; the structure falls out of ensemble statistics.
arxiv-2606-06773:
Leptons are the light building blocks of matter: electrons, muons, taus, and neutrinos. Francener surveys how they interact across an enormous energy span in this 2026 arXiv paper. The work is a doctoral thesis from studies at Campinas and Amsterdam. It ranges from collider energies up to the extreme energies of cosmic neutrinos.

Several studies sit inside the thesis. One examines how tau leptons from neutrino collisions keep their polarization, a clue to their production. Another treats the rare neutrino trident process, where one neutrino creates extra particles. A third probes deep inelastic scattering at the LHC, including hidden charm inside protons. For neutrino observatories like IceCube, he models how Earth's inner structure filters incoming neutrinos. He also checks faint extra channels in track like events, and scattering beyond the Standard Model during the long trip to Earth.
arxiv-2606-07073:
Even a meson has an inner mechanical life: pressure, shear, and forces holding it together. Dwibedi, Puhan, and Ghosh map that life for two heavy mesons in this 2026 arXiv paper. The subjects are pseudoscalar charmonium and bottomonium, bound states of a heavy quark and antiquark. The tool is the light-front quark model, built for relativistic bound states.

Gravitational form factors are computed from the model's wave functions. Fourier transforms turn them into spatial maps across the meson's transverse plane. The pressure map shows a node: positive and pushing outward near the center, negative and pulling inward farther out. The force distribution stays positive everywhere, satisfying a known stability condition. Most maps depend on the assumed wave function shape near the center. Toward the edge they converge regardless of the choice. Shear stress is the exception, staying sensitive at middle distances.
arxiv-2606-07673:
June-Woo Kim and co-authors tackle a voice-medicine problem in this 2026 arXiv paper: telling apart two kinds of vocal hyperfunction from a neck sensor. Vocal hyperfunction is a pattern of strained voice use. One kind, phonotraumatic hyperfunction, involves tissue injury such as nodules, while the other involves muscle tension without such injury.

The team uses the NeckVibe Challenge recordings of neck-surface acceleration. They build features in four layers: steady patterns, changes over time, and ratios between measures. A fourth layer, coupling features, captures how airflow and sound interact. Their classifier separates the injury-related group from controls far better than the tension-related group. It reaches an area under the curve near eighty-nine hundredths for the first task and about seventy-three hundredths for the second. Coupling features prove essential for both tasks, suggesting the tension-related form hides in interactions between measures.
arxiv-2606-07873:
Zhenqi Liu, Brown, and Paarporn deliver a cautionary result about vehicle-to-vehicle communication in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cars sharing hazard warnings are expected to make roads safer. But drivers are strategic: information changes behaviour, and changed behaviour feeds back into system safety. Earlier work hinted partial adoption could backfire, raising congestion or risk.

The authors propose a corrected version of an existing equilibrium model and analyse it as adoption varies. They show that, in some cases, increasing adoption itself raises accident probability, a direct inversion of the technology's promise. The news is not all bad. Under an optimally designed signalling policy, controlling what information equipped cars reveal, the system can guarantee accident probability never increases with adoption. For regulators, safety depends not just on how many cars join, but on how the shared information is designed.
arxiv-2606-08173:
Bilal Hussain and co-authors survey how 6G networks should defend the physical systems running on them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In 6G, billions of cyber-physical systems, grids, robots, and surgical equipment, will ride ultra-reliable low-latency slices. The time between a breach and physical harm shrinks to milliseconds. Perimeter firewalls and centralised centres cannot react that fast.

The survey reframes defence as a closed, AI-native loop. Sense at the network edge, decide locally with compressed models, mitigate network-wide through software-defined control, and retrain through federated learning and digital-twin replay. It formalises a per-slice latency contract bounding the whole chain at the ninety-ninth percentile. Organising one hundred twenty-eight studies under a PRISMA protocol, the authors map the threat surface and unify detection results across twelve datasets. They synthesise the controls into one reference architecture and consolidate open problems into five directions.
arxiv-2606-08273:
Prisha and co-authors search for signs of new particles in rare meson decays in this 2026 arXiv paper. The focus is a family of decays where a bottom quark turns into a strange quark plus a neutrino and antineutrino, particles that escape unseen. A recent Belle II measurement of one such decay, a charged B meson producing a kaon plus the invisible pair, deviates from the Standard Model prediction. That mismatch motivates testing whether right-handed neutrinos, hypothetical partners absent from the Standard Model, could explain it.

Working in a model-independent effective theory, the authors focus on dimension-six vector operators involving right-handed neutrinos. They combine the Belle II result with an upper limit on a related decay to constrain the new interactions. They then study correlations with partner decay rates and with a polarization fraction describing spin alignment.
arxiv-2606-08473:
Xin Li and colleagues defend power grids against stealthy data falsification in this 2026 arXiv paper. False data injection attacks alter sensor measurements to mislead state estimation, the grid operator's picture of voltages and flows. Even small changes can cause large estimation errors. That happens when injected signals align with the pseudo-null space of the system model, directions the measurements barely constrain. Existing detectors fail here: residual tests ignore changes hidden in that space, while subspace methods miss physical consistency.

Their framework detects such low-magnitude, high-impact attacks by preserving the geometric match between the physical null space and the measurement-derived pseudo-null space. A key step re-expresses measurements in the physical coordinate frame before subspace extraction. Attacks crafted to hide in the model's blind directions thus become visible.
arxiv-2606-08673:
Remy builds a word aligner specialized for clinical text in this 2026 arXiv paper. Word-level cross-lingual alignment, matching each word in a text to its counterpart in a translation, is central to annotation projection and translation auditing. Existing neural aligners are rarely adapted to specialized domains, where terminology is dense and errors are costly. Remy's aligner targets biomedical and clinical text and is initialized from a clinical encoder model, with a training recipe inspired by an established alignment method.

The training target is built by sharpening a cost matrix for parallel clinical texts with optimal transport, the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm, fusing sentence-level, phrase-level, and token-level signals into soft alignments. This sharpened matrix is distilled into the student aligner by teaching its cosine-based token similarity scores to match the target. Evidence comes from a shared task on a multilingual clinical corpus.
arxiv-2606-08873:
Fan and colleagues design SCOPE, a control system for error-corrected quantum networks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum networks will link quantum devices, but their signals are fragile, so error correction wraps data in codes. Network controllers pick routes using simple link quality scores, ignoring how each link's noise pattern interacts with the chosen code, and probing that noise directly would interrupt service.

SCOPE instead listens passively. Decoders produce syndromes, parity-check outcomes that flag where errors occurred, and SCOPE harvests these byproducts during normal traffic. From them it rebuilds a map of network error patterns and pushes better route-and-code choices to senders. In simulations calibrated on IBM hardware data, SCOPE cut estimation error by more than sixty percent against a standard baseline. In large networks, that precision lowered logical error rates by thirty to thirty-five percent, up to sixty-five percent in the best cases.
arxiv-2606-09073:
Hahami and colleagues show that three popular defenses against reward hacking in AI training are secretly one formula wearing different hats, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning from human feedback trains models against a reward model, which the policy can game for high scores without quality. A natural defense is pessimism: discount rewards where the model is uncertain. Standard models output one number, with no uncertainty. The authors argue for a distributional reward model, a distribution over rewards per response.

Under Bayesian or robust-optimization lenses, the training objective collapses to a closed-form effective reward: a logarithmic average of exponentiated rewards, with a sign choosing optimism or pessimism. The pessimistic branch is the unifying object. Mean aggregation, worst-case optimization, and uncertainty-weighted optimization, the standard ensemble heuristics, all emerge as limits of that expression. The unification exposes each heuristic's hidden assumptions, showing when each should hold or break.
arxiv-2606-09173:
Cai and Liu prove a stabilized scheme for noisy partial differential equations stays accurate forever, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such equations describe systems like phase separation under random forcing. Superlinear ones, as in the stochastic Allen-Cahn equation, break naive schemes: errors explode or stability demands tiny steps. A tamed finite-element scheme, damping the nonlinearity, is unconditionally stable and preserves the Lyapunov structure, the energy-like decay.

This paper supplies the error analysis. They establish sharp, uniform-in-time error estimates: accuracy at year ten equals day one, no drift. They prove exponential ergodicity, long-run statistics settling to a unique equilibrium, and bound the invariant measure's distance from its numerical counterpart in the Wasserstein-2 metric. Experiments confirm the ergodicity, sharpness, and time-independence of the rates. For long simulations of noisy phase-field models, that package, stability, sharpness, no time degradation, is the guarantee needed.
arxiv-2606-09673:
Tattwamasi Amrutam, Pierre Fima, and Yongle Jiang carry a group-theory notion into operator algebras in this 2026 arXiv paper. The notion is the uniformly recurrent subalgebra, a counterpart of uniformly recurrent subgroups. A group acts on a finite von Neumann algebra, a vast number system with a trace, and some subalgebras recur under that action in a tight way.

One early result sorts the room these objects live in. The space of subalgebras is compact just when the algebra has no diffuse part. Inside that room, recurrent subalgebras can take any shape a minimal Polish space can take. In crossed products with tame coefficients, the new objects give a fresh test for C-star simplicity. A group passes just when no tame recurrent subalgebra sits strictly between the base and the whole. A state-space machine built with Baire tools then catches cases the plain room misses.
arxiv-2606-09873:
Aditya Sharma, Christopher Pal, and Amal Zouaq prime a model's thinking by rotating its inner compass in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reasoning models write out long thought traces before they answer. The team find that prompt vectors and thinking vectors each bunch into a tight cone. The two cones point in unlike ways, for many models and tasks alike.

That gap reads as a rotation, one with a closed-form fit from the Procrustes method. Their Rotate2Think learns the turn from a few solved cases. At run time, it slips a fake thinking vector in at the head of the trace, a primer made by math, not words. No training is spent. Scores rose in thirty of thirty-two model-test pairs, across maths, science, and code.
arxiv-2606-09973:
Barber and colleagues validate a young planet and measure how its orbit aligns with its star's spin, in a 2026 arXiv paper on exoplanets. Young planets reveal formation in action, but active stars make adolescent systems, aged one hundred to five hundred million years, hard to find. The host belongs to the Alessi 84 group, whose age the team updates to about one hundred thirty-five million years from color, rotation, and variability.

The validated planet is about three point six times Earth's radius and orbits in ten and a half days, with transit dips arriving early or late, called transit timing variations. A candidate second planet, near a three-to-two resonance, likely causes those shifts but remains unvalidated. With the MAROON-X instrument, the team measured the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect and found the orbit near-aligned with stellar spin. That matches similar aged planets, linking planetary infancy to maturity.
arxiv-2606-10073:
Levin and Zuevsky unify two approaches to analysis on rough spaces, in a 2026 arXiv paper on functional analysis. Their setting is a metric measure space, a space with distance and volume but no smooth structure. It satisfies a doubling condition and a Poincaré inequality, a key link between functions and their gradients. One approach studies the isoperimetric profile, which measures the smallest boundary needed to enclose a given volume.

An explicit transform, built from an inverse integral of the isoperimetric profile, converts geometric data into grand Lebesgue parameters. They prove sharp embeddings of the Sobolev space into the grand scale, with explicit constants, and a converse: controlled grand embeddings imply lower bounds on the profile. Concrete examples cover genuinely non-Euclidean settings, including the Heisenberg group, a model manifold with logarithmic volume growth, and Gaussian measure space. Gradients are handled through upper gradients, avoiding any need for charts.
arxiv-2606-10173:
Chung and Badhe argue that running AI locally on a device does not by itself guarantee privacy, in a 2026 arXiv paper on technology policy. Operating-system assistants can assemble email, calendars, files, screenshots, and notifications, retain summaries, invoke tools, emit telemetry, or route hard requests to the cloud. Local inference answers only where computation happens, not who may assemble context, what derived state persists, or which actions are authorized.

Their OS-centered framework specifies a threat model, a six-part privacy risk taxonomy, privacy-by-architecture controls, and a four-level audit rubric. They demonstrate the rubric through a documentation-bounded comparison of Apple Intelligence, Android's AICore with Gemini Nano, and Microsoft Recall. Meaningful privacy, they conclude, depends on constrained information flow, bounded authority, visible user control, and auditable governance across the whole operating-system lifecycle, including how updates change an assistant's authority over time.
arxiv-2606-10273:
Vyas analyzes how a four-legged robot should walk on the Moon's loose granular soil, in a 2026 arXiv paper on space robotics. Lunar regolith is soft and shifting, so foot contacts behave nothing like rigid ground. Locomotion algorithms trained with rigid contact assumptions become unstable and track poorly on such surfaces. For effective mechanical design of a lunar exploration quadruped, motor torques, energy expenditure, and cost of transport all need careful study under realistic contact physics.

Vyas applies physical modeling of granular surface and foot contacts inside a simulation environment where locomotion is trained by reinforcement learning. Policies trained on rigid contacts are compared with policies trained on soft contacts, analyzing gait and performance metrics. The results argue that lunar legged robots must be designed and trained against granular contact models from the start, rather than adapting Earth-style rigid-ground controllers.
arxiv-2606-10473:
Gao and a team of co-authors improve computer simulations of liquids in this 2026 arXiv paper, where high-resolution particle simulations are accurate but expensive. Coarse simulations run fast but lose fine surface detail. Most fixes generate extra particles, eating the savings. AnisoLift instead enriches each existing coarse particle with a learnable anisotropic ellipsoidal component, a stretched virtual shape that records directional structure in the nearby flow. The model then predicts corrections that move each particle toward a high-resolution reference.

Training supervises both particle motion and geometric structure, for physical and visual consistency. Across paired two- and three-dimensional benchmarks, including a dam-break scene, the method consistently improves fidelity to fully resolved flow under a fixed particle budget. Limits remain: the approach needs paired trajectories, corrects frame by frame, and cannot recover global transport the coarse run missed.
arxiv-2606-10773:
Schroedter, Bonitz, and Joost speed up simulations of correlated quantum matter in this 2026 arXiv paper. Nonequilibrium Green functions track real-time dynamics with memory, but their cost grows with the cube of the time steps. Their variant, delta NEGF, replaces the stored two-particle correlation function with fluctuations of field-operator products, evolved as an ensemble of independent Hartree-Fock-like paths.

The factorization keeps the dynamics stable by preserving positivity of the reduced density matrices, and scaling stays linear in time. Basis sizes reach about ten thousand states, roughly a hundred times beyond earlier time-dependent runs. Benchmarks on lattice systems stay stable even at strong coupling, and the team simulates diffusion in two-dimensional Hubbard lattices.
arxiv-2606-10873:
Nardini and Gevertz compare two modeling styles for spatial biology in this 2026 arXiv paper. A wound-healing dataset can be fit by a partial differential equation model, smooth and averaged, or by an agent-based model that tracks individual cells. No guideline says which to pick. Their pipeline uses approximate Bayesian computation for fitting, uncertainty estimates, and model choice, testing both on artificial data and real scratch-assay wounds.

Both styles recover parameters about equally well, though agent-based estimates carry wider uncertainty, and the equation models run more than a thousand times faster. Surprisingly, the pipeline often picks the smooth equation model even for data the agent model generated. On real wound data it favors an equation model with cell pulling and a time delay.
arxiv-2606-11173:
Semih Kara and Ersoy study how context given to a self-teacher shapes self-distillation in a 2026 arXiv paper. In self-distillation, a student sees only the question, while a self-teacher, the same model, also sees extra context, and the student learns to match it unaided. What context works best was unexplored.

The authors train a solver on feedback from a frozen critic under three conditions: a binary reward as in GRPO, the reference solution, and a step-by-step critique aligned to the solver's trace. The step-aligned critique won clearly, beating GRPO by 16.11 points and the reference-solution setup by 5.27 points. Per-token analysis explains why: aligned feedback pressures only the tokens where reasoning fails, leaving correct steps intact. Reference solutions push the model to change everywhere, even where it was right. The catch is cost, since good critiques need a capable critic model.
arxiv-2606-11273:
Broms, Tornberg, and Barnett speed up viscous flow simulation around nearly touching particles in a 2026 arXiv paper. Simulating dense suspensions of rigid particles in two-dimensional Stokes flow faces two problems: iterative solvers converge poorly as gaps shrink, and lubrication flows need many unknowns. The authors introduce a two-body preconditioning strategy, implemented with the method of fundamental solutions.

For each close pair, the hard interaction is represented in a basis precomputed from a local fine-grid boundary value problem. The basis is then compressed onto a coarse surface so all other particles feel only coarse sources. Iteration counts stay low even in dense packings. In one test, a random close packing of ten thousand disks at area fraction 0.65 has minimum separation one thousandth of a radius. It solves the mobility problem in forty-seven GMRES iterations. Accuracy reaches five digits with seventy-two unknowns per body.
arxiv-2606-11473:
Heredge and co-authors at JPMorgan Chase speed up tabular foundation models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Prior-fitted networks do in-context learning: the whole labeled training set serves as context, and predictions come in one forward pass. But quadratic self-attention makes inference prohibitive for large training sets. Their CRUMB wrapper attacks the context size instead of the model.

CRUMB clusters test queries, then greedily selects a small training subset per cluster matching its distribution, minimizing maximum mean discrepancy. Exact inference runs on each reduced batch. The wrapper needs no retraining. Across 51 TabArena datasets and three architectures, CRUMB beats rival context-selection strategies at identical budgets. It also resists covariate drift, since matching aligns training context with the current test distribution. Its edge over the MICP baseline grows from about five to about seventeen percent as drift intensifies. The method does require all test queries upfront.
arxiv-2606-11573:
Qiu and five co-authors, of Zhejiang University, harden radar-camera perception against sensor change in a 2026 arXiv paper. Bird's-eye-view perception fuses camera images with radar point clouds, but performance degrades across datasets as scenes, sensor configurations, and conditions alter both observations and fused representations. Their framework models source-domain variation, without target-domain samples.

The method characterizes visual scene variations in the frequency domain and synthesizes diverse source-domain views from them. Comparing the resulting fused representations captures how image-level variations influence multi-modal features. These variation patterns then regularize the detector, keeping the learned fusion space stable under latent scene changes. The framework applies only during training, leaving inference unchanged. On cross-dataset detection between View-of-Delft and TJ4DRadSet, it improves performance consistently over multiple fusion backbones. Gains persist when a small amount of target-domain data is available.
arxiv-2606-11673:
Jian Xu and four colleagues build a quantum attention head in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ordinary self-attention compares tokens only in pairs within one layer. Capturing interactions among three or more tokens at once needs much larger layers or many stacked layers classically. Their Quantum Higher-Order Attention head creates such interactions inside a shallow quantum circuit.

Using data re-uploading and an entangling circuit, the head reads its result from one qubit. The authors prove an expressivity separation: one head represents order-k correlations that a classical layer below a stated size cannot. For a local version they prove gradients avoid the barren plateau, the flat landscape stalling quantum training. With a budget six and a half times smaller, the quantum head learns hidden-subset parity up to order six, where the classical head fails past order two. A trained head also ran on IBM hardware at full accuracy.
arxiv-2606-11973:
Dominik Lüthi and seven colleagues try to slip a molecular carpet under graphene ribbons in this 2026 arXiv paper. Graphene nanoribbons grown on gold are coupled to the metal, which distorts their properties and complicates device use. Sliding a molecular layer underneath could decouple them. The team used N-heterocyclic carbenes, reactive carbon-based molecules that form ordered monolayers, on ribbons exactly seven atoms wide.

Microscopy, spectra and simulations show the carbene's shape decides everything. Methyl carbenes lie flat as pairs and partially intercalate, producing locally decoupled ribbon segments. Bulkier isopropyl carbenes stand upright as single molecules and instead embed the ribbons inside the monolayer, preventing intercalation entirely. Overall yields are low, showing that lifting a ribbon off gold is costly in energy. The results identify geometry and packing as the key design factors for decoupling layers. That guidance matters for using nanoribbons in real electronic devices.
arxiv-2606-12673:
Nguyen and colleagues propose AlignGAD, a framework for finding abnormal nodes in graphs it has never seen, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A graph shows items as nodes joined by links, and anomaly detection means flagging nodes that break the usual pattern. Detectors trained for one network usually fail on another, because features and structures differ between domains. AlignGAD is zero-shot, so it applies to new graphs without any retraining there.

Three parts do the work. A unification module aligns mismatched features and normalises signals. A clustering module builds group-level views that expose collective oddities. A scoring module reconstructs each node and measures how badly the reconstruction fits. Nodes that reconstruct poorly look anomalous. The authors test the framework on nine real datasets, including Cora, Reddit, Amazon, and YelpChi, and report that it detects anomalies effectively across these very different graphs under the strict zero-shot setting.
arxiv-2606-12773:
Shelton classifies the 3-dimensional real associative algebras with identity, which he calls near-trinions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Frobenius' theorem rules out any 3-dimensional real division algebra, sitting between the complex numbers and the quaternions, but it does not say which 3-dimensional associative algebras exist. Shelton answers that question up to isomorphism.

The answer is exactly 6 isomorphism classes, for which he gives canonical forms, multiplication tables, and invariants that tell every pair apart. It sorts algebras by the dimension of their radical, the largest nilpotent ideal, which can be 0, 1, or 2. The semisimple case is settled by the Wedderburn-Artin theorem. With a 1-dimensional radical, a Peirce decomposition places the radical generator in a corner, producing two branches. With a 2-dimensional radical, the split turns on whether the radical's square vanishes. A characteristic sign obstruction rules out any near-trinion with residue field equal to the complex numbers.
arxiv-2606-13373:
Bedrouni studies webs of curves on the complex plane in this 2026 arXiv paper. A web is a family of foliations, sets of curves filling a region in several directions, like families of contour lines. Each web carries a curvature, a quantity whose poles, points where it blows up, signal special behaviour. Bedrouni considers a web built by combining two webs, one of which leaves a curve invariant, meaning its curves map the curve to itself. The second web crosses that curve transversally everywhere.

He proves the web's curvature is holomorphic along the invariant curve, free of poles, when the smaller web's curvature is. When it is non-degenerate along the curve, holomorphy follows. A numerical condition on the discriminant, the locus where the web's directions collide, gives a sufficient criterion. The result generalises work that required the curve to have minimal multiplicity in the discriminant.
arxiv-2606-13673:
Seokju Cho and colleagues study the action interface of spatial reasoning agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial reasoning, judging where objects are and how they relate in three dimensions, remains a basic challenge for vision-language models. Tool-augmented agents delegate perception to modules, but their power is bounded by the interface through which tools are invoked. Existing spatial agents either run single-pass code, committing to a full strategy before seeing any result. Or they use structured tool calls that limit free composition of operations.

The authors' system, SpatialClaw, rethinks that interface to support open-ended analysis, where the agent can adapt its strategy as evidence arrives. The study isolates interface design as a variable, showing how much of an agent's capability is interface capability. For builders of embodied agents, the lesson: before scaling the model or adding tools, fix the channel through which the model acts.
arxiv-2606-13873: Dated 2026 on arXiv, this preprint reports a new research result. The paper is titled around Natively Unlearnable Large Language Models. Its discipline is artificial intelligence: the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. It records a new contribution to human knowledge.
arxiv-2606-14173:
Zhou and colleagues render holograms by tracing light waves the way graphics traces rays, merging two computations usually kept apart. Standard holography pre-renders scene brightness on discrete sectors, then propagates waves separately, limiting focus cues and effects like glossy reflection and refraction. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents HoloPathTracer, a Monte Carlo method solving the rendering equation and the Rayleigh-Sommerfeld diffraction integral at once, encoding full 3D cues into phase-only holograms.

Path Reuse generates multiple time-multiplexed holograms at minimal extra cost, and an ambient radiance cache gives an order-of-magnitude convergence speedup. Validation ran in simulation and on a spatial light modulator prototype. Reconstructions showed natural defocus blur, view-dependent effects, and realistic highlights on complex materials, with close-ups at depths of zero point five, zero point nine, and ten meters against ground truth. No pre-trained network or fixed primitive set is required.
arxiv-2606-14373:
Mokhtar, Pata, Kagan, and Duarte show a network trained to reconstruct collisions learned representations rich enough to power other analyses: a foundation model for collider physics. Event reconstruction is traditionally modular: the particle-flow algorithm turns detector signals into candidates, and downstream tasks start over, losing low-level information. Their 2026 arXiv paper repurposes a machine-learned particle flow model, appending its per-particle latents as extra features.

The tasks: jet flavor ID, jet energy regression, missing momentum regression. Adding the latents improved all three over kinematic-only baselines. More strikingly, one linear layer on the latents matched state-of-the-art models, and for missing momentum regression beat the baseline with roughly 35 times fewer parameters. For flavor ID, a 387-parameter linear classifier performed well with no hand-crafted track features. With earlier cross-detector transfer results, they emerge as foundation models on two axes, geometry and task.
arxiv-2606-14773:
Wen presents a geometry-based visual sampler in a 2026 arXiv paper. It squeezes images into tiny signals. Double-Helix Vision samples a picture along two phase-shifted spiral paths inspired by the golden ratio. It mimics biological foveation. Sampling is dense at the center and sparse at the edges, instead of reading every pixel uniformly.

At 4K resolution the sampler claims a compression ratio above fourteen hundred to one. It preserves the scene's geometric structure. The full pipeline runs in about half a millisecond at 1080p on CPU-only hardware. It includes spatial mapping, temporal collision detection, and structural disparity estimation. No neural networks are needed. On CIFAR-10 at extreme budgets of one hundred twenty-eight points per helix, it beat uniform random sampling. The gain was about six accuracy points. A robotics API delivers sub-millisecond reports in packets under three kilobytes.
arxiv-2606-14873:
Shankar, Van Acoleyen, and Haegeman extend a quantum simulation method to continuous systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Matrix product states are a compact way to write quantum states of chain-like systems. They work naturally on lattices. Real problems, like gases in traps, live in continuous space. The authors build a finite-element version using non-orthogonal basis sets.

The trick maps the physical problem to an auxiliary space. There the overlap operator becomes a matrix product operator, as long as the orbitals stay localized. The ground-state search turns into a generalized eigenvalue problem. A generalized DMRG algorithm solves it. As the main test, they study the Lieb-Liniger gas, a line of interacting bosons, with impurities in its density. The finite-element setting also allows exact lattice refinement. That enables multigrid optimization, refining the mesh where it matters most.
arxiv-2606-14973:
Khoperskov and coauthors view the Milky Way as if it were a distant galaxy in a 2026 study. Astronomers know our galaxy star by star, yet study other galaxies through blended light. The team builds mock integral-field datacubes of the Milky Way. They then fit those cubes with the spectral tool pPXF.

Two routes build the mocks: stacked stellar populations from an orbit-based solution tied to APOGEE data, and radiative-transfer modeling with SKIRT. The fits recover rotation and dispersion patterns of the thin disc, thick disc, and bar. The chemical split of disc stars, though, cannot be read from the blended data. The star-formation history comes back, but false bursts appear from the age-metal trade-off. Radiative-transfer mocks prove harder, with weaker recovery of higher-order motion and population traits. The results warn that forward modeling of galaxy surveys remains demanding.
arxiv-2606-15473:
Dixon builds a mathematical framework for measuring the model risk of agentic AI in a 2026 paper. Agents do not merely predict: they form beliefs, call tools, act, and reshape their own future information. The framework casts the agent as a partially observed decision process over hidden regimes. A language model serves as the observation model, converting evidence into a probability vector over regimes. A Bayesian filter smooths the beliefs over time into an auditable trail.

Uncertainty and risk are kept apart. Entropy, drift, and calibration error describe the beliefs. Loss distributions under the induced decisions carry the risk, summarized with value-at-risk style tail measures from finance. A case study on daily equity returns shows the pipeline producing regime probabilities and diagnostics end to end. The aim is governance with numbers, giving AI risk officers the discipline financial model risk applies to trading models.
arxiv-2606-15673:
Chung and colleagues build WebStep in 2026, a benchmark that grades web agents on how they work, not just whether they finish. Existing benchmarks score only final success, throwing away everything about the path taken. WebStep instead runs a deterministic semantic model underneath each site, recording states and transitions automatically as the agent clicks.

Its eighteen hundred tasks span ten self-hosted websites with controlled difficulty. Three agents with success rates within two points of each other differ sharply in exploration reach versus execution accuracy. On one housing site, a leading agent beats a rival by about twenty-four percent on commit actions yet trails it by about sixteen percent on filtering, a reversal invisible in totals. Bifurcation analysis pins down the single decisive error that doomed each failed run, and shows the error differs by agent. Process-level scores like these tell developers exactly which skill to fix.
arxiv-2606-15773:
Zhang and colleagues project how well the CEPC collider could measure CKM matrix elements from W-pair decays in 2026. The CKM matrix encodes quark flavour mixing, and several of its elements remain imprecise. Using simulated collisions producing W pairs that decay semileptonically, with jet flavour tagging by ParticleNet, they target the hadronic decays.

With the simulated dataset at 240 GeV, projected precision reaches about six tenths of a percent for the element Vcb and about one hundredth of a percent for Vcs. The results are direct and model-independent, unlike many extractions that lean on theory inputs. Systematic uncertainties, dominated by detector response and tagging calibration, are treated conservatively, with data-driven calibrations expected to shrink them. Such measurements would stress-test the Standard Model's charged-current flavour structure and could expose new physics. Turning hadronic W branching fractions into precision CKM probes is the opportunity the study quantifies.
arxiv-2606-15873:
Troger and colleagues give a complete relational account of spin in 2026: can a quantum spin be described with no classical background frame? Standard quantum mechanics defines spin directions against fixed external axes — the laboratory walls. Poulin tried this twenty years ago with one large reference spin: group-averaging yielded only a classical bit in a probabilistic mixture, and the quantum description was lost.

Adding a second large reference spin, pointing orthogonally, changes everything. After the incoherent group average over rotations removes every external axis, the remaining state encodes the qubit by how it aligns with the reference spins. When the reference spins' quantum numbers grow large, the standard spin state is recovered: the encoding becomes faithful in the frame's classical limit. They also settle a standing dispute: the averaging loses coherence only between total-angular-momentum sectors, not the spin's own.
arxiv-2606-15973:
Dheeraj and colleagues study whether the sound of breathing, recorded at the back, tracks spirometric airflow limitation in asthma in 2026. Spirometry's FEV1/FVC ratio is the standard, but a stethoscope-based acoustic marker would be cheaper and easier to repeat. The team computes the expiratory-to-inspiratory spectral power ratio at four sites in 141 participants aged twenty to sixty, correlating it with FEV1/FVC across subbands.

Two bands, one to two hundred and two to four hundred hertz, show significant correlations. Lower sites associate most strongly overall, but the map shifts with demographics. Younger adults correlate best at the left lower site, older adults at the left upper; men pattern with the younger group, women with the older. The correlations are moderate, between two-tenths and four-tenths, so the authors read them as exploratory evidence, not a spirometry replacement. Location-, age-, and gender-specific models are the next step.
arxiv-2606-16073:
Korolev and colleagues teach a sampler when to stop in a 2026 paper on Bayesian computation. Sampling from complex densities underlies Bayesian inference, where analysts update beliefs from data. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods guarantee correct answers in the limit, but fixed trajectory lengths waste computation and mix slowly. The authors make termination itself a learned part of the dynamics.

Framing the sampler through generative flow networks, they train neural classifiers to end a trajectory once it reaches a high-density region. Theory links the optimal classifier to the target density through detailed balance conditions. A multilevel training scheme helps exploration in complex geometries. Across benchmark densities, the method significantly shortens average trajectory lengths versus standard baselines in the reported experiments. Mode coverage and mixing also improve. Adaptive stopping could cut routine sampling costs without giving up correctness.
arxiv-2606-16273:
Micheli and co-authors introduce in 2026 the first deep generative framework for data that lives on a metric graph, such as a road network. A metric graph gives each edge a length, so probability distributions can spread continuously along it. Their approach embeds the graph into a smooth ambient space where transport is easier to compute.

Inside that space, they solve an entropic optimal transport problem with a neural semidual parameterization, then project samples back onto the graph. Two embeddings are studied: a plain Euclidean one, and a tropical Abel-Jacobi embedding into the Jacobian torus that respects the graph's own geometry. The authors prove the learned generator converges to a valid transport coupling as the network grows more expressive. On test graphs it matches or beats discrete graph transport baselines while scaling better. A demonstration trains on one million Uber pickup locations across Manhattan's street network.
arxiv-2606-16373:
Stankewitz and Wahl sharpen in 2026 the spectral theory of kernel matrices, the workhorse arrays behind kernel methods in data science and machine learning. A kernel matrix mirrors a kernel integral operator, and its eigenvalues drive smoothing, principal component analysis, and manifold learning. The authors prove spectral concentration bounds under weak assumptions: a Mercer condition on the kernel and a local Weyl law on the data geometry. Heavy machinery from earlier proofs is avoided.

The bounds tolerate the traits that make kernel matrices hard: large multiplicities, large effective dimension, and heavy-tailed data distributions. Uses run to manifold learning and Bayesian nonparametric statistics. Two cases carry the theory: the heat kernel on the sphere, and a wavelet prior. As the second paper in a series on higher-order spectral perturbation, it supplies the backbone for finer expansion results.
arxiv-2606-16473:
Dubey and Varshney measure in 2026 how ready the public internet is for quantum computers that can break today's encryption. TLS, the protocol securing web traffic, rests on RSA and elliptic curve cryptography, both vulnerable to quantum attacks. The authors scan 32,011 domains across sectors, recording protocol versions, cipher suites, key exchange mechanisms, and certificates. The picture is a transition half finished.

Modern TLS 1.3 and QUIC are spreading, yet 15.70 percent of domains still rely on TLS 1.2, with banking and government sites prominent among the laggards. Hybrid post-quantum key exchange, pairing ML-KEM-768 with X25519, is supported by 49.3 percent of domains. The other 50.7 percent remain fully exposed to quantum attack through classical key exchange alone. Adoption of hybrid post-quantum certificates stands at zero. The driver of progress is ML-KEM-768, standardized as FIPS 203, now built into browsers, cloud platforms, and content delivery networks.
arxiv-2606-16673:
Akarken, Kupyn and Rupprecht present MMDiff in a 2026 paper on diffusion transformers, the models behind much modern image generation. During generation, these models compute rich internal features at each denoising step, then throw them away once the image is rendered. MMDiff instead decodes those features into extra outputs, such as depth maps and object outlines, at the same time.

Lightweight decoder heads are trained on top of a frozen generator, so the image model itself never changes. The key finding is that useful information is spread across the whole denoising path, not held in one step. Fusing features from many steps, with weights that vary by location, lifts segmentation scores sharply over single-step extraction. The system performs strongly on segmentation, salient object detection and depth estimation. It also produces synthetic training data at scale, showing frozen diffusion features can rival specialist encoders like DINOv3.
arxiv-2606-16773:
Llorens-Terrazas and Meitz propose a new way to forecast whole distributions in a 2026 economics paper. A forecast distribution describes all the uncertainty around a time series' future, not just its expected path. From it come fan charts, value at risk and tail risk measures used in finance.

Their method writes a general forecast distribution in a generative form based on a classic probability result. That form can be sampled directly, so means, spreads and tail measures are easy to compute. Fitting uses a conditional generative adversarial network, set up as a minimax problem. The authors prove the fitted sets settle toward the truth under weak time dependence. Tests on stock returns, realized variance and realized covariances show the method works in practice. Fitting in their examples takes about a minute on a standard laptop, fast enough for routine forecasting work at banks and funds.
arxiv-2606-16973:
Eduardo Ferreira da Silva, Oliveira and Pires ask how much text reviews really add to recommender systems in a 2026 paper. Recommenders often enrich user and item profiles with review text, hoping the words reveal tastes that star ratings miss. Whether that text helps once a strong collaborative model is in place was unclear.

The team builds three enrichment strategies on one matrix factorization backbone. A learnable gate balances collaborative and textual signals during training, fed either by topic profiles from review histories or by full text embeddings. A cross-attention variant instead picks out the most informative text dimensions before fusion. Six model variants are compared across several review datasets. Hybrid models do improve error metrics like root mean square error. They tend to hurt ranking quality, though, and the marginal gain from text stays small beside the collaborative backbone, a structural trade-off the authors support with statistical tests.
arxiv-2606-17173:
Goetting and colleagues entangle three atomic qubits across separate nodes in a 2026 quantum networking paper. A quantum internet needs multipartite entanglement across distant memories, for modular computing, sensing and secure protocols. Photonic links are the way to connect the nodes.

The team reports the first fully distributed GHZ state of individual atomic qubits across a three-node network. Earlier three-node GHZ states used solid-state qubits or atomic ensembles; single atoms offer replication and individual control. Photonic interconnects herald the shared state at a modest generation rate, with fidelity bounded comfortably above the entanglement threshold. The state also violates Mermin's inequality, the three-party Bell test, while closing the detection loophole, a first for a fully distributed multipartite state. That combination matters: loophole-free shared entanglement across real nodes is a building block for distributed quantum computing and self-checking protocols.
arxiv-2606-17473:
Bo, McWilliams, and Chamecki present a 2026 arXiv paper on how submesoscale ocean fronts move material from the surface down into the interior. These fronts sit between big eddies and small boundary turbulence, and they drive vertical exchange that ocean models must capture. The puzzle is how front-driven currents and turbulence combine to carry tracers such as nutrients or pollutants across density surfaces, a process called diapycnal transport in the field.

Large-eddy simulations of a forming front show intense turbulence developing as the front sharpens over time. Part of the downward tracer flux comes directly from turbulent mixing, as expected from earlier work. A substantial share, though, rides an advective flux driven by the mean downward velocity at the front. That mean flow grows from the evolving secondary circulation where turbulent mixing acts on density, revealing an overlooked pathway.
arxiv-2606-17673:
Villani and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper showing that graphene Josephson junctions act as superconducting diodes, passing supercurrent more easily one way than the other. Such non-reciprocal devices could rectify signals in superconducting electronics and probe broken symmetries in mesoscopic systems. The effect needs inversion and time-reversal symmetry broken together. Here it appears under a small out-of-plane magnetic field, in junctions so clean that graphene serves as a near-perfect transmission medium for the supercurrent flowing through the device.

Rectification efficiency passed a fifth near the nodes of the interference pattern, where the effect strengthens markedly. The team's model pins the symmetry breaking on long-range scattering potentials left by residual disorder in the junction. Even unavoidable disorder in a clean two-dimensional system is enough, they show, to create the effect. Gate design could tailor the breaking deliberately in future devices.
arxiv-2606-17773:
Illiano and De Risi set out a 2026 framework for routers in a future quantum internet, written from the University of Naples Federico II. Classical routers copy, buffer, and inspect data, but quantum rules forbid copying and restrict measurement, so forwarding needs a different basis. Their design uses multipartite entanglement as the resource that moves quantum information through a node.

A graph state serves as the switching fabric, and forwarding happens through local Pauli measurements on it. The authors translate the classical idea of a non-blocking switch into quantum terms and derive an edge-controlled design principle. They build it two ways, a monolithic crossbar and a modular Clos-type fabric, and show the modular version can cut the switching-qubit overhead in the right size range.
arxiv-2606-17973:
Tieleman and colleagues teach a language model to estimate depression severity straight from therapy chat transcripts, in a 2026 study. The standard PHQ-9 questionnaire tracks symptoms well, but few patients complete it, leaving biased gaps in monitoring. A passive estimate drawn from conversations people already have with an AI mental health app could fill those gaps without extra burden.

The team fine-tuned a large Qwen model with a regression head to predict PHQ-9 totals from conversation text alone. Real labels for about three thousand users were expanded with pseudo-labels from a reasoning model and from earlier trained versions, more than doubling the data. On a held-out set of over eight hundred users, the best model landed within a few points of true scores on average. It also separated clinical cases from non-cases with strong accuracy at every severity cutoff tested.
arxiv-2606-18073:
Palitta and Pasha slim down a workhorse algorithm for giant inverse problems, in a 2026 numerical paper. The generalized Krylov subspace method solves large Tikhonov regularization problems, the kind that recover images or signals from noisy data with a general smoothing matrix. As its search subspace grows, two costs dominate: repeated QR factorizations of tall matrices, and re-orthogonalizing every new basis vector against all the old ones.

Their sketched variant, sGKS, performs the factorizations on compressed matrices kept current by rank-one updates, shrinking the tall problems to small ones. Boldly, they also drop re-orthogonalization entirely, arguing no step of the method truly needs an orthogonal basis, and the approximation quality survives. Without sketching in the inner solve the iterates match the original method exactly, and with it the residual norms stay near-optimal for any reasonable sketching choice.
arxiv-2606-18373:
Blaschke, Röpke, and Röpke investigate why the relative amounts of heavy elements made by the rapid neutron-capture process look nearly the same in star after star, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. That shared pattern is striking because the sites where these elements form are still debated, and a minority of stars break the pattern in telling ways.

Their approach treats heavy element formation as a freeze-out that never reaches equilibrium, described by just three Lagrange parameters linked to temperature and to neutron and proton chemical potentials. Fitting observed abundances in several astrophysical objects, they find those parameters barely wobble between ordinary stars, while metal-poor stars show larger spreads. Outlier cases, including actinide-boost stars and patterns that drop off at the heavy end, also fit through modest parameter changes. The authors suggest the fitted values could help identify which environments produced the heavy elements.
arxiv-2606-18473:
Su, Shah, and Le study whether the collateral damage caused by making a large language model forget selected knowledge can be predicted in advance, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Unlearning aims to remove specified information while sparing the rest, but distant knowledge is entangled with the target.

Measuring effects across layers of decreasing relevance to the forget set, they find a steady decay pattern. Harm is strongest near the material slated for removal, weakens with semantic distance, yet does not vanish at domain boundaries. They then frame auditing as a prediction task and test which data features forecast the damage. Features describing the interaction between the forget set and the evaluation set gave the strongest signals, beating properties of the forget set. The authors propose such audits as an early warning screen that flags risky unlearning runs before model updates are committed.
arxiv-2606-18573:
Researchers at the University of Rochester's Audio and Music Engineering program argue that models of range compressors should be graded on the gain signal they produce, in a 2026 audio engineering paper. Compressors are the studio processors that tame loud passages. Normally such models are scored with proxy metrics on the processed waveform.

The team captured that gain signal directly as a control voltage from a hardware SSL bus compressor, alongside its audio output, and released the recordings as a dataset. Training a gray-box compressor model on the true gain trajectory beat models trained on two standard proxy losses when judged against that trajectory. The waveform metrics scored the clearly separated models almost identically. The authors conclude that proxy objectives can hide exactly the behavior a model is meant to copy, and they offer direct gain supervision as the fix.
arxiv-2606-18873:
Mellinand and the team report the design of a motorized mount for a folding mirror inside a future Very Large Telescope instrument, in a 2026 paper. BlueMUSE, a blue integral field spectrograph, needs key optics placed with care again and again, to hold stability. Its second folding mirror needs three degrees of freedom: tip, tilt, and vertical shift.

The paper tests candidate mechanical designs through theoretical sim runs. It then details the chosen approach: a ball-and-slope design from the instrument's first folding mirror mechanism. Its high motion reduction shields the mirror from actuator backlash. Control runs through the project's Beckhoff EtherCAT setting, using homing and open-loop placement from calibration tables. A dedicated optical setup with an autocollimator was designed to measure repeatability, precision, and thermal stability. A thermo-mechanical check tested stainless steel against Invar alloy, which reduced heat-caused warping and stress.
arxiv-2606-19073:
Gao and colleagues tackle image editing of human-object interactions in 2026. Current editors handle static traits well but fail on complex interactions, like a person lifting or pouring with an object. Past benchmarks mix interaction with static traits and use global scores. Those scores cannot judge both the dynamic act and the preservation of the human-object pair at once, so a key editing skill has gone unmeasured.

Their HOI-Edit benchmark has three progressive levels of cognitive demand and an automated metric that uses grounded question answering on the pair. The team benchmarks image-to-video models and finds them naturally suited to dynamic editing through their temporal generation. Video also replays how a failure unfolds, aiding diagnosis. Their SCPE framework then corrects itself through iteratively refined prompts, constraining the video model step by step. Frames from the corrected video form the final edit.
arxiv-2606-19173:
Boulanger and colleagues prove a nonlinear graviton theorem for higher-spin self-dual gravity in 2026 using twistor space. Interacting theories of massless higher-spin fields are hard to construct, and chiral higher-spin gravity is a rare candidate expected to be integrable. The authors study small deformations of twistor space and the planes embedded through its origin.

That space of planes is an infinite-dimensional manifold with a projection onto a four-dimensional self-dual spacetime. Solutions of higher-spin self-dual gravity arise by choosing an embedding of spacetime into the higher-spin space, with higher-spin symmetries from the different embedding choices. Integrability appears as a Lax pair for the system, which the authors present. They conjecture chiral higher-spin gravity arises the same way from deformations unconstrained at the origin. The twistor route thus geometrizes a hard interacting theory.
arxiv-2606-19273:
Kryukov runs computer tests in 2026 for a random-matrix theory of how quantum states reduce. The companion theory says random Hamiltonians push states to spread through state space. The tests check the main claims of that theory. They check even spread from GUE Hamiltonians, how that spread limits to Brownian motion on the classical surface, and Born-rule rates for outcome classes set by detectors.

More tests cover Newtonian motion for large systems watched repeatedly by their surroundings. The GOE ensemble fails to give the needed even complex spread, while the GUE ensemble succeeds. Tests also cover detector records in the double-slit setup and the Zeno stability of recorded classes. One-way behavior from high-dimensional dynamics and lost path data is checked too. The results present state reduction, stable records, and classical behavior as faces of one shared mechanism, not as separate postulates.
arxiv-2606-19373:
O'Hara and colleagues introduce cAPM in 2026, a continual AI-assisted pace-mapping system for ventricular tachycardia ablation. Pace-mapping is a standard procedure for finding the intervention target. Clinicians pace sites in the ventricles and read the resulting electrocardiograms to choose the next site. Existing methods, though, retrain from scratch for each target and cannot transfer knowledge across targets in one patient or across patients.

cAPM learns continually, carrying knowledge from past pace-mapping into future cases. A task-agnostic surrogate network learns the mapping from pacing sites to twelve-lead ECG morphology. An active learning strategy refines that surrogate by picking the most informative new pacing sites as the procedure proceeds. Each new case starts from what earlier cases taught. Fewer pacing sites means shorter procedures for patients with a life-threatening rhythm disorder. Continual transfer is what makes the guidance practical across a clinician's whole case load.
arxiv-2606-19473:
Joseph MacManus and Bobby Miraftab develop median decompositions as a tool for structural graph theory in 2026. A median decomposition generalises the tree decomposition, a standard way to break a graph into linked bags of vertices. Vertex separations, sets whose removal splits a graph, sit at the heart of the theory.

Nested systems of separations are known to yield tree decompositions over a structure tree. MacManus and Miraftab show that any system, nested or not, yields a median decomposition instead. The median graph inside it is Sageev's dual median graph, and nested cuts recover the tree case exactly. They prove the decomposition is uniquely minimal and explain Sageev-Roller duality inside it. One payoff extends Stavropoulos: for every graph, median-width equals clique number. Links to coarse embeddings into median graphs then characterise when a group acts well on such a graph.
arxiv-2606-19873:
Han Yan builds random three-dimensional quantum codes that dodge two classic obstructions in 2026. Self-correcting quantum memories fail when string-like logical operators let errors grow at fixed energy cost. Haah's fracton codes ban strings but host fractal logical operators with only logarithmic barriers.

Yan's qutrit random cubic codes keep Haah-style cube checks with spatially varying stabilizers. Randomness replaces translation invariance as the organising principle. The no-string property is proven for the new family. Numerical work then probes how the codes differ from fracton kin. Ground-state degeneracy exponents take small values split by lattice parity. Plane-like logical operators span the whole logical space. Charge-push diagnostics find no self-similar fractal operators at all. Constrained randomness thus reshapes code behaviour and improves self-correction prospects.
arxiv-2606-19973:
Swaraj Biswas and Santanu Maiti design thermal logic gates in a phononic ring in 2026. Logic gates are the atoms of computing, and heat-carrying lattice vibrations, phonons, could in principle carry the signals instead of electrons. Two atomic sites near a ring serve as inputs for two-input gates, and one extra site handles single-input gates. The output is read from the phonon transmission probability, computed with non-equilibrium Green's functions.

By adjusting how the ring joins its electrodes, all seven standard gates appear, three basic and four combined, each in its own frequency range. The operations hold across broad frequency bands, which supports the scheme's generality. Heat-based computing remains theoretical, but a complete gate set in one tunable device is a useful milestone. Nanoscale thermal management could borrow the same physics.
arxiv-2606-20173:
José Manuel Suárez, Luís Mariano Bibbó, Joaquín Bogado, and Alejandro Fernandez use language models guided by retrieval to migrate quantum code between Qiskit versions. Their 2026 paper targets a fast-moving problem: quantum kits change so quickly that working code rots, and general models asked to fix it often hallucinate plausible but wrong migrations.

Their hybrid approach pairs an LLM with retrieval over an automatically built taxonomy of migration scenarios, giving the model structured, version-specific knowledge. They tested Google Gemini Flash-2.5 and OpenAI's Gpt-oss-20b under open and restrictive retrieval schemes. The taxonomy setup, especially with restrictive retrieval, cut hallucinations and improved suggestion quality. Gemini proved better at spotting complex refactoring cases. Such assistants can protect quantum software from API churn and flatten the learning curve.
arxiv-2606-20273:
Lili Fan, Hongjun Gao, and Ji Li determine when small periodic waves of the modified Camassa-Holm equation are stable. Their 2026 paper studies an equation with cubic nonlinearity, proposed for nonlinear water waves and now known to govern shallow water waves of moderate amplitude. The team analyzes the spectrum of the linearized operator around small-amplitude periodic traveling waves, near the origin of the spectral plane, adapting Kato's perturbation theory.

The analysis gives a complete description of the spectrum near the origin. Such waves are not subject to modulational instability, the slow sideband growth that destroys many wave trains. But a sharp threshold appears: waves with wavenumber squared at most three are spectrally stable, while instability emerges above three. A threshold this clean gives modelers a precise boundary between safe and unstable regimes.
arxiv-2606-20473:
Illia Rohozhkin constructs invariants of the colored braid groupoid by treating braids as dynamical systems. In his 2026 paper, the states of the system are Delaunay triangulations of points moving in the plane. This geometric setup yields an abstract groupoid that represents the colored braid groupoid.

Rohozhkin defines homomorphisms from this groupoid into general linear groups over the rationals and the complex numbers. An algorithm computes the invariants these maps produce. Turning braids into triangulations links braid theory to computational geometry in a concrete way. The resulting representations give new algebraic handles on colored braids, objects that appear in topology and in anyon models of quantum computation.
arxiv-2606-20673:
Matin Fallahi, Patricia Arias-Cabarcos, and Thorsten Strufe introduce NeuroShield in 2026, a foundation model for brainwave authentication. EEG systems identify people from electrical signals recorded at the scalp. Most models tie tightly to the headset used in training. Changes in hardware, channel layout, or signal length break them. Each new device then becomes a fresh model project. That fragmentation limits learning across datasets and reuse.

NeuroShield learns identity features from recordings with varied channels and lengths. It uses a dual-stage transformer design. Pretraining covers three public datasets with 15,762 subjects and 28,116 sessions. Tests on two unseen datasets follow. After fine-tuning, equal error rate falls by 0.44 to 8.06 points against prior best results. A device-agnostic model could make EEG login more practical, because clinics and labs rarely share the same headset or recording setup.
arxiv-2606-20873:
Yueming Wang and five colleagues present SciLens in 2026, a framework for checking scientific claims against multimodal evidence in papers. Claims often mix numbers, comparisons, scope limits, and context. Evidence sits in tables and figures with distinct structures. Asking a vision-language model for one direct judgment handles that mix poorly. SciLens instead breaks each claim into atomic parts.

Central empirical atoms are separated from background atoms. Central atoms are grounded to specific evidence witnesses. Tables ground atoms to rows, cells, arithmetic links, and scope. Figures ground them through panels, axes, legends, trends, and ranks. An atom-level entailment rule then gives the final label. A claim counts as supported only if every central atom checks out. That audit trail matters for automated science, where a verdict without located evidence cannot be trusted by researchers.
arxiv-2606-21073:
Zhiyao Xiong, Xiaokui Yang, and Shing-Tung Yau prove an analogue in 2026 of a classic theorem using a prescribed Hermitian-Yang-Mills flow. That theorem links stable bundles to special metrics. A vector bundle sits over a compact Kähler manifold. A slope condition on subsheaves is assumed.

For any starting metric and any prescribed positive tensor, the flow admits a global smooth solution for all time. As time grows, the flow converges smoothly to a metric that solves the prescribed equation exactly. An application is given on Fano manifolds. Flow proofs are prized in geometry. They construct the desired metric as a limit. The object and a process that finds it both come out of the proof.
arxiv-2606-21273:
Vasileios Aravantinos-Sotiropoulos and Panagis Karazeris study locales inside presheaf toposes in 2026, a topic in category theory that recasts topology without points. A presheaf topos organizes data indexed by a base category, and structures inside it can be viewed internally or as families of ordinary structures. For suplattices and frames, the two views differ: not every family of frames forms an internal frame.

The authors construct the free internal suplattice or frame on a presheaf of such structures, giving a left adjoint to the forgetful passage between the views. They then test which properties pass to the sections over each base object. Compactness and stable local compactness transfer. Local compactness needs extra care with transition maps. The Hausdorff property does not transfer. The results clarify how point-free topology behaves inside variable worlds.
arxiv-2606-21473:
Aaron Johnson, Katerina Chatziioannou, and Jake Summers write a self-contained guide in 2026 to the Wilson-Daubechies-Meyer time-frequency transform for gravitational-wave analysis. Time-frequency methods sit between fast frequency-domain tools and flexible but costly time-domain ones, suiting signals buried in slowly varying noise. Despite growing use, the approach is far less documented in the gravitational-wave literature than its frequency-domain cousin.

This first paper of a series derives the WDM basis from scratch and builds intuition for its orthogonality and tight localization in both time and frequency. Practical material covers edge effects at the lowest and highest frequencies, forward and inverse transforms and their implementation, and the noise covariance matrix and likelihood written in the time-frequency domain. The account collects lessons learned for analysts adopting the method.
arxiv-2606-21973:
Gui and colleagues present SPOTR in 2026, a self-supervised method for learning from physiological signals such as brain, heart, and pulse waveforms. Existing self-supervised methods distort clinically meaningful structure or learn shortcuts from redundancy, and usually serve one signal type at a time. SPOTR aims for one universal pretraining recipe across modalities.

The method squeezes each waveform into a single-token representation, one compact summary code, and must reconstruct the signal from that code alone. A compaction module keeps computation and memory costs down. Pretrained on twenty datasets spanning EEG, intracranial EEG, ECG, and PPG signals, SPOTR beat the strongest baseline under linear probing on every modality. Average AUC gains ranged from about five percent for pulse signals to over twenty percent for intracranial recordings. It also ran with about seventy-eight percent lower latency and half the peak memory of a general foundation model.
arxiv-2606-22373:
The BESIII Collaboration, a large particle-physics collaboration whose author list is headed by M. Ablikim, reports a search for a forbidden decay in this 2026 paper. The decay would turn an eta meson into an electron and a muon. Such charged lepton flavor violation is banned in the standard model and would signal new physics.

The team analysed more than ten billion J/psi events recorded by the BESIII detector, looking for eta mesons produced through a specific chain of decays. They found no sign of the forbidden decay in the data. The collaboration therefore sets an upper limit on its branching fraction, the share of eta decays taking that route, below seven in ten million at the ninety percent confidence level. That limit improves the previous best bound by a factor of ten, tightening the space where new physics could hide.
arxiv-2606-22873:
The SingGuard Team presents a safety guardrail for vision-language models in this 2026 paper. Such models now serve consumer, medical, financial, and enterprise products, and each setting carries different moderation rules. Most existing guardrails use fixed risk taxonomies or cover only narrow interaction types, so they adapt poorly when policies change at deployment time.

SingGuard treats the active policy as a runtime input. Given rules in natural language, it checks content against the policy rule by rule and predicts both the safety label and which rule was triggered. It offers fast, hybrid, and slow inference modes, from direct judgments to policy-grounded deliberation, tuned by a fast-slow decoupled reinforcement learning method. The team also built SingGuard-Bench, with 56,340 examples spanning more than eighty fine-grained risk types. Across six benchmark families covering thirty-five datasets, SingGuard achieved the best average F1 in every family.
arxiv-2606-23073:
Jun Wu and colleagues survey covert wireless communication that uses sensing in a 2026 article. Covert communication hides not the message content but the very fact that a transmission happened. Enemies listening in must be unable to tell signal from background. Older designs relied on blind interference or passive uncertainty, which falter when radio conditions keep changing. Adding sensing lets the system learn about the adversary and the environment, then adapt its sending and jamming choices in real time.

Wu and colleagues explain how sensing shifts design from passive hiding to state-aware decision making. Sensing also brings fresh costs, including exposure risk and extra resource use. They review smart sensing schemes that gather task-relevant information with little active probing. A case study on low-altitude networks shows sensing-assisted beamforming improving spatial resource use and delivery reliability. Open problems close the survey.
arxiv-2606-23573:
Berardi, de' Liguoro, Kimura, and Osorio-Valencia extend a logic system for infinite computations, in a 2026 extended abstract on proof theory. Lambda calculus is the formal backbone of functional programming, and its infinitary version allows terms, meaning expressions, that run on without end. The authors enrich that calculus with zero, successor, and conditional operations, plus a type system modeled on Gödel's System T, a classic scheme for defining computable functions.

They then add a Global Trace Condition, a rule borrowed from cyclic proof theory that watches how a computation unfolds over time. For well-typed terms meeting that condition, every infinite reduction, any sequence of simplification steps, converges strongly. A key payoff follows: any closed term of natural-number type reaches an actual numeral under every reduction path. For regular terms, the calculus defines the total functions of Gödel's System T exactly, no more and no fewer.
arxiv-2606-23673:
Wanjari and colleagues combine standard mental health screening tools into one decision support system, in a 2026 paper on digital health. Assessment today often relies on single questionnaires or opaque data driven models. Tools such as the PHQ-9 for depression and the GAD-7 for anxiety are validated, but each is usually applied alone. That leaves out cognition and personality, which also shape mental health.

Their framework, PsyBridge, unifies the two screeners with cognitive evaluation and personality profiling in one modular design. A weighted aggregation mechanism merges the parts into interpretable risk classes with recommendations. Testing uses a semi synthetic set of five hundred patient profiles from clinically grounded score distributions. PsyBridge reaches an overall accuracy of about eighty four percent, beating either screener alone on precision, recall, and F1 score. Ablation tests show the cognitive and personality parts steady the hardest middle risk predictions.
arxiv-2606-23873:
Devi estimates how long a financial market takes to settle into equilibrium when its statistics follow a generalized entropy rather than the classical one, in a 2026 paper on econophysics. Market returns have sharp peaks and fat tails, defying the Gaussian shape classical theory predicts. Tsallis entropy, designed for nonextensive systems, produces distributions with exactly those features. The equilibrium state maximizes the chosen entropy, and the relaxation time measures how quickly a system reaches it.

Devi tracks the market's distribution through a Euclidean gradient flow climbing toward maximum Tsallis entropy. The distribution stays in the q Gaussian family, with only its shape index and inverse temperature drifting. The resulting relaxation times exceed those from ordinary Shannon entropy. Longer relaxation suggests prediction may be possible over longer horizons than classical theory allows.
arxiv-2606-23973:
Holcombe builds an infinite family of regularized versions of Wallis's classical product for pi, and evaluates them in closed form, in a 2026 paper on mathematical analysis. Wallis's product expresses pi through a ratio built from all integers. Its reciprocal factor telescopes to one half. Holcombe raises that factor to growing polynomial powers, one product per power. The naive products diverge, so each is rescued by a minimal exponential counterterm cancelling exactly the non summable pieces of the logarithm's expansion.

The rescued products evaluate beautifully. Each logarithm becomes an explicit tail of the zeta function. The even members have closed forms built from pi, odd zeta values, and harmonic numbers. The odd members reduce to logarithmic gamma moments, bringing in Euler's constant and zeta derivatives. The products also connect to Kurokawa's multiple sine functions.
arxiv-2606-24173:
Patel benchmarks whether small transformer models are worth running on the device itself for fault detection. On-device systems must flag failures in real time, with no cloud to lean on, and tight hardware forces trade-offs among accuracy, speed, and size. Writing alone in 2026, Patel compares classic methods, random forests, gradient boosting, support vector machines, and logistic regression, against light transformers such as DistilBERT, TinyBERT, and MobileBERT. Three public datasets are used.

They cover turbofan engine wear, chip manufacturing, and predictive maintenance. On clean, well-separated sensor data, the transformers merely match the classic methods, while costing vastly more size and latency. TinyBERT-4L emerges as the most deployable transformer. Compressing weights to 8-bit integers shrinks models by a quarter and barely dents accuracy. Patel's two-stage adaptive pipeline sends nearly all cases through a tiny triage model. Only a small fraction goes to a larger expert.
arxiv-2606-24373:
Bickerton and colleagues test whether a famous bound on the solutions of Pfaffian equations can actually be attained. Pfaffian functions are built through chains of differential equations. Khovanskiĭ's theorem bounds the number of isolated real solutions of such systems. It uses three complexity parameters: chain degree, the functions' degrees, and the chain's order. The bound anchors Pfaffian geometry and o-minimality, yet its sharpness was largely unknown.

Parameter by parameter, the team constructs extremal examples. For chain degree, they build, for every degree and order, a single Pfaffian function. Its count of nondegenerate real zeros matches the predicted growth. For the degree parameters, systems are constructed whose regular common zeros grow at exactly the rate the theorem allows, as degrees increase. Two of the three dependencies are thus asymptotically sharp, the 2026 paper shows. The classical bound cannot be improved in those directions without extra hypotheses.
arxiv-2606-24673:
Qian-Nan Huang and seven colleagues report a new kind of magnonic frequency comb. A frequency comb is a set of evenly spaced spectral lines, like the teeth of a comb. Here the lines come from magnons, the quanta of spin waves inside a magnet. Normal combs of this kind keep one fixed spacing, which limits how finely they can measure. The team adds a second, weak microwave drive, precisely detuned, to a magnetic sphere.

With the extra drive, the spacing shrinks to a rational fraction of the original. The result is a dense grid holding hundreds of lines. Huang and colleagues trace the effect to parametric three magnon scattering, which their theory shows dominates the observations. The mechanism is special to magnets and needs far less power than comb formation in optomechanical systems. Like a vernier caliper for frequency, this comb suits precision metrology.
arxiv-2606-24773:
