Jaehoon Yoo introduces Posterior Refinement, a way to make fast language generation correct itself. Two families dominate, each with a flaw. Masked diffusion models lose quality when they generate many tokens at once, through factorisation error. Flow map language models generate whole sequences well in few steps, but cannot revise flexibly at inference time. Yoo's framework, FMLM plus, equips flow map models with masking style noise schedules.

While producing a full sequence in one step, the model also scores each token's global consistency after the fact. Posterior Refinement uses those scores to target weak tokens for adaptive self correction. The method matches discrete baseline quality with thirty two times fewer function evaluations. Benchmarks across diverse tasks show a better speed quality trade off than both parent families. Yoo presents the framework as a scalable base for high fidelity language modelling.
arxiv-2606-24873:
Guillermo Capobianco, Ulises Chialva, and Horacio Rotstein ask how to tell whether a reconstruction of a dynamical system from noisy data can be trusted. Researchers increasingly rebuild systems from measured time series with machine learning tools. Checking the rebuild by loss value alone is tempting. The authors show that loss based criteria, and standard metrics borrowed from deterministic dynamics, have real limits for stochastic systems.

Their alternative is an exploratory two step test of adequacy and reliability. It assesses a rebuild generally, without arbitrary error tolerance thresholds set by hand. The test's reach has limits, though, and the authors discuss them openly. System degeneracy and non identifiability blur what any test can certify. Features intrinsic to stochastic dynamics add further constraints. The test is framed as a diagnostic instrument that states where its own verdicts stop.
arxiv-2606-24973:
Malachy Fox, Kavi Samra, and Paul Jung ask whether off the shelf language models can mark school exams as reliably as human examiners. Their benchmark is real: over thirty two thousand double marked responses by students to GCSE mock exams. GCSEs are the national exams British pupils take at sixteen. The set spans 328 questions across five subjects and includes handwritten work.

Models match the examiner consensus well across subjects. The top performers agree with examiners more closely than the examiners agree with each other. High scores appear even on subjective work like English essays. Messy handwritten mathematics scripts are handled well too. Agreement stays uniform near the examiner line rather than collapsing on borderline scripts. Model size does not drive the differences much. Fox and colleagues read this as evidence for cost effective automated marking, with human level consistency on real exam material.
arxiv-2606-25573:
Radio telescopes with thousands of antennas produce data faster than it can be stored. Reconstruction methods must therefore be proven in simulation before precious observations are trusted to them. Ezequiel Centofanti and colleagues present argosim in 2026, a Python package that simulates radio interferometric observations end to end. Antenna positions go in one side; synthetic measurements and a cleaned image come out the other. The package stays modular and lightweight across major operating systems.

Its computing backend is written in JAX, which brings two advantages at once. Hardware acceleration handles large simulation volumes. Full differentiability lets gradients flow through a simulated observation into the methods being tested. That second property fits the coming era of giant arrays, where reconstruction is increasingly learned rather than hand tuned. The project is fully open source, with code public on GitHub.
arxiv-2606-25873:
Gregg Gallatin examines a quiet weakness in a standard optics tool: fitting wavefront measurements with Zernike polynomials, the round functions used to describe optical aberrations. His analysis asks how much the fitted values shift when the edge of the measured wavefront is placed slightly wrong. Because the data must be rescaled onto a unit circle, any error in that edge position feeds straight into the results. Modern sensors make the question pressing.

Working through the mathematics directly, Gallatin shows the sensitivity grows steeply with the order of the Zernike terms used. High-order fitted values become unreliable unless the true edge is known very precisely, and the edge error also breaks the clean separation between terms, producing spurious cross terms. His practical conclusion is blunt: pushing fits to ever higher orders quickly becomes pointless, and the leftover part of the wavefront is better handled with Fourier methods instead.
arxiv-2606-25973:
Giulian Biolo, Michael Tezza, Yuanjun Gong, and Fabio Massacci set up a human experiment on a timely question. Does help from a large language model make people better or worse at patching security flaws in code? Fixing vulnerabilities demands specialist knowledge most developers lack, so AI assistance is tempting. The risk is plausible-looking patches that pass ordinary checks while leaving the hole open.

Participants will patch real-world flaws twice in a balanced crossover design. One round uses model help, and one does not. A custom web application hosts the work. Hidden ghost tests probe patch integrity beyond the visible functional requirements. Speed, correctness on both functional and security tests, and participant perception are the planned measures. A small pilot run has already been completed, and its lessons shape the full study design the team lays out.
arxiv-2606-26373:
Sergey Kurilenko designs semantic search that does not leak the documents it indexes, a real risk because stored embeddings can be inverted back into readable text. Fully encrypted search is too slow at million-document scale, and adding noise wrecks ranking quality.

Kurilenko's hybrid splits the defense: documents are geometrically scrambled by truncation and a secret rotation, while queries are encrypted under CKKS. On a million-document corpus the protection kept, and slightly improved, ranking quality at sub-second speed, and an inversion attack fell to noise level. He also maps the limits: enough leaked pairs let an attacker undo the rotation.
arxiv-2606-26573:
Yu Wang, an independent researcher in Shenyang, proposes Pingquanqi, a framework for governing how people interact with AI agents. The name means Equalizer. Wang argues that language model agents are becoming permanent infrastructure, like the electrical grid. When the chain from builders to users leaks, users pay with their lifetime, their least replaceable resource.

Pingquanqi is meant as a design standard built into agent frameworks, much as accessibility rules are built into websites. Four components are specified. A user-state model reads conversation text to level knowledge proactively. A stop-loss rule based on Bayesian reasoning caps the cost of each session. Controlled friction breaks dependency loops that feed on themselves. The stated goal is adoption as a standard, not sale as a product.
arxiv-2606-26673:
Bryan Currie and nine colleagues ask whether the wiring of evolutionary networks can be recovered from genetic data. A phylogenetic network models species history with hybridisation, so lineages merge as well as split. Triangles inside such networks are notoriously hard to orient. Earlier work showed standard algebraic tools cannot fix triangle directions under some models.

The authors study three small networks with three leaves and embedded triangles. Their model uses the Jukes-Cantor rule for DNA change and no merging of lineages within populations. They give a complete semialgebraic description of each model, inequalities as well as equations. For any pair of models, the shared and differing regions are full-dimensional. The models are therefore genuinely different, yet neither is identifiable from data, even generically. The signal distinguishing them is too weak to orient the triangles.
arxiv-2606-26873:
Snehal Raj and five colleagues build quantum graph neural networks with guaranteed expressivity and a path to scale. Graph neural networks learn from relational data by passing messages between nodes. Quantum versions existed but barely used message passing and offered few guarantees. Trainability is a known bottleneck for quantum circuits generally.

Their network performs genuine message passing on quantum hardware. It respects graph symmetries exactly, treating relabelled graphs identically. Within the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, the standard yardstick for telling graphs apart, its distinguishing power can be placed at a chosen level. Training can start on small graphs, as with classical networks. That pre-training softens the usual training pathologies. Readout cost stays low as graphs grow, addressing scalability directly.
arxiv-2606-27273:
Liu builds a category of vector-space-like objects over perfect idylls, algebraic structures broader than fields. Idylls generalise fields and hyperfields, and modules over them mimic vector spaces. Naive linear algebra there stumbles: independence need not obey the matroid axioms that make dimension behave. Liu adds a sufficient axiom restoring those matroid properties for independence inside these linear spaces. Basic categorical features of the new setting are then mapped, in an algebra paper published in 2026.

One stark finding: the category of these linear spaces has no products. That absence explains why naive product-based linear algebra fails over idylls. Links among three worlds are drawn out: linear spaces over a perfect idyll, ordinary matroids, and matroids over an idyll. Existing theories of matroids and modules meet through those links. Tropical and sign hyperfield examples sit inside the same frame. Abstract algebra gains a cleaner map of a slippery borderland.
arxiv-2606-27573:
C Vardar-Acar and M Çağlar study processes that jump only downward. These are called spectrally negative Lévy processes. The authors ask how deep the worst falls can be. A drawdown is the drop from a past peak to a later low. The infimum is the lowest value reached. Their 2026 work watches the process up to a random exponential time limit.

The path is split at its lowest point. One split gives a part before the low and a part after it. A second split adds a middle section when the low comes before the high. The authors describe the early part with scale functions, special functions that encode these processes. The laws they derive are Doob h-transforms, reweighted versions of killed processes. The formulas give the largest drawdown on each separate piece. They also confirm the classical results known for Brownian motion.
arxiv-2606-28173:
Rui Luo, Pan-Pan Wang, Lin-Lin Yang, Xin-Lei Zhao, and Cheng-Gang Shao work on space-based detectors that will listen for gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime, from fleets of spacecraft exchanging laser beams. Instrument noise there dwarfs the signal, so a technique called time-delay interferometry recombines delayed measurements to cancel the worst noise.

Luo and colleagues offer a general recipe that builds each detector's response function, its expected output for a given wave, directly from the geometry of its laser links. They rewrite forty-five second-generation interferometry combinations in this language. For several combinations the new expressions are much simpler and physically clearer, and the recipe cuts the computing effort needed to process data for future missions.
arxiv-2606-28473:
Kirill Khoruzhii, Patrick Gelß, and Sebastian Pokutta finish a classification that the field had left open. Boolean cubic forms, polynomials in zero-one variables with terms up to degree three, come in families related by invertible linear changes of variables. Classifying them in ten variables means listing one representative of every family.

The list holds nearly three point seven million nonzero families. For each, the authors give a representative with few monomials, the size of its symmetry group, and an alternating rank with a written-out decomposition. Counting rank by rank did the heavy lifting, and two separate counting arguments, Burnside's lemma and the orbit-stabilizer identity, confirmed the list was complete. By polarization, the result also classifies alternating trilinear forms in dimension ten over the two-element field, completely and for the first time.
arxiv-2606-29273:
Liyanarachchi and four colleagues study how people and language models label the emotions in song lyrics. Lyrics need not match a song's overall emotion, so labelling them is subjective and little studied. The team built a new sentence-level dataset of lyrics and compared human labels with model labels to see where the two align.

Their observations highlight how subjective the task is and where annotators diverge. On that basis they present a hybrid framework that predicts where human and model labels are likely to misalign. Cases flagged as risky can then get more human attention, while clear cases lean on the model. The aim is to spend scarce human effort where disagreement is most likely, improving lyric emotion annotation without labelling everything twice. The framework and dataset are released openly for other researchers.
arxiv-2606-30073:
Robert Weiß, Sandro Wimberger, and David Guéry-Odelin turn dissipation from obstacle into tool for quantum control. In open quantum systems, slow relaxation modes usually set the manipulation speed limit. Their idea is to exploit the fast relaxation channels instead. A qubit with uneven, non-unital Bloch relaxation is their test case. The strategy has a bang, drift, bang rhythm.

A short coherent pulse first aims the Bloch vector along a fast direction. Free relaxation then carries the state most of the way to the target. At most one final corrective pulse finishes the move. Coherent control picks the channel; the bath does the transfer. For targets on the axis, they derive a closed-form speedup factor. Off-axis targets gain a further geometric amplification from an interception effect. That extra factor reaches about four to five. The mechanism fits magnetic resonance spins, nitrogen-vacancy centers, and superconducting circuits.
arxiv-2606-30373:
Yacong Gu and eight colleagues audit the security of AI demo apps hosted on model-sharing platforms. These apps give browser access to pretrained models for inference and tuning. Many are built by untrusted parties with weak isolation. Settings are often misconfigured as well. The team maps the app lifecycle to known risk taxonomies.

Five threat categories and ten attack vectors organize the study. Findings include broken access control and insecure resource reuse. Weak input validation and sensitive data exposure also appear. Three novel flaws stem from the platforms' architecture itself. Their framework, Insightor, scans over nine hundred seventy thousand public apps. Thousands leak credentials, the scan finds. Hundreds allow input injection leading to arbitrary code execution. Tens contain embedded backdoors suggesting active exploitation. All findings were responsibly disclosed to platforms and developers.
arxiv-2606-30573:
Mohit Raghavendra and three colleagues argue that coding-agent benchmarks miss how developers really work, and their 2026 response is a new testbed. Existing software-engineering tests hand agents complete requirements up front and grade solo implementation. Real users, the authors note, start vague, reveal needs gradually, inspect the workspace and add constraints along the way. SWE-Interact recreates that loop with a carefully designed user simulator.

Across frontier and open-weight models, skill at single-turn tasks transferred poorly to these interactive sessions. The best models solved about half of the single-turn baseline tasks but only about a quarter of the matching SWE-Interact tasks. Top models coped better with vagueness, kept going until every requirement surfaced, and wrote cleaner code. Even they overreached at times, forgot requirements and made technical mistakes. Weaker models stalled early, ignored instructions and reworked code more often.
arxiv-2606-30673:
Chunshi Wang and eleven colleagues present PolyFlow, a system that generates artist-style 3D meshes. Top mesh generators are autoregressive transformers. They build meshes one piece at a time and run far slower than parallel methods. Diffusion methods cannot handle meshes directly. Mesh connectivity is discrete, while their noise processes need continuous values.

PolyFlow bridges the gap with a compact topology embedder. It projects each vertex's position and normal into a continuous embedding. From that numeric code, the original connections can be recovered by a distance rule. With the embedder frozen, every mesh becomes a continuous state space mixing position, normal and topology. A transformer flow-matching model then denoises all vertices at once, guided by point-cloud features. On the Toys4K benchmark, PolyFlow beat step-by-step baselines on both Chamfer and Hausdorff distance, while letting users set the exact vertex count.
arxiv-2606-30773:
Sehmimul Hoque, Roger Melko and Pooya Ronagh use a generative model to warm-start simulations of a classic magnet model. The XY model places continuous spins on a lattice and underlies phenomena from magnets to superfluids. Markov chain Monte Carlo, the standard sampler, explores such continuous landscapes slowly, and reaching equilibrium can take very long. Worse, chains trained behaviour does not transfer across lattice sizes.

The team train a diffusion model, conditioned on temperature, on small XY lattices only. The model then generates plausible states for much larger lattices directly. A few Monte Carlo steps polish those generated states into accurate samples, judged by spin correlations and other physical observables. Compared with random starts, diffusion-warm sampling cut thermalization time by about an order of magnitude. The authors present the result as evidence that such models can help study continuous condensed-matter systems at scale.
arxiv-2606-30873:
A. D. Krupin, V. V. Strelkov and M. Yu. Ryabikin study how two kinds of resonance interact when intense laser light generates high harmonics in xenon. High harmonic generation turns laser light into extreme ultraviolet pulses. One resonance family, channel-closing resonances, appears when the energy needed to free an electron plus its quiver energy matches a whole number of photons. The other comes from bound-to-bound transitions whose energy gap, shifted by the field, likewise matches whole photons.

Using a simplified xenon model, the team compute harmonic yields across laser parameters. Where the two resonance systems cross, the yield shows a pronounced dip rather than a peak, with enhancement regions shifted slightly away. They link this to Fano-type spectral lines and note one resonance system can be controlled, which suits experiments.
arxiv-2606-30973:
Yifan Zhu, Kyeongmin Rim and James Pustejovsky extend a theory of dialogue friction to partners who literally see different worlds. Frictive Policy Optimization treats misunderstanding and repair not as noise but as a signal that helps partners build common ground. Its earlier forms assumed both speakers share one scene and differ only in how they interpret statements about it. The authors generalise to perceptual asymmetry, where each partner holds partial information, so the same phrase can point to different things depending on whose view grounds it.

Testing on the HCRC MapTask and with model probing, they find the friction measure stays valid only when judged inside each participant's own information horizon. A small class of ambiguous map layouts caused a disproportionate share of failures, including dialogues that looked successful while silently diverging. In probing, one informed viewpoint beat access to both.
arxiv-2606-31073:
Zhang and five colleagues build MultiUAV-Plat, a simulation platform for testing how large language models plan missions for teams of drones. Existing simulators stress flight physics or low-level control, and existing agent benchmarks rarely capture aerial constraints like partial observability, coverage, and vehicle assignment. MultiUAV-Plat exposes simple web-style interfaces, role-based information access, and hidden validation, so agents must work through realistic tool use.

On the platform the authors build a benchmark of 75 mission sessions, 1,500 natural-language tasks, and 9,396 validation checks covering target assignment, area search, and patrol. Their agent framework, Agent4Drone, organizes memory, planning, execution, and verification into separate stages. It passes 57.9 percent of tasks, well above a ReAct baseline at 30.6 percent, and cuts the failed-task rate by more than half.
arxiv-2606-31273:
Li offers a way to judge whether claims made with AI help stay within the evidence behind them. AI tools now draft ideas, run tests, and write papers, so the hard part is no longer output alone. The hard part is whether a final claim says only what the proof in hand allows.

Li breaks research into five steps: making a hypothesis, drawing out what a model implies, checking it against the outside world, updating belief, and fixing the claim. The gap between a claim and its proof gets its own name, as does the debt built up by claims made too soon. Sorting claim meanings into four kinds lets the frame grant some strong claims and block others.
arxiv-2606-31673:
Polletta and six others propose catching active galactic nucleus feedback in the act, using the future SHARP instrument on the Extremely Large Telescope. Their targets are eleven luminous but dust-obscured nuclei at cosmic noon that also host young radio jets and recent starbursts. This is a short-lived phase where feedback should be suppressing star formation while clearing the nuclear dust.

Integral-field spectroscopy with the VESPER mode would map stellar ages, star formation rate density, gas density and ionization state. It also maps the motions of stars and ionized gas, for direct comparison with the radio structures. That comparison separates jet-driven effects from radiative ones. The multiplexing capability extends the resolved mapping to at least 110 surrounding galaxies within 55 hours, characterizing environments and nuclear activity as one.
arxiv-2608-00073: A 2026 arXiv paper on unsupervised spatio-temporal stratification. The authors move beyond random partitioning. The clustering research. The archive keeps the paper open to all. The paper remains available to readers. Kept for readers. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
arxiv-2608-00273: A Focal-plane X-ray Polarimeter with Spectral and Timing Capabilities, arXiv 2608-00273. The X-ray polarimeter. Scholars can read the full paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Writers of history may cite it later in their work.
arxiv-2608-00373: Facility integration of the NASA IRTF adaptive secondary mirror, arXiv 2608-00373. The IRTF mirror. Scholars can read the full paper. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
bastiat-sophisms-stirling-1873:
Frederic Bastiat was a French writer who defended free trade with wit sharp enough to outlive his century. His Economic Sophisms, in Stirling's 1873 translation, collects short essays that mock the fallacies behind tariffs and protection. Each piece takes a popular error and walks it into absurdity.

The most famous piece is the candlemakers' petition, which asks the state to block the sun as unfair foreign competition. Another tells of a broken window, showing that repair spending is loss, not gain, once the unseen costs count. Free traders still quote Bastiat more than any other nineteenth-century writer.
cairnes-essays-political-economy-1873:
Cairnes gathered his Essays in Political Economy, Theoretical and Applied, in 1873. By then the Irish economist, plagued by ill health, had become one of the clearest voices of the classical school. The volume joins papers on pure theory with papers on the live questions of the day.

The theoretical essays work on value and on the wages question, while the applied ones take up the Irish land problem and other public issues. Cairnes tests theory against fact and is willing to follow the evidence against his own side. Readers meet classical economics at its most humane and practical in these pages. The essays show why Cairnes was valued as the conscience of his science in the years before the new marginal economics took over.
calderon-wonder-working-magician-maccart:
Pedro Calderón de la Barca wrote El mágico prodigioso in Spain in the 1630s, and Denis Florence MacCarthy gave it complete English verse in 1873. The Wonder-Working Magician tells the legend of Saint Cyprian of Antioch. Cyprian, a learned pagan, loves the Christian maiden Justina and seeks a demon's help to win her.

The demon fails against Justina's faith, and Cyprian starts to question his bargain. Study turns to conversion, and both lovers face martyrdom together. Calderón treats the Faust theme a century before Goethe, from the side of grace. MacCarthy's translation was part of his life work on Calderón. The play shows Spanish Golden Age drama at its most searching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jesuit-genera: This 1913 reference piece on the Jesuit generals — the pre-suppression chiefs. John Hungerford Pollen lists the mighty line. Ignatius founded the holy rule. Ricci faced the papal storm. The order bless their names. Their 1541 founding is famed. Their 1773 end is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-suppressi: The suppression of the Jesuits was the fall of 1773. This very long entry examines its Clement, its Bourbons, and its causes. The brief of the dissolved Society: its fatal 1773 crowned Rome in the Quirinal of the old Clement.
cia-0000009773:
Hoa Lo prison in Hanoi is sketched in a July 1971 CIA paper on the detention and interrogation center for American prisoners. Hoa Lo, called the Hanoi Hilton by its inmates, was the system's best-known site. A sketch implies layout: walls, blocks, and rooms drawn from sources.

Knowing the layout served interrogation studies, rescue thinking, and debriefing of freed men later. Former prisoners could confirm or correct each drawn detail. The sketch also preserves how the prison looked to those watching from outside. It is an architectural record of the war's most famous address of captivity.
cia-0000010873:
One year after its first look, the CIA returned in March 1952 to the question of what Communist China could do and what it wanted. The Korean War had settled into a grinding stalemate by then. The new estimate reweighed Beijing's capabilities and intentions, with Taiwan still the prize both Chinese regimes claimed.

Analysts drew on the hard lessons of Korea, where Chinese armies had fought the United States to a standstill. They asked how much risk the young People's Republic would accept in pressing its claims. The paper shows Washington's central unanswered question of the era: how far the new China would go.
cia-0000012273:
The chalk problem is the subject of letter number seven, sent from Sledge to Compass in January 1961. Chalk was one of the marking methods in the Penkovsky operation. Such small signs told a source or a courier that a meeting or a drop was on. A flaw in those marks was no small thing; a missed or doubled signal could expose the whole case.

The letter works through the trouble in the flat tone of case correspondence. It shows officers tending the machinery of contact, detail by detail. For readers, it reveals how great operations hung on marks as small as a scrawl of chalk.
cia-0000012373:
In November 1962 the CIA and Britain's Secret Intelligence Service negotiated over a letter to the KGB and GRU. A record preserves the talks between the two services. Penkovsky had been arrested weeks before, during the Cuban missile crisis. The allies now weighed how to play the exposure. What could a message to Soviet intelligence win for the men in Soviet hands?

Endgame diplomacy around a blown case was stage-managed as carefully as any operation. The cousins counseled together over signals to send east. For readers, the record shows the case's last act being written jointly in London and Washington.
cia-0000013873: North Vietnamese teams that questioned new prisoners are the subject of a CIA report dated August 4, 1967. The report lays out how prisoners were processed after capture. Intake steps decided a man's camp, his file, and often his treatment. Knowing the system helped U.S. officials guess what captured men would face in their first hard weeks.
cia-0000015273: Talks with Soviet scientists on unidentified flying objects fill a CIA report dated July 5, 1967. Scientists who would speak at all on the topic were rare finds. Their views hinted at how much the Soviet state cared, or did not. The report preserves a cross border chat on a subject both sides handled with care.
cia-0000015473: Unidentified aircraft were reported over Spain, Greece, and North Africa in a CIA record dated in 1954. The three places ring the Mediterranean Sea, a busy crossroads of air and sea traffic. Reports from its shores reached Washington through many channels. Gathered in one entry, they show officials watching the whole inland sea for strange traffic in the mid nineteen fifties.
cia-0000020273: Whether Britain and France might resort to military action against Egypt is weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1956. The clipped title ties the question to the crisis of that year, when Egypt seized the Suez Canal. Two old allies were furious, and Washington had to guess their next step. The paper's task was forecast, the hardest kind of intelligence work.
cia-0000037173:
Two alleged American prisoners were detained at the Cam Thuy detention camp, a CIA record dated October 3, 1983 states. Cam Thuy is a district in Thanh Hoa province, south of Hanoi. The report is one of many camp claims filed during that busy year.

Inside, the detention claim is recorded with its camp and its number of prisoners. A named camp gave analysts something solid to compare with older camp reports. The file adds one more point to the map of places where Americans were said, in the early 1980s, to still be held against their will.
cia-0000042873:
An update on the Jesuit killings fills a CIA record dated January 1, 1990. Unlike its numbered companions, this update carries no series number. It belongs to the same steady flow of case reporting that winter.

Inside, the latest state of the case is set down for the record. Steady updates kept the file current for officials reading abroad. They also built the paper trail by which the case can now be followed. Without that trail, the probe's slow turns would be far harder to trace today. Month by month, the updates show an investigation moving through arrests and courtrooms under the eyes of the whole world.
cia-0000045273:
Managua reported that Salvadoran army officials met on the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated August 4, 1985. Nicaragua's capital watched its neighbor's crisis with close interest. The two countries stood on opposite sides of the region's wars.

Inside, the Nicaraguan report of the officers' meeting is preserved. Neighbors report each other's troubles with a mix of news and advantage. A generals' meeting in San Salvador was worth a dispatch in Managua. What the Salvadoran army decided behind closed doors could shift the whole region's balance within a week. The file holds that watchful neighbor's view, the last of this set's many angles on a kidnapping that the whole region followed.
cia-0000049273: Declassified CIA document 0000049273, dated January 2, 1990, records a briefing on Central America prepared for Lee H. Hamilton, a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. The file's subject is the briefing itself and the region it covered. It survives as a brief agency record of a session meant to inform a senior member of Congress about Central American affairs.
cia-0000102973:
USSR: Forced Labor System is a CIA Special Analysis released as declassified document 0000102973, dated October 5, 1985 in the catalog. The sample text is dated November 29, 1985. It puts forced laborers at more than four and a half million people, about three percent of the total Soviet labor force.

More than two point three million laborers were confined, and the camp population had grown by fourteen percent since 1977, it says. Most forced laborers worked in construction and manufacturing, with others in logging, oil, chemicals, and concrete work. They also mined coal, gold, and other minerals, the analysis adds, under inhumane conditions.
cia-0000106273: Agreement of Coup Group to Postpone Action Until After Elections is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000106273, dated June 5, 1965. The title reports a decision: a coup group agreed to wait until after elections. No country or leader is named in the heading itself. The brief record is a coup timing item, dated in the summer of 1965.
cia-0000108073: Status of Imprisoned American Pilots in the SAM Neua Area of Houa Phan Province is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000108073, dated July 6, 1966. The heading asks after a status: American pilots held in one area of Laos. Sam Neua and Houa Phan Province are both named in full. The brief record is a prisoner status item from the summer of 1966.
cia-0000108473: Weekly Situation Report on Internatioal Terrorism Report - 2 July 1980 is the heading, with international misspelled, on declassified CIA document 0000108473, dated May 1, 1980. The title dates its week to July 2, 1980, two months after the file date. That gap stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record preserves the misspelling exactly as released.
cia-0000109073: Dated July 2, 1967, with its publication date marked as an estimate, declassified CIA document 0000109073 reports on the economic prospects for Communist China. Its heading breaks off at Communist Ch, mid-name in the title. Report is the form named at the front of the heading itself. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000112273: British Guiana Moves Toward Independence is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000112273, dated September 5, 1965. The heading describes a colony in motion, toward independence, in five plain words. No leader or date for independence is named in the title itself. The brief record is an independence item, filed in the autumn of 1965 as released in the files.
cia-0000119173:
Written on April 3, 1964, this CIA report describes the political situation in Brazil. Its timing gives it weight: Brazil's military seized power that same month and pushed out President Goulart. The report therefore catches the country at the exact moment its government changed hands.

Inside, the agency sets out its reading of the forces at work in Brazil as the takeover unfolded. Reports written in the middle of events show what Washington knew, what it guessed, and what it got wrong. For readers, this one offers a front-row view of how a coup looked to American analysts while it was still fresh and its long rule still ahead.
cia-0000126873: Dated August 1968, this CIA report tallies the costs of the invasion to Czechoslovakia and to the Warsaw Pact powers alike, the heading breaking off. Occupation proved expensive for everyone involved in it. The paper gives the price on both sides of the action. Two-sided cost papers were written for officials weighing pressure, since knowing the invasion's price to Moscow helped Washington judge how firmly the Kremlin would hold on.
cia-0000126973: A June 1975 CIA Weekly Review covers Angola: a new ceasefire, a front regrouping, and an open Soviet role, the heading breaking off. The proxy war over the colony was taking shape in plain sight. The review gathers that week's developments for senior readers. Headline strings in weekly reviews were written to be scanned, and this one compresses a whole turning week of Angola's war into four short phrases.
cia-0000132573: Cuban foreign exchange reserves reportedly exhausted fill item 1 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated October 3, 1960. Empty reserves meant the revolution would depend on Soviet aid to pay for imports. Hard currency had been draining away since Castro took power. The short item reports the state of the reserves as analysts understood them.
cia-0000132673: Panama throwing out one more Cuban consul fills a CIA paper dated March 1, 1961. The word another in the headline tells its own story about that year. Cuban consuls in Panama were being shown the door one by one as ties soured. The short paper records the latest expulsion and the charge said to stand behind it.
cia-0000132773: Three CIA papers on Cuba carry the date July 4, 1960, and this entry completes the set. The triple filing shows the priority the island held in the summer of 1960, when the series was a key reporting product. Each paper in the set approaches the same fast-moving story separately. The declassified copy comes via the CIA Reading Room and the Internet Archive.
cia-0000134273: Fresh communist bids to run Cuban labor fill a CIA paper dated October 4, 1959. It stands beside a paper on the Cuban labor congress from the same season. The party was moving on the unions post by post that fall. Control of labor meant control of the docks, the mills, and the streets. The short paper tracks the latest bids and their outcomes.
cia-0000135873: Dated about March 1954, a declassified CIA document deals with operational death notices, with the name in the heading deleted by the censors. All of it feeds into PBSUCCESS, the agency operation against the Arbenz government in the months before the June 1954 coup. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136273: The open CIA files hold a cable dated 1 May 1954 that deals with speeding tactical messages to Sherwood, traffic too urgent for the regular cable channel. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136373: Situation reports for 6, 7, and 8 July fill this 9 July 1954 LINCOLN cable to ONTRICH. An officer met CALLIGERIS early on 7 July, cracked down hard, and told him communists must be controlled immediately and he should take over the junta before Friday. On 8 July CALLIGERIS was unanimously elected permanent president of the junta, a mass demonstration was stopped, and appointments in the ministries favored his group. Oscar Mendoza became chief of the armed forces.
cia-0000136773: From 1960, a Spanish document in the 2506 Brigade files, dated only to the year in the catalog. The brigade was a CIA-trained exile force in its buildup period, its members Cuban volunteers against Castro. The record states no month or subject for this item. It is preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, one of the brigade's early records, its contents for the reader of the text to establish.
cia-0000136873: KUSODA rejects a team's exit plan in this March 1954 cable. A flight manifest would show the subjects passing through. That might start a check-back at the far end. The airline might also refuse to let them off. Neither man has proper entry papers. Headquarters offers other routes instead. One man can fly commercial under alias and return. Or he can fly under his true name on a direct flight. The men should arrive apart and meet only at the end point.
cia-0000137473: Kennedy's Venezuela visit was a decisive victory over communist extremists. These comments on the December 1961 trip argue that case. Security rested on the armed forces. The visit strengthened their unity. It tested their loyalty to constitutional government, and they passed. The Union Republicana Democratica was weakened as legitimate opposition. It will take long to recover, if it ever does. Castroite student leaders took a severe blow. The propaganda effort was very successful and well timed. Catholic Church support removed doubts and fears. A large, enthusiastic turnout followed.
cia-0000139473: Document 0000139473 is a second 1986 report from the hostage location task force that served the Director of Central Intelligence. The mid-1980s were the worst years of the Lebanon hostage crisis, and Washington kept a standing effort to learn where the captives were held and by whom. Reports in this series recorded that search for the DCI. Which hostages this file covers, the catalog does not state. It endures as part of the paper trail of a grim, often fruitless mission.
cia-03172473: September 1958 opened with this daily intelligence briefing. The bulletin covered the communist bloc and beyond. The Cold War's daily pulse, captured. The library keeps the document safe. This file preserves that declassified CIA bulletin. Kept for readers.
cia-03185373: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1957/08/13, a CIA publication. Another August briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-06475773: SPECIAL DAILY REPORT ON NORTH VIETNAM - 1968/01/10, a CIA publication. The Vietnam report. This file preserves that declassified paper. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
cia-06485473: MEETING OF DR. MARTIN LUTHER KING WITH ITALIAN LEFTIST, a CIA document. The King meeting. This file preserves that declassified paper. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-06844973: TASK FORCE REPORT ON HISTORICAL REVIEW PROGRAM DECLASSIFICATION GUIDELINES, a CIA document. The declassification rules. This file preserves that declassified paper. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-family-jewels-1973:
The CIA once made a list of its own sins, and the list stayed sealed for thirty-four years. The Family Jewels, drawn up in 1973 for Director James Schlesinger, gathers acts that might break law or charter. The sheaf of memos came out at last in 2007.

Mail opening, wire taps, plots on foreign chiefs, and drug tests crowd the pages in the agency's own flat prose. The file fed the great probes of the mid 1970s once its gist leaked out. It is the agency confessing to itself, act by act. Few files show Cold War spy work's dark side so raw.
constitution-bahamas-1973:
The Bahamas adopted this constitution at independence from Britain in 1973. Chapter one declares the constitution itself the supreme law. Chapters then cover citizenship and the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms of the individual. Those rights include life, liberty, fair trial, and freedom of conscience, speech, and assembly.

A Governor General represents the monarch as head of state. Real power sits with a cabinet led by a prime minister, drawn from Parliament. Parliament has two houses, an appointed Senate and an elected House of Assembly. Later chapters cover the courts, the public service, and public finance. The orderly layout, shared with other Caribbean independence charters, still frames Bahamian government today.
d-johannis-tackii-triplex-phasis-sophicu: D. Johannis Tackii Triplex phasis sophicus, 1673. The triple phase. The archive keeps it. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc10026873:
Merenstein and many co-authors review emerging questions about probiotic safety in a 2023 paper. Probiotics are live microbes sold for gut and general health. Healthy shoppers use them widely, and clinics use them with patients who are frail or very ill. Most use looks safe, but rare harms have been reported.

The authors survey known and possible risks as new strains reach new groups of users. They call for clearer labels, better tracking of harms, and care with high-risk patients. The paper is a measured guide for clinicians and makers alike.
europmc-pmc10086073:
Li and co-authors review blood vessel diseases caused by diabetes, their mechanisms, and treatment strategies, in a 2023 paper. Vessel damage is the main source of harm in diabetes, driving heart attacks, strokes, kidney failure, and blindness. Care aimed at one vessel problem at a time no longer fits how the disease behaves.

The authors present the idea of diabetic panvascular disease, damage across the whole vessel network. They trace shared mechanisms, from high sugar to inflammation. They then survey treatments that protect vessels as a system, not organ by organ.
europmc-pmc10367273:
Proctor and co-authors looked back in 2023 on ten years of research into how new practices take hold. In 2011 the lead author had named eight signs of success, such as whether staff accept and keep using a new method. The team traced all later work that cited that paper. They screened 1,346 items and kept 400 studies with real data.

Acceptance was the most studied sign, in 52.1% of the kept work. Cost was the least studied, at just 7.8%. Most studies sat in health or mental health settings. Proctor found few tests of which steps cause which signs of success. Few studies tied those signs to better health for patients either.
europmc-pmc10514873:
Gentilini led the SOUND trial in 2023, with the SOUND Trial Group, on whether some breast surgery can be skipped. The question was if women with small tumours still need a check of armpit lymph nodes. That check, a sentinel node biopsy, samples the first nodes a cancer might reach. Women entered with tumours of 2 cm or less and a clear ultrasound scan of those nodes.

In all, 1,463 women were split at random to biopsy or no armpit surgery. Gentilini found that five-year freedom from distant spread was no worse without surgery. The result says such women can safely skip armpit surgery. That holds when the lost node facts would not change the care plan after surgery.
europmc-pmc10869273:
Hie and co-authors used AI language models to improve human antibodies in this 2024 study. Antibodies are proteins the immune system makes to grab germs and toxins. Finding better versions by chance mutation is slow, since most changes do harm. Language models are AI systems trained on protein sequences, and they learn which changes nature tends to allow.

The team let such a model suggest changes for seven antibodies, with no facts given about their targets. They tested 20 or fewer variants per antibody over just two lab rounds. Binding strength rose up to sevenfold for four mature medical antibodies. For three young ones it rose up to 160-fold. Many designs also held up well to heat and blocked test viruses. The authors say the trick works across many protein types.
europmc-pmc1181873:
Wearing, Rohani, and Keeling asked in 2005 which math models truly fit disease outbreaks. Such models guide health officials who must judge control options. They also predict how well each option might work. Two hidden assumptions sit at the core of most models in use.

One assumption skips the latent period, the quiet gap after infection before spread starts. The other treats those waiting times as simple random draws. Wearing shows both choices lower key spread estimates and flatter control plans. Careful model design gives safer advice for real outbreaks. The team also fitted these models to data from a real flu outbreak for a check.
europmc-pmc1233573:
Frand, Russel, and Ruvkun hunted the genes behind worm molting in 2005. Molting is how worms and insects shed their outer shell. Its hormone controls and shell-making steps were poorly known. The roundworm C. elegans offered a clean test case.

A genome-wide screen silenced genes one by one. It found 159 genes needed for normal molting. They include hormone signals, secreted peptides, and shell enzymes. Many switch on in a pulse just before each molt. Frand notes shared genes in parasitic worms. Those genes could become targets for new pest drugs.
europmc-pmc1360673:
Xue and co-authors taught a computer to tell real microRNA precursors from fakes in 2005. MicroRNA precursors fold into hairpin shapes. Genomes contain many similar hairpins that are not real precursors. Most search methods relied on species comparisons to filter them.

New features captured local structure and sequence patterns together. A support vector machine learned from those features. On human data it reached about 90 percent accuracy. Remarkably, the human-trained classifier transferred to other species data. Xue supplies a match-free route to discovering new microRNAs. The training set came from known human hairpins.
europmc-pmc1475773:
Tiny RNAs called microRNAs can mute a gene without cutting its message. Chu and Rana pinpointed a helper protein for that muting in 2006. The protein, RCK/p54, unwinds RNA and partners with the silencing machinery in human cells. It also helps form P-bodies, cell spots where messages are stored or broken down.

Removing RCK/p54 scattered those spots and freed genes from microRNA control. Yet cutting of messages by a sister process went on fine. Chu proposes that silencing complexes use RCK/p54 to block protein building. The microRNA itself picks which message gets blocked, by matching its tail end.
europmc-pmc1487173:
Sticky films of yeast on catheters cause stubborn infections. Nobile and co-authors traced how Candida albicans, a fungal pathogen, builds those biofilms in 2006. A control protein, Bcr1, was known to govern film growth on plastic. They found it switches on surface proteins that glue cells down.

One glue protein, Als3, proved key in lab tests. Yeast lacking Als3 failed to form films in a dish. Extra Als3 rescued film growth in mutants lacking Bcr1, both in dishes and in a rat vein catheter model. Nobile notes other Bcr1 targets, Als1, Hwp1, and Ece1, also help. Bcr1 clearly works inside living hosts, not just in lab glass.
europmc-pmc1578573:
Cadmium, a metal long used in industry, harms the body in quiet ways. Godt and co-authors reviewed its toxicity in 2006. The metal came under scientific scrutiny in the mid-1900s, after severe poisoning cases drew attention.

The review traces where exposure comes from, how the body absorbs the metal, and how it damages organs. Kidneys bear a heavy share of the burden, since cadmium builds up there over years. Bones and lungs also suffer. Godt sums up old and new findings to size the hazard cadmium poses to human health today.
europmc-pmc1636673:
Protein complexes, not lone proteins, do most cell work. Levy and co-authors built the first full classification of them in 2006, called 3D complex. Over half the structures in the Protein Data Bank are complexes of two or more chains.

Representing each complex as a graph of its subunits, they built a hierarchy of forms. Between half and two thirds of known structures are multi-chain, depending on counting rules. Most complexes hold four subunits or fewer, and symmetry is common even in mixed complexes. Levy also flagged likely errors in database assignments of biological units. The resource is public online.
europmc-pmc1892573:
Tang, Thornton and Stoneking presented in 2007 a sharper way to spot recent positive selection in human DNA. A selective sweep, where a helpful variant races upward in one population, leaves a telltale stretch of uniform DNA around it. Scans for such signals map how humans adapted locally.

Their method contrasts the length of that uniform stretch, called extended haplotype homozygosity, between populations. It targets sweeps that are nearly or just completed, the hardest to catch. Applied to two large public datasets, it found widespread local selection signals, both finished and partial sweeps. Because human history itself can mimic selection, they built the test to stay robust across many population-history and sampling models. Simulations showed strong power for strong sweeps that had already swept through most of a population.
europmc-pmc2124873: A medical paper on studies in isoagglutination, transfusion and intravascular questions. The blood groups. This article preserves that hematology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2125273: A medical paper with further investigations on substances inhibiting tumor growth. The cancer blockers. This article preserves that oncology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2125373: A medical paper on the action of the lethal dose of strophanthin in normal animals and in animals with heart disease. The deadly heart drug. This article preserves that pharmacology. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2126073: A medical paper on antibody production after partial adrenalectomy in guinea pigs. The glandless immunity. This article preserves that immunology. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128473: A medical paper with studies on oxidation and reduction by pneumococcus, peroxide production. The germ's chemistry. This article preserves that biochemistry. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2140473: A biology paper on the phagocytosis of solid particles, quartz. The eaten sand. This article preserves that cell biology. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2361173:
Karakas, Bachman, and Park reviewed mutations in the PIK3CA gene in 2006. PIK3CA makes a working part of PI3K, an enzyme in a signal path that tells cells to grow and survive. That path had already been tied to cancer, and new reports kept finding PIK3CA faults in tumors.

The authors gathered reports from the previous year covering many cancer types. They found the gene mutated again and again across human malignancies, marking it as a true cancer driver rather than a bystander. Because the enzyme can be blocked by drugs, they discussed what the mutations could mean for diagnosis and for targeted therapy. Testing a tumor for PIK3CA faults, they argued, might one day guide which patients get PI3K-blocking drugs.
europmc-pmc2375073:
Giatromanolaki and colleagues measured oxygen-sensing proteins in lung cancer in 2001. The proteins, HIF1 alpha and HIF2 alpha, rise when cells run short of oxygen and switch on genes for blood vessel growth and energy use. The cancer was operable non-small-cell lung cancer, the common form.

They stained 108 tumor samples. HIF1 alpha appeared in 62% of cases and HIF2 alpha in 50%, while healthy lung stained weakly or not at all. Both proteins tracked high levels of vessel growth factors such as VEGF. Patients whose tumors showed HIF2 alpha died sooner, and this held even in tumors with few blood vessels. In the combined analysis HIF2 alpha stayed an independent warning sign of poor outcome. HIF1 alpha showed only a weak trend the same way. The authors suggested drugs aimed at the HIF pathway.
europmc-pmc2387073:
Dugan and a large team mapped bird flu diversity in wild birds in 2008. Wild birds are the natural home of type A influenza viruses, the family behind human flu pandemics. The team read the full genomes of 167 viruses gathered from 14 bird species at four US sites.

The viruses spanned 29 combinations of the two surface proteins used to name flu subtypes. Up to 26% of samples showed signs of mixed infection with more than one subtype at once. Family tree analysis, the largest of its kind then, revealed constant genome reshuffling. Flu viruses swap their eight genome segments when two infect one bird, and here segments mixed with no fixed pattern. Some segments had even crossed between hemispheres. The authors called these short-lived genome constellations, unlike the stable sets seen in mammal flu.
europmc-pmc2429973:
McIntosh, Kovacevic, and Itier measured brain signal variability during development in 2008. Adults answer more steadily than children on mental tasks, so the natural guess was that mature brains also fluctuate less. The team recorded scalp electrical signals, called EEG, while children aged 8 to 15 and adults aged 20 to 33 did a face memory task.

Children were indeed slower, less accurate, and more variable in response times. Yet their brain signals varied less from trial to trial than adults' signals did. Brain variability rose with age and tracked performance: more variability meant steadier responses and better accuracy. The authors read this as growing neural complexity. A more variable brain holds a wider stock of states and switches between them more fluidly, they argued, making variability an index of mental capacity.
europmc-pmc2435273:
Supekar, Menon, Rubin, Musen, and Greicius mapped resting brain networks in Alzheimer's disease in 2008. Even at rest, brain areas pulse in coordinated networks with a small-world layout: tight local clusters joined by short paths. The team asked whether that layout breaks down in Alzheimer's, the commonest dementia.

They scanned 21 patients and 18 matched healthy adults with fMRI, a brain imaging method, while they rested. In healthy adults the networks showed the expected small-world pattern at low frequencies. Patient networks had lost it: the clustering measure was significantly lower, signalling weakened local links. The drop centred on the hippocampus, a memory structure, on both sides of the brain. Clustering alone separated patients from controls with 72% sensitivity and 78% specificity. The authors proposed network measures as imaging markers of the disease.
europmc-pmc2447873:
Gao and colleagues catalogued the bacteria living on psoriatic skin without growing them in dishes in this study. Psoriasis is an inflamed, scaly skin disease of unknown cause. Earlier work relied on cultures, which miss most skin microbes, so the team read bacterial DNA directly from skin samples.

They took 19 samples from six patients, 13 from lesions and six from healthy-looking skin, and sequenced 1,925 gene clones. About 95.6% matched known bacteria, spanning 189 species-level groups. Lesions were dominated by the Firmicutes group at 46.2% of clones, far above its 24.4% share on healthy volunteers' skin. The usual skin leaders, Actinobacteria, fell from 47.6% on healthy skin to 37.3% in lesions in this data. One common skin genus, Propionibacterium, dropped from 21.1% on healthy skin to 2.9% in lesions.
europmc-pmc2559873:
Dunker and colleagues reviewed in 2008 a decade of work on intrinsically disordered proteins, proteins that never fold into a fixed shape. The classic view held that a protein's function flows from its folded structure, like a key fitting a lock. Yet experimenters had long reported proteins that work while unfolded, and a predictor from the authors' group had opened the field ten years earlier.

Genome-wide predictions now show disordered proteins are everywhere, across all three domains of life, and number far beyond the few early examples. Many key functions depend directly on the unfolded state, including signalling and binding that folding would prevent. The authors argue textbooks still ignore this evidence. Disorder prediction, they say, has forced a rewrite of how structure relates to function.
europmc-pmc2667673:
Danaei and colleagues counted in 2009 how many American deaths could be blamed on fixable risks, from smoking to poor diet. Death certificates name the final disease but not the habits and body measures that led there. Earlier counts had used patchy methods and left out diet almost entirely, so the authors rebuilt the tally on one shared footing.

They combined national survey data on exposure with known risk sizes for each disease. Smoking and high blood pressure came out as the two largest killers, ahead of excess weight, inactivity, and high blood sugar. Both leaders already have proven treatments and public programs, which makes their toll a policy choice as much as a medical fact. The study gives officials a ranked list of where prevention would save the most lives.
europmc-pmc2700273:
Kalmar and colleagues showed in 2009 that embryonic stem cells are not a uniform pool. Each cell's level of Nanog, a core stemness factor, flickers up and down over time. The flicker steers its fate. Stem cells keep the ability to become any tissue, held by a small gene network. The textbook picture treated that state as stable and identical in every cell.

Tracking single living cells, the team watched Nanog levels rise and fall on their own. Cells caught in a low phase were primed to specialize, quick to answer a differentiation signal. Cells in a high phase resisted and stayed flexible. Crucially, low cells could climb back: the fluctuation is reversible, not a one-way exit. Fate decisions in the dish, the authors argue, are partly a matter of timing, of which phase a cell happens to occupy when the signal arrives.
europmc-pmc2729073:
Patrick and co-authors ran a randomized trial in 2009. They tested a weight-loss program built mainly on daily text and picture messages to mobile phones. No prior study had tested whether weight control could be driven this way in overweight adults. Seventy-five adults were assigned to monthly print materials alone, or to the message program plus print and brief monthly counselor calls.

After four months, the message group lost more weight than the print-only group, an adjusted difference of about two kilograms. Average loss in the message group was close to three percent of body weight. Nearly all message-group participants who finished said they would recommend the program to friends and family, which suggests phone messaging is a practical channel for weight support.
europmc-pmc2750773:
Osborne, Wakeling, and Nicholson reviewed in 2004 fulvestrant, a new breast cancer drug. It blocks the estrogen receptor and lowers the receptor itself. It has no estrogen-like effects. Hormone therapies are favored for hormone-sensitive metastatic breast cancer because they are well tolerated. Older drugs such as tamoxifen partly mimic estrogen, and cross-resistance limits how long similar drugs can be sequenced.

Their review explains estrogen signaling and how fulvestrant differs. It binds the receptor, blocks it fully, and drives its loss, so receptor levels fall in the cell. Lab and clinical data support that novel mechanism. A drug that is not cross-resistant lets doctors extend tolerated hormone treatment before turning to harsher chemotherapy. Women who still respond to hormone drugs gain more time on gentler care first.
europmc-pmc2791173:
Lorincz and colleagues recorded single nerve cells in awake cats to learn how the brain's alpha rhythm shapes visual signals. Alpha waves are slow rhythms tied to sight and attention. The team watched relay cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus, a relay station that passes visual news from the eye toward the cortex.

Relay cells fell into two groups whose firing was briefly hushed at opposite peaks of the alpha wave. That timed hushing came from bursts of inhibition, meaning calming signals, sent by nearby interneurons between relay cells. The pattern chops the stream of visual signals into timed frames, which may match how seeing itself comes in brief snapshots.
europmc-pmc2825373:
Stephan, Penny, Moran, den Ouden, Daunizeau, and Friston wrote ten simple rules in 2010 for dynamic causal modeling, a math approach that infers hidden brain activity from scans. The method estimates how strongly brain regions drive each other and how tasks change those links. It has spread fast across brain imaging since its debut in 2003, but its complexity traps new users.

The rules walk through good practice, from setting up the model to reading its outputs with care. Each model states how unseen neuron groups evolve over time, then links that hidden activity to the measured signal through a body-based forward model. Judgments stay Bayesian, meaning prior knowledge shapes every estimate and models are compared by evidence. The authors aim the tutorial at the growing user community.
europmc-pmc2831073:
Boyko and colleagues showed in 2010 that stressed Arabidopsis plants pass a tougher state to their offspring, and that the handoff needs chemical tags on DNA. Offspring of plants hit by salt, cold, heat, flood, or ultraviolet light rearranged their DNA more often. They also carried more genome-wide methylation tags and withstood stress better than offspring of sheltered plants.

The boost lasted one generation, not more. A drug that strips methylation tags changed both tag levels and tolerance in the offspring. Plants missing either of two enzymes that make small silencing RNAs, called DCL2 and DCL3, lost most of the inherited response. The authors tie the effect to altered methylation plus the small RNA silencing pathway working together.
europmc-pmc2836773:
Webb, Joseph, Yardley, and Michie pooled results in 2010 from eighty-five trials of internet programs meant to change health behavior, covering over forty-three thousand people. Websites can coach smoking quits, exercise, or diet at scale, yet earlier reviews never coded what the programs actually contained, so nobody knew which ingredients worked.

On average the programs nudged behavior by a small but real amount. Effects grew when a program leaned harder on theory, and programs built on the theory of planned behavior, which weighs intentions and social pressure, did notably better. Programs using more behavior change techniques also did better. Extra contact channels helped most of all, above all text messages to phones.
europmc-pmc2857873:
Pancreatic cancer is rarely curable once it spreads, so Gillen and colleagues asked in 2010 whether treatment before surgery could help more patients reach an operation. Their systematic review and combined analysis covered studies of pre-surgery drug or radiation therapy. The therapy is called neoadjuvant, meaning it is given first to shrink the tumor.

Pooling the published studies, Gillen found that tumors judged removable shrank or stayed stable in most treated patients, and surgery rates stayed high in that group. Among patients whose tumors first looked unremovable, about one in three could still have surgery after treatment, a rate close to that group overall. The authors argue such patients belong in pre-surgery treatment programs rather than being ruled out at once.
europmc-pmc2887173:
Schöchl and colleagues reported in 2010 an Austrian trauma program that treats bleeding by replacing specific clotting factors, guided by a bedside clot test. The test, thromboelastometry, watches a blood sample clot in minutes and shows which ingredient is missing. The analysis covered one hundred thirty-one major trauma patients who each needed at least five units of red cells within a day.

Nearly all received fibrinogen concentrate, the protein that forms the clot mesh, as their first treatment. Most also received a concentrate of several other clotting factors, and a few needed platelets when the mesh stayed weak. Deaths in the group ran lower than two standard injury scores predicted for such severe cases. Test-guided concentrates may cut blood product use, the authors argue, though only a randomized trial can prove it.
europmc-pmc2955973:
Merrall and co-authors pooled studies on drug deaths shortly after release from prison in a 2010 meta-analysis. Time inside lowers tolerance to drugs such as heroin, making the first weeks outside especially dangerous.

Six prison systems contributed follow-up covering tens of thousands of person-years and over a thousand early deaths, most drug-related. Risk in the first two weeks ran several times higher than in later weeks, though the multiple varied by country, from about threefold to more than eightfold. Weeks three and four stayed moderately risky. The authors urge release planning focused on that window.
europmc-pmc3028573:
de Boer and colleagues tested in 2011 whether a blood protein called galectin-3 can forecast outcomes for people with heart failure. The protein had looked promising in smaller studies, mostly in patients whose hearts pumped weakly. The team measured it in nearly six hundred patients admitted to hospital with heart failure, then followed them for a year and a half.

Higher starting levels meant a higher risk of dying or returning to hospital, even after accounting for age, kidney function, and other markers. The signal was strongest in patients whose pumping strength was still preserved, a group that is hard to assess. Combining galectin-3 with another common marker improved prediction beyond either one alone. Repeat levels months later added little beyond the first reading.
europmc-pmc3031573:
Flutre, Duprat, Feuillet, and Quesneville tackled in 2011 a practical problem in genome science: how to label jumping genes in a fresh DNA sequence automatically. These mobile pieces, called transposable elements, copy themselves around genomes and shape their size and function. New sequencing projects need fast, accurate ways to find and group them.

The team benchmarked grouping methods against two well finished genomes, from a fly and a small plant, where expert labels already exist. Only one pairing of methods recovered the known families well. They then added a step that merges rival groupings and classifies the pieces in a single pipeline. The combined approach also reveals how copies within a family have diverged over time. That view helps track how jumping genes spread and change across species.
europmc-pmc3072373:
Lafos and colleagues showed in 2011 that a gene silencing mark in plants is busily added and removed as cells take on their final identities. The mark, a triple methyl tag on a DNA packaging protein, is placed by the Polycomb system and was thought to lock genes off in a lasting way. The team mapped the mark genome wide in stem cells of the growing tip and in mature leaf cells of Arabidopsis.

Hundreds of genes gained or lost the mark during the shift, and losing it generally let genes switch on in the matching tissue. The mark directly silences only certain regulator families, yet it frees others indirectly by silencing the tiny RNA genes that restrain them. A whole plant hormone pathway, from making to sensing the growth hormone auxin, sits under its control. The authors propose the mark as a main sculptor of tissue specific patterns.
europmc-pmc3072973:
Burridge and coauthors built in 2011 a single recipe that turns any human pluripotent stem cell line into beating heart muscle cells, solving a notorious reliability problem. Heart cells grown from patient stem cells promise safer drug testing and disease models, but older recipes worked well on some lines and barely at all on others. The team tuned more than forty five variables to find one universal method.

Their recipe clusters the cells into balls, feeds them a defined broth, lowers oxygen to body like levels, and times two growth signals carefully. The recipe was tested across eleven stem cell lines of several origins. Nearly all cell balls started beating within nine days. Most of their cells were genuine heart muscle by protein and electrical tests. The cells answered heart drugs as expected. The authors offer the method as a cheap, scalable source of human heart cells.
europmc-pmc3103473:
Luca Cucullo and colleagues published a laboratory study in BMC Neuroscience in 2011 on how blood flow shapes the barrier between blood and brain. They worked with a human cell model grown under flow, asking whether the push of moving fluid helps vessel cells take on barrier traits.

Flow raised levels of proteins that seal gaps between cells and made the layer tighter and harder for test substances to cross. It also lifted drug pumps, ion channels, and carrier systems for sugars, while shifting energy use away from simple sugar breakdown toward fuller respiration. Flow further slowed cell division. The work shows that fluid force alone helps build and keep a selective brain barrier.
europmc-pmc3123173:
Katrin Loeschner and colleagues fed rats silver in two forms for a month and tracked where it went, in a 2011 paper in Particle and Fibre Toxicology. Tiny silver particles are added to food-related products for their germ-killing power, so swallowing them is a realistic exposure. The team compared the particle form with a dissolved silver salt.

Both forms spread through the body in the same pattern, settling most in liver and kidneys, with some reaching lungs and brain. Total tissue levels were lower for the particle form, matching greater loss in faeces. Under the microscope, small granules containing silver sat in gut wall tissue in both groups, at sizes much like the fed particles. The overlap suggests the two forms may act alike once swallowed.
europmc-pmc3163573:
Nabil-Fareed Alikhan and colleagues built a desktop program that draws circular comparison maps of bacterial genomes in a 2011 paper in BMC Genomics. Ring diagrams, with one reference genome in the centre and matches from others as coloured rings, reveal differences between close relatives at a glance. Existing tools capped the number of comparisons, handled draft genomes poorly, or demanded scripting skill.

Their program removes the comparison cap and runs the underlying matching itself through a point-and-click interface. Rings shade by match strength, and extra tracks can show assembly gaps, repeat collapses, or raw read coverage. Unassembled reads can also be mapped onto references. The cross-platform tool is free, putting large multi-genome comparisons within reach of any lab.
europmc-pmc3167373:
Pedro Valdes-Sosa, Alard Roebroeck, Jean Daunizeau, and Karl Friston closed a journal debate series on mapping directed influence between brain areas in a 2011 paper in NeuroImage. Simple correlations show areas active together, but claims about which area drives which need models of cause. The authors argue such claims stand or fall on models grounded in brain biophysics.

They compare the main approaches, including their own dynamic causal modelling and a rival based on prediction timing, and connect both to older statistical ideas about influence and dependency networks. Models, they insist, must include realistic observation and state equations, prior knowledge about parameters, and checks that parameters can actually be identified from data. The paper maps promising fixes for the field's known challenges.
europmc-pmc3242773:
Gretchen Hofmann and a large team compared natural swings in ocean acidity across ecosystems, in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Predicting how ocean acidification will affect sea life suffers from a basic gap: few measurements describe the acidity conditions organisms actually live in. The team deployed autonomous sensors that recorded pH continuously in places from polar waters to coral reefs.

Month-long records varied enormously by site. Some places were nearly steady, while others swung through more than a full pH unit, with daily, tidal, and irregular rhythms of different strengths. Many resident organisms already endure acidity extremes not expected on average until the next century. The authors say knowing each habitat's exposure history should sharpen laboratory experiments and help identify refuges and vulnerable areas as the ocean changes.
europmc-pmc3260173:
Ronny Herzog and colleagues introduced LipidXplorer, open-source software for lipidomics, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Lipidomics aims to inventory the fats in a sample, and shotgun mass spectrometry produces huge datasets toward that end. LipidXplorer reads those spectra to describe complex lipid mixtures and measure their amounts.

The software works with spectra from any brand of tandem mass spectrometer. It identifies and measures molecular species from any ionizable lipid class by reasoning from known or assumed fragmentation pathways, without depending on libraries of reference spectra. It supports routines from high-throughput screening for diagnostic markers to precise absolute measurement of scarce species. The paper points users to a wiki carrying full documentation, a tutorial, interpretation scripts, a question archive, and a forum.
europmc-pmc3285573:
Purvesh Khatri, Marina Sirota, and Atul Butte reviewed the first decade of pathway analysis in this 2012 paper in PLoS Computational Biology. Faced with long lists of changed genes, researchers turned to pathway analysis, which interprets results through known biological routes, reducing complexity and adding explanatory power. It became the method of first resort, and the authors trace how it evolved.

They divide knowledge-base-driven methods into three generations, each fixing limitations of the one before, and explain which limits remain specific to each. Annotation problems, gaps and errors in the pathway knowledge bases themselves, now look like the binding constraint, alongside methodological challenges the next generation must meet. Their agenda aims at methods that exploit modern genomics and proteomics for sharper, more relevant results.
europmc-pmc3323073:
Van den Hoogen and colleagues sorted out the varieties of a newly recognized respiratory virus, in a 2004 study. Human metapneumovirus, found only a few years earlier, causes cold like illness and more serious lung infections, especially in young children. Early gene readings hinted it came in several lineages, as its close relatives do, but whether those lineages behaved as distinct types for the immune system was unknown.

The team compared gene sequences from many virus samples and tested how well antibodies against one lineage neutralized another. Two clear serotypes emerged, meaning immunity to one does not fully cover the other. Each serotype split further into two genetic lineages, though those inner splits mattered little for antibody recognition. The sorting helps explain repeat infections and guides vaccine thinking.
europmc-pmc3346773:
Halldorsson and colleagues followed Danish children from before birth to age twenty to test whether a persistent chemical affects weight, reporting in 2012. The chemical, PFOA, is used in many products and shows up in people worldwide. In mice, low doses before birth made female offspring heavier after puberty. The team checked humans next, using blood samples from six hundred sixty five pregnant women recruited in the late nineteen eighties.

Daughters of mothers with the highest chemical levels were about three times as likely to be overweight at twenty as daughters of the lowest group, with larger waists to match. Their blood also showed higher insulin and appetite hormone levels and lower levels of a protective hormone. Sons showed weaker, less certain hints of the same pattern. Related chemicals showed no independent link. The authors say the human results line up with the animal warning.
europmc-pmc3348673:
Booth and colleagues described the building of an international register where systematic reviews are logged before they are done, in a 2012 article.
