Portable fifteen-minute checks could help teams adjust training loads on altitude camps before fatigue builds into injury risk.
plos-pone-0353773:
Bao and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, build a model that summarizes videos by picking their most important shots. A good summary lets a viewer grasp a long video in moments, which matters for surveillance review and short-video apps. Earlier graph-based methods struggled to blend close-up detail with the whole video's shape.

Their model turns each shot into a point in a graph, linked to shots with similar meaning. It then reads the graph at two scales: one attention method draws out local links between neighboring shots, and another network draws out global structure. The three views, original, local, and global, are fused to score each shot's importance. On two public benchmark sets, the method scored competitively against leading approaches. The authors offer it as a practical way to cut long footage down to its essentials.
plos-pone-0354073:
Lijuan Zhao and coauthors published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on automating the building of multibody dynamics models, the virtual machines engineers test before cutting metal. Hand-building such models in the RecurDyn software is slow and error-prone. Their method reads a design file's assembly features, identifies components with a wording-and-meaning system backed by a multilingual language model, then generates code that assembles the model automatically.

They tested the pipeline on the cutting unit of a drum shearer, a coal-mining machine, at three levels of structural complexity, then checked simulations against a test rig. Model building took less than one percent of the usual manual time. Simulated shaft speeds matched reality almost exactly, and drum vibration errors stayed within a few percent. The authors present the rule-driven approach as transferable to other complex machinery, turning weeks of modeling into an automatic step.
plos-pone-0354173:
Tanjina Rahman and six colleagues document how common malnutrition is among kidney dialysis patients in Bangladesh, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. One hundred and eighty-one patients on regular haemodialysis across four districts were assessed with two standard nutrition scoring systems. By the stricter criteria, over two fifths were malnourished, and about one in ten severely so; the other score flagged nearly three quarters.

One practice stood out sharply: patients who reused their dialysis filter more than twice had far higher odds of malnutrition. Age, body weight, and diabetes also played a part. In poor health systems, the authors argue, routine nutrition checks and safer equipment practices could save lives cheaply.
plos-pone-0354373:
Robi Cynthia Chacha and Ermias Mergia Terefe published this 2026 study of prescribing habits at Thika Level 5 Hospital in Kenya. With yardsticks from the World Health Organization, they reviewed six hundred prescriptions, a hundred patient visits, and the facility itself, comparing results with global benchmarks for sensible medicine use.

Prescriptions carried more drugs on average than recommended, few were written by generic name, and antibiotics appeared in well over half of visits, though most medicines came from the essential list. Chacha urges stronger antibiotic stewardship, generic prescribing, and better counseling for patients at the dispensing counter.
plos-pone-0354473:
Niazy and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, test an old cancer drug against a stubborn hospital germ. The germ, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, harms patients with weak defenses, and its swimming, crawling, and slime-building habits help it cause disease. Repurposing an approved drug is a fast route to new anti-germ tactics, so the team tried 5-fluorouracil at rising doses.

All three forms of movement shrank as dose rose, and genes for the germ's propellers and grappling hairs were turned down. So were genes for a tissue-chewing enzyme and for soap-like chemicals that help it spread. The picture for genetic material leaked from cells was mixed: it fell after one day, then rose at high doses after two days, alongside genes for DNA repair. The authors read the drug as a brake on this germ's attack tools, while noting the later DNA rise needs explaining.
plos-pone-0354673:
David J Lewkowicz and Julia McClellan published this 2026 eye-tracking study of the cocktail party problem: following just one talker among many when faces and voices arrive together. Adult volunteers watched competing talking faces on screens while the researchers varied lip-sound timing, face shape, and identity cues from face, voice, and word choice.

Timing synchrony separated talkers without needing a standard face layout. Word-choice identity helped on its own, and pupil size showed the mental effort each cue combination cost. Lewkowicz maps which clues adults actually use to untangle crowded conversation.
plos-pone-0354773: Akinyemi and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on loneliness and death risk in the United States. They examined whether people who report loneliness die sooner from any cause than those who do not. Loneliness is now common enough to count as a public health issue. If the link is strong, doctors may one day screen for loneliness like they screen for smoking.
plos-pone-0354973:
Carlos Abraham Herrera-Amante and co-authors checked how badly standard formulas estimate resting metabolism in professional footballers. Resting metabolic rate drives daily energy needs, yet measuring it directly needs costly gas analysis. Their 2026 study compared twelve common equations and a machine learning model against direct measurement in forty male professionals.

Every equation overshot the measured rate, by margins from small to more than a third. Agreement scores were poor across the board. The learning model, built from body measurements, made smaller errors than any formula. Even so, it explained only a limited share of the differences between players. The authors warn practitioners that off-the-shelf formulas can badly mislead diet planning for athletes.
plos-pone-0355173:
José García-Moreno and co-authors interview in 2026 patients waiting for spine surgery about what stops or helps them stay active before the operation. Activity before surgery may improve recovery from narrowed or slipped disc conditions in the lower back. Interviews used each person's own activity data as a prompt and were sorted through a behaviour framework, with a patient partner shaping the work.

Pain, low physical capacity, fear of harm, poor settings, and negative feelings blocked activity. Motivation, good settings, social support, positive feelings, workarounds, and daily habits helped. Tailored programmes before surgery should attack fear and pain while building on habits and support, the authors suggest.
plos-pone-0355373:
Bashige Chiribagula Valentin and co-authors recorded plants used to start or strengthen labour in Lubumbashi, in the Haut-Katanga region of Congo. Traditional birth practice there relies on plant knowledge passed down by healers and herbalists. For their 2026 study, the team interviewed more than two hundred local informants, including housewives, herbalists, and traditional healers.

Informants named close to a hundred plant species across many families, with the pea family most common. Leaves featured in most of the recorded labour remedies, often applied as a paste. Dozens of species had never before been reported for this use, and several were new medicinal records for the country. The inventory gives pharmacologists a starting list for safety and effect testing.
plos-pone-0355473:
Na Li and colleagues study a small helper protein in eye cells damaged by high sugar, a lab model of diabetic eye disease. Diabetes can harm the retina over time, and earlier work had linked this protein to several illnesses but not to this one. The team grew human retinal cells in very sweet conditions, then switched the protein down and read which genes changed activity or changed how their messages were cut and rejoined.

High sugar lowered both cell growth and the protein's level. Switching it down shifted hundreds of genes, mostly ones that run the cell division cycle, and altered the cutting of many more. Li and colleagues suggest the protein helps coordinate growth control in retinal cells, making it a candidate lead for protecting sight in diabetes.
plos-pone-0355673:
Matt Vogel and three colleagues question a growing habit in violence research in this 2026 paper. A federal index built to gauge how well communities withstand natural disasters, called the Social Vulnerability Index, is now often used to flag places at risk of gun violence. The authors ask whether a disaster tool really fits that job.

They compared the index head-to-head with a long-standing measure of concentrated disadvantage across census tracts in more than eighty American cities. The disaster index consistently explained firearm violence less well, and what power it had came almost entirely from its economic component. The authors argue that borrowing the index amounts to conceptual drift. It measures how a community absorbs outside shocks, not the local conditions that breed violence. Using it could steer prevention money to the wrong places.
plos-pone-0355873:
Anjali Saini and Shalini Rai present a plan to map laboratory evidence on traditional Indian mineral and herb mixtures used against cancer. The formulations come from the Ayurveda and Siddha systems of medicine. Their 2026 protocol asks what cell and animal studies actually show about these mixtures, since that evidence is scattered.

The paper reports a method, not finished findings. Two reviewers will search selected databases and sort studies using set eligibility rules. Results will be shown in tables and summary text, following standard reporting guidance for scoping reviews. Saini and Rai hope the map will help researchers pick the most promising formulations for closer study.
plos-pone-0355973:
Gabriel Haddad and three colleagues sort out which forms of an invasive malaria mosquito are living in Djibouti City, in this 2026 entomology study. Anopheles stephensi, an Asian species first found in Djibouti in 2012, has been linked to rising urban malaria across the Horn of Africa. It exists in three biological forms with different habitats and different abilities to transmit malaria, distinguishable by ridges on their eggs and, supposedly, by a scent-related gene.

Six hundred eggs collected at six city sites in April 2023 covered all three forms living side by side. Surprisingly, the form thought rural and a weak transmitter dominated even in high-malaria urban districts. The gene test did not match the egg-based identification, so the authors judge it unsuitable for telling the forms apart. They say the forms' actual roles in city transmission must be pinned down before control policy can be well aimed.
plos-pone-0356073:
Yang Wang, Asif Ali Safeer, and Yewang Zhou ask what makes travelers bond with artificial intelligence chatbots, in this 2026 survey study. Their respondents were Chinese tourists who use chatbots to plan and manage trips. Nearly seven hundred responses were analyzed with two statistical approaches, one tracing average pathways and one hunting for winning combinations of traits. The model connects chatbot features, through trust, to engagement and emotional connection, with the bot's social presence as a booster.

Personalization, interactivity, and ease of use each built trust, and trust in turn raised engagement and emotional connection; engagement itself deepened the emotional bond. A stronger sense of social presence further amplified engagement. The combination analysis singled out a personal touch, ease of use, and engagement as the key ingredients of emotional connection. The authors advise travel firms to design chatbots as relationship partners, not transaction machines.
plos-pone-0356173:
Chiel van der Laan and Alessandro Corbetta published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on how pairs of pedestrians move through crowds. Most people in public spaces walk with a companion, side by side to talk, but crowds force pairs to adjust. The authors mined a huge dataset from Eindhoven Central Station, millions of walking pairs tracked over years, modeling how pair speed and formation respond to crowd density and flow.

Pairs slowed and reshaped themselves predictably as crowds thickened. Walking abreast favors conversation, while falling into single file favors pushing through, and pairs traded between the two as conditions changed. They built diagrams linking pair behavior to crowd state and introduced a number for how strongly a pair prefers side-by-side over in-file walking in a given situation. That measure breaks into two standard crowd diagrams, giving engineers a grounded way to include social groups in simulations.
plos-pone-0356373:
Petko Karagyozov, Inna Dobreva, and Ivelina Zhecheva report a Bulgarian tertiary center's experience with liver biopsy performed through an endoscope, in this 2026 study. Using ultrasound guidance from inside the stomach, doctors can sample the liver while watching in real time, avoiding some drawbacks of needle-through-skin and vein-based routes. The team reviewed three years of consecutive cases done with a fine 22-gauge Franseen-tip needle and a gentle slow-pull technique, for both widespread liver disease and focal lesions.

All seventy-two patients yielded tissue that pathologists judged adequate for diagnosis. About three quarters proved to have malignant disease and the rest benign conditions. No complications appeared in the first two days or over a month of follow-up. The authors present the technique as safe and effective, with shorter recovery than conventional biopsy routes, aided by live imaging that helps the needle steer clear of blood vessels.
plos-pone-0356473:
Lidong Hou and five colleagues explain why water quietly destroys mudstone from the inside, in this 2026 multi-scale study motivated by oil drilling. Mudstone formations that drink water make boreholes unstable, and the chief suspect is a swelling clay mineral, montmorillonite. The team combined mineral analysis, mechanical tests on soaked rock cores, and molecular dynamics simulations that watch individual water molecules at work.

Soaking cut the rock's compressive strength by more than half. The simulations show why: water slips between the clay's layers in stages, forming one, then two, then three molecular films, prising the layers apart unevenly while sodium ions shuffle among the water. That staged swelling explains why real cores first flake, then fragment, the longer they sit in water. The authors say blocking this interlayer hydration is the key to stable boreholes.
plos-pone-0356773:
Tae-Eun Kim and colleagues link an eye condition of early birth with later development using nationwide Korean health screening records. The eye condition scars the retina of premature babies. Records covered more than eight hundred thousand children screened near age five, including several thousand with a history of the condition, and tested six areas of development from language to movement.

Children with the eye history faced higher odds of delay in every area tested, with the largest gap in large-muscle skills. Risk ran higher still when eyesight at screening was also weak. Kim and colleagues propose the eye history as an easy flag in records, marking children who deserve close developmental watch and joined eye and development care.
plos-pone-0356873:
Nobuo Nagano and colleagues pool three Japanese clinical trials of tenapanor, a newer drug for the phosphate build-up that plagues dialysis patients. Failing kidneys cannot clear phosphate, which drives bone and heart harm; older binder pills work but pile up daily doses that patients skip. Tenapanor instead blocks phosphate absorption in the gut, and its dose is raised step by step until blood levels respond, though stomach side effects make some patients resist higher doses.

The pooled analysis asks which patient traits mark those who end up needing the high end of the dose range. Knowing the profile in advance could help doctors counsel patients and set expectations before titration begins. Nagano and colleagues draw on the three registered trials' combined records for this prescribing question.
plos-pone-0357173:
Abdul Mannan and co-authors model hepatitis C spread with a twist. Alcohol use deepens liver damage in infected people. Here it enters the transmission equations as its own factor. The virus drives much chronic liver disease worldwide. Their six-group model tracks people through stages of infection and drinking. Classic numerics can solve the stiff equations, but slowly. So the team also trained a deep learning solver. They compared its answers against trusted methods.

The learning solver matched the classic results with strong stability and convergence in their tests. Stability analysis located the thresholds where infection dies out or settles in, and sensitivity checks named the parameters that matter most. Mannan and colleagues present machine solving as a practical extra tool for epidemic forecasting.
plos-pone-0357273:
Hyeon Ah Kim and colleagues describe, organ by organ, what healthy tissue looks like under a microscope in baby common marmosets. Marmosets serve widely as lab primates, yet reference detail for the first weeks of life is thin. The team compared five major organs from infants in their first three weeks with the same organs from adults, using several standard stains and a marker of dividing cells.

Infant livers still made blood cells and held loosely layered tissue, while adult livers showed tidy plates. Infant kidneys were still building their filtering units, spleens held small pale zones, lungs had thick walls between air sacs, and hearts packed muscle loosely. Adult organs looked mature on every count. Kim and colleagues offer the atlas for judging normal growth against disease.
plos-pone-0357473:
Tancredo José Carlos and colleagues run field trials in Mozambique on feeding cowpea plants extra zinc and iron. Cowpea is a staple bean, and enriching it in the field could fight hidden hunger while raising yields. Their 2026 trial crossed three ways of applying the minerals, on soil, on leaves, or both, with several dose levels of each mineral in blocked field plots.

Combined soil and leaf feeding gave the best yields, and a growth curve pointed to one dose pair for the largest harvest. The profit peak, however, sat at lower doses, especially for iron, which could be cut nearly in half while keeping almost all of the yield gain. Risk checks stayed positive across treatments. The authors advise farmers to aim for the profit point, not the biggest harvest.
plos-pone-0357573:
Simon Alexander Berry and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for PAINLESS, a trial asking whether smoothing blood sugar can ease the burning pain of diabetic neuropathy. Painful neuropathy is common and hard to treat, and hints link flare-ups to glucose swings rather than average levels. Hybrid closed loop pumps, automating insulin delivery from continuous glucose readings, flatten those swings. The two-center crossover trial will recruit just under fifty adults with type 1 diabetes and painful neuropathy.

Each participant spends twelve weeks on the closed loop and twelve on standard care with glucose monitoring, in random order, keeping daily pain diaries. The main comparison is change in average daily pain. Secondary measures cover responder rates, quality of life, mood, and global change, while exploratory tests probe nerve function, sleep, and activity. If pumps relieve pain as a side benefit, the funding case widens beyond glucose numbers.
plos-pone-0357673:
Belal Elmarhoumy leads a lab study of the soft silicone used to rebuild faces after surgery or injury, asking how tiny added particles change its strength over time. Some samples sat outdoors in a hot, humid climate for two full years, while matching samples stayed indoors. The fillers were two common mineral powders mixed at low and higher shares into a medical silicone.

Fresh samples with a low share of silica powder tore and stretched far better than plain silicone. After two years outside, every mix lost stretch, but filled samples kept far more of theirs than the plain control, which lost about half. Elmarhoumy and colleagues conclude that a small silica dose helps prosthetic material survive harsh weather, a practical point for clinics in tropical regions.
plos-pone-0357773:
Yi Luo led a team of eight authors tracing air pollution damage in rats, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Breathing fine particles, PM2.5, harms the lungs first, but this team found effects far beyond them. Nasal exposure to the particles caused testicular injury and switched on a form of inflammatory cell death called pyroptosis.

Luo's group also tested inhibitors of that pathway and checked public gene data to support the chain. Their work suggests pollution's reach may extend to male fertility. If the damage route can be blocked, a future treatment path opens, though human evidence is still needed. The study adds weight to clean-air arguments by showing harm in organs people rarely connect with breathing.
plos-pone-0357973:
Rosella Muresu, Monica Rodriguez, and Andrea Squartini published a 2026 analysis in PLOS ONE questioning how well a standard bacterial barcode identifies Rhizobium, the root bacteria that help legume plants capture nitrogen. Identification usually rests on one gene, called 16S, assumed to match species, host plant, and origin. The team pulled thousands of Rhizobium sequences for that gene from the GenBank database and compared every pair that matched perfectly.

Among identical sequences with full records, about two-thirds disagreed on all three labels: species name, host plant, and country. Only a tiny share agreed on everything, and the single most common sequence appeared under dozens of host plants, many countries, and several species names. The gene, they argue, changes too slowly, while key traits move between bacteria on mobile DNA. Naming species needs genome, trait, and ecology data together.
plos-pone-0358073: Sowińska and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on bedsores as a safety problem in hospital care. Pressure injuries form when patients lie or sit too long without moving. The team reviewed cases at a specialist hospital from 2013 to 2020, treating each injury as an adverse event. Tracking these wounds over years shows whether prevention efforts are working.
plos-pone-0358773: Entwistle and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on why promising animal results often fail in people. They traced therapies for acute injury that began in small rodents. The trail runs from early promise through human testing to approval and safety results. As a systematic review, it gathers the full record. Seeing where the trail breaks can save money and spare patients false hope.
plos-pone-0358873:
Daniel Y Tsybulnik, Justin J Gillette, and Thomas F Heston ask whether language models agree with each other when grading clinical trial reports, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Journals expect trials to follow the CONSORT reporting checklist, and automated checking would help editors, if the checkers were consistent. The team had three leading models independently score twenty randomized trials from immunology journals against thirty-seven checklist points.

The models diverged sharply. One awarded an average compliance score of about eighty-one percent, a second about sixty-four, and the third about fifty-five. Against a strict ninety percent quality bar, the most generous model passed five papers while the other two passed none at all. Agreement between models was too weak for interchangeable use. The authors warn that swapping one model for another silently changes the verdict, so any editorial workflow needs a fixed, validated checker.
plos-pone-0358973: Hwang and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on drug-resistant gut germs in long-term care hospitals. Some patients carry carbapenem-resistant bacteria without being sick, yet can spread them. The team actively checked patients over time to measure how common carriage is and how people pick it up. They also hunted risk factors. Quiet carriers are a hidden route for outbreaks in care homes.
plos-pone-0359573:
Muna Elsadig, Shamsa Kanwal, Rab Nawaz, and Qazi Muhammad Zaigham Zia wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in applied mathematics. It studies beam-foundation systems, structures where a beam rests on a supporting base, with viscoelastic constraints, materials that behave partly like solids and partly like thick fluids. The authors model the system's computational dynamics.

Their focus includes damping-induced transitions, moments when energy loss shifts the system from one pattern of motion to another. Bridges, rails, and building foundations all involve beams on elastic supports, so these transitions matter for safety. Structural engineers and mathematicians share this ground where equations predict how real structures vibrate and settle.
plos-pone-0359773:
Orarat Karnjanawanichkul and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a prospective observational study of Thai adults under general anesthesia. The authors hunt for predictors of needing airway adjuncts, extra devices that keep the airway open, during mask ventilation.

Predicting who will be hard to ventilate lets anesthetists prepare equipment and help before trouble starts. Observing patients prospectively, as care unfolds, captures real practice rather than records alone. Anesthesia teams are the readers, since failed mask ventilation is one of the emergencies their specialty trains hardest to prevent.
pmc-13155173:
Milani and colleagues screened blood donations in Manaus, Brazil in 2026 for Oropouche virus during the 2023 to 2024 outbreak. A reshuffled virus lineage then caused tens of thousands of cases and was linked to brain complications and infections in pregnancy. No transfusion spread has been reported, but silent infection in donors could hide a route. The team tested pooled donations with a genetic assay, sequenced reactive samples, and tracked antibody levels in the population.

Among nearly twelve thousand donations, about six and a half percent of pools carried viral RNA, peaking in January 2024, and the donor viruses matched the outbreak lineage. Population antibody rates more than doubled across the outbreak, implying roughly 390,000 infections in the city, far above reported cases. The detectable window in blood was about five days. The authors say the findings raise real blood safety questions and demand continued donor and recipient watch.
pmc-13199673:
Jun P Hong and Michel C Nussenzweig present a 2026 protocol for a gene screen in mouse immune cells. Germinal center B cells mature antibodies inside lymph nodes, but no lab dish copies their biology well. Genetic screens must run in living mice, so the protocol adapts CRISPR tools, which cut or silence genes, for that setting.

Steps cover building a guide RNA library, delivering guides with a mouse-only retrovirus, and running the screen in an immunization model. Sequencing and analysis steps close the workflow. Tweaks include a refined guide scaffold and matched primers. Animal and biosafety approvals are stressed throughout. As a protocol, it reports no results; it gives labs a tested recipe for in vivo screens.
pmc-13200373:
Anett Mau-Moeller and colleagues compared inpatient versus outpatient rehabilitation after knee replacement in Germany in a 2026 trial. German care usually adds a three-week rehab stay after knee joint replacement surgery. Whether patients must stay in a facility or can attend daily was little tested, so the team ran a blinded comparison.

Patients chose their setting: twenty-six went inpatient and sixteen outpatient. Tests ran before rehab and three months after surgery. Outpatients logged far more daily steps in the first rehab week. At three months, outpatients also showed better joint position sense, the feel for where the knee sits. Other measures covered pain, swelling, motion, and timed walking tasks.
pmc-13200473:
Ayman Shaban and colleagues tested nano fertilizer sprays on olive trees in a 2026 field study. Olive trees often bear heavily one year and lightly the next, a pattern called alternate bearing. Spray feeding in the off-year might even out yields, so the team sprayed nano NPK and calcium-boron mixes on fifteen-year-old Picual trees.

Trials ran across the 2023 and 2024 seasons. The best blend raised flower counts, perfect flower share, and fruit set above controls. Off-year yield peaked under that blend, while fruit drop fell by about half versus controls. Leaf and fruit mineral levels rose. Oil kept its extra virgin grade with a richer share of oleic acid, its main healthy fat. Alternate bearing severity fell sharply.
pmc-13211873: A correction notice from Si-Ting Chen and co-authors, published in 2026, fixes figure errors in their 2023 eLife paper on embryo-derived TNF and uterine decidualization. Assembly mistakes had duplicated a loading-control band across two figures, copied immunoprecipitation bands into a later figure, and repeated one histogram in place of another. The authors replaced the affected panels, updated the source data, and apologized for the inadvertent errors. Only the correction notice itself survives here, so the study's data are not re-presented.
pmc-13212173:
Jiezhi Lin and co-authors review, in 2026, what regulatory T cells do in the slow healing of wounds among people with diabetes. These immune cells normally calm inflammation and help tissue rebuild, so their failure may help explain why diabetic foot ulcers linger.

The narrative review pulls together work on inflammation, new blood vessel growth, and cell regeneration in diabetic wounds. It also surveys therapies that aim to boost or guide these cells, including new biomaterials and molecular approaches. Problems remain, from obtaining good-quality cells to risks of infection and over-suppressed immunity. Still, the authors see cell-based care as a promising direction worth careful trials.
pmc-13212673:
Tatiana Palotta Minari reviews in 2026 how population surveys should measure nutritional status in a digital age. No single method captures the full picture: body measurements are cheap but blunt, while laboratory markers are sensitive yet hard to collect at scale.

The review weighs body measurements, body composition tools, and biochemical indicators side by side. Composition methods reveal tissue distribution but need costly equipment, and blood tests face logistical and ethical hurdles in large surveys. The pandemic exposed fragile data systems, while digital tools now offer new ways to combine sources. Minari argues surveys must blend methods and invest in staff, infrastructure, and fair data governance.
pmc-13213173:
Xueyuan Li, Ming Hu, and Yi Shen compare in 2026 two drug regimens for bone loss in women after menopause. One group received an active vitamin D compound alone with calcium, while the other added denosumab, an injected antibody that slows bone breakdown.

Records for 306 women treated over twelve months showed the combined group gained more bone density at spine, hip neck, and total hip. Bone turnover markers fell further, calcium balance measures improved, and pain, disability, and daily function scores all improved more. Side effects stayed low and similar in both groups, with none judged serious. The pairing looks promising, though the retrospective design invites a confirming trial.
pmc-13214273:
Zuyun Yan and colleagues engineer in 2026 an implantable scaffold meant to finish off bone cancer after surgery while rebuilding the bone it leaves behind. Drug-resistant osteosarcoma poses all three problems at once: leftover tumour, weak immune attack, and a large defect.

Their scaffold releases two agents in response to tumour acidity and a light trigger. One agent blocks DNA repair so the other's platinum damage lands harder, reversing resistance, while together they provoke an immune-visible form of cell death. Silicon released from the scaffold plus the second agent encourage blood vessels and new bone. Animal tests showed tumour suppression first, then substantial bone bridging, without obvious whole-body toxicity.
pmc-13214573:
Esteban Villar-Rodríguez and colleagues examine in 2026 whether the brain sides used for speaking, listening, and reading agree with each other in left-handers. This group includes more people with right-sided or split language organisation, which makes it ideal for testing independence among components.

Brain scans of sixty-nine selected left-handers showed speaking and listening lateralised together strongly, while reading aligned more loosely with both. Forty-four people were consistent across all three tasks, and twenty-five had one component straying, usually reading, most often within overall rightward dominance. Inconsistent organisation, especially between speaking and reading, came with slightly slower reading speed. Language sides, the authors conclude, are coordinated but not locked together.
pmc-13215373:
Yuya Nakajima and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study on cognitive testing and driving among older adults living in the community in Japan. The team asked which tasks within the Japanese-language version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment relate to driving as a person's main way of getting around.

The study covered 199 participants in a long-term preventive care program, of whom 156 mainly drove themselves and 43 used other transport. Drivers scored higher on trail-making, digit span, and verbal fluency tasks, yet only trail-making stayed linked to driving after regression adjustment, with an odds ratio of 2.82 in the model. The authors suggest this single task could help clinicians guide older patients on driving decisions.
pmc-13216373:
Mugahid Ali and Fumin Huang present a 2026 optics paper giving simple formulas for how layered, stretched nanoparticles interact with light. Such particles, treated as stacked spheroids, are workhorses in plasmonics, sensing, and Raman spectroscopy.

With the particle far smaller than the wavelength, the authors solve Laplace's equation layer by layer with the light polarized along the long axis. The key surface factor falls out as a ratio of two matrix determinants, and from it they derive one general expression for the particle's polarizability, which drives scattering and absorption. Worked examples with two, three, and five layers check the formulas' accuracy and speed against heavier number-crunching approaches.
pmc-13218173:
Ayuba Issaka and co-authors set out a 2026 protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis of voice-assisted AI in cardiovascular care. Heart and vessel diseases remain a leading cause of illness and death, and how patients manage their condition affects outcomes. Voice assistants and apps are a hands-free way to support self-management, but their value for heart patients is unproven.

The review will search MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, and the Cochrane register for studies from 2010 to 2025. Eligible work includes randomized trials, non-randomized studies, and observational work on voice-based tools for heart self-management. The primary outcome is cardiovascular death. Secondary outcomes are quality of life, blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose measures, diet, and physical activity. Quality will be judged with Cochrane and Newcastle-Ottawa tools, and results will be pooled with random-effects models, using subgroup analyses and meta-regression to explain differences.
pmc-13219873:
Takanori Komada and colleagues report organized lymphocyte clusters inside kidneys damaged by potassium deficiency in a 2026 research letter. Hypokalaemic nephropathy, kidney injury from long low potassium, is usually treated by replacing potassium, and its long-term course was assumed benign. Inflammation's role in the condition, however, had drawn the team's earlier interest.

Five kidney biopsies from patients all showed T-cell infiltration, and three contained clusters of T and B lymphocytes resembling tertiary lymphoid structures, the outposts familiar from chronic inflammation and cancer. None of the patients progressed to kidney failure over an average of eight years of supplementation. In a mouse version of the disease, potassium and kidney function recovered on a normal diet, yet scarring and the same lymphoid clusters developed anyway, and both amounts rose. The authors suggest these structures may flag kidneys at risk of chronic decline and keep inflammation smoldering after the deficiency is fixed.
pmc-13220073:
Dmytro Kobzev and colleagues wrote this 2026 review of medicines that switch on only when triggered by a signal, such as light, heat, sound, or body chemistry. Such control could let a drug act at the right place and time instead of spreading through the whole body.

The authors mapped research from 2014 to 2024, covering over 90,000 papers and 1,000 clinical trials. Light was the most used outside trigger, while internal triggers like acidity and enzymes made up nearly half the work. They also list six barriers slowing use in patients, from complex designs to cost, and offer practical fixes for each.
pmc-13222773:
Hanyi Wang and co-authors test the enzyme PepO against ulcerative colitis in mice, in a 2026 study. It was given to mice with drug-induced colon inflammation. Disease scores, colon length, tissue damage, and tissue signals measured the effect, while cell and gut tests traced the mechanism.

Treated mice showed milder disease, longer colons, and less tissue damage. The enzyme directly cut output of CCL2, a macrophage-attracting signal, reducing immune cell invasion of the colon. Gut microbe mixes also shifted toward helpful species such as Lactobacillus and Akkermansia. Wiping out gut microbes erased the protection, and transplanting treated gut contents reproduced it.
pmc-13223973:
Karina Cancino-Maldonado and co-authors present a 2026 single-cell study of ampullary carcinoma, a rare cancer arising where the bile and pancreatic ducts meet the intestine. The tumour accounts for a small share of gut cancers, and its awkward anatomy often makes diagnosis hard. The team profiled gene activity cell by cell in tumour tissue.

Their atlas separates malignant epithelial cells from the surrounding immune environment. Known cancer drivers appeared more active, alongside a gene program specific to this tumour that may yield markers detectable without invasive sampling. Immune cells looked suppressive in character, with macrophage and T cell groups showing limited anti-tumour activity, which may guide later treatment research.
pmc-13229473:
Tai-Cheng Kuo and colleagues compare in 2026 two layered skin templates for rebuilding injured fingertips and nail beds in Taiwan. Thirty patients with Allen type one to three injuries were treated between 2020 and 2022. Twelve received Integra and eighteen received Terudermis, both used instead of flap surgery.

At six months the two products gave closely similar results across healing, appearance, feeling, and movement. Skin closed fully in about thirty-nine days on average, and satisfaction averaged near the top of a five point scale. Two-point discrimination averaged under six millimeters on the injured side. The findings support either template as a choice that avoids taking tissue from another site.
pmc-13230673:
Yudai Murayama and colleagues review in 2026 eight cases where the drug eribulin was given after surgery for soft tissue sarcoma. Most patients were older or had other health problems that made standard anthracycline chemotherapy risky. Records from one hospital captured dosing, side effects, and cancer outcomes after curative surgery.

Blood side effects such as low white cell counts were fairly common but were handled with dose changes and support care. Nerve tingling and taste changes stayed mostly mild to moderate, and no treatment deaths or major heart events occurred. Six patients stayed free of cancer during follow-up, while two died of the disease. The small series suggests the drug is workable after surgery, though benefit size cannot be judged from eight cases.
pmc-13231073:
Xiaojie Yao and Ziqing Cheng review in 2026 a nursing model meant to turn gum disease advice into lasting daily habits. Gum disease affects more than a billion people and needs steady self care, yet knowing what to do rarely changes behavior. The model follows a chain from information to knowledge, then attitude, then practice.

Care unfolds in three phases covering digital preparation before visits, skill building and motivational talks in the clinic, and remote follow-up afterward. Trials gathered in the review show better gum measures such as shallower pockets and less bleeding. Patients also reported stronger self-management skills, confidence, and quality of life. Joining behavior science with ongoing nursing contact may close the gap between intention and action.
pmc-13233473:
Jing Chen, Fei Chen, and Shuang Qiu published a 2026 questionnaire study of test anxiety among medical students in China. Drawing on surveys from 1,067 students at three medical universities, the team weighed academic stress, social support, and two kinds of perfectionism, healthy striving versus harsh self-judgment. Psychological resilience, the capacity to recover from pressure, sat at the center of their model.

Academic stress and maladaptive perfectionism raised test anxiety, while social support and adaptive perfectionism lowered it. Resilience carried part of every effect, transmitting over half of the benefit linked to social support. The authors recommend resilience training as a lever medical schools can pull to protect both mental health and academic performance.
pmc-13233573:
Karen M. Buch-Olsen and colleagues published a 2026 randomized trial report comparing two advanced scans for staging newly diagnosed prostate cancer. One scan targets prostate-specific membrane antigen, a tumor marker, while the other, a sodium fluoride scan, highlights bone. Both were paired with contrast CT imaging, and patients were followed for progression-free survival.

The tumor-targeted scan found more disease, so fewer patients were classed as nonmetastatic, a shift called stage migration. Survival without progression looked visually better beyond two years in that group, but the difference was not statistically significant. The authors warn that comparing outcomes between studies using different scans can mislead, because the imaging itself changes who counts as high or low risk. Longer follow-up is planned.
pmc-13233773:
Jinhao Chen and colleagues published a 2026 materials study on improving a bismuth-based metal-organic framework for splitting water with sunlight. These crystalline, sponge-like materials can act as photocatalysts that release oxygen from water, one half of making hydrogen fuel. The team added bromine during a one-pot synthesis and varied its ratio to bismuth, which reshaped the crystals from rods to mace-like and flower-like forms.

The mace-like version, made at a balanced ratio, offered more surface area, favorable crystal orientation, and more exposed active sites. It kept electric charges apart longer, reaching an oxygen evolution rate well above the undoped and heavily doped versions, and stayed stable over ten hours. The work shows shape engineering and light doping can be combined in one simple, template-free recipe.
pmc-13237173:
Lohitaksh Badarala published a correction in 2026 to a paper on Q-CaDD, a drug-design framework that mixes quantum computing with standard methods and targets the epidermal growth factor receptor. The notice replaces several wrong passages in the original text. Most of all, the hybrid model's headline accuracy figure was too high.

The corrected text gives an AUC-ROC near 0.76 rather than 0.83 for the mixed model. It still claims the mixed model holds up better on new data than standard models alone. Other fixes widen the write-up of the framework and restate why a toxicity test endpoint was picked, now calling it a hard test with few active compounds. Readers should use the corrected numbers.
pmc-13237273:
Ali Rteil and co-authors used the TriNetX research network in 2026 to compare Achilles tendon repair outcomes in patients with and without a recent mental health diagnosis. From nearly 11,800 repair patients, matching on age, sex, body size, and other conditions built two groups of 1,767. Follow-up stretched to two years.

At three months, the mental health group had higher odds of wound problems, ankle stiffness, and ankle pain, along with more emergency visits, readmissions, reoperations, and opioid use. Most gaps persisted at six months, and pain and opioid use remained higher at one year. The authors urge surgical teams to plan pain control, rehabilitation support, and follow-up with mental health in mind. Tendon healing, they suggest, is not only mechanical.
pmc-13239073:
Andrew J. Hearn and colleagues surveyed the Endangered Bornean ferret badger with camera traps across Sabah's western mountains in 2026, its only confirmed home. Sixty camera stations logged 407 independent detections, including the first confirmed records from a reserve east of the known axis. Habitat modeling and connectivity analysis then refined where the animal likely lives and moves.

One forest reserve and a mixed farmland site held the highest occupancy, and habitat suitability tracked landform position and soil type, fitting the animal's digging habits. pmc-13242373:

pmc-13246373:

pmc-13249073:

pmc-13250873:

pmc-13252573:

Paula Alcazar and colleagues report a 2026 case of extra breast tissue on the back of a child as a sign of spine defect. Extra nipples or breasts form when a fetal milk line fails to shrink back. They sit most often on the line from armpit to groin. Back sites are rare and can link to spine closure defects. Their patient was an eleven year old girl.

A back midline swelling present from birth was first called a lipoma, a fat lump. Growth and a dark centre spot led to closer checks, which proved a nipple and areola complex. Spine MRI showed a fat tumour inside the spine cover at chest level, with a fibrous tract to the skin lump. The cord was tethered, or held tight, by the tract. Teams removed the tissue and did spine surgery in one plan. Back midline marks in children merit spine scans.
pmc-13279873:
Thaer A. Tumar and colleagues report a 2026 case of a low grade brain tumour in a young infant with a gene fault. Child low grade gliomas grow slowly and often end well. Early infancy cases in the back brain with wide spread are rare. Their patient was a four month old girl with signs of high skull pressure and sunsetting eyes. Scans showed a mass on the medulla, the low brain stem, with a large cyst.

The mass blocked fluid flow and swelled all four ventricles. A shunt drained fluid and surgery eased pressure. Tissue tests proved a low grade glioneuronal tumour with low growth rate. Gene tests found an FGFR1 mutation, a growth gene fault, plus a chromosome arm loss. Despite benign tissue looks, the tumour spread to neck cord and spine linings. Targeted therapy was started. Gene class can warn of fierce acts that tissue grade hides.
pmc-13281873:
Yiwei Zhang and colleagues followed women after pelvic support surgery for over seven years in a 2026 study. Pelvic organ prolapse lets the womb or bladder sag into the vagina. The surgery lifts the top of the vagina with its own ligaments through small cuts, alongside womb removal. Thirty-four women had the operation at a Beijing hospital from 2015 to 2019. Thirty-one stayed in follow-up past seven years. Checks joined exams with standard questionnaires.

By strict joint rules, about four in ten women counted as full successes. By body measures alone, more than three in four held up. No sag returned at the lifted top. Returns clustered in the front and back walls instead. More than nine in ten women never needed a second fix. The authors call the support durable, while noting strict success rules flatter no one.
pmc-13282173:
Maria Papaefstathiou and co-authors describe a 2026 wearable sensor made wholly from fabric that tracks body posture during yoga. The sensor is a stretchy capacitor, a device that stores charge and changes its signal when stretched, woven into clothing in a comb-like pattern. It is light, comfortable, and washable. Lab tests showed it kept working through six thousand five hundred stretch cycles.

Built into garments, the sensor recorded electrical signals during four yoga poses: two lunges, a squat, and a tree pose. A machine learning program, which learns patterns from examples, sorted the poses with about ninety-four percent accuracy. Signals linked to capacitance, the stored charge, carried the most useful information. Other signal types added detail on how each pose moved the fabric. The authors say such clothing sensors could support digital fitness coaching and home movement checks without stiff hardware.
pmc-13282473:
Perihan Kubra Akman and co-authors report a 2026 food study on fermenting reduced-calorie sour cherry drinks with lactic acid bacteria. Fermentation can raise how much of a food's useful compounds the body can access. The team used three single probiotic strains and one mixed culture, comparing the drinks with unfermented controls over twenty-eight days of cold storage. They tracked acidity, colour, plant compounds, antioxidant power, and bacterial survival.

Fermented drinks ended more acidic and kept live bacteria above the probiotic threshold for three weeks. Their key plant compounds were identified, though most declined in storage. Despite higher starting plant compound levels, controls were beaten on recovery after simulated digestion, meaning better bioaccessibility. Calorie cuts reached nearly half in the best recipe. Antioxidant capacity stayed higher in fermented drinks. The authors present fermentation as a practical upgrade for functional cherry beverages.
pmc-13282673: Adwall and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their 2022 study of complications and risk factors in breast cancer surgery. One sentence in the limitations paragraph of the Discussion was wrong. It explained why neoadjuvant chemotherapy, treatment given before surgery, was excluded, citing an earlier department cohort study and a hazard ratio for surgical site infection. The corrected sentence cites instead a 2014 to 2015 department study, gives an odds ratio near one, and marks the data as unpublished. The authors apologise for the error.
pmc-13282873:
Atom-by-atom maps for chemical reactions get a rigorous theoretical treatment from Marcos E Gonzalez Laffitte and collaborators, writing in 2026. Such maps link each atom in starting compounds to its place in products. Databases often lack these links, yet synthesis planning and isotope studies need them.

The authors focus on partial maps that cover only the reaction center, where bonds change. Using the Imaginary Transition State graph, they prove a clear rule for extension. A full unique map exists exactly when the partial map covers the reaction center. They also extend the result to cases where hydrogen atoms are not shown. Algorithms follow from the proof.
pmc-13283173:
Chicago's school stock inhaler rollout is audited for fairness in a 2026 district-wide analysis under Mariya Patwa. Stock inhalers are shared rescue inhalers kept for breathing distress at school. Asthma is common in the city, but access gaps hit Black and low-income students hardest.

Data covered 517 district schools and more than 266,000 students in total. High schools had higher asthma rates than elementary schools in the data. Black students had higher asthma odds than Hispanic students in adjusted models. Yet they had lower odds of a formal support plan for asthma. Low-income and unhoused students also had higher asthma odds. The rollout itself was judged fair across schools.
pmc-13283373:
Ultrasound stiffness of the cervix outpredicts the classic Bishop score before labor induction, Ping Li's prospective team shows in 2026. Failed induction raises risks for mother and baby alike. The Bishop score relies on hand exam and can vary between examiners.

A total of 106 first-time mothers with single babies joined from January 2024 to August 2025. Ultrasound measured neck length, angles, and tissue stiffness of the cervix. Of the group, 83 had successful induction and 75 had vaginal births. Ultrasound traits differed clearly between outcome groups in the analysis. Bishop traits showed no clear gaps in this study. Tissue stiffness alone predicted both outcomes best.
pmc-13283473:
Uncertainty bands make GPT-4o death forecasts from ICU notes more honest, Fatemeh Shah-Mohammadi's conformal study shows in 2026. Clinical notes hold rich detail but are hard to use in structured models. Large language models can read notes, yet their confidence per patient is unclear.

Notes from the first 24 hours of intensive care were fed to GPT-4o. Cases came from the MIMIC-III set for kidney failure patients admitted via emergency care. A conformal method wrapped predictions with patient-level uncertainty ranges. The model spotted death cases well, with high recall in that class. Survival calls were weaker by comparison in the test results. Clear uncertainty bounds may make AI forecasts safer for clinical use.
pmc-13283873:
Yi Zhong and a large team built a prediction chart in 2026 for death risk in children with moderate-to-severe head injury. Brain injury is a leading cause of child death and disability, and spotting high-risk cases early guides care. Records of 289 children admitted with such injuries were reviewed, and statistical selection pulled out the strongest predictors of dying in hospital within thirty days.

Four factors made the final chart: the Glasgow Coma Scale score, which grades consciousness, blood lactic acid, blood albumin, and trauma-driven clotting failure. Half the children were under about five years old. The chart sorted risk with high accuracy and matched observed outcomes well in checks. Decision analysis suggested value across a wide range of risk thresholds. The authors offer it for early risk sorting at admission.
pmc-13284773:
David Baud and co-authors report a 2026 cohort study on sexual function twelve years after childbirth injury to the anal sphincter. Such tears can cause pelvic floor problems, and short-term work has found more pain and less pleasure after injury. Long-term evidence was scarce, so the team re-surveyed the same women with a standard sexual function questionnaire.

Replies came from 52 women with injury and 141 controls, a high return rate for this long follow-up. Total and domain scores were alike between groups overall. Still, women with injury more often reported poor lubrication and pain on penetration. A past gap in reaching orgasm had faded by year twelve. The authors show broad recovery with some lasting symptoms.
pmc-13284873:
James Muscat and co-authors give a 2026 case report and literature review on a rare open midfoot injury. A 30-year-old woman fell six meters and suffered an open fracture-dislocation of the medial cuneiform bone, plus tearing of the tibialis anterior tendon from its anchor. Such cuneiform injuries are uncommon and often hide within wider foot trauma.

Urgent care included washing and cleaning the wound, realigning and fixing the midfoot, and repairing the tendon through a bone tunnel with strong sutures. At six months, X-rays held the alignment with no hardware failure. Pain was minimal, no infection appeared, and she walked on her own. The authors call this the first report of this exact pairing.
pmc-13285173:
Rumaisa Riaz and co-authors give a 2026 overview of drug care for Alzheimer disease, centered on the newly approved antibody donanemab-azbt. Older drugs lift a brain chemical or calm a receptor, easing symptoms but with side effects such as nausea or dizziness. New antibodies aim at amyloid clumps, yet can cause imaging faults tied to swelling or bleeding.

Trial data show donanemab-azbt lowers amyloid load and slows thinking decline in early symptomatic disease, the authors report. That gain comes with a need for close clinical and scan monitoring during treatment. The overview weighs donanemab beside standard drugs and the earlier antibody aducanumab to guide early-stage care choices.
pmc-13285373:
Greener straw pulping with soda ash help is the advance in a 2026 study by Qixi Xu and co-authors. Normal oxygen-alkali pulping of wheat straw runs hot, chews up cellulose, and lets silicon foul the process. Their low-heat method adds sodium carbonate and recycles the alkali mix.

At set heat and alkali levels, pulp yields rose over the standard method, and the test paper grew stronger on both pull and crush measures in the trials reported here. Far less dissolved silicon stayed in the waste liquor than under the old method, easing a key snag. The authors say the route gives steady, high-grade straw pulp with less waste strain.
pmc-13285573:
A tail stretch of viral RNA steers how well Getah virus grows, sickens, and rides mosquitoes, Tongwei Ren and co-authors show in a 2026 study. This mosquito-borne virus threatens farm stock and people, with fresh outbreaks growing harsher. The team snipped parts of the tail stretch, called the 3 prime untranslated region, and watched each mutant.

The tail proved bendy: cutting up to three hundred ten letters still left live virus. Losing repeat bits slowed growth in some cells and blunted illness in mice. The biggest cut crippled spread to mosquitoes and caused only brief sickness, with no deaths. Joint gene reads tied the softening to immune path shifts. A weakened vaccine seed is the goal.
pmc-13285673:
Yuhai Dang and Jinliang Kong describe an 80-year-old woman in rural Guangxi, China, who carried two infections at once, in a 2026 case report. She had coughed and run a fever for a month. Her lungs were already scarred by past tuberculosis, and she had eaten raw rodent meat, a known route of exposure to a tropical fungus.

Standard tests found nothing, although a nose swab detected the COVID-19 virus. Gene sequencing of fluid washed from her lungs identified both that virus and the fungus Talaromyces marneffei. Her immune counts were modest and she had no HIV. Treatment paired an antiviral with antifungal drugs, and her condition and scans improved. Damaged lungs, the authors note, can invite such fungi.
pmc-13285973:
Reda Amrani Souhli and colleagues compare four laboratory tests for tuberculosis in Tangier, Morocco, in a 2026 study. Fast, accurate diagnosis limits spread and guides treatment. The team ran smear microscopy, a rapid molecular test, and two culture methods side by side on the same samples, using liquid culture as the reference.

The study covered 386 specimens over nine months, from lungs and from other body sites. The molecular test found more cases than microscopy in both sample types while staying highly specific. Solid culture landed between the two in sensitivity. Results for drug resistance matched well between the molecular test and standard methods. The authors recommend combining molecular testing, microscopy, and culture rather than relying on one method.
pmc-13286073:
Elizabeth R Boskey and co-authors run a 2026 randomized trial on whether readers notice gender-inclusive health writing. Handouts on sexual and reproductive health can use wording that fits all genders, yet critics claim general readers dislike the style. The trial handed adults paired versions of teen handouts, one inclusive and one gender-specific, in random order.

The study held 454 adults assigned female at birth, about a third of them LGBTQ+. Most readers never spotted a difference between the paired sheets, even in the first pair they saw. Many who said they favored gender-specific wording still picked the inclusive sheet as the one they liked better. Those who favored inclusive wording chose it far more often when they did notice. Quiet inclusion, the authors conclude, passes without friction across the political range.
pmc-13286373:
Sepideh Cheheltani, Megan Coffin, and Velia M. Fowler study what happens to the eye lens when a protein that remodels its internal skeleton is removed. Published in 2026, the mouse study targets CAP2, which helps break down actin filaments. Lens fibers need that skeleton to stay flexible as they mature.

Lenses without CAP2 looked normal in size, shape, and clarity, yet they were stiffer under pressure and bounced back faster. Total actin stayed the same, but proteins that cap, stabilize, and bundle filaments increased in fiber membranes, while a cross-linking protein fell. The pattern suggests filaments became over-stabilized without CAP2's trimming. The work links one regulator to the mechanical feel of a whole tissue.
pmc-13286573:
Megan S Laham and a large team refine a fingerprinting assay for liver X receptor drugs in a 2026 pharmacology study. These receptors command cholesterol handling genes tied to Alzheimer's risk, and their activators help in animal models of several diseases. The blocker has always been the liver: the same drugs switch on fat making there. Their assay reads, with glowing molecular tags, which partner proteins a drug recruits or dismisses at the receptor.

A combined version now watches a partner swap happen in real time. Strength at recruiting partners to one receptor form tracked how well drugs switched on a cholesterol export gene in brain tumor cells. Fat-gene activation followed murkier rules. Fingerprints ranged from full activation to outright blockade within single drug families, giving designers a precision screen for cholesterol-friendly candidates that spare the liver.
pmc-13286673:
Giuseppe Dell'Anna and colleagues describe fishing a stray gallbladder stent out through a second one in a 2026 case vignette. A 74-year-old woman with heavy comorbidity first received external gallbladder drainage elsewhere for moderate acute gallbladder inflammation, then arrived with leaking bile and lingering fever. The team converted her to internal drainage under ultrasound guidance, seating a 10 by 10 millimeter metal stent through the gut wall into the gallbladder.

A month later, checks showed the stent had slipped entirely inside the gallbladder. Rather than operate on a frail patient, the team placed a second stent beside it, widened the passage, and pulled the migrated stent out with grasping forceps through the new channel. A large gallstone followed with a basket tool in the same session. No complications ensued, and the authors commend the rescue route for expert centers.
pmc-13286873:
Chukwuka Elendu and co-authors recount a goat saved by timely surgery in a 2026 veterinary case report. A proven mother doe under smallholder care strained in active labor for about fourteen hours with nothing to show for it. Examination found an alert but exhausted animal, weak contractions, and a cervix that stayed firm and barely open, admitting at most two fingers despite the long labor.

Gentle manual stretching failed, and the team deliberately skipped drugs that would strengthen contractions against a closed cervix, fearing rupture. An emergency cesarean through the left flank under local anesthesia resolved the obstruction directly. The report's lesson targets field practice: when a rigid cervix ignores both time and manipulation, earlier surgery, not more tugging, protects both doe and kid.
pmc-13286973:
Ting Lei and colleagues report long-term results for a modified hip operation in children born with a dislocated or poorly formed hip joint. The 2026 study reviews fifty-five children, seventy-one hips, treated between 2004 and 2025 with open reduction plus the modified Pemberton cut. The classic version risks damaging the growth cartilage because its deep path is partly blind.

The modification ends the cut a few millimeters above a notch in the pelvis, hinging above the Y-shaped cartilage instead of through it. Average follow-up exceeded seven years. Socket angle measures improved dramatically and stayed stable. Roughly nine in ten hips earned excellent or good ratings on both function and imaging scales. Bone death in the femoral head affected about one hip in nine, within historical norms.
pmc-13287073:
Yue Fei and colleagues lay out the protocol for a randomized trial comparing two sedatives in older patients having both upper and lower digestive tract endoscopy in one session. Published in 2026, the protocol responds to a real risk: sedation in the elderly can drop blood oxygen and blood pressure. Ciprofol, a newer relative of the standard propofol, may keep breathing and circulation steadier.

One hundred eighty-four patients aged sixty-five and over will be assigned evenly to one drug or the other, with neither patients nor assessors told which. The main outcome joins oxygen dips and blood pressure drops during sedation. Secondary measures cover airway help, recovery times, drug totals, and satisfaction. The registered trial aims to give firm guidance for a common procedure.
pmc-13287973:
Sultan M Alsharif and co-authors sequenced bacteria in 2026 from soil hugging the roots of four date palm varieties grown near Madinah in Saudi Arabia. A marker gene survey named the resident groups, and a prediction tool inferred what growth-helping jobs those bacteria might carry.

One large bacterial phylum led in most samples, while a second led in one variety. Known helper genera appeared throughout, including Bacillus and Paenibacillus. Predicted genes for moving phosphate and sulfur, grabbing iron, and handling oxidation were plentiful. The authors present the root zone as a rich source of helper microbes that could support greener date farming after strain-level testing.
pmc-13288973:
Xinyan Chen and colleagues give a 2026 trial plan for pain drugs after heart surgery. The trial sits at one center in China. It deals with small-cut valve replacement. Pain care after such surgery is tricky. Strong pain drugs can cause side effects.

The trial will enroll 130 patients in all. Half will get oxycodone by a pain pump. Half will get sufentanil instead. Neither side will know their drug. The main test is pain on coughing at 24 hours. Staff will also track drug use and side effects. The goal is to match, not beat, the standard drug.
pmc-13289373:
Tracey Smythe and coauthors ran a 2026 pilot in Luuka district, Uganda, on group work to improve health care access for people with disabilities. Barriers to care are steep in low-resource areas, and few community fixes have been tested. The Participatory Learning and Action for Disability approach lets groups name local barriers and act on them together.

Five groups ran from May 2023 to March 2024, each with roughly 35 to 48 members, totaling 204 people meeting every two weeks. Trained facilitators led 11 sessions per group cycle. Interviews, group watching, activity logs, and surveys before and after checked appeal, demand, and early effects. Members found the groups relevant and wanted them to continue, though mentor support for facilitators lagged at times.
pmc-13289673:
Louisa Horvath and Silke Pawils explored a 2026 mixed-methods study on trauma-sensitive obstetrics from the provider side in Germany. Traumatic birth experiences draw growing concern, yet most research asks birthing people, not staff. An online survey ran from October 2024 to February 2025 with 102 providers, plus four expert interviews for depth on causes and fixes.

Most providers defined traumatic birth through loss of control and negative emotions for the patient. Poor communication and information topped causes at 97.1 percent, followed by lack of emotional support as reported. Emotional support also ranked as the top preventive step by mean score. Lack of time and staff shortages were the main barriers named.
pmc-13289773:
Shivangini Duggal headed a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on infection after cholangioscopy, a scope procedure that views bile ducts directly. The method helps with complex bile disease but seems to carry higher infection risk than standard duct procedures. Proof to guide preventive antibiotics for this specific scope was thin, so pooled rates were needed.

Five databases were searched through March 2025, yielding twelve studies with 4413 procedures for pooling. Blood infection pooled near 6.68 percent, with wide uncertainty and high variation across studies as reported. Duct inflammation and pancreas inflammation pooled lower. Technical success was very high and clinical success also high overall. Study design explained part of the variation.
pmc-13289973:
Muhammad S Shabbir, Mary Ayad, and Christian S Jackson compare two treatments for bleeding vessel tangles in the upper gut, in 2026. These tangles, called angioectasias, often cause anemia, hospital stays, and transfusions. Using the TriNetX database, the team sorted patients into endoscopic therapy or drug therapy with somatostatin analogues. Outcomes were tracked at six months, three years, and five years.

Endoscopic treatment led on nearly every measure at six months. Its patients had lower hospitalization, fewer repeat scopes, and lower death rates than the drug group. The gap persisted at three years, including fewer transfusions for the scope group. At five years the endoscopic advantage still held across the same outcomes. Average hemoglobin also ran higher in the endoscopic cohort at every checkpoint. The authors call for randomized multicenter trials to confirm the pattern. Their data favor treating the lesions directly over drugs alone.
pmc-13290573:
Testing whole blood, not just plasma, catches more infections in patients with blood disorders, a 2026 real-world cohort study from northern China by Cuicui Lyu and colleagues shows. Infection is a leading killer in this group, and standard blood culture misses most culprits.

The team reviewed 231 blood samples from patients with suspected infection who received metagenomic sequencing. Whole-blood sequencing, which reads plasma plus blood cells, detected pathogens far more often than culture and found 13 organisms that plasma-only testing missed among its 101 detections. Its agreement with final clinical diagnoses was also the highest of the methods compared. Treatment improved for most patients as a result, with needless antibiotics stopped and therapy better aimed. Lyu and colleagues back the combined sample for early infection care in these fragile patients.
pmc-13291073:
Yiwei Chen and colleagues report a 2026 case where gene sequencing of spinal fluid found the true cause of meningitis after standard treatment failed. Their patient was a 67-year-old man with chronic lung disease who arrived with four days of high fever and confusion, and first antibiotic cover with meropenem brought no gain.

Metagenomic sequencing named Listeria monocytogenes, a foodborne germ that strikes hardest at older and weakened patients, as the cause of meningitis alongside a flare of his lung disease. Care switched to ampicillin-based treatment plus gentamicin for set courses, and his symptoms and blood markers improved fast afterward. The case backs early use of broad sequencing when brain infections resist usual diagnosis.
pmc-13291273:
Xiaochan Wang and co-authors measure how grass roots change water entry into loess soil, in a 2026 study. Loess covers China's Loess Plateau, where rain is scarce and restoration planting is widespread. The team grew tall fescue in soil columns and tested infiltration at five growth stages up to ninety-nine days. Root mass grew steadily across those stages. Water behavior was then modeled with a standard flow equation.

Older root systems let water finish infiltrating much faster than bare soil did. Saturated conductivity rose in a straight line with the root-to-soil mass ratio. Other water traits followed smooth exponential curves as roots grew. The team folded those relationships into the Richards equation for unsaturated flow. Simulations with the HYDRUS program matched measured wetting fronts and moisture profiles closely. The work gives modelers growth-stage parameters for vegetated loess slopes.
pmc-13291473:
Remote rehab may beat home exercise for sore tendons. Shijie Fan leads a 2026 review of telerehabilitation trials. Tendon pain often gets exercise care without surgery. Remote coaching could add support that home plans lack.

Ten trials with 412 people were pooled. Remote care cut pain more than home exercise alone. Function also improved more with remote support. Against in-person therapy, remote care tied on both scores. No clear gap showed for pain or function. Study quality and bias were graded with care. Remote care thus looks like a fair swap for clinic visits. It may widen access for rural patients.
pmc-13291773:
Theodore Z Cook and co-authors present a 2026 data paper assembling the first specimen-backed occurrence dataset for stoneflies across West Virginia. Stoneflies signal clean water, and the state holds unusually rich diversity for the eastern United States. The team merged museum specimens, fresh statewide collecting, and trusted literature records, with funding from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and northeastern states.

The dataset holds more than 4,500 records from all 55 counties, spanning 134 years and drawn from 17 institutions and private collections. Checking specimens confirmed 150 species from all nine eastern North American families. Fourteen species reported earlier could not be found again, most likely because of naming changes. The records will anchor a planned distribution atlas and checklist.
pmc-13291873:
Suqing Zhou and colleagues stop DNA origami pieces from clumping in a 2026 study. DNA origami folds a long strand into precise shapes that can dock onto patterned chips. The team worked with an asymmetric right triangle meant to land in a chosen orientation. Instead, triangles stuck to each other at one corner, cutting single-piece placement sharply. Microscopy traced the clumping to the hypotenuse arm's vertex.

Twisting along that arm exposed loose staple ends that grabbed neighboring triangles. Trimming short staples at that corner softened the vertex and hid the sticky ends. Single, unclumped triangles rose from about seventy-two to about eighty-seven percent. A competing fix, adding poly-T tails, helped only slightly, ruling out simple base stacking. On patterned surfaces, correctly oriented placement jumped from about thirty-three to seventy-seven percent. Tiny local tweaks can rescue placement fidelity.
pmc-13292573:
Lidan He and co-authors trace a 2026 protective circuit in the placenta that fails in preeclampsia, the dangerous pregnancy disorder. The deubiquitinase USP22 runs low in preeclamptic tissue while the necroptosis machinery, RIPK1, RIPK3, and MLKL, runs high. In oxygen-starved trophoblast cells, necroptosis proved the dominant death route among several tested with targeted blockers.

Removing USP22 worsened the necrotic signaling, while restoring it revived histone acetylation marks and calmed cell death. Gene scans after knockdown found 1,186 changed genes, including the silenced Wnt antagonist SFRP1. The mechanism: USP22 grips the acetyl writer KAT2A and shields it by snipping off K48-linked ubiquitin chains, keeping SFRP1's promoter acetylated and active. A rat model induced with L-NAME backed the pathway in living tissue.
pmc-13292773:
R. M. G. van Vuren and co-authors ask whether the COVID-19 pandemic widened income gaps in Dutch surgical cancer care, in a study published in 2026. Using national quality registries, they compared patients operated on for lung, esophageal, stomach, pancreatic, or liver tumors during the pandemic with a group treated in the two years before it. Social position was estimated from postal code scores.

Nearly thirty thousand operations were analyzed across both periods. The mix of patients by social position stayed much the same, and the median wait for treatment held at twenty-seven days in both groups. Rates of surgery for advanced tumors also showed no income pattern. The authors credit near-universal coverage and pandemic prioritization of cancer care for keeping access fair under pressure.
pmc-13293373:
Benjamin N Rome and colleagues test, in a 2026 validation study, whether live prescription fill data can stand in for slow official insurance counts by state. Coverage data often lag, which delays judgment of new health policies.

Quarterly state coverage and fills by payer type were compared from 2013 to 2024 for Medicaid, private cover, and uninsured groups. Medicaid fills tracked Medicaid coverage closely, while cash-pay fills tracked uninsured rates fairly well, and both links were stronger for adults than children. Private cover links were weak. The authors suggest fill data could give fast early reads on policy effects, above all for Medicaid.
pmc-13293473:
Junghee Yoon and co-authors build, in a 2026 expert study, a first framework for virtual reality health literacy in clinical care. Headset-based virtual reality can teach and treat patients, yet the skills patients need to use it well had not been defined.

A three-phase Delphi process ran from January to April 2024, starting with a literature scan and a panel of 15 experts in health care, virtual reality, and health literacy. Two survey rounds rated draft parts, and 13 experts stayed for round two. The final framework holds 5 domains and 14 subdomains, covering expected benefit, effort, and other readiness traits. The work gives clinics a shared language.
pmc-13293673:
Aparna Meher, Riya Chaudhary, and Himanshu Kumar identify a circular RNA that helps the body fight influenza A, in a 2026 laboratory study. Circular RNAs are ring-shaped molecules that fine-tune gene activity, yet their role in the first-line immune defense against flu was poorly defined. The molecule they studied, circCPSF6, normally falls during infection, and the team probed what happens because of that drop.

Experiments in cells and animals showed the ring works through two routes at once. It soaks up a small RNA that otherwise suppresses several antiviral defenders, freeing those defenders to act. It also binds a protein that normally restrains a key signaling hub, keeping interferon responses switched on. Together these actions raise cytokine and interferon-driven gene activity, marking the ring as a possible target for antiviral therapy.
pmc-13294273:
Jun-Chen Liu and coauthors pool early evidence on albumin-bound paclitaxel for advanced small cell lung cancer in a 2026 single-arm meta-analysis. Later-line options have improved survival, but the best regimen stays debated and trials of this drug were small and uncontrolled. Four databases yielded nine studies with 334 patients, covering response, survival, and side effects.

Pooled response rate was 25.0% and disease control rate was 62.5% in the reported figures. Median-style pooled survival values reached 3.16 months without progression and 7.23 months overall. Low white cell counts and anemia dominated side effects. Adding immunotherapy looked numerically better in subgroup checks, a lead for controlled trials.
pmc-13294373:
Ziqiang Ding and coauthors build a nanobody T cell engager that can reach targets inside cancer cells in a 2026 proof-of-concept study.
