pmc-13441373:
Cwik and a long list of colleagues argue that open science habits matter even more in clinical psychology. The habits include preregistration, data sharing, and open-access publishing. Studies in this field rest on small, hard-to-recruit patient samples and sensitive data. Their commentary aims to help clinical teams take a stance and apply the habits despite real hurdles.

The authors map where openness already gains for clinical science and practice. It also aligns with the field's ethical standards of transparency and patient welfare. They then work through the tensions. Privacy duties surround patient data. Complex therapy methods resist one-size formats. And sharing could harm at-risk patients if handled badly. A final push urges including experts by experience, the patients themselves, as partners in the research process. The authors say clinical psychology has missed that facet of openness.
pmc-13444373:
Zixiang Ye and colleagues hunt for care targets in a web that links family function and self-insight in schizophrenia in a 2026 study. The pool held 785 adults in community follow-up care in Pengzhou City, China, with 414 men and 371 women. Online scales graded family closeness, family flex, and insight into one's own thoughts.

Network models treated each scale item as a node with ties to its kin. A play-acting tool then poked each node to see which pokes ripple most, a way to spot core and bridge items. One flagged item marks low family say in shared choices. The authors stress that pokes in a snapshot web give hints, not proof of cure. Trials must test whether family work on those items pays off.
pmc-13444473:
Wenyi Tang and colleagues map silent brain injury on MRI in heart failure patients in a 2026 study. Weak hearts starve the brain over time, and scans often show infarcts, white matter scars, and shrinkage long before clear mind loss. Their team hunted which patient traits foretell each injury type on scans.

Smoking, diabetes, and a high NT-proBNP mark foretold large brain infarcts in the cohort. Age, high blood pressure, clot protein levels, and HDL marks tracked white matter scar load. Age plus a broad inflammation index tracked brain shrinkage. One patient type, marked by hot inflammation and poor nutrition, faced the highest injury risk in the split. The authors urge brain checks for that high-risk heart group.
pmc-13445573:
Luyan Chen and colleagues build a scoring chart to sort thyroid cancer patients by the size of their lymph node spread after surgery, in a 2026 methods study. Guidelines split patients at a two-millimeter focus size, since larger spread calls for closer follow-up and, at times, added radioactive iodine. No tool yet graded that burden for patients with proven node spread.

Records came from 212 patients with the classic form of papillary thyroid cancer and confirmed node spread, treated at one center from 2021 to 2025. Ninety-two fell in the tiny-spread group and one hundred twenty in the larger group. The team screened thirteen tissue traits with a penalized method built to stay steady on rare traits, then shaped the strong ones into a chart for bedside risk sorting.
pmc-13446173:
Charith Raj Adkar-Purushothama and colleagues open a journal collection on non-chemical ways to guard crops against disease and harsh conditions, in a 2026 editorial. Outbreaks and climate stress press world food supply, while heavy pesticide use raises worries over pollution, harm to bystander species, and drug resistance in pests. The collection gathers work that leans on biology and ecology instead.

Pieces in the set span friendly microbes that suppress disease, bred-in plant resistance, care of the soil microbiome, and breeding plans that harden crops. Highlights include a multi-omics study of how microbe teams quell bacterial wilt in tomato and a review of the fight against a deadly citrus and olive pathogen. The editors frame the set as a systems-level push for crop care with fewer synthetic inputs.
pmc-13447073:
Yun Chai and colleagues map the blood chemistry that sets tumor-induced osteomalacia apart from common osteoporosis, in a 2026 records study. The rare syndrome comes from small tumors that leak a hormone, FGF23, which drains phosphate through the kidneys and softens bone. Its low bone density is often misread as plain osteoporosis, which delays the cure.

Eleven syndrome patients and twelve osteoporosis patients, seen over fourteen years, were compared in depth. The syndrome group ran far lower blood phosphate and phosphate reclaim by the kidney, lower calcium, and a bone enzyme level about four times higher. Bone density and parathyroid hormone did not split the groups. The authors lay out a step path from blood tests to tumor proof.
pmc-13447973:
Giacomo Butta leads a team defining immune signatures of silent HIV infection inside a special memory T cell pool in 2026 work. Hidden HIV copies that make no virus form the main barrier to a cure, yet how such non-productive infections settle during the very first round in human cells was unclear. A reporter virus let the team separate silently infected cells from productive ones.

Stem cell memory cells, a long-lived T cell subset, carried a distinct signature of over one hundred raised genes when harbouring silent virus. Top signals included migration chemicals that bind a specific receptor, enzymes that break down an amino acid, and proteins that rearrange cell scaffolding. Flow tests confirmed enrichment for two of those markers together in this subset. The profile may help silent cells dodge immunity and persist, the authors suggest.
pmc-13448273:
De La Cruz-Villanueva and colleagues studied which breast cancer patients develop brain spread early, using records from a specialized cancer center in Central America. Their 2026 retrospective cohort covered women treated between 2019 and 2023 whose invasive breast cancer later reached the brain. Early brain spread cuts survival and quality of life, so knowing who is at risk could guide closer monitoring.

De La Cruz-Villanueva compared 63 women with brain spread within two years against 49 whose spread came later. Early cases were far more often HER2-positive or triple-negative tumors, meaning cancers driven by a growth receptor or lacking hormone receptors, and they more often had advanced stage at diagnosis. Luminal A tumors, a slower hormone-driven type, clustered in the late group. Brain spread appeared at a median of 14 months in early cases versus 41 months in late cases, supporting risk-based brain surveillance.
pmc-13448873:
Elif Ekinci and colleagues analyze in 2026 stored data from two phase 2 trials of survodutide, a drug that activates both glucagon and GLP-1 receptors. One trial randomized 413 people with type 2 diabetes on metformin for 16 weeks; the other followed 387 people with overweight or obesity and normal blood sugar for 46 weeks. The question was whether the drug improves insulin-making cell function and insulin sensitivity.

In the diabetes trial, survodutide raised a standard index of beta-cell function and lowered insulin resistance, glucagon, and fasting glucose versus placebo. In the second trial, beta-cell indices barely moved, likely because participants started with normal sugar, while insulin resistance and fasting measures still improved. Weight loss explained the largest share of change in fasting insulin and resistance, yet most other shifts were independent of weight, hinting at extra metabolic action.
pmc-13449073:
Juan Manuel Arteaga-Diaz and co-authors present in 2026 the Latin American findings of SUCCESS, a real-world study of a once-daily combination injection for type 2 diabetes. The product, iGlarLixi, pairs basal insulin glargine with the GLP-1 drug lixisenatide in one pen, lowering fasting and after-meal glucose together. Across Latin America fewer than 55 percent of treated patients reach their glucose targets, so simpler regimens matter.

SUCCESS was a twelve-month international observational study of people whose diabetes stayed uncontrolled on oral drugs, with or without insulin or GLP-1 therapy. The parent study found better glucose control after starting the combination, with little low blood sugar and no weight gain. This subanalysis focuses on participants from the Latin American region, checking whether those effectiveness and safety patterns hold in local routine practice, where undiagnosed diabetes and cost pressures shape care.
pmc-13449773:
Chandok and colleagues reviewed in 2026 every in-hospital cardiac arrest on general wards at a Singapore hospital. A cardiac arrest means the heart stops while a patient is already in hospital care. They read records of all arrests during 2022 and sorted each case by its pre-arrest state. 

There were 50 arrests among more than fifty thousand admissions, and most patients were frail older adults. Three in five arrests met the criteria for possible suboptimal end-of-life planning. Yet only three in ten patients had any written note on the extent of care they wanted. Just five patients survived to leave hospital. Shorter resuscitation, witnessed arrests, and lasting return of a heartbeat were each tied to survival. The authors urge earlier, routine talks about care goals for frail inpatients.
pmc-13449973:
Zhuoyun Tong and colleagues publish in 2026 a protocol for tagging antibody-making plasma cells inside one mouse thigh bone without disturbing the rest of the body. Long-lived plasma cells shelter in bone marrow niches and keep protective antibodies flowing for years, yet tracking whether they stay, wander, or get mobilized has lacked a clean tool. Injecting labeled antibody into a single femur marks only that bone's residents.

The method walks through injecting dye-linked antibodies directly into the marrow cavity, harvesting marrow afterward, and reading the tags by flow cytometry. Cells carrying the mark that later turn up in other bones, blood, or tissues reveal themselves as emigrants from the labeled femur. The protocol has been validated in standard laboratory mice. The authors note the same trick could label other marrow populations by aiming at their distinctive surface markers, opening studies of retention and release across immunology.
pmc-13450273:
Dias and colleagues study sorting nexin 5, or SNX5, a protein that helps move cargo inside cells, and ask what it does in tuberculosis infection. Their 2026 study infects mice lacking the protein with a low dose of the tuberculosis bacterium through the air, then compares them with normal mice. The team also tests infected macrophages, the immune cells that swallow bacteria, in the lab to find where defense breaks down.

Mice without SNX5 died more often, though their lungs held the same number of bacteria as normal mice. Their lungs showed worse inflammation without shifts in which immune cells arrived. In macrophages, loss of SNX5 left bacterial killing intact. But it cut the breakdown of swallowed proteins and weakened MHC class II presentation, the display of bacterial pieces that wakes helper T cells. Helper cell activation fell, though the display molecules on the cell surface stayed normal in number.
pmc-13451873:
Zartashia Ghani and a large team report in 2026 an eighteen-month trial of a tablet app for people with mild memory loss and their family carers. The app, SMART4MD, sends drug reminders and visit alerts, aids whose proof past short trials was weak. The trial ran in Spain and Sweden and enrolled 1,078 patients with carers.

Quality of life, the main score, ran a touch higher in the app group at both six and eighteen months. Drug taking and mind test scores, though, did not split by group at the end. Early gains in quality-weighted life years showed for patients, carers, and pairs alike. The authors call the app a modest help, not a cure path.
pmc-13452173:
Thiloka Ratnaike and a very large team pilot in 2026 whole genome reads for British children and youth with cerebral palsy. Past world work finds a single-gene cause in up to a third of cases, yet the health service had not tested genome reads for this group. The pilot enrolled 86 patients from clinics in five towns, most as parent-child trios.

Reads found a firm or likely disease gene in about an eighth of cases, with a further third holding unclear variants. Each firm find shaped forecasts, care plans, and family risk advice. A learning model used symptom terms to sort who was likeliest to gain a label. The team offers the pilot as a case for wider NHS use.
pmc-13452273:
Shraddha Vaidya and Jatinderkumar Saini set out in 2026 a protocol for scoring how repeatable a large language model's answers are. The same prompt can yield changed words, shape, and length on each run, since the models sample by chance. Their frame runs prompts again and again and grades the spread.

A single score, the Composite Consistency Score, blends sense likeness with shape wobble across the runs. Checks cover heat settings of the sampler, prompt wording shifts, and the score's own trust. A public notebook carries the code. The authors offer the frame as a shared yardstick for a trait that model cards rarely report.
pmc-13452573:
Arman Moini Jazani and five co-authors shrink a polymer growing method so labs can make many polymer and protein hybrids at once, fast. These hybrids pair man made chains with DNA, peptides, or proteins to help drugs last longer in the body. Their 2026 method, called OPTIMA ATRP, grows the chains with light in open air, with no need to purge oxygen first.

Each run takes under ten minutes in less than 50 microlitres of water, in pipette tips or a 96 well plate. A common salt, sodium pyruvate, works with UV light to keep the growth fast and controlled, even at fridge level cold. The team made DNA, peptide, lipid, and protein hybrids side by side on the cheap. The setup lets non specialists screen large libraries of hybrids, work that older methods made slow and costly.
pmc-13453073:
Hsiao and colleagues work toward building a natural antibiotic in the lab in this 2026 chemistry study. The target, microcin J25, is a bacterial peptide tied into a lasso shape, a loop with its tail threaded through, which makes it remarkably heat-stable and potent against Gram-negative bacteria. Making this knotted structure chemically has eluded chemists since its discovery in 1992.

Their plan used unusual amino acids carrying sulfur on a side carbon to pre-staple the peptide into shape with sulfur bridges. The strategy did not achieve the lasso configuration, and the authors report that plainly. They did develop reliable routes to those sulfur-bearing building blocks. The form suits standard peptide synthesis. They also summarize prior work on making microcin J25 and its analogs for future attempts.
pmc-13453673:
Donatella Di Corrado and five co-authors ask whether felt stress explains why football referees run more anxious than coaches. Their 2026 study surveys 177 regional level football professionals, 94 referees and 83 coaches. Each person filled in scales for anxiety, stress, and personality traits.

Referees reported clearly higher felt stress and trait anxiety, the deep set kind, than coaches. Coaches scored higher on openness, agreeableness, and care with duties. Felt stress tracked both passing and deep set anxiety, and it proved the strongest predictor of anxiety overall. A mediation test showed stress carries part of the role effect: being a referee raises stress, which in turn raises anxiety. The authors urge programs that teach stress appraisal, not just workload cuts.
pmc-13453773:
Xing Xiong, Shanrui Yang, Xinyi Jiang, and Qinghai Zhang use AI built rural scenes to test which parts of a view restore a stressed viewer. Their 2026 study makes 27 country scenes with set depth layers, swapping what sits in the foreground and midground while the backdrop stays fixed. Thirty people did a stress task, then viewed the scenes or a blank screen while blood pressure, heart rate, brain waves, and mood were tracked.

The rural scenes beat the blank screen on every recovery measure, with heart rate down 5.85 beats per minute more. Within the scenes, water in the foreground lifted liking scores, while a foreground road sank them. Brain wave signs of stress dipped with water and forest settings, though that part of the proof ran weaker. The authors present AI scenes as a workable lab tool for landscape research.
pmc-13453873:
Miller and co-authors used Japanese death certificate data from 2020 and 2021, before vaccines were widespread, to test whether universal health coverage protected non-Japanese residents from COVID-19 as well as citizens. Of 20,775 COVID deaths, 358, under 2 percent, were among non-Japanese residents in the national registry.

The overall age-standardized rate looked reassuring for non-Japanese residents at 14.9 per 100,000, below the nationwide 16.5 figure. Among those 65 and older the picture inverted sharply: non-Japanese mortality reached 152.3 per 100,000 against 52.5 for the general older population. Korean residents accounted for 193 of the 358 deaths, 53.9 percent, with an older-adult rate of 162.1 per 100,000 in that subgroup. Years of life lost per capita ran three times higher for non-Japanese residents and over four times higher for Koreans.
pmc-13454073:
Nicole I Y Z Tan and thirteen co-authors ask how two brain fluid systems work together with thinking power in memory clinic patients. One system is the choroid plexus, a tissue that makes spinal fluid; the other is the glymphatic flow that clears waste. Their 2026 study scans 100 patients, grading thinking with two standard tests and flow with a diffusion scan index.

A larger choroid plexus came with a lower flow index, after adjusting for age, schooling, and a blood tau marker tied to Alzheimer disease. Neither measure alone tracked thinking scores. The two together did: a larger plexus meant worse scores only when the flow index ran high, a link that held on both thinking tests. Blood tau tracked worse thinking on its own but did not change the pairing. The authors suggest the two fluid systems interact in a state dependent way.
pmc-13454873:
Merve Boyraz and five colleagues review, in a 2026 study, warning signs seen before the most severe suicide attempts by children and teenagers. The team studied patients aged 8 to 18 admitted to one Turkish intensive care unit between 2017 and 2025 after intentional self-harm. Survivors were interviewed in person, and families supplied details for those who died.

Of 256 patients, 116 met the study rules, about 70 percent of them girls, with an average age near 15.5 years. Roughly seven in ten had seen a health provider in the prior year for signs that, in hindsight, warned of risk. The group with no such contact skewed younger, especially ages 8 to 13, and suffered worse outcomes. The authors argue that clinics miss chances to intervene, and that staff should treat certain visits by young patients as prompts for careful screening.
pmc-13455273:
Troost and collaborators widened their earlier air pollution study in 925 children and adults with primary glomerular kidney diseases. They re-ran the analysis with a national air research dataset and longer follow-up. More pollutants were tested against disease decline. Decline meant a 40 percent drop in filtering rate or kidney failure.

The new pollutant data repeated the original adverse findings for fine particles and black carbon in this patient cohort with extended observation. Nitrogen dioxide emerged as an additional culprit, with a hazard ratio of 1.12 per doubling of exposure for decline in the survival models. Specific chemical components of fine particulate matter also showed new associations with faster decline in the wider analysis reported. The authors argue the replication across independent exposure datasets strengthens the case that air quality is a modifiable driver of glomerular disease outcomes.
pmc-13457073:
Yu Chen and six colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether cheap inflammation scores from a routine early pregnancy blood test can warn of preeclampsia months ahead. The condition, marked by dangerous blood pressure in pregnancy, strikes three to eight percent of mothers and still lacks a useful early predictor. Blood drawn between weeks six and twelve was compared for 109 women who later developed it and 177 who did not.

White cell families ran higher in the future cases, while two cell types stayed level. All four combined inflammation indices were significantly raised in the women bound for preeclampsia. The signal tied mainly to the late-onset form of the disease. Severity, once the disease arrived, did not track the early scores. The authors present the indices as candidate early flags drawn from a test clinics already run, pending wider validation.
pmc-13459173:
Guojun Yue and co-authors tested whether a simple nutrition and immunity blood score, tracked after lung cancer surgery, can flag patients heading for recurrence. The score, the prognostic nutritional index, combines albumin, a blood protein, with lymphocyte counts. Their 2026 study enrolled 119 patients having curative surgery for stage I to III non-small cell lung cancer. It focused on 94 who were alive and cancer free at three months with complete score data.

By three months, 51 patients had recovered their score to target levels and 43 had not. During follow up, recurrence or death events struck 41.9 percent of the non recovered group against 17.6 percent of the recovered group. Two year recurrence free survival was 59.2 percent versus 82.3 percent in the comparison reported. Failing to recover the score more than doubled the recurrence hazard after adjustment. Adding the recovery measure improved the prediction model's accuracy.
pmc-13459273:
Marisa Iborra and co-authors surveyed gastroenterology trainees across Spain about their training, skill gaps, and well-being, on behalf of the national society SEPD. Their 2026 cross-sectional survey drew 241 anonymous responses from residents and specialists within five years of finishing, most training in university and tertiary hospitals. Respondents rated satisfaction and named weak areas on five-point scales, and the team modeled which working conditions were associated with burnout, a major concern in medical training.

Overall satisfaction scored 3.99 out of 5, with practical training rated 4.25 but theoretical teaching only 3.30 in the survey results. The most requested reinforcements were clinical nutrition, digestive ultrasound, and endoscopy, each named by roughly a quarter of respondents. Burnout was reported by 63.5 percent of respondents, a strikingly high share. Inadequate rest strongly raised burnout risk, while satisfaction with working conditions protected against it. Nearly nine in ten wanted an extra training year.
pmc-13459373:
Arlene Jiang and co-authors describe how they built the statistical starting assumptions for a children's emergency trial without ever meeting in person. Bayesian trials need prior distributions, expert informed starting estimates, and gathering them usually requires costly face to face workshops. Their 2026 study ran three remote workshops, each with two survey rounds separated by group discussion. The topic was two steroid doses for croup, the barking cough childhood illness, in a planned trial comparing a low dose with the standard dose.

Experts reviewed the same literature beforehand and gave judgments merged using bivariate distributions, a method that preserves how beliefs about the two doses hang together. The resulting prior supported a planned sample size of 1,850 children at a four percent non-inferiority margin. The authors report the elicited beliefs matched published evidence on both doses. They present remote elicitation as a workable, cheaper replacement for in person panels.
pmc-13460173:
Zi-Wei Zhang and Qiu-Hua Wan combined in 2026 a global literature map with a bedside test of the SAVE score. That score predicts survival for patients on veno-arterial ECMO, a machine that takes over heart and lung work in refractory shock. Bibliometric tools charted publications from 1988 to 2024, while a separate check ran the score on 101 intensive care patients drawn from the MIMIC-IV database.

The United States, France, and China led publishing, and hot topics since 2020 include assist devices, guidelines, and in-hospital cardiac arrest. At the bedside the score disappointed: discrimination was weak, predicted survival was badly calibrated against actual hospital deaths, and decision analysis showed little net benefit. The pairing warns clinicians that celebrated scores need local validation before guiding real ECMO decisions.
pmc-13461173:
David Alsina and co-authors modeled in 2026 two disease-causing variants of POLRMT, the sole enzyme that copies mitochondrial genes in mice, mirroring mutations recently found in patients. People with these variants show varied problems from low muscle tone to developmental delay. The team engineered the dominant and recessive substitutions into mice and tracked survival, mitochondrial DNA, and gene transcripts.

Mice carrying two copies of the recessive variant died around birth without obvious developmental defects, seemingly failing the metabolic switch to oxygen-based energy that birth demands. Mice with the dominant variant lived, with depressed mitochondrial transcripts yet normal DNA levels, matching patient biology. The comparison separates two jobs of the enzyme: starting fresh transcription versus priming DNA copying.
pmc-13461373:
Ligia Patricia Laverde and colleagues pooled in 2026 randomized trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists at obesity doses to ask what these powerful weight loss drugs do to muscle. Seven trials with 821 patients were combined, tracking lean mass three ways: its share of total weight, its absolute change, and its percentage change, alongside side effects.

The share of weight made of lean tissue actually rose, because fat fell faster. Absolute lean mass nevertheless dropped by an average of a little under two kilograms, with wide variation between trials, and semaglutide showed the largest absolute loss. The authors conclude that muscle loss alone should not disqualify these drugs for obesity, while insisting that protein intake and exercise accompany treatment to protect strength and function.
pmc-13461573:
Dergaa and colleagues mapped in 2026 the evidence on generative artificial intelligence in sports medicine, where chatbots are already used for training plans, rehab, nutrition, mental health support, and writing. Adoption has outrun proof of accuracy and safety. The team searched six databases for work from 2022 to March 2026 and sorted the studies by use area, accuracy, and ethical concerns.

Dergaa kept 32 studies from over eighteen hundred records. Uses spread across seven domains, with academic writing and ethics the largest groups. Accuracy swung widely: in one check, a newer model met validity bars for sleep and jet lag advice while an older one fell short on both. Made-up content, called hallucination, was rated a critical risk for general chatbots but much lower for systems tied to retrieved sources. The authors call for governance matched to the fast uptake.
pmc-13461873:
Akash Shambharkar and co-authors characterized the first virus enzymes ever tested from phages of Proteus mirabilis, a bacterium behind stubborn catheter urinary infections increasingly resistant to antibiotics. Endolysins are phage proteins that dissolve bacterial walls from outside, but none from Proteus phages had been described experimentally. In their 2026 study, the team produced two endolysins, LysPM1 and LysPM2, with different wall cutting domains, and tested killing against several Proteus species alongside agents that breach the outer membrane.

Both enzymes killed Proteus when paired with permeabilizers such as EDTA or citric acid, worked best near neutral pH, and stayed active up to sixty degrees. Their metal appetites differed: stripping metals killed all activity, and calcium plus zinc partly revived LysPM1, while calcium plus manganese revived LysPM2. LysPM2 is also the first single CHAP domain endolysin characterized from a Gram negative phage. Distinct cofactor needs matter for formulating the enzymes as drugs.
pmc-13462073:
Dsouza and Mendon ran a 2026 school-based study of digital exposure and health behaviours in South Indian adolescents. Habits for eating, activity, and screen use form during the teenage years and track into adult health. Their cross-sectional survey covered students aged twelve to fifteen in a school setting.

A total of 192 adolescents completed structured questionnaires on food habits, physical activity, and screen time for this study. Dsouza found most students scored in the neutral middle range for eating behaviour overall. Activity split sharply, with about fifty-five percent highly active and about forty-five percent in the low activity group. Between fourteen and twenty percent reported two or more hours of screen time daily across domains. Activity linked significantly to sex, family type, exercise status, and age.
pmc-13462873:
Huijing Wu and colleagues build, in a 2026 cohort study, a time-aware computer model that predicts the risk of distant spread in early-stage breast cancer from routine clinical traits. Spread to distant organs is a leading cause of death in this group, yet current tools are imprecise.

The system stacked four survival models under one combining learner, and an explanation method showed how each trait pushed risk. Node stage and a cell growth marker, Ki-67, drove risk most, with curved effects and interactions between traits. Five-year freedom from distant spread was about ninety-five percent in the low-risk group, seventy-nine in the middle, and near half in the high-risk group. A competing-risk check, accounting for deaths from other causes, told the same story. Decision analysis confirmed practical benefit. The authors offer the model as a transparent aid for tailoring follow-up and extra treatment.
pmc-13463973:
Mosaddeghi-Heris and colleagues studied in 2026 how oxidative stress, mood, and thinking skills interact in people with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis who have mild to moderate disability. Oxidative stress means damage from unstable oxygen molecules that the body's defenses fail to mop up. Whether blood markers of that damage explain thinking problems in early disease was unclear.

The study assessed 83 patients with thinking tests, mood scales, hand skill tasks, and a panel of blood markers. Disability level and years of schooling were the strongest predictors of thinking scores, with more disability tied to slower processing and weaker working memory. One damage marker, malondialdehyde, tracked with abnormal thinking in simple analyses but faded once other factors were weighed. Most other stress markers showed no firm links. The authors stress support for cognition even at low disability.
pmc-13464873:
Bezen and colleagues ran a randomized trial in 2026 comparing three nerve blocks for pain after modified radical mastectomy. That breast cancer operation is known for moderate to severe soreness. Ninety women were divided evenly among three techniques. They were an erector spinae plane block, a thoracic paravertebral block, and a pectoral nerve block. Each delivered the same local anesthetic before standard general anesthesia. Morphine use over 24 hours was the main measure.

The erector spinae group needed the most morphine, a median of 10 milligrams against 9 in each other group. The gap was small but statistically firm. Those patients also asked for their first morphine soonest. They reported the lowest quality-of-recovery scores on a standard 15-item scale. The paravertebral block lasted longest before wearing off. Pain scores, rescue opioid use, and nausea rates otherwise matched. The authors recommend the pectoral or paravertebral techniques as stronger building blocks for pain plans.
pmc-13465473:
Melissa Castillo-Lizardo and Enrique Viguera test how magnesium levels steer copying slips by DNA polymerase enzymes in the lab. Slippage at repeated DNA letters inserts or deletes chunks and destabilizes genomes. Seven enzymes, from mild-temperature and heat-loving germs alike, copied a repeat-laced template across magnesium levels.

Low magnesium curbed slips in four enzymes, while two others slipped at every workable level. The link ran through strand displacement: enzymes that pushed the old strand aside harder slipped less. Proofreading skill, by contrast, moved slip rates not at all. Normal free magnesium inside cells may quietly guard genome steadiness, the pair suggest, by keeping displacement strong. The setup offers a clean bench model for fidelity studies.
pmc-13465573:
Xijing Fei, Kai Liu, and Narayanaswamy Balakrishnan describe a system, published in 2026, that suggests radiotherapy-based choices for people with head and neck cancer. They built a plain Cox hazards model as a baseline, then a DeepSurv deep-learning model, using records for 3,266 patients drawn from the RADCURE collection held in The Cancer Imaging Archive.

On held-out test data the two models scored close together, and the small gap between them was not statistically clear. Older age and more advanced tumors pointed to higher risk, while people who had quit smoking or never smoked fared better than current smokers. The authors stress that the outputs are decision support, not proof that one treatment causes a better outcome.
pmc-13466273:
Maria Martinez-de-la-Casa and colleagues link the health of the cornea's inner cell layer to eye measurements and general illnesses in a large group of cataract patients, in a 2026 study. Just over a thousand eyes, one per patient, were examined before surgery, with an average age near seventy-six. A microscope counted the lining cells and rated their shape and size spread.

Cell density averaged a little above two thousand per square millimeter, and small deposits called guttae appeared in about fifteen percent of eyes. Older age tracked with fewer lining cells. Models adjusted for age and sex, and separate looks by eye length tested whether long or short eyes changed the pattern.
pmc-13466373:
Ipponi and co-authors ask whether bone tumour surgery by curettage lets patients return to sport. Their 2026 study reviews 138 cases of benign and locally aggressive bone tumours scraped at one institution between 2016 and 2024. Activity was tracked with the UCLA scale. Readings came before the tumour was found, before surgery, and at latest follow-up. Standard oncology scores, the authors note, miss this performance dimension.

Activity collapsed with illness, the average score falling from 7.7 to 5.1, then recovered to 7.0 after surgery. About 87 percent of patients who had played sport regularly returned to their main sport, though over a quarter did so less often. Postoperative complications struck about 6.5 percent of cases. Patients who needed plates and screws, or who suffered complications, regained less activity, while younger patients fared best. Curettage, the authors conclude, suits an athletic life for most.
pmc-13466673:
Ciołkiewicz and colleagues examine the liver-heart axis in rheumatoid arthritis, the autoimmune joint disease whose patients also face raised cardiovascular risk, in 2026 clinical research. Liver scarring is common in the disease, yet whether the standard drug methotrexate drives it remains disputed. The study enrolled 51 patients, 46 of them women, with a mean age of 48.8 years and median disease duration of 12 years, and measured liver stiffness by ultrasound elastography plus two blood-based fibrosis scores.

Blood signals called organokines behaved differently against the stiffness readings: myostatin rose with stiffness, while resistin moved in the opposite direction. One fibrosis score also tracked with heart measures, tracking with a rheumatoid-specific heart risk score and with ultrasound signs of the heart's relaxation problems. Methotrexate use, weekly dose, and lifetime dose showed no link to any fibrosis measure. Ciołkiewicz calls the findings early, but they shift suspicion away from the drug itself.
pmc-13468373:
Yessica San Miguel and colleagues test in 2026 whether fungi that live inside desert plants can lend their heat tolerance to tomato. Rising temperatures flood plant tissues with reactive oxygen species, damaging growth, and tomato is especially sensitive. Tomato plants were inoculated with one of two desert-derived endophytic fungi, Talaromyces minioluteus or Serendipita indica, and grown at normal or heat-stress temperatures of 35 degrees by day.

Heat cut growth and raised oxidative damage, but inoculated plants fared better on both counts. They kept higher shoot and root biomass. They also carried less of the damage marker malondialdehyde and less hydrogen peroxide. pmc-13469273:

pmc-13470373:

pmc-13471673:

pmc-13474373:

pmc-13474673:

pmc-13474873:

pmc-13477373:

pmc-13478473:

pmc-13479573:

pmc-13479673:

pmc-13483673:

pmc-13486473:

pmc-13487673:

pmc-13488073:

pmc-13488173:

pmc-13488573:

pmc-13489573:

pmc-13489673:

pmc-13489773:

pmc-13490573:

pmc-13490873:

pmc-13493473:

pmc-13494673:

pmc-13495173:

pmc-13495273:

pmc-13499173:

pmc-13499473:

pmc-13499873:

pmc-13500373:

pmc-13501573:

pmc-13501673:
