pmc-13501773:
Yujing Gu leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 mixed-methods study of kinesiophobia, an excessive fear of movement, in older stroke survivors in Wuxi, China. Between January 2024 and June 2025, 307 patients aged 60 or older in subacute or chronic recovery completed questionnaires on physical function, psychological state, and illness adaptation. Eighteen of them later gave semi-structured interviews, read through a life-course lens that weighs early experiences, relationships, and timing across a lifetime.

Kinesiophobia affected 64.8 percent of the sample, 199 of the 307 patients counted in the survey. Muscle weakness, fear of falling, frailty, and anxiety each raised the likelihood, while being over 81, confidence in exercising, and acceptance of the illness lowered it. Interviews distilled four themes covering historical setting, linked lives, life timing, and personal agency. The authors urge nurses to screen for movement fear routinely and to shape rehabilitation plans around each patient's history.
pmc-13501973:
Alsuwied and co-authors report removing a jaw tumour and rebuilding the bite in a single operation. Their 2026 case report and literature review describes a 36-year-old woman with pain on biting and swelling near her right ear. Examination found facial asymmetry with her chin shifted left and limited mouth opening. She also had an open bite at the back right and a tilted biting plane. All traced to an osteoma, a benign bone tumour, on her jaw condyle.

Rather than staging the work, the team resected the condylar tumour and performed orthognathic surgery, corrective jaw surgery, simultaneously, guided by virtual surgical planning. The authors argue the combined approach restored facial harmony that tumour removal alone would not have achieved, while sparing the patient a second operation and a second recovery. Their review places the strategy among options for condylar osteomas where asymmetry is significant.
pmc-13502773:
Tibenderana and colleagues analyzed a 2022 national health survey to find what predicts cervical cancer screening among Tanzanian women aged fifteen to forty-nine, in a 2026 study. Cervical cancer is the most common cancer in Tanzanian women of reproductive age despite being preventable through early detection, and screening uptake is low. Their weighted sample covered more than fifteen thousand women, analyzed with multilevel models that account for clustering.

Tibenderana found screening odds rising steeply with age and with education. Odds were modestly higher among employed women, contraceptive users, and women who had visited a health facility in the past year. Women living with HIV had more than fivefold higher odds of being screened, likely reflecting their contact with HIV care services. Rural residence cut the odds substantially. The authors call for outreach to younger, less educated, rural, and poorer women, plus access and health literacy, to close the screening gap.
pmc-13503873:
Fan Ding leads a team that made carbon nanodots glow red for minutes after the light stops, in a 2026 study. Long afterglow in red is prized for imaging and light devices, yet most materials fade in seconds at room heat. Carbon dots are cheap and safe, but their red glow has been short-lived.

The team tuned the dots' energy states with help from machine learning searches. The best dots kept glowing for more than 4,000 seconds, with a glow life of 353 seconds by the standard measure. Light studies showed two decay paths, one fast and one very slow; the slow path rules the long tail of light. As a test, the team built a wearable lamp marker that keeps signaling after power is cut.
pmc-13504973:
Souleymane Ouedraogo leads a team reporting a patient carrying two water-linked parasite infections at once, in a 2026 case report. The man, aged 37 and visiting France from Djibouti, had belly pain and a cough that had lasted three months. Both parasites favor regions with poor water safety.

Blood tests showed a surge in allergy-linked white cells and mild liver strain. Scans found odd tube-like liver lesions. Parasite eggs in samples, plus positive antibody tests for both liver fluke and blood fluke, confirmed the pair. He recalled eating local greens and bathing in fresh water years before. Two drugs, one for each parasite, were given together. He improved with no side effects. The authors urge checking for both when liver signs and travel history align.
pmc-13505073:
Ryuichi Nakayama and colleagues asked whether long use of high-flow nasal oxygen before intubation predicts worse outcomes on lung-support machines. The patients had severe ARDS, a lung failure syndrome, and all later received veno-venous ECMO, a machine that oxygenates blood outside the body.

Registry data covered 209 adults treated between 2012 and 2022 who had high-flow oxygen before ECMO. Each extra day on high-flow oxygen raised the odds of death within 60 days by a factor of 1.22 after adjustment. Patients on it three days or more, 69 people, faced about double the death risk and freed themselves from ECMO less often. Nakayama reads long high-flow use as a risk marker of delayed escalation, not proof the oxygen itself harms.
pmc-13505573:
Lei Zhou and colleagues built a generative computer model that mimics how tumour-associated macrophages shift between attack and support states during immunotherapy for digestive cancers. Only a minority of patients respond to such therapy, and fixed biomarkers miss these moving immune changes. Their digital-twin platform learned from more than a million single-cell profiles, tissue maps, and clinical records covering 2,847 people with five cancer types.

Attention-based links between cells and time-aware modules let the model simulate immune state changes and search for patient-specific moves that push macrophages toward the anti-tumour state. It predicted therapy response more accurately than standard biomarker models in their tests. Among 156 cases where its advice clashed with doctors' choices, model-guided care coincided with higher response rates and longer time before progression. The authors flag possible selection bias in that comparison and call for randomised prospective trials before clinical use.
pmc-13508273:
Ying Zhang and eight co-authors compare two surgical routes for putting a slipped jaw joint disc back in place, in 2026 work. The disc can slide forward and fail to return, locking the jaw in later stages of the disorder. The study reviewed 132 patients with 218 affected joints treated at a Guangzhou hospital in 2023 and 2024. Surgeons reached the joint either in front of or behind a bundle of nerves and blood vessels on the temple. Scans and early outcomes were compared between routes.

Scans after surgery confirmed the disc was back in place in 211 of 218 joints. The behind route bled more and took longer, and it brought more fevers and infections. The front route caused more temporary facial nerve weakness and a few skin flap injuries. The study gives jaw surgeons a clear trade-off table when choosing how to reach the joint.
pmc-13508373:
Sara Farinone leads a nine-author letter from an Italian kidney center arguing that pain alone does not explain lost quality of life in polycystic kidney disease, in 2026 correspondence. The letter answers a study linking kidney size to worse physical quality of life, with mental effects flowing largely through kidney pain. Enlarged organs can squeeze the gut, causing early fullness, indigestion, and constipation. Survey data they cite put about three in ten clinic patients at nutritional risk, with kidney and liver size the strongest predictor.

Body measures in cited work show low muscle mass with extra body water, a wasting pattern appearing even when kidney function holds up. Women face more liver enlargement over time, and body image strain seems stronger in women, which may deepen mental health effects. The letter urges sex-split analyses and nutrition-aware thinking in future studies of this disease.
pmc-13509373:
Francesco Paolo Lo Muzio and eight co-authors test whether heart sounds can reveal how the left side of the heart works under stress, in a 2026 pig study. The group studied twelve minipigs in three groups: healthy ones, animals with a weak pumping heart, and animals whose hearts relax poorly while pumping strength stays near normal. Sensors recorded heart sounds, heart rhythm, and oxygen levels while direct pressure readings gave the reference values.

A computer model learned to predict the pressure-based measures from the outer signals and sorted the three groups with high accuracy in standard tests. Accuracy stayed strong in a tougher test that left one animal per group out of training entirely. The poor-relaxation animals showed the most change in sound features as heart rate rose. The authors say the method could aid diagnosis, though human testing still lies ahead.
pmc-13510273:
Bo Lyu, Zhixuan Liu, and Xiaozi Gao report a longitudinal study, published in 2026. It tracks how executive function and motor skills influence each other in preschool children. Executive function covers the mental skills for goal-directed behaviour. More than two thousand children were assessed. They were aged three, four, and five. Parent reports supplied the data. The team modelled the two-way links over time.

Early executive function predicted its own later levels. Fine motor skills did the same. This was as expected. The striking result ran from fine motor skill. It significantly predicted later executive function at every step. It also predicted later gross motor skill. The reverse paths were weaker. The authors argue for combined motor and thinking training in preschool programmes.
pmc-13511973:
Jiahui Zhang and Dongxin He investigate how silicone gel used to seal power electronic devices fails under high voltage and high heat, in 2026 work. The gel insulates modules that convert electric power, and long service under harsh loads eats into reliability and lifespan. The team aged samples under combined electrical and thermal stress, varying pulse edge speed and aging stage.

They tracked tree-like damage channels, breakdown strength, charge-driven molecular vibration, leakage current, and softness by cone penetration. Failure traced to two forces acting together: fast pulse edges drove repeated charge damage inside the gel, while heat broke down its part-solid, part-liquid structure. Each force alone explained only part of the decline. The authors say the paired mechanism gives a base for reformulating the gel and redesigning modules for longer sealing life.
pmc-13512673:
Zhu and colleagues proposed GLUQ, a system for judging the quality of ultra-high-definition images without a reference copy, in a 2026 computer vision study. Scoring such huge images directly is computationally expensive. Shrinking or chopping them into independent patches loses distortions that only appear at certain scales and disconnects local flaws from the whole scene's context.

Zhu instead samples patches aligned to the image's aspect ratio and links them as nodes in a graph. The graph is built from spatial closeness and feature similarity, letting information flow between regions through graph convolution, a method that pools data across connected nodes. Attention-based pooling then weighs patch evidence into one quality score, trained with a combined loss balancing accuracy, correlation, and ranking. On the standard ultra-high-definition benchmark the system achieved the lowest prediction error among compared methods with competitive correlation scores, supporting graph relations as the key improvement.
pmc-13514373:
Jiajia Lu, Yue Shen, Xu Wang, and Fuyang Ke present a robotics study, published in 2026. It improves SLAM for self-driving in cities. SLAM lets machines locate themselves while mapping their surroundings. Single sensors drift or fail in built-up areas. The team tightly combined three data sources. They used laser scanning, motion sensing, and GPS data.

Their system extracts features from laser scans. These include lines, surfaces, and ground. It corrects height drift frame by frame. Motion and GPS data are fused with an error-state filter. GPS-checked loop closure avoids false matches. In tests, average position error fell by nearly half. This was against laser-only methods. Against laser-inertial methods, the cut was about a quarter.
pmc-13516073:
Juan Mauricio Ramírez-Vidal leads a ten-author team testing an essential oil against two parasites in a 2026 study. The oil comes from Plectranthus amboinicus, a medicinal plant grown in Mexico City. Chemical analysis found forty-six compounds, led by camphor at about thirty-one percent, with several aromatic oxides and carvacrol behind it. The team then exposed amoebae that cause gut disease and the Chagas-disease parasite Trypanosoma cruzi to the oil.

The oil killed amoeba trophozoites at moderate strength. Against the blood form of the Chagas parasite it worked better, landing near the potency of the reference drug benznidazole, while the insect-stage form needed a stronger dose. Tests on monkey kidney cells gauged collateral harm to host tissue. Ramírez-Vidal's team plans to trace the oil's molecular effects and test its parts singly, in mixes, and beside standard drugs.
pmc-13516773:
Hossein Omidian, Sumana Dey Chowdhury, and Luigi X Cubeddu argue, in a 2026 review, that inhaled RNA medicines must be designed as whole products, not just clever molecules. Breathing RNA into the lungs can place gene-silencing, protein-making, or editing cargo exactly where lung disease sits. The authors survey cargo types and the carriers that ferry them, from fatty nanoparticles to polymer bundles and dry powders.

Progress is real but patchy, they find. Many studies show a carrier can work, yet few prove it survives the inhaler, crosses mucus, enters the right cells, and stays tolerable on repeat doses. The review urges target-first design: define the patient, cell, and outcome, then gate each manufacturing and device step with hard measures. Success, in their framing, means RNA still working after production, spraying, landing, and cell entry.
pmc-13517973:
Haupt and colleagues reported a 2026 case of hepatopulmonary syndrome, a liver-driven cause of low blood oxygen, in a ten-year-old boy whose breathing tests had looked normal. The boy, who had obesity, sleep apnea, and asthma, arrived with low resting oxygen and drops during exertion. Yet his lung examination and outpatient lung function were unrevealing, and inhalers did not help.

Haupt describes how the workup instead uncovered liver cirrhosis and an enlarged liver and spleen. It found swollen veins in the food pipe. There was a widened gap between oxygen in the air sacs and in the blood, the signature of blood bypassing oxygen pickup through dilated lung vessels. A liver center confirmed the syndrome, whose only established cure is transplantation, and the boy underwent liver transplant. The authors urge emergency physicians to consider this liver-lung connection when a child's low oxygen defies the usual explanations.
pmc-13518373:
Vivien Min Er Lee and eight colleagues study disabled patients who teach medical students in a 2026 qualitative paper. Patient educators bring lived experience into family-medicine training, yet nobody had asked those with physical disabilities how the role feels from inside. All seven educators from a workshop on communicating with disabled patients gave in-depth interviews, and reflexive thematic analysis sorted their accounts.

Each educator blended three roles: patient, teacher, and advocate, in personal proportions. The team sketched four types, from patient-led to advocacy-led, with the middle types, where teaching stood equal, proving most confident and best aligned with course aims. Pure advocacy sometimes pulled sessions off the lesson plan. Lee's team recommends structured training and guided reflection to help educators balance story, advocacy, and syllabus, so disabled voices strengthen teaching instead of being flattened into a single testimony role.
pmc-13518973:
Kartick Bag and four colleagues build a 2026 learning system for managing hospital outpatient queues as demand swings through the day. Fixed staffing models assume steady arrivals and identical servers, while real clinics see surges plus different handling for first-time and returning patients. Their model separates those two provider types and lets arrivals follow a time-varying pattern.

A Q-learning agent, guided by a supervised exploration rule, decides when to add or move providers. Separate value tables for arrivals and departures capture their different costs and rewards, which also shift over time. Simulations showed clear cuts in total waiting time and system cost versus conventional uniform queue models. The design extends to wider hospital resource planning.
pmc-13519273:
Fonseca and colleagues reviewed drug treatment for olfactory reference disorder in a 2026 analysis. The disorder is the conviction that one emits a foul body odor others barely notice. The analysis also traces how prescribing changed over decades. Following standard review guidelines, the team extracted patient, symptom, and treatment details from every report they could find on medicines for this condition.

Fonseca located 52 studies covering 87 patients, almost all single case reports or small series, with no controlled trials at all. Serotonin reuptake inhibitors were used in about three fifths of cases and antipsychotics in about half. These inhibitors are a class of antidepressants. The reported response rate ran above eighty percent, which the authors discount for publication bias. Antipsychotics dominated earlier decades, while serotonin drugs took over after the nineteen nineties as the disorder was reclassified within the obsessive-compulsive spectrum, and no patient feature reliably predicted response.
pmc-13520273:
Gabriel Cubillos and nine colleagues train machine learning models in 2026 to predict which babies will be born large for their gestational age. Such size is a risk factor for delivery injury to mother and child. Twelve algorithms were tuned and tested using routine prenatal variables, with data augmentation and feature selection to sharpen performance.

The leading model balanced sensitivity and specificity at 0.84 each using 14 variables, while a leaner 10-variable model reached 97 percent specificity, beating the classic ultrasound formula's balance of errors. Maternal body mass index, maternal weight at first and last checkups, and estimated fetal weight drove predictions most. Cubillos's team argues standard clinic data, gathered early, can flag risky pregnancies in time to act.
pmc-13520373:
Wu and colleagues compared in 2026 human-led and ChatGPT-assisted analysis of the same nursing interview data. Artificial intelligence tools promise faster coding and tidier organisation for qualitative research, but nursing stories carry emotion, context, and culture that software may flatten. The team ran both methods side by side on interviews from a larger nursing project and compared where the results agreed and split.

Wu found the software helped with rapid sorting, first-pass coding, and spotting clear, surface themes. Its output read smoothly yet simplified context, missing tacit nursing know-how and the feel of experience-based stories. Four ethical themes emerged: privacy and data safety, loss of emotional and contextual grasp, algorithmic narrowing with cultural bias, and shifting roles for researchers. The authors treat the tool as a support for human judgement, not a replacement for it in nursing inquiry.
pmc-13520473:
Haijia Tang and colleagues review in 2026 how support cells around tumours and lymphoid-like clusters inside tumours jointly shape anti-tumour immunity through their layout in tissue. Support cells can block immune entry and fuel resistance, while lymphoid clusters help prime immune cells locally and track with better outcomes.

Recent single-cell and spatial studies show varied support-cell states, some of which even help organise lymphoid clusters. The authors frame outcome as a balance between stromal restriction and lymphoid organisation. That balance may guide tumour classification, patient grouping and combination treatments that reprogramme stroma or encourage lymphoid cluster growth.
pmc-13520873:
Soufyane Elkadiri and colleagues review in 2026 twenty patients treated surgically for eyelid cancers at a university hospital in eastern Morocco over three years from 2023 to 2025. Eyelid tumours demand full removal while preserving eye function and appearance.

Average age was about 63 years, with women slightly outnumbering men. Long sun exposure appeared in nine of ten patients, while the lower lid was the commonest site. Basal cell tumours made up three quarters of cases, with squamous tumours making up the rest. All patients had wide removal with margin checks, mostly rebuilt with local flaps, and no return of cancer was seen during follow-up.
pmc-13522473:
D Rex Mitchell and colleagues study how extinct armored fishes from Devonian Australia crushed hard prey in a 2026 analysis of eight species. Fossils came from the Gogo Formation, a site known for detailed preservation. Computer models simulated biting stresses in the lower jaw, while tooth surface complexity was measured to infer how each species handled resistant food.

Species with broad, flat teeth showed low strain, suiting them to crushing armored prey small enough to swallow whole. The largest species paired a very strong jaw with complex teeth able to pierce and tear prey too big for its mouth. Medium-sized forms seemed suited to slicing softer tissue. Feeding therefore depended on prey size relative to the predator, not on predator size alone.
pmc-13522573:
Li and co-authors report in 2026 that a splicing factor called CELF2 drives production of the 4R form of tau, a brain protein whose abnormal buildup marks several dementias. Splicing decides which protein version a gene makes, and too much 4R tau is linked to disease. The team found that CELF2 works not as scattered molecules but by gathering into clusters inside the cell nucleus.

These clusters form through the protein's intrinsically disordered region, a floppy segment that lets molecules assemble, and one residue, D388, proved essential for clustering and for the splicing effect. Two other splicing factors, NOVA2 and SFPQ, joined the same clusters. In animal tauopathy models, the capacity for this nuclear assembly tracked with 4R tau levels and with movement and thinking performance. The authors identify CELF2 clustering as a possible drug target for tau diseases.
pmc-13523173:
Christos Psevdos and Giovanni Ianniruberto analyze how friction falls as polymer melts flow in a 2026 theoretical study. Recent experiments on three unentangled polystyrene melts of different chain lengths showed complex thinning and stress patterns under fast shear. Single-chain simulations that let friction drop as chain segments align were compared with the measurements and with many-chain simulations.

The analysis confirmed that the friction coefficient must fall significantly as segment alignment rises. The extracted relationship matched earlier results from stretching experiments for the two longer-chain melts, while the shortest melt showed a weaker dependence. Single-chain models missed some effects that many-chain simulations captured, especially in stretching flows. The authors conclude that interactions between chains still hold part of the missing physics.
pmc-13523973:
Lhoucine Naanaai and others describe a 2026 strategy, run on computers, to find antidiabetic compounds that block alpha-amylase, an enzyme that digests starches. Slowing this enzyme can improve blood sugar control. The team studied a family of hybrid compounds built around an indenoquinoxaline core.

Their workflow joined three-dimensional QSAR modeling, which relates molecular shape to activity, with absorption and toxicity profiling, docking into the enzyme, molecular dynamics simulation, transport checks, and retrosynthesis planning. The best model showed strong fit and predictive power. The ligands fit the enzyme active site from a known crystal structure, stayed stable in hundred-nanosecond simulations, and showed sound drug-like profiles. A lead compound emerged, with a synthesis route sketched, ready for lab testing.
pmc-13524073:
Rahpeyma and colleagues probed the purpose of stromules in 2026, the thin fingers that plastids, the plant cell's energy and chemical factories, extend under stress. Two ideas compete: the fingers might pass raw material to neighboring peroxisomes for making the hormone jasmonate, or they might carry signals from plastid to nucleus. Using tobacco cells with glowing markers and automated image counting, the team tested both accounts.

Two plant hormones each tripled stromule numbers within about an hour, mainly by starting new fingers rather than lengthening old ones. Blocking the cell's microtubule rails stopped the response, while blocking a jasmonate-making step prevented one hormone's effect. When finger growth was suppressed, hormone-driven gene switching grew stronger, hinting the fingers temper the signal. The exporter protein for the jasmonate precursor favored the fingers, and most fingers touched peroxisomes. The authors lean toward a signaling role that also aids metabolic hand-off.
pmc-13525173:
Dokos and colleagues investigated in 2026 prescription errors inside a regional psychiatric hospital in Germany. As part of a year-long study, the team reviewed treatment plans at St. Josef hospital in Oberhausen. They identified errors by a modified EQUIP method, then interviewed prescribers in a double-blind way and built a codebook of error themes.

From 6,020 treatment plans, 150 errors were detected, an error rate of about two and a half percent. A Delphi consensus process clarified the nature of each error type. The authors argue that psychiatric prescribing has its own error profile shaped by ward routines and drug mix. Understanding those circumstances, they say, is the first step to targeted safety work in mental health facilities.
pmc-13525573:
Raphael Fernandes Casseb leads a large team in a 2026 study of a free deep-learning tool that automatically outlines the cavity left after epilepsy surgery on brain scans. Measuring resected tissue matters clinically and in research, yet manual outlining is slow and imprecise. Their system, ResectVol DL, was built on a UNet-like network.

Training used postoperative scans from 72 patients, with testing in 48 more, plus healthy controls and brain tumor cases to check false alarms and generalizability. The tool reached the highest median overlap score with manual outlines, beating three rival automated methods after statistical correction. Volume agreement was comparable with the best rival, but that rival falsely marked cavities in three control scans while the new tool marked none. The authors offer the software freely for surgical research.
pmc-13526073:
Leyun Pan and colleagues ask, in a 2026 prospective study, whether dynamic PET imaging adds value for liver metastases from uveal melanoma. This eye cancer's liver spread can be faint on standard scans. Dynamic imaging tracks tracer movement over an hour and builds parametric maps, yet technical complexity has kept it from routine oncology use.

Twenty-six patients with 126 lesions, including 58 liver metastases, underwent an hour-long dynamic scan plus a later whole-body scan on a long-field scanner. Three image sets were compared, parametric maps, standard static images, and delayed static images. Total lesion detection did not differ significantly between approaches. One true liver metastasis appeared on the parametric map and was confirmed by MRI after being unclear on static images. Quantitative contrast ratios were measured for every lesion.
pmc-13526473:
Naidu and colleagues mapped in 2026 the United Kingdom's research output on artificial intelligence in medical imaging. They analysed Scopus-indexed papers from 2017 to 2025 on generative and foundation AI methods. Globally they found 13,452 publications with about 195,000 citations. UK-affiliated papers numbered 889, about seven percent of the world total, and the UK ranked fourth by volume.

UK papers averaged twenty-one citations each, higher than several larger producers, despite the UK's smaller share. Output grew roughly eighteen-fold across the nine years, with a citation lag in recent years because new papers need time to be cited. The authors describe a fast-growing, high-impact national ecosystem. They note the analysis shows where UK imaging AI concentrates and how its themes connect internationally.
pmc-13527473:
Shabnam Afzal and colleagues report a 2026 dermatology case of a rare pigmented purpuric disorder appearing during pregnancy. These disorders leak red blood cells into the skin, leaving brown patches from iron pigment. The Majocchi variant forms ring-shaped or geographic plaques, reported more often in young women, usually on the legs.

A twenty-nine-year-old woman developed painless darkened patches during pregnancy eighteen months earlier, which enlarged, darkened, and then stabilized without fading. Examination found well-demarcated violet-brown, slightly thinned ring plaques across both lower legs and feet, and over-the-counter moisturizers had not helped. A punch biopsy of the ankle showed escaped red blood cells and iron pigment in the upper skin layer, matching the clinical picture. The authors stress biopsy plus clinicopathologic correlation to confirm this uncommon diagnosis.
pmc-13528073:
Laura Kirkpatrick and four colleagues interview pediatric clinicians about sharing hard newborn screening results in a 2026 study. Infantile Krabbe disease joined the United States screening panel in 2024. It is a rare, fast nerve disease of babies. Families often want their own pediatric clinician involved in the news. The team interviewed twenty-five clinicians in western Pennsylvania.

Clinicians named three big barriers. They knew little about Krabbe disease. Their schedules had no slack. Specialists were hard to reach. Helpful factors included past training in breaking bad news and trusted online resources. Requests were practical: fact sheets, scripts, and care pathways. Education bundled with the result notice was another idea. Better links with specialists would help too. The authors say primary care can play this role if systems support it.
pmc-13529673:
Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 study of how a malaria parasite protein punches holes in cell membranes. Plasmodium parasites must cross several cell types, and perforin-like proteins do the piercing. One, PLP2, is essential for bursting out of red blood cells at the sexual stage. Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team resolved its shape on membranes.

The protein assembles into arcs and rings of varying size on fat membranes. One complete pore held seventeen copies: the pore-forming domains line up as a central barrel through the membrane, while tail domains anchor the ring to the surface. A locked mutant form caught the complex just before insertion, showing the steps of the attack. The pore's build gives drug designers a concrete structure to block.
pmc-13530173:
Wojciech Piasecki and colleagues give a fresh account of a widespread freshwater fish parasite in 2026 using modern imaging and DNA tools. The tiny crustacean has been cited in fish disease writing for nearly two centuries, yet its form and identity stayed fuzzy. Specimens came from ide fish in a Polish lake.

Electron microscopy revealed fine details on mouthparts, legs, and other structures never shown before. DNA barcodes, the first for this species, confirmed its separate identity and close kinship with a relative. Two names long treated as distinct species were folded into this one, and the group diagnosis was rewritten.
pmc-13531973:
Isobel K Dunstan leads a 2026 chemical profile of blood and spinal fluid in osteoarthritis, hunting molecules tied to pain. Samples from 81 patients and 70 pain-free controls underwent magnetic resonance profiling of metabolites plus targeted inflammation protein tests. Modeling separated the groups with high accuracy in both fluids.

Two amino acids, histidine and glutamine, ran low in patient blood across every subgroup. Lower levels meant stronger pain, disability, sleep trouble, and overall symptom burden. Women showed the deepest drops and the heaviest symptoms. The pair emerges as candidate markers for sorting patients and targeting pain pathways.
pmc-13534373:
Ilker Sengul, Demet Sengul, and Cagri Akalin discuss in 2026 why HER2-positive breast cancer splits into two distinct groups by hormone receptor status. Cancers with both marks tend to fare better, while those without hormone marks grow larger and present at later stages. Large database work backs this split with gene activity data.

The double-positive group showed richer drug-processing pathways, which may explain better response to hormone therapy. Immune cell mixes in tumours also differed by group, while key gene mutations stayed similar. Readers are urged to treat the two groups as separate diseases in trials.
pmc-13534673:
Tengfei Long and colleagues track in 2026 how changes in estimated glucose disposal rate, a stand-in for insulin resistance, link to death in middle-aged and older Chinese adults. Single baseline measures miss how risk shifts over time. Data from a national ageing study held 5,966 people with measures in 2012 and 2015.

Four change patterns emerged, and patterns with falling values carried higher death rates than the steadiest group. Total exposure over time linked inversely to death risk in follow-up. Readers see why repeated and cumulative checks add warning value beyond one reading.
pmc-13534773:
Rebecca Lievesley and colleagues chart in 2026 treatment pathways for people convicted of sexual offences who take medication to manage problematic sexual arousal in the United Kingdom. The service is little studied beyond before-and-after outcome reports. Service records covered all 139 users at the first evaluation site.

Six distinct pathways emerged from starting drug class, dose or drug changes, and stopping patterns. Each pathway paired with positive shifts in arousal problem measures, while journeys varied a lot between users. The team also offers an ethical prescribing frame that weighs benefit and user experience.
pmc-13536573:
Wenqiang Liu and colleagues clone in 2026 DT1, a cytochrome P450 gene that boosts drought tolerance in rice. Drought limits rice output worldwide, and new protective genes aid breeding of hardier varieties. Near-isogenic lines narrowed the trait to a small stretch of chromosome 3 with several candidate genes.

Gene tests singled out one candidate: knockout plants became more drought sensitive, while overexpressing lines tolerated dry spells better. The gene acts mainly in stems and leaves, and one form common in japonica rice looked favourable. Breeders gain a fresh genetic resource for drought-resistant varieties.
pmc-13536673:
Usama Yaseen and co-authors report a 2026 field experiment on black soybean grown in poor, low-fertility soil called Inceptisol. Plants received organic soil additions, either biochar or vermicompost, alone or with two helpful microbes. One microbe helps roots fix nitrogen from the air, while the other helps roots absorb nutrients. Growth, nutrient uptake, and root colonization were tracked across treatments.

Plants given both organic additions plus both microbes grew the tallest and fullest canopies. Biochar with both microbes gave the largest shoot and root mass and the highest root colonization, reaching 80 percent of roots. Phosphorus uptake also rose, and nitrogen-fixing bacteria were most numerous under the combined treatment. The authors conclude that pairing biochar with both microbes offers a practical route to stronger soybean growth with less reliance on chemical fertilizer.
pmc-13542073:
Muhammad Shazib Hameed and colleagues write a 2026 mathematics paper. The topic is fairer ways to merge expert judgements. The judgements are fuzzy and uncertain by design. The formalism is called intuitionistic fuzzy Z-numbers. It grades both support and doubt about a claim. Group decisions in e-learning form one test case.

New aggregation operators anchor the paper. They rest on proportionate weighting of support and doubt. Weighted versions serve groups where experts carry different weight. Worked examples apply the machinery to multi-criteria choices. A grey relational analysis step double-checks the rankings. The authors claim more accurate results than existing models. They also claim more consistent results across comparisons.
pmc-13542173:
Hasti Nouraei and colleagues test a laboratory risk in 2026. The subject is the yeast Candida albicans. Labs regrow this yeast again and again for experiments. The team asked whether that routine strips away dangerous traits. If it does, research findings may mislead. Ten clinical isolates went through twenty passages.

Adhesion gene activity fell steadily across passages. Two genes, ALS1 and ALS3, both declined. Biofilm building weakened in nearly all isolates. Most isolates had lost biofilm growth by the final passage. Surface water-repellence slid as well. Every isolate scored low on that trait by passage fifteen. The authors urge low-passage isolates for realistic work.
pmc-13542673:
Karimwabo writes to press health leaders to give rehabilitation a full place in care and policy. Rehabilitation helps people regain daily function after stroke, injury, or long illness. Across much of Africa, and in Rwanda, such care stays low in funding and planning.

Many patients leave hospital with no referral to rehabilitation and no follow-up plan. That gap can turn a survivable illness into lasting disability and lost work. Karimwabo asks ministries to fund rehabilitation inside main health budgets. He also asks that rehabilitation staff join care teams and policy talks. Training for doctors on what rehabilitation offers forms part of the plea.
pmc-13543073:
Dikra Suleyman George and colleagues published a 2026 case report of endemic Kaposi sarcoma disguised as morphea, a skin-hardening condition, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Kaposi sarcoma ranks among the most frequent cancers in sub-Saharan Africa and is driven by human herpesvirus-8. Its endemic form mainly affects children and younger adult men in the region, often without HIV infection, and usually appears as nodules or swollen limbs rather than flat hardened patches.

Their patient was a 28-year-old HIV-negative man with four months of skin hardening on both sides of the groin. The authors state they found no earlier description of morphea-like Kaposi sarcoma in an HIV-negative person. The case matters because endemic Kaposi sarcoma in Africa is classified into recognised patterns, and a hardening presentation that mimics a benign skin disease risks delayed diagnosis and treatment.
pmc-13543373:
M van der Ven and colleagues published a 2026 evaluation of SPICE, a Dutch workplace programme teaching trainee doctors to collaborate across the primary and secondary care boundary during a geriatrics rotation. Learning to hand patients smoothly between family medicine and hospital care matters for older adults with complex needs. Instead of a standard survey, the team used an effects forum: residents, supervisors, and patients together built a timeline of learning moments from the programme and the six months after it.

Seventeen people took part in two forums. Residents said they understood the patient's whole care journey better and understood each other's worlds, which led to more proactive handovers. They also carried the habits into new settings through reflection and conversation, a ripple effect beyond the original placement. The authors present collective evaluation as a way to see how workplace learning becomes changed practice over time.
pmc-13543473:
Yassine Kallel and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a stab wound that pierced the common bile duct straight through. Such injuries appear in only a small fraction of penetrating abdominal trauma and are easily missed at first. A 35-year-old man arrived two hours after being stabbed in the upper right abdomen, stable, with a scan showing a liver laceration and abdominal fluid. Care began non-operatively, but within six hours fever, racing pulse, and abdominal tenderness forced a change of plan.

Exploration found bile-stained fluid and a through-and-through injury of the duct above the duodenum. Surgeons repaired the back wall through the front opening, widened it carefully, placed a T-shaped drainage tube, and added a drain. Recovery was smooth, and dye studies on day eight and at two months showed no leak or narrowing. A year on, the patient remained well.
pmc-13543573:
Gobeille and colleagues compared three visual function surveys in low vision patients to judge which best suits clinic use, in a 2026 study. Seventy-four patients completed the Activity Inventory, a veterans' low-vision questionnaire with forty-eight items, and the vision subscale of a National Eye Institute questionnaire. Testing ran before and six months after a low vision exam, with Rasch analysis applied to the scores.

Gobeille found each tool flawed in a different way. Two surveys showed ceiling effects, bunching patients at the top. The third subscale targeted ability best yet mixed dimensions, with the most responses that fit. Scores tracked each other across tools. On ease of use, the veterans' questionnaire was answered fastest per item before the exam. The authors conclude no questionnaire wins on all counts and recommend the veterans' survey when patient ability sits below its ceiling, while calling for fixes to all three.
pmc-13543873:
Klouda and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of pulmonary vein stenosis returning after a double lung transplant in a young child. The disease narrows the veins that carry blood from the lungs to the heart. Transplant is the last-resort cure for severe forms of this disease that resist other care. The girl had the transplant at 17 months of age after many earlier procedures, on top of other birth conditions.

Klouda describes how early checks showed open veins, but about 34 months after transplant tests revealed severe narrowing again in several veins of the new lungs. Flow scans showed the left lung getting far less blood than the right. Doctors used balloon widening, which eased pressure in the heart, and switched her to sirolimus, a drug that slows tissue growth, instead of placing stents. The authors urge counselling families that the disease can return, plus close monitoring after transplant.
pmc-13544173:
Aubrey and co-authors reviewed a 2026 decade of lung transplants at one centre, comparing recipients aged seventy and above with younger patients. Whether an upper age limit should exist is controversial, since guidelines flag age over sixty-five as high risk. The review covered all transplants performed over the ten year period.

Of 380 transplants, seventy-three went to patients seventy or older and 307 to younger patients, Aubrey reports. Older recipients more often received a single lung and more often had restrictive lung disease as their diagnosis. Length of stay, early graft dysfunction, and kidney injury did not differ between the age groups postoperatively. One, three, and five year survival were statistically indistinguishable, and age seventy plus was not an independent predictor of death.
pmc-13545373:
Sujay Jaju and colleagues reported in 2026 on whole-exome sequencing for 113 people with retinitis pigmentosa seen through an eye disease registry in South India. Retinitis pigmentosa slowly destroys the retina, and many families in this region have parents who are related, which raises the share of recessive disease. The team sequenced the protein-coding genome and judged each variant by standard clinical rules.

Among 109 unrelated patients, testing found 186 rare variants across 92 retinal genes and settled a molecular diagnosis for about 46 percent. Recessive inheritance dominated, and even patients without related parents often carried two identical copies of a variant. Three genes, EYS, USH2A, and ADGRV1, appeared most often, giving counselors a region-specific picture to work from.
pmc-13546573:
Priyadarshini Pathak and colleagues mapped in 2026 how gastrointestinal cancers escape targeted drugs, using DNA shed into the blood after treatment stops working. They reviewed 106 patients with bile duct, colorectal, and other gut cancers who had tumor profiling before treatment and a blood test at progression. The drugs involved targeted a range of growth switches, including EGFR, HER2, and KRAS.

A likely resistance change appeared in just over half the patients, and a third carried two or more. About half the changes altered the drug's own target, while the other half opened a bypass route, most often through RAS and MAPK signaling. Colorectal cancers favored bypass routes, whereas bile duct cancers more often changed the target itself. The authors support blood testing at progression to guide next steps.
pmc-13547273:
Qianqian Bai and colleagues reported in 2026 that a cellular helper protein, HSPA8, fuels the inflammation behind a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. The protein was more abundant in the spinal cords of sick mice, in step with disease severity, and concentrated near microglia, the brain's immune cells. Lowering it through spinal injection eased the illness, calmed inflammation, and reduced damage to nerve insulation and fibers.

Cell experiments traced the effect to an internal alarm complex, the NLRP3 inflammasome, which HSPA8 helps both prime and assemble. Without enough HSPA8, inflammatory messengers and a fiery form of cell death fell. Restoring the protein partly reversed the protection. The authors nominate HSPA8 as a drug target for multiple sclerosis and related inflammatory brain diseases.
pmc-13547373:
Tingxing Wu and colleagues built in 2026 a prediction model for how fast the protective epoxy coatings on power equipment break down in humid substations. First they studied how failed coatings change shape and chemistry over service time. Then they fed six environmental and operating factors into a gradient boosting model whose settings were tuned by an automated search method. The factors included peak temperature, daily temperature swing, vibration, humidity, ultraviolet exposure, and service age.

The tuned model explained about 96 percent of the variation in degradation rates and beat support vector and random forest rivals. It matched a far heavier neural network's accuracy while running much faster. Repeated checks across time periods held up, and the authors propose the model for lifespan planning of grid equipment.
pmc-13548473:
Resta Emanuela and colleagues modeled in 2026 the mental health of Italian regions from 2016 to 2023, blending lifestyle behavior data with environmental, social, and governance indicators drawn from national statistics. The country's mental health index held fairly steady nationally while regional gaps persisted, with the north and center ahead of the south.

Inactivity, smoking, and living with several chronic conditions tracked consistently with worse regional mental health, while good nutrition and city green space looked protective. Job security and effective courts also played a part, which the authors read as mental health being shaped by institutions and surroundings, not only personal habits. Calabria and Campania bucked the southern pattern with notable gains. Policy advice joins lifestyle programs with green investment and better governance.
pmc-13550573:
Xiaohua Xu, joined by five colleagues, presented a 2026 remote sensing model for picking water bodies out of satellite images. Finding lakes and rivers automatically supports flood control, city planning, and environmental monitoring, yet tangled shapes and limited labeled data cause errors in older methods. Their design, called ResDDSCUNet++, rebuilds a familiar segmentation network for this task.

New building blocks widen the area each decision can draw on, an attention module highlights key information, and a lighter convolution design cuts computing cost. Training mixed labeled examples with self-supervised learning on unlabeled images. In experiments the model beat rival methods, raising two standard accuracy scores by modest margins that the authors report in full.
pmc-13551673:
Eugene Ham, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 study asking whether a signaling protein in immune cells drives liver cancer. Hepatocellular carcinoma grows amid many infiltrating myeloid cells, and focal adhesion kinase, called FAK, links adhesion and inflammatory signals. Human tumor data showed higher FAK gene activity in myeloid-rich tumors tied to worse survival, with the strongest pattern in one macrophage type.

The team bred mice lacking FAK only in myeloid cells and triggered liver tumors with an established model. Baseline livers looked normal, and tumor survival, burden, and growth did not change significantly without myeloid FAK in the reported results. Macrophage accumulation inside tumors did fall, so the authors conclude FAK recruits macrophages yet its loss alone cannot slow this cancer.
pmc-13551773:
Franco Poma-Soto, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 benchmark of software that decodes DNA barcodes when copying errors are heavy. Barcodes tag molecules in pooled sequencing, and light-printed arrays reach huge library sizes yet err on ten to twenty percent of letters. The team tested three decoders on simulated and real data across barcode lengths, library sizes, and error rates up to about a third of letters.

A GPU-accelerated tool called QUIK recalled the most barcodes while keeping precision above 99.5 percent at medium error rates in the reported runs, and it processed reads far faster than its rivals. Longer barcodes helped every tool, and on real array data QUIK assigned the most reads with perfect precision, leading the authors to recommend barcodes of at least 34 letters.
pmc-13554273:
Asia Othman Aljahdali presents a federated learning system that spots cyber attacks across spread-out networks without pooling raw data in a 2026 study. Each site trains a small local detector on its own traffic. A central step merges the local models by averaging, while a regularizer keeps local and global models aligned. Calibrated noise added to updates gives formal privacy protection.

On a public benchmark of network traffic, detection accuracy reached near ninety-eight percent. That beat standard federated rivals by about five points. Precision and recall both ran high and balanced. Message costs fell by more than a third, and privacy loss shrank compared with baselines. The author pitches the system for live defence in linked device networks.
pmc-13555873:
R V Shravya, A I Ananthakrishnan, and Ranajit Das compare inherited risk for autoimmune diseases in Indians with and without type 2 diabetes in a 2026 study. Their group held 474 people from Gujarat, ninety-nine of them diabetic. Polygenic scores summed many small gene effects for eleven autoimmune diseases. Two diseases separated the groups clearly.

People with diabetes carried higher genetic risk for lupus. People without diabetes carried higher genetic risk for rheumatoid arthritis. Genes behind the patterns clustered in immune pathways covering antigen display, helper T cell growth, and responses to viruses. The authors frame the split as a clue to how diabetes reshapes immune inheritance, useful for future risk sorting and tailored care.
pmc-13555973:
Wanyue Xu leads a six-author team revealing how skin cells help prune fruit fly nerve branches during development in a 2026 study. Young neurons grow excess branches that later get trimmed for precise wiring. Skin cells were known to eat the trimmed debris afterward. The team found a scaffolding protein, Patronin, working earlier in those skin cells, before any eating begins.

Lowering Patronin in the skin left sensory neuron branches unpruned. The protein normally restrains a surface receptor in skin, which keeps the neuron's own copy working and triggers branch breakage near the cell body. A growth enzyme inside neurons also joined the chain. The work recasts skin as an active signalling partner, not just a cleanup crew.
pmc-13556073:
Xuan Chanh Tran and five colleagues validated in 2026 a built-in dialysis monitor and a machine learning predictor for patients in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Dialysis adequacy is usually judged by a formula-based measure called Kt/V, while machines can estimate the same quantity live through online clearance monitoring. Data from Southeast Asian patients were scarce, so the team compared both measures in 97 people on maintenance dialysis.

The monitor's readings tracked the reference formula very closely, though they ran slightly low on average. Two thirds of patients met guideline adequacy targets. Machine learning models that combined the monitor reading with age and body mass index predicted the continuous value well, and a classification model separated adequate from inadequate treatments almost perfectly in testing. With local calibration, the live monitor could guide sessions in real time.
pmc-13557473:
Audrey Beaufils and a large international group of colleagues built in 2026 an image-based marker that aims to predict which chemotherapy a pancreatic cancer patient will benefit from after surgery. Choice between the two standard regimens, gemcitabine and a modified FOLFIRINOX combination, is usually guided by how fit the patient is rather than by tumour biology. The team trained deep learning models on routine microscope slides from 231 patients treated at several centres.

Separate models learned outcome patterns under each regimen, and their outputs were combined into a score called PANCprAId that estimates personal benefit from one regimen over the other. The score was then checked in a randomised trial cohort of 313 patients, where it separated outcomes within both treatment arms. The authors propose that tumour appearance on ordinary slides carries treatment-relevant information that current practice ignores.
pmc-13558673:
Mohammad Tahami and three colleagues ground copper ore concentrate in acid in 2026 to break the crust that normally stalls its leaching. Chalcopyrite resists chemical attack because a passivation layer seals its surface. Their mechanochemical approach mills the concentrate in sulphuric acid without oxidants, and one variant uses pyrite itself as the grinding medium so abrasion and galvanic chemistry work together.

Optimised milling recovered about twenty-seven percent of the copper in three hours, seventy percent better than still leaching, while activation energy fell and rates rose several fold. Microscopy confirmed stripped surfaces and fresh mineral exposed. Pyrite media pushed recovery to about forty percent in six hours. Grinding too fine backfired by choking later leaching, so particle size needs control. The authors see industrial promise once periodic milling and oxidant dosing are tuned.
pmc-13558773:
Laura Ospino and five colleagues epoxidised sesame oil in 2026 using solid acid resins instead of dissolved catalysts, a greener route toward bio-based plastics ingredients. Epoxidised vegetable oils feed polymer production, and the trick is converting double bonds into reactive oxygen rings without wrecking them. Two commercial ion exchange resins were compared across three temperatures and three reaction times, with hydrogen peroxide and acetic acid generating the active oxidant in place.

Falling iodine values confirmed the double bonds were consumed, and spectra verified the new oxygen rings. Eighty degrees proved best for both resins, and four hours gave the highest conversions, above ninety-five percent for the stronger resin. Stretching to six hours gained nothing and likely fed side reactions that degrade the rings. The authors map the sweet spot where conversion and ring stability balance.
pmc-13558873:
Siti Nafisah and four colleagues asked in 2026 which ordinary patient traits travel with more worrying ultrasound grades in thyroid nodules. A Korean reporting system sorts nodules into risk classes by their scan appearance, and why some patients land in higher classes was unclear. Their cross-sectional study at a Banda Aceh hospital in Indonesia gathered 109 patients holding 171 nodules, recording age, sex, body mass, and thyroid hormone levels beside the scan grade.

Most patients were women with a median age in the mid forties, and most nodules fell in the two middle risk classes. Age alone tracked with higher grading in first-pass analysis, and it survived in the adjusted model that accounts for several nodules sharing one patient. Sex, body mass, and hormone level showed no clear link. The authors suggest age deserves weight when clinicians judge how hard to chase a nodule.
pmc-13562273:
Jeanette Koeppe and colleagues ask how treatment choice after a shoulder-end fracture shapes older patients' long-term care dependency. Their 2026 propensity-matched analysis uses nationwide German insurance data to compare non-operative care, locked-plate fixation, and reverse shoulder replacement. Most studies of this fracture chase X-ray results; this one chases independence.

Reverse replacement carried a higher risk that a patient's formal care level would deteriorate within a year of the fracture. Locked-plate fixation showed no such difference from non-operative care in the matched comparison. Surgery overall was associated with lower death rates, yet no strategy changed progression to severe dependency or nursing home entry. The authors advise weighing care-level consequences beside survival when choosing treatment for an older patient, and framing the choice around geriatric priorities rather than the fracture film alone.
pmc-13562573:
Verónica Santos-Pulpón and ten colleagues publish a dataset on breathing support in intensive care, built for teams who study how patients and ventilators interact. Waveform-level data from ventilators is rarely kept in standard hospital records, which limits work on mismatches between a patient's effort and the machine's push. The 2026 resource, called RAMIC-I, covers 155 critically ill adults treated at Hospital Universitari Parc Taulí in Sabadell, Spain, between 2015 and 2019. Names were removed before release.

Derived measures flag patient-ventilator asynchronies, the clashes that can harm lungs. The set follows FAIR sharing principles through a shared repository. The authors aim it at prediction models and at safer, better-tuned ventilation.
pmc-13563773:
Aylin Taghipour and four colleagues follow 390 patients through the Whipple operation, the sweeping surgery for pancreatic and nearby cancers, with lymph node clearance included. The operation cures some and burdens many, so knowing who gains matters. Their 2026 retrospective study covers one tertiary centre's cases from 2019 to 2023, all of one cancer family to keep the group clean. Follow-up reached 299 patients, about three-quarters, through records and structured phone calls.

Chemotherapy after surgery cut the death hazard by about a third. Recurrence struck hardest in the first three years. The authors press two levers: count and clear nodes properly, and get eligible patients to chemotherapy.
pmc-13566373:
Lara Lewis and colleagues ask, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether moving stable HIV patients to community medicine collection also improves clinic care for people just starting treatment. Those new patients cannot yet use the community option. Records from 112 clinics in KwaZulu-Natal covered 36,865 people who began therapy between February 2022 and September 2023.

When a clinic's community referral share rose from twenty to thirty percent, new patients became slightly more likely to complete key blood tests. The clearest gain was for six-month virus checks. No gain appeared for staying in care at six months. The spillover benefit looks real but small, a useful calibration for claims about freeing clinic capacity.
pmc-13571373:
Arturo Giacaman and colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a 79-year-old man with torrential leakage of the tricuspid valve whose catheter repair succeeded only after the team switched entry route. They moved from the leg vein to the neck vein. His history included a protein-deposition heart disease, atrial fibrillation, lung hypertension, kidney disease, and repeated heart failure admissions.

The standard leg approach failed because a prominent ridge inside the right atrium pushed the delivery tube off line. Entering through the right internal jugular vein gave a straight path, and two clips reduced the leak from torrential to mild with no harmful narrowing. The case offers a backup route when anatomy blocks the usual one.
pmc-13574773:

Its design aims to hold detail for tiny nodules while still seeing the wide context that sorts real lesions from look-alikes. Multi-scale handling is central, since a nodule may span a few pixels or a broad patch in the same scan. Sharper calls at low compute cost would suit mass screening, where scans pile up fast. The authors frame the work as a step toward screening that catches cancer while it is still curable.
pmc-13578273:

The water loving side held tannins, plant acids, and pigment compounds. The work is a map, not a measure, since amounts were not counted. It sets a base for later studies that count amounts and test uses for the harvest.
pmc-13579773:

Five learning methods were raced inside a strict nested testing frame to keep scores honest. Sorting was fair to good: the tools separated depressed patients from healthy adults best, and the two patient groups from each other least well. One hub region at the back of the brain, the precuneus, stood out as the sharpest divider. Its activity rose with anxiety severity yet fell with depression severity, a mirror pattern the authors flag for diagnostic tools.
pmc-13579873:
Fengqian Yang and colleagues harvest a fructose rich slime from a salt loving bacterium found in Qinghai saline soil, in a 2026 study. The purified coat proved to be almost pure fructose chains, with traces of glucose and an acidic sugar. It held together until a high heat near two hundred seventy six degrees, dissolved well in water, and soaked up more than three times its weight in oil. Under the lens it formed a dense, layered web. The authors suggest trials as a stabilizer for hot food processing and as a helper for healing salty, alkaline soils.
pmc-13580273:
Jialin Li and colleagues grow a porous ceramic skeleton to host better cathodes for proton carrying fuel cells, in a 2026 study. Such cells run cooler than classic solid oxide designs, yet their air electrodes still limit output. Baking heat governed how well the sponge linked up. The praseodymium based catalyst won clearly, posting very low resistance at seven hundred degrees in damp air. It also survived one hundred hours of switching between power making and splitting modes.
pmc-13582973:

pmc-13584273:

High levels of that protein switched the T cells on at first, then pushed them toward wear-out and death. Blocking the cells' own receptor removed that wearing effect. The authors propose that easing this pathway could make T-cell transfer work better for ovarian cancer.
pmc-13586773:
Yi-Jui Liu and colleagues use a special MRI method to study a slim strip of tissue beside the brain's top center line. Standard scans cannot easily separate its water movement from the fluid and brain around it. Ten healthy volunteers underwent high-detail scans at a strong field strength.

The method, called IVIM imaging, splits water motion into true spreading and flow-like motion. The dura strip landed between spinal fluid and brain tissue on plain spreading, while showing stronger flow-related signals than brain tissue itself. Two ways of running the scan agreed closely, one with less warping and one with cleaner signal. The authors offer the measures as a no-dye way to probe brain fluid movement.
pmc-13587073:

Most studies used image quizzes or written cases rather than real clinic visits, and only three tracked real misdiagnosis rates. Eleven studies found worse diagnostic accuracy on skin of colour than on light skin overall. Certainty in the pooled evidence rated very low, so Ding calls for stronger, real-world studies of the gap.
pmc-13587373:

Breaking any link in this chain, the authors suggest, could unmask the cancer for immune clearance.
pmc-13589373:
Zheng and colleagues validated in 2026 a Chinese version of a scale measuring nurses' attitudes toward telehealth. The scale has nineteen items in three dimensions: satisfaction, rejection, and development.

The Chinese scale proved reliable, with strong internal consistency and stable scores on retesting. Experts rated its content as sound, and factor analysis confirmed the three-part structure fit well. Fit indices all met standard thresholds for a good model. The authors conclude the scale works well for measuring Chinese nurses' attitudes toward telehealth.
pmc-13589873:
Wang and co-authors trace a copper-driven cell death pathway in children whose sepsis injures the lungs. Mechanistically, SF1 binds the FDX1 gene's promoter to switch it on, and SF1 physically partners with cJUN so the two amplify that activation together. Removing cJUN cancelled the SF1 effect. The authors name this axis as a candidate drug target.
pmc-13590473:
Yi Chen and ten colleagues report, in 2026, that a sleep drug may fight glioma, a harsh brain tumor with few good treatments. The drug, tasimelteon, is approved for sleep rhythm disorders and reaches the brain well. In lab tests it slowed glioma cell growth in step with dose and time. No clear harm to major organs showed up. Chen and colleagues offer the drug as a candidate worth testing in patients.
pmc-13591273:

Hoang and the team stress that a careful scan read can spare patients a wrong call and guide the right treatment.
pmc-13594473:

The authors show this is possible when the slow pathway conducts almost not at all in the upward direction. That leaves it free for the downward trip. One treatment settled both problems: ablating the slow pathway abolished the double response and the tachycardia together. The case gives clinicians a tidy mechanism for an otherwise baffling tracing.
pmc-13595673:
