Their 2026 matched study measured quality of life alongside depression, fatigue, sleep, pain attitudes, walking capacity, and daily functioning.

The long COVID group scored dramatically lower on quality of life. They also scored worse on nearly everything else. Fatigue and depression scores were far heavier, sleep was poorer, and the six-minute walk ran roughly seventy-five meters shorter. Fewer than four in ten were employed, against eight in ten controls, and more carried additional post-COVID conditions. Modeling within the long COVID group then singled out the factors independently tied to the worst quality of life. The authors say care should treat the whole biopsychosocial cluster, not chase single symptoms.
pmc-13598073:
Jialin Xiang and co-authors pooled ninety brain imaging studies of local activity synchrony. The studies covered 3,764 patients with depression, bipolar disorder, or schizophrenia. They also covered 3,590 healthy controls. The team asked what these three diagnoses share in the brain and where they part ways. Their 2026 meta-analysis searched the literature to March 2025.

One shared signature emerged: heightened local synchrony in the right inferior frontal gyrus across all three disorders. The differences spread by diagnosis. Depression-specific changes sat mainly in the default mode and subcortical networks, bipolar changes concentrated in the default mode network, and schizophrenia showed the broadest dysfunction, reaching into frontoparietal and movement networks. The authors argue the blend of one common node and distinct network fingerprints supports a transdiagnostic view, useful for precision diagnosis and for choosing treatment targets patient by patient.
pmc-13603873:
Machado and co-authors evaluated a 2026 set of quinoidal compounds, redox active molecules, against Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite behind African sleeping sickness. New treatments are needed because current drugs are limited, toxic, or hard to deliver in rural settings. Twenty-four previously described derivatives were tested in cell culture.

Several compounds killed the parasite potently, Machado reports, but most also harmed human kidney and liver cells in parallel tests. Only quinone-triazole hybrids showed significant antiparasitic activity as a class in the whole series of compounds. One compound stood out with strong potency plus the best selectivity margins over both human cell lines tested. Computer analysis confirmed the novelty of its scaffold against this parasite, and the authors propose it as a platform for safer analogues.
pmc-13614873:
Bruno Costa Poltronieri leads a team asking whether more hours of digital brain training give older adults longer-lasting gains in thinking and daily function. Participants were aged 60 or older and had mild neurocognitive disorder, a stage of thinking decline beyond normal ageing. In a double-blind trial, groups received either the training or standard computer games as a control, stepping up from 10 to 20 hours of practice.

Sixty-seven people finished the training and were tested before, after each dose, and at follow-up visits. The 20-hour group improved in daily function and satisfaction, plus processing speed, word fluency, and self-control, and kept much of the gain at three and six months. The 10-hour group improved in narrower areas. The results suggest dose matters: enough practice may be what turns short gains into lasting independence.
pmc-13617073:
Christina Donatti and three colleagues interview people living with HIV in the United States about what they want from treatment, as long-acting injectable options expand. The team first reviewed the literature and settled on five regimen features to probe: how treatment is given, where, how often, where on the body injections go, and side effects. Fifty patients and five healthcare providers took part in individual interviews.

Side effects ranked as the top concern for patients and providers alike, followed by dosing frequency and mode of administration. Most patients preferred injections over daily pills when all injection types were weighed together, and clinic-given injections every four or six months were especially popular because they fit existing appointment routines. The authors say these priorities should shape new products, and a larger choice experiment is planned to test how widely the findings hold.
pmc-13617673:
Ruijun Wang and four colleagues critically review Lachnospiraceae, a gut bacterial family that ferments dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate and propionate, compounds with immune-calming potential. The review separates established findings from hypotheses, stressing that function varies sharply by strain, so results from one genus cannot be generalized to the family. Diet components such as inulin, pectin, resistant starch, and arabinoxylan steer what these bacteria produce.

Mechanistic claims rest mostly on rodent work, while human evidence remains correlational. Only one strain has been tested in causal human trials, and only for metabolic disease, and regulatory approval for food use is nearly as narrow. Oxygen sensitivity and survival inside food products add practical hurdles. The authors suggest postbiotic and synbiotic preparations as near-term alternatives, while concluding that current evidence does not support clinical or commercial health claims for these bacteria.
pmc-13617873:
Joseph Ntagerwa Ntaganzibwa and sixteen colleagues study perinatal asphyxia, oxygen deprivation around birth, among newborns admitted to a tertiary intensive care unit in Bukavu, Democratic Republic of the Congo. Local evidence is scarce, so the team reviewed admissions from January 2021 to December 2025, measuring how common asphyxia was and how severe it proved. They also asked which factors tracked with death in hospital.

Among two thousand three hundred thirty-three admissions, two hundred fifty-seven babies had documented asphyxia and nearly a quarter of them died. For term babies, mortality climbed steeply with brain injury stage, from under five percent at the mildest stage to about a third at the most severe. Lower birth weight and being born elsewhere before transfer signaled higher risk in initial analyses, though adjusted estimates were imprecise given few deaths. The authors call for better recognition and referral pathways for asphyxiated newborns in the region.
pmc-13618273:
Huaiyuan Zhu and colleagues report a chemistry study, published in 2026. It widens a classic five-part carbon ring. A silicon bridge makes the ring larger. The team used short-lived silicon compounds called silylenes. A cobalt complex was the partner. They cleaved a strong carbon-carbon bond in the ring. Such bond breaking is normally very hard.

The products carry the silicon bridge across the ring. Tests of electron spread supported true homoaromatic character. This is ring stability that survives a gap in the ring. Experiments and quantum maths point the same way. A metal helps the ring expand. The path is modelled on the classic Büchner reaction. Routes to odd silicon ring systems widen as a result.
pmc-13619073:
AlMothana Manasrah led a team of twelve authors on a 2026 systematic review comparing two treatments for obstructive sleep apnea. One treatment, continuous positive airway pressure, pushes air through a mask to keep the airway open. The other, a mandibular advancement device, holds the lower jaw forward during sleep. The review asks which option better protects heart and metabolic health.

Pooling fourteen randomized trials with 1,241 patients, the authors found airway pressure lowered LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, and dipping diastolic blood pressure more than the jaw device. Glucose, triglycerides, HDL, average blood pressure, and heart rate showed no clear difference. Their reading favors airway pressure for patients whose cardiovascular risk is already raised, while both therapies still treat the apnea itself.
pmc-13621673:
Lennart Evers, Jessica M Grein, and C Alexander Boecker traced what happens to alpha-synuclein inside nerve endings when a regulatory phosphatase goes missing. Alpha-synuclein is the protein that clumps in Parkinson's disease, and the kinase LRRK2, a major genetic culprit, tags helper proteins called RABs with phosphates. The phosphatase PPM1H removes those tags. Using cultured mouse neurons lacking PPM1H, the team measured where synuclein sits relative to a presynaptic landmark.

Without the phosphatase, synuclein drifted farther from its usual presynaptic position, as if the terminal's organization had loosened. Blocking LRRK2's kinase activity with a drug restored normal positioning, proving the displacement runs through that pathway. The authors read the result as evidence that excess phosphorylated RAB proteins disturb the nanoscale arrangement of synuclein at the synapse. That misplacement, long before clumps form, may be one early step in how LRRK2-linked Parkinson's begins.
pmc-13623273:
Eunice X X Tan leads a multicentre study charting the natural history of liver decompensation, the point where a scarred liver starts to fail openly. Patients move through stages: silent advanced disease, a first crisis such as fluid build-up or bleeding, further crises, and death. The team modelled those moves step by step in a mainly Asian cohort.

The study followed 1,777 patients across nineteen institutions, all with stiff livers on a scan test. During follow-up of over four years, about fifteen percent had a first decompensation. Once that first crisis struck, the next one came far faster, at a yearly rate many times higher than the first. Alcohol-related liver disease pushed patients into the first crisis quickest, while hepatitis B patients were slowest to reach a second. Most patients stayed stable for years, the authors note, so effort should focus on the turning point.
pmc-13623373:
Samuel C Eziuzor writes a first-person essay about an early research career that crossed three worlds: West Africa, East Germany, and Western Canada. A German Academic Exchange Service scholarship took him to Leipzig for a doctorate, the turning point he describes with clear gratitude. The essay dwells on what acceptance letters never mention.

Life outside the lab ran in German, from tenancy contracts to grocery runs, and that daily language gap slowly eroded his sense of belonging. German supervisors expected independence early, which felt both freeing and abandoning to a scholar raised in a more guided system. Loneliness carried a measurable cost, and the essay cites survey evidence that many doctoral students face serious psychological distress. Underfunded posts after the doctorate added money worries and unclear job titles. Eziuzor closes with suggestions for universities on both sides of the Atlantic that host travelling researchers.
pmc-13626473:
Diana M Karosas and co-authors model how an epileptic seizure recruits quiet brain tissue, and show the answer depends on the seizure's dynamotype, its pattern of starting and stopping. Earlier models handled only one such pattern, so the team used a flexible seizure model with two linked nodes, one that fires on its own and one that can be pulled in. They varied the nodes' inner settings and the strength of the link between them.

Seizures that began with a baseline shift, a step in the resting signal, spread less often and more slowly than those without. Seizures that opened with swelling amplitude almost never spread at all. The model also forecast odd mixes, like a shift in the recruited node only, and human brain recordings confirmed such cases occur, which may sharpen how doctors locate seizure sources.
pmc-13626673:
Ruchi Patel and Bhuvnesh Bharti frame swarms of field-driven particles as tiny distributed machines. Active colloids, grains a millionth of a meter wide, can be pushed and steered by electric or magnetic fields applied from outside. In this Perspective the authors split the machine across parts: the particles move, the fields supply power, cameras sense, and computers close the loop with feedback and learning algorithms.

Judged by motion alone, the field has dazzled, yet real jobs ask more: finding a target, hauling cargo, catching, treating, releasing, and assembling on cue. Power delivery, material fit with living tissue, and fast feedback in messy settings still limit deployment. The authors urge builders to score success by task outcomes, and to wire sensing, computation, and actuation into one adaptive loop.
pmc-13627273:
Yan and colleagues reviewed in 2026 primary central nervous system lymphoma, a rare and aggressive cancer confined to the brain, spinal cord, eyes, and nearby membranes. High-dose methotrexate chemotherapy remains the backbone of first treatment, but lasting control is hard, above all in older or frail patients and when the disease returns. The authors gathered recent genomic and multi-layer studies to map what drives the cancer and how care is shifting.

Yan shows that repeated gene changes cluster in a few pathways that drive B cell growth signals, immune evasion, and adaptation to the brain setting. Liquid biopsy, testing tumor DNA or cytokines in spinal or eye fluid, now offers a less invasive way to aid diagnosis and tracking. New targeted and immune drugs, including BTK blockers and engineered CAR T cells, show activity mainly in returned disease. Most proof still comes from small early studies, the authors caution.
pmc-13627873:
Yanbing Wang and colleagues chart the world literature on GLP-1 medicines for type 2 diabetes, the gut-hormone drugs that have reshaped diabetes and weight care. Their bibliometric sweep of the Web of Science gathered 3,736 original articles from 2004 to 2025 and mapped who publishes, who partners with whom, and which themes rise and fall. Single-target GLP-1 studies still form the core pile, while head-to-head and multi-receptor studies have surged lately.

The United States leads in output and in international ties, and two drug makers, Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly, stand out as the most present institutions. Landmark outcome trials and joint diabetes guidelines drew the heaviest citations. Topics have swung from basic hormone biology toward heart, kidney, and weight outcomes and real-world use, the field's center of gravity in one map.
pmc-13628573:
Kerstin Müller and Hans-Achim Wagenknecht fixed light-up dyes onto sydnones. Sydnones are stable ring compounds that react with tagged DNA inside living systems. Their 2026 paper builds five dyes of one family. The glow switches on only after the tagging reaction. That lets researchers watch DNA being marked in real time.

The dyes reacted with changed nucleosides at modest speeds. With strained-ring-tagged DNA, the reaction sped up sharply. The glow grew up to seventeen times stronger. The DNA itself helped by acting as a template. One product also shifted its colour a lot. That could help scientists tell tagged building blocks from tagged DNA. Tests in HeLa cell cultures confirmed the chemistry works inside living cells.
pmc-13631273:
Elizabeth V K Ledger and four colleagues show that human blood serum itself teaches one bacterium to become harder to kill. The bacterium is Staphylococcus aureus. Their study appeared in 2026. It causes infections from skin boils to fatal bloodstream disease. Its biofilms shrug off antibiotics. Yet most biofilm research uses artificial media, not anything like blood.

They found the trigger is triglyceride fat in serum. A bacterial enzyme clips glycerol from the fat. The glycerol fuels extra production of a cell wall polymer. That polymer drives biofilm growth plus tolerance to two last-resort drugs. Blocking the enzyme or the polymer's making collapsed the biofilm. Drug sensitivity returned. The authors propose both steps as drug targets.
pmc-13635873:
Mikaeli Carmichael and three colleagues present a model for putting menstrual cycle tracking to work in sports teams. Tracking is widely discussed under the female athlete research theme, and clubs already log cycles to plan training. Yet practitioners said they lacked guidance on rollout, not on which app to pick. Drawing on their own series of studies plus the wider literature and athlete voices, the authors built the ConNECT model.

The model rests on education and communication as levers of change. Done well, those levers can shift habits at three levels: the individual athlete, the organization, and the surrounding culture. Better uptake and follow-through should follow. The authors present the model as a preliminary, practice-grounded starting point rather than a finished system. It also gives researchers a frame for naming the next questions, since evidence for phase-based training remains thin while practice races ahead.
pmc-13637273:
Thobani Cele and Xolile Mkhize published this 2026 survey study of depression severity among students at a university in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Student mental health suffers where money stress, food insecurity, and disaster shocks pile up. Four hundred forty-five registered students answered an online questionnaire. A standard nine-item scale sorted their depression into five levels from none to severe, and a statistical model weighed social, economic, food, and disaster factors together.

Nearly six in ten students reported moderate-to-severe symptoms. Women faced a notably higher chance of the severe grade than men. Eating a more varied diet lowered that chance, while relying on shakier funding sources raised it. Exposure to the 2021 unrest and the 2022 floods each pushed severe depression upward. Older students enjoyed a modest protective edge. The authors urge universities to pair counseling with food support, steadier funding guidance, and disaster resilience help.
pmc-13637373:
Sabah Al-Marwani, Zaidah Murang, and Nik AA Tuah published this 2026 scoping review of digital tools for managing obesity in adults. Apps, video visits, and trackers promise support between clinic appointments, yet the field's shape was unclear. Following established scoping methods, the team screened a decade of studies, from 2015 to 2025, in four databases. Forty-three studies qualified, spanning clinics, workplaces, and community programs.

The tools clustered into five delivery styles: telehealth, mobile apps, web programs, multi-tool bundles, and hybrids that mix digital contact with face-to-face care. Content ranged from diet coaching and activity plans to fasting schedules, games, and psychological support. Connected scales and wearables often fed the self-monitoring loop. Some studies showed real weight loss and better habits, yet reporting varied wildly. The authors flag short follow-up and thin evidence from low-income countries as the gaps that matter most.
pmc-13641773:
Kim and co-authors compared a 2026 pair of obesity definitions in Korean children, one based on body mass index and one on body fat percentage. BMI cannot tell fat from muscle, so growing children may be misclassified during puberty. Children aged seven to twelve were sorted into five obesity groups plus a large control group.

Children labelled obese by BMI were taller with more muscle, while those labelled by body fat were shorter with more fat mass. Kim found those contrasts sharpened with age across the seven to twelve range studied. By ages eleven to twelve many boys met the BMI cut-off through lean mass gains rather than fat. Girls more often showed the reverse pattern, carrying excess fat that BMI missed entirely. Waist to hip ratio separated obese from non-obese children but not the two definitions.
pmc-13643773:
Ye-Ji Kim and colleagues present OptOrch, a software toolkit that helps tree breeders decide how to deploy clones and families in forest seed orchards. Their 2026 paper describes a modular optimization system built in AMPL, a mathematical programming language, that keeps biological assumptions, input data, and solvers separate.

Unlike earlier optimal-contribution software, OptOrch exposes its objective function and constraints so breeders can adjust orchard-specific rules, including diversity thresholds, contribution limits, graft availability, relatedness restrictions, and outside pollen flow. The authors demonstrate the toolkit with simulated scenarios that vary diversity thresholds and pollen contamination. The simulations quantify the trade-off between genetic gain and diversity and compare feasible deployment strategies under realistic conditions.
pmc-13645573:
Lin Zhou and four colleagues build a machine learning model to flag patients at risk of osteoporosis, a disease that weakens bones and raises fracture risk. Their data came from 187 patients treated at a Beijing military hospital between January 2023 and September 2024. The team measured sixteen immune signals in blood, called cytokines, along with other routine markers. Eleven different learning models were trained and compared.

Sixteen features, including the cytokine IL-8, were kept as risk markers for the final work. A gradient boosting model performed best, with strong accuracy and a fair balance between catching cases and avoiding false alarms. A tool called SHAP was used to show which features pushed each prediction up or down. The authors say such a model could help doctors spot high-risk patients earlier, before fractures occur.
pmc-13645773:
Andrés Ramírez maps the scientific literature on measuring adolescent dating violence in a bibliometric review written on his own. Dating violence covers physical, sexual, emotional, and online abuse between young partners, and measured rates depend heavily on how studies define and ask about it. His search of two databases in March 2026 gathered 6,125 records published from 1987 to 2026. He charted growth, sources, authors, countries, and keyword patterns.

Output grew fast after 2014 and reached its highest yearly count in 2025. Work clustered in journals on violence, psychology, and assessment, with themes around validation, reliability, gender, and prevalence. Measurement adapted for minority sexual and gender identities, and for less-studied regions, stayed at the field's edges. Ramírez warns that a fast-growing literature is not the same as a mature one. His map shows where measurement tools are strong and where young people's experiences remain poorly captured.
pmc-13646173:
Saira Sheikh and four colleagues argue that cell therapy for lupus may be offered too late to show its full power. Engineered immune cells called CAR T cells have produced deep, drug-free remissions in severe lupus, including kidney disease from lupus. Today the therapy is reserved for patients who have failed other treatments, under regulatory guidance. By then, the authors note, organs may carry fixed damage and scarring.

When treatment comes late, weak results may reflect permanent damage rather than a weak therapy, which can mislead judgment of the approach. The authors propose trials in early severe disease, when the chance to change the disease course is greatest. They weigh the known risks and benefits from evidence so far. Their piece is a call to test timing itself as a treatment variable, before the salvage-only habit hardens into doctrine.
pmc-13647173:
Zi-Yao Wang, Na Liu, and Min-Bin Chen review how artificial intelligence fuses many layers of data to sharpen breast cancer care. Single tests miss much of this cancer's variety across molecules, space, and time. AI tools can extract patterns from gene, protein, imaging, and tissue data and tie the microscopic scale to what doctors see. The review covers early detection, precise diagnosis, prediction of immunotherapy response, drug sensitivity, and outlook.

The authors sort the field by how close each approach is to real clinic use, and they appraise evidence across data types rather than within one silo. Obstacles get full weight: messy data, lab batch effects, hard-to-explain models, privacy, regulation, and fitting hospital workflow. New foundation models are weighed as an opportunity. Their conclusion is that these tools promise genuinely personal treatment choices, once prospective trials and auditable systems catch up.
pmc-13647973:
Alexander Muacevic and six colleagues ask whether obesity and heart failure reshape the heart's electrical signature along shared directions, using national survey data. The data cover 8,324 adults aged forty and older examined between 1988 and 1994, each with a twelve-lead heart tracing. Forty-seven tracing features were adjusted and standardized, then compressed into two-dimensional maps for obesity and heart failure. A shuffled-data test repeated the whole pipeline five thousand times to judge whether any overlap was real.

The two maps aligned far beyond chance, and the overlap survived clinical adjustment and exclusions of prior heart attacks and conduction defects. The shared direction was dominated by T-wave size and frontal T-axis features, tied to the heart muscle's recovery after each beat. Alignment weakened after the strictest exclusions yet stayed positive. The authors read this as evidence that fat and failing hearts push cardiac electricity down partly common paths.
pmc-13648273:
Abdul Azeez and eight colleagues study how fluorinated zinc phthalocyanine molecules, flat ring-shaped compounds used in electronics and sensors, settle into films on gold surfaces. By varying the number of fluorine substituents and the symmetry of each molecule, they ask what controls whether molecules lie flat or stand on edge.

Films were formed simply by soaking gold in solution, then measured with X-ray spectroscopy, adsorption curves, and water contact angles. Mid-range fluorination gave the strongest adsorption and highest coverage, with molecules standing edge-on in head-to-tail rows, while the extremes lay face-down. Modelling traced the difference to molecular dipoles and steric crowding, offering design rules for other supported molecular films.
pmc-13650573:
Lauren Hallewell and four colleagues design a service pathway that would place dietitians inside children's primary dental care in the United Kingdom. Diet drives both tooth decay and wider health, yet dental teams usually offer only brief sugar advice, and no established route connects young patients to full dietetic support.

Eight professionals, four dietitians and four dental clinicians, mapped the pathway in a structured online workshop held in April 2026, building on earlier expert consensus statements. Their design puts dietitian-led triage at the center, coordinating referrals, communication, and continuity between services. Discussion surfaced uncertainties about staffing shapes, escalation routes, and whether outside services could absorb new referrals, plus questions of family engagement and system readiness. The authors label the pathway conceptual and early-stage, needing pilot testing and evaluation before any service adopts it.
pmc-13650973:
María Elisa Peichoto and four co-authors, writing with two regional collaboration networks, set policy priorities for venomous bites and stings across Latin America and the Caribbean. Snake, scorpion, spider, and caterpillar envenomation remains a major regional burden, and climate and ecological change are shifting where the dangerous species live.

The team studied survey data coordinated through Pan American Health Organization networks for 2019 to 2024, modeled trends, projected them to 2030, and mapped how incidence and deaths vary across countries. Overall incidence is rising, led by spider bites and caterpillar contacts, and spider case fatality is projected to climb if trends hold. Surveillance quality, risk mapping, clinical readiness, and follow-up of lasting damage all showed weaknesses, and antivenom output, purchasing, and actual use often mismatched the burden for each envenomation type. Regional cooperation has sharpened coordination, yet access gaps persist, and the authors lay out strategic fixes.
pmc-13651773:
Jintao Song and four co-authors show that the visual system files spatial relations between objects into topological categories, such as inside versus outside and connected versus separate. Geometry treats these relations as the deepest invariants, unchanged by stretching, and the team asked whether perception honors those boundaries while hunting for targets.

Search performance jumped whenever the difference between target and distractors crossed a topological category line, even with distances held equal. Control experiments stripped away a depth-from-overlap explanation and showed that removing the inside-outside boundary restored a smooth dependence on plain metric distance. The categorical edge reappeared across several forms of connectivity. The authors read the results as evidence that vision represents relations abstractly and categorically. That would explain why a phone in a basket and a knife in a cup feel similar at a glance despite sharing nothing else.
pmc-13651873:
Frank Förster and five colleagues report a laboratory study of how weathered volcanic rock affects reef-building corals. Working with material collected on the island of St. Vincent, the team exposed three coral species to weekly additions of untreated tephra and its leachate over six weeks. The question was whether long-term contact with remobilized sediment helps or harms the animals that build reefs around volcanic islands.

Every exposed colony showed stronger photosynthetic light harvesting, while most other measures of coral health stayed unchanged. Chemical analysis found that the tephra released small amounts of dissolved trace metals into the seawater, including iron, manganese, and copper. The authors argue that this slow supply of metals may quietly support reef growth near volcanic coasts, a role for eroded volcanic sediment that earlier work had largely overlooked.
pmc-2836773:
Webb, Joseph, Yardley, and co-authors review internet programmes that aim to change health behaviour. The internet is used ever more to deliver such interventions, from quitting smoking to eating better. Earlier reviews had not sorted out, in a systematic way, which features make online programmes work.

The team pooled results across studies and linked effectiveness to three things: the theory behind a programme, the behaviour change techniques it uses, and how it is delivered. Their findings give designers evidence for building online health tools that do more than inform; they actually shift habits.
pmc-3163573:
Alikhan, Petty, Ben Zakour, and co-authors present BRIG, the BLAST Ring Image Generator, for comparing microbe genomes. Seeing genome matches as pictures is of great use for spotting genetic differences between closely related microbes. Fresh ways to draw genomes were needed to check, read, and share sequencing results well.

BRIG draws genomes as ring-shaped bands, aligning shared and missing regions at a glance. Differences that signal new traits, such as resistance or virulence, become easy to point to. The simple format made genome comparison accessible to labs without specialist graphics skills.  Doctors use such matches when a familiar microbe behaves in a new way in patients.
pmc-3599573:
Akbarzadeh, Rezaei-Sadabady, Davaran, and co-authors review liposomes: their kinds, how they are made, and their uses. Liposomes are sphere-shaped vesicles made of one or more fat-like layers, much like cell membranes. First described in the mid-1960s, they have become useful models, reagents, and tools in many sciences.

The review covers fields from physics and chemistry to medicine, where liposomes carry drugs inside their shells. Sorting types and making methods helps researchers choose the right carrier. Liposome delivery now supports approved medicines and vaccine tools used worldwide.  Cosmetics and food science also use liposomes, a breadth the review covers.
pmc-3933873:
Zhang, Kobert, Flouri, and co-authors present PEAR, a fast and accurate tool for merging Illumina paired-end reads. Illumina paired-end technology reads DNA fragments from both ends at once. When fragments are short enough, the two reads overlap and can be merged into one longer read.

Tools for merging already existed for some cases, but accuracy and speed varied. PEAR was built to merge reads reliably at scale. Longer, cleaner merged reads improve assembly and variant detection in sequencing projects of every kind.  Amplicon studies merge reads first, so merger quality shapes all downstream ecological conclusions.
pmc-4081273:
Van der Walt, Schönberger, Nunez-Iglesias, and their team presented scikit-image in 2014. Scikit-image is a library for image processing in the Python language. It supplies algorithms and helper tools for work in research, teaching, and industry.

The library is released under a liberal open source license, so anyone may use and adapt it. Its interface is well documented, which lowers the bar for new users. Tasks range from cleaning and filtering images to finding edges and shapes. As part of the wider Python science stack, it helps labs build image workflows that others can run and check.
pmc-4261873:
Bardou, Mariette, Escudié, and their colleagues built jvenn in 2014, an interactive viewer for Venn diagrams. Venn diagrams are a common way to compare lists, showing what is shared and what is unique. Biologists use them often to compare gene lists from different analyses.

Unlike a static picture, jvenn lets users click and explore the overlaps directly in a web browser. Lists from different conditions or species can be swapped in and compared at once. The shared part often holds the genes most worth studying further. A clear, hands-on view saves time and helps teams agree on what a list comparison really shows.
pmc-4839673:
Talevich, Shain, Botton, and their colleagues built CNVkit in 2016. Copy number variants, where a DNA stretch is deleted or repeated, matter in inherited syndromes and in cancer. Targeted DNA sequencing is increasingly used to infer such changes from read depth.

CNVkit detects genome-wide copy number changes and draws them for inspection. It works with the targeted panels that clinics use for cancer and genetic testing. Clear plots help analysts judge whether a change is real and where its edges fall. Reliable copy number calls from standard sequencing panels widen access to this layer of diagnosis.
pmc-5014473:
Martin, Murrell, Golden, and their co-authors released RDP4 in 2015. RDP4 is the latest version of a recombination detection program for sequence alignments. Recombination, where viruses swap genome pieces, can distort evolutionary trees if it goes unseen.

The Windows program runs a wide array of methods to detect and visualize recombination in virus genomes. It can also strip the evidence of recombination from an alignment so other analyses run cleanly. Viruses such as HIV recombine often, which affects vaccine and drug work. RDP4 helps researchers spot those events and judge how virus families truly evolved.
pmc-5267473:
Sekhon, Cartwright, and Francis studied the acceptability of healthcare interventions in 2017. Acceptability, whether patients and staff find an intervention suitable, is increasingly seen as something to consider when designing, evaluating, and putting care into practice. The literature gave almost no guidance on defining the term or measuring it.

The authors reviewed existing reviews on the topic and built a theoretical framework for acceptability. A clear framework gives trial teams questions to ask before and during a study. Interventions that patients dislike fail in real life, however well they work in theory. The framework helps designers catch that problem early and improve uptake.
pmc-7296073:
Bianca Parker and co-authors surveyed in 2020 a genus of gut bacteria called Alistipes, a group scientists are only beginning to understand. Members of this genus were first isolated mostly from medical samples, and they belong to the Bacteroidetes, a large bacterial phylum with a strong role in gut imbalance and disease. Interest grew as studies began linking these bacteria to conditions well beyond the gut.

The review gathers evidence tying Alistipes to inflammation, to cancer, and to mental health, and weighs where the links look protective and where they look harmful. The authors are candid that findings conflict and that context seems to matter a great deal. Their summary gives researchers a clear starting map of a microbe whose story is still being written.
pmc-7319273:
Xiandong Chi and colleagues reported in 2020 that they had found a human antibody able to block SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19. Their target was the viral spike protein, the three part structure the virus uses to latch onto cells and fuse with them. Most antibody work at the time aimed at the spike's receptor binding region, the part that grips the cell.

This antibody instead attaches to a different stretch of the spike, its N-terminal domain, and still stops the virus from infecting cells. That result mattered because it showed the spike has more than one vulnerable spot. Drugs and vaccines that press on several spots at once are harder for a changing virus to escape.
pmc-7619273:
Stephen Potter and Mark Hawley survey what older people living independently actually think about digital technology. Services delivered through apps and connected devices are often proposed as the way to help people age well at home, yet uptake among older users is patchy. The researchers questioned 230 people aged fifty-five and over, drawn from independent-living schemes and local communities, and compared attitudes across generations within that group.

Views were more varied than the stereotype of the reluctant older user suggests, with experience and perceived usefulness shaping opinion more than age alone. Missed chances to help, the authors argue, come from services designed around assumptions rather than these stated attitudes. For councils and care providers rolling out technology-enabled care, the survey offers a corrective: ask first, and build around the answers people actually give.
racine-athaliah-donkersley-1873:
Athaliah, Racine's last tragedy, stages a child king hidden in the Temple of Jerusalem. J. Donkersley's 1873 English blank verse renders the biblical drama of Joash and the high priest Jehoiada. Queen Athaliah, who seized the throne by blood, dreams of a child she cannot name.

The priest guards the boy until the hour comes to crown him before the people. Racine drew the tale from scripture and gave it the tight, singing form of French classical tragedy. In English dress the play completes a shelf of Racine's tragedies, and many judge it his most sacred work.
ralston-russian-fairy-tales-1873:
W. R. S. Ralston, a Scots scholar at the British Museum, made this first great English set of Russian tales in 1873. He read Russian well and drew from the best stores of tales in that tongue. No such set had been made for English readers before his work.

The tales hold the rusalka, the water maid of Slav lore, in her gay and grim forms. House spirits, wood demons, and bold young heroes fill the rest of the rich store. Ralston's set gave the English world its first true sight of the fairy lore of Russia.
riemann-hypotheses-geometry-clifford-187:
Bernhard Riemann gave his famous lecture on the foundations of geometry in 1854, though it was printed only after his early death. William Clifford's 1873 English version brought it to a wider world. Riemann asks what we truly know about space itself.

He argues that space need not be flat, and that its shape is a fact to be measured, not assumed. Curved spaces of many kinds become open to math for the first time. Einstein later took Riemann's tools to build general relativity. Few short lectures have changed physics and math so deeply. Clifford, himself a fine geometer, kept the translation close and clear.
stowe-palmetto-leaves-1873:
Palmetto-Leaves, printed at Boston in 1873 with pictures, gathers Stowe's sketches of Florida. She wintered at Mandarin on the St. Johns River and wrote as a delighted newcomer. The contents open with Nobody's Dog and A Flowery January in Florida.

Orange groves, alligators, and steamboat trips fill the bright early pages. She also describes freed Black families building new lives after the end of slavery. Part travel book and part gentle sales pitch, the sketches urge Northern settlers south. Historians credit the book with helping to spark Florida's first great land boom in the years that followed its release.
the-alchemy-of-happiness-1873: No page of the book named by this record stands here. The full Google Books front wrapper stands in its place. It gives notes on public domain status. It gives notes on legal use. It tells of the search project itself. A Harvard College Library stamp ends the copy. No title page appears. No contents or text of the 1873 printing appears. Nothing of the work itself can thus be told from what is present.
the-alchemy-of-happiness-tr-from-the-tur: No page of the book named by this record stands here. In its place stands the full Google Books front wrapper alone, with its notes on public domain status, legal use, watermarks, and the search project. No title page, contents, or text of the 1873 Turkish-abridgement printing appears, so nothing of the work itself can be told from what is present.
the-fatal-jealousie-1673: Henry Nevil Payne wrote The Fatal Jealousie, a play of 1673, and this copy is a 1948 reprint by the Augustan Reprint Society with an introduction by Willard Thorp. Only the front matter of the reprint is present here: the series page, the names of the society's editors, and the note that the text was lithoprinted at Ann Arbor in 1949. No scene or speech from the play itself shows up in these pages.
the-german-classics-of-the-nineteenth-an: Volume six of The German Classics is a patrons' edition of 1914. It is named for Heinrich Heine, Franz Grillparzer, and Ludwig van Beethoven. Only the front matter and start of contents are present here. The Heine part opens with a life by William Guild Howard. Poems and songs then follow. They stand in versions by Sir Theodore Martin and Charles Wharton Stork. Other hands helped too. No full work is included in this portion. So the texts cannot be judged from the front pages alone.

Volume eight of The German Classics was printed in 1914. It holds Berthold Auerbach, Jeremias Gotthelf, and Fritz Reuter. It holds Adalbert Stifter and Wilhelm Heinrich Riehl too. Only the front matter and start of contents are present here. An essay on the novel of provincial life opens the volume. Auerbach's Little Barefoot stands first among the tales. Gotthelf's Uli, The Farmhand stands with it. No full work follows in the pages given here. So the texts cannot be stated here.
the-great-riots-of-new-york-1712-to-1873: Hon. J. T. Headley wrote The Great Riots of New York, 1712 to 1873. The title page promises a full and complete account of the four days' draft riot of 1863. Headley dedicates the book to the Metropolitan Police. He praises their unwavering fidelity and courage in the past. Only front matter is present here: the title page, the dedication, and the start of a list of illustrations. The plates named are the burning of the Provost-Marshal's Office and the Old New York Hospital. No chapter text is present.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
The English, part of In London and Moscow in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, comes from Arthur Machen's rendering of the 1894 London edition, with chapters Arthur Symons discovered. Chapter Ten opens after a night like a never-ending nightmare. Casanova rises sad and savage, feeling his fine house hang like a millstone. Knowing no English, he watches the crowd in a coffee-house until two men discuss a suicide in French.

One speaker, a creditor of the dead Tommy, coolly calculates that the man might have lived comfortably six months longer before killing himself. The arithmetic amuses and steadies Casanova. At the Exchange, the banker Bosanquet supplies money and prices passers-by on request: one worth a hundred thousand, another not worth a ten-pound note. The chapter promises English eccentricity, a betting club, and the Charpillon affair. Readers see London through a foreigner's eye for money talk.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Columbia College in New York fills the Mirror's No. 323, dated Saturday, July 19, 1828, under a joke from Swift's Tale of a Tub about an academy for the island's wits. The editors note that London itself is becoming a seat of learning, with one college nearly complete and subscriptions pouring in for a second. A respected correspondent supplies the view and description of the American college as equally important to Prince Posterity.

Columbia College ranks among America's chief seminaries of learning, the correspondent writes. It was founded principally by voluntary contributions of the province's inhabitants, assisted by the general assembly. The principal building in the sketch represents the college to English readers. The article treats a New York college as news fit for a London miscellany hungry for improvement stories. Readers watch the magazine congratulate its own city by way of Manhattan.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-19:
Headed volume twenty in its own pages, though the record calls it volume nineteen, this portion covers 1572 and 1573 in chapter eight. Patriots besiege Tergoes, and Mondragon relieves it by an audacious march across drowned land, while Zutphen suffers a horrible sack.

Naarden refuses terms, Romero betrays the admitted Spaniards' faith, and garrison and burghers are massacred before the town burns. Orange is warmly received in Holland and negotiates secretly with the estates, while Don Frederic plans from Amsterdam and Haarlem prepares for siege. Relief marches and massacres measure the war's stakes.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-20:
Headed volume twenty-one in its own pages, though the record calls it volume twenty, this portion covers 1573 in chapter nine. Alva, hated by great personages, quarrels with Medina Coeli, trades complaints to the king, and watches Spanish troops mutiny before obedience is restored.

At Alkmaar his bloody threats meet steady defense, a first assault is repulsed, soldiers refuse a second storm, and Orange orders the country flooded. A carpenter-envoy's captured dispatches frighten the Spaniards further, and the siege is raised. Water, Motley shows, could defeat even Spain's best army in the field.
the-yankee-tea-party-or-boston-in-1773: Henry C. Watson wrote The Yankee Tea-Party, or Boston in 1773, for the Young American's Library. Title pages from its Philadelphia publisher, Lindsay and Blakiston, are what appear here. Watson also wrote The Camp-Fires of the American Revolution. The book carries illustrations of the Boston Tea Party story. A publisher's catalogue begins at the end of the pages shown. The story itself does not appear within the pages present in this record.
tob-10173:
Hosea is the twenty-eighth book in this King James ordering, named for the prophet at its center. Unusually, Hosea lived out his message. According to the text, God told him to marry an unfaithful wife, so his broken home became a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness to God.

Through grief, accusation, and forgiveness, the short book pleads for the nation to return. Judgment speeches give way in the closing chapters to promises of mercy reaching beyond punishment. Readers feel the argument in domestic terms: betrayal, anger, and a love that refuses to end the story at divorce. That personal frame sets Hosea apart among prophetic books.
tob-10273:
Enoch, the patriarch who walked with God, became the hero of writings that the Hebrew Bible left out. R. H. Charles translated the Book of Enoch, or 1 Enoch, the version kept as Scripture by the church in Ethiopia. Its visions shaped ideas found later in the New Testament.

Enoch tours heaven and watches the fall of the Watchers, angels who came down to earth and sinned. He sees stores of wind and fire, thrones of judgment, and the fate of the wicked and the just. Charles's careful work made the strange, vivid book readable again for modern students.
tob-10473:
Psalms through Malachi complete the Douay-Rheims Old Testament in Part Two, in the revision associated with Bishop Richard Challoner. The translation began at the English College in Douai in 1609, made for Catholics living under a Protestant crown. Its language is solemn and formal, close to the Latin Vulgate behind it.

The Psalms in this rendering carry a distinctive music long used in Catholic prayer, and the prophets speak with grave weight. Wisdom books and the later histories fill out the volume. As a monument of recusant scholarship, the Douay-Rheims remained the Catholic Bible in English for generations and is still prayed by traditional Catholics.
tob-10573:
A letter known as First Clement went from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth near the end of the first century. Tradition credits Clement, an early leader at Rome, as its author. It ranks among the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament.

Corinth had thrown out its elders, and the letter urges the church to restore them and live in order and humility. It cites the Old Testament, the words of Jesus, and examples of envy and its harms. Early churches read it aloud beside scripture, and it shows how Christian leaders taught within living memory of the apostles.
tob-4073:
One architectural treatise survives from ancient Rome: the Ten Books of Vitruvius, written under Augustus. Joseph Gwilt's translation of 1826 carried it to English builders. Temples, theaters, houses, waterworks, and war machines all fall within the Roman architect's brief.

Vitruvius demands that building unite firmness, usefulness, and beauty, a trio still quoted in schools of architecture. He treats proportion, site, climate, and materials with a practitioner's care. Renaissance masters from Alberti to Palladio rebuilt the classical world from his pages. Checked from the 1919 printing, Gwilt's version remains readable, direct, and full of working detail.
tob-4273:
Lewis Spence surveyed The Myths of Mexico and Peru in 1913, introducing English readers to the gods of the Aztecs, Maya neighbors, and Incas in one illustrated, wide-ranging volume. Quetzalcoatl the feathered serpent, Huitzilopochtli the war god of Tenochtitlan, and Viracocha the creator in the Andes receive full treatment, along with creation stories and flood tales.

Behind the myths stands the calendar-stone cosmos: ages of suns, each ending in destruction, and rituals meant to keep the current world alive. Spence also records what the Spanish conquest did to these traditions and their texts. Readers get the pre-conquest religions of two civilizations as a popular scholar of his era understood them.
un-ga-res-a-69-73:
Central Africa's states built a standing team on safety in 1992, and Resolution A/69/73, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, backs its work. The United Nations Standing Advisory Committee on Security Questions in Central Africa was set up by the Secretary-General. Its task is to spur arms limits, disarmament, and calm in the sub-region, and to rebuild trust among its member states.

The text recalls the guides for full disarmament from the first special session of 1978. It notes the shared stand the team's states took at Sao Tome in 2011, on the world arms trade pact then in the making. Trust steps and arms limits, worked out by the region for the region, are the core of the call.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/73, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, reviews regional confidence-building measures through the United Nations Standing Advisory Committee on Security Questions in Central Africa. It notes the Kinshasa Convention on small arms control. It notes a road map against terrorism and proliferation. It notes concern over the Central African Republic crisis and the creation of the MINUSCA mission in April 2014. It notes shared action against threats such as Boko Haram and the Lord's Resistance Army.
un-sc-res-1073:
Clashes over a tunnel exit at Jerusalem's holy places drew the Council on 28 September 1996. Saudi Arabia's letter of 26 September, for the Arab League states, told of Israel opening an entrance to a tunnel near the Al Aqsa Mosque. Days of fighting followed in Jerusalem, Nablus, Ramallah, Bethlehem, and Gaza. Many Palestinian civilians died, and Israeli soldiers and Palestinian police also clashed. Foreign ministers joined the Council's debate on 27 September.

The Council called for the instant halt and reversal of every act that had worsened the state of affairs. The safety and protection of Palestinian civilians had to be secured. Talks inside the Middle East peace process had to resume at once on their agreed basis. The agreements already reached were to be applied on time. The Council decided to follow the situation closely and stay seized of the matter.
un-sc-res-1373: One of the Council's formal texts, Resolution 1373 is carried in this catalog under 2001. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1473: Resolution 1473 is a voted act of the fifteen-member Security Council, preserved from the official UN record through English Wikisource. Such texts matter because their wording can bind every UN member state. The entry gives the full decision, from its opening clauses recalling earlier steps to the closing paragraphs that set the action in motion.
un-sc-res-1573:
Timor-Leste's United Nations support mission received its final extension on 16 November 2004. The Council praised the Timorese people and government for their peace, stability, and institution building. The mission, UNMISET, was in its consolidation phase under resolution 1543 (2004). Yet the country had not reached self-sufficiency in public administration, law enforcement, or security.

The Council extended UNMISET for a final six months, to 20 May 2005, keeping its tasks, shape, and size unchanged. The mission was told to focus on its exit strategy and on Timorese ownership of the work. Donors were urged to keep giving, and United Nations agencies were told to plan a smooth shift to a development framework. The Council noted the Serious Crimes Unit's push to finish its probes by November 2004. It also conceded the unit might not fully answer the call for justice over the 1999 violence.
un-sc-res-1673: Kept under number 1673, a Security Council resolution survives as a record transcription from English Wikisource. The Council's authority on peace and security comes from the UN Charter, and resolutions are its exercise in writing. This entry preserves one exercise entire: the findings the members adopted and the steps those findings set in motion.
un-sc-res-173:
Security Council Resolution 173, adopted on July 26, 1962, recommended Burundi for membership in the United Nations. The small central African kingdom had gained independence from Belgium on July 1 of that year, ending decades of rule first by Germany and then by Belgium under League and UN mandates. Its leaders at once sought a seat in the world body.

The council found Burundi fit under the Charter and sent the bid to the General Assembly, which seated the new state that September. Burundi joined in the great wave of African nations entering the UN as empires wound down. The brief text is one tile in that larger picture of decolonization.
un-sc-res-1773: Kept as Resolution 1773, this Security Council text comes from the official record through a transcription by English Wikisource. The format will be familiar to any reader of UN documents: concern weighed in the preamble, action ordered in the clauses. Preserving the format along with the words keeps the entry faithful to the original act.
un-sc-res-1873: Adopted in 2009, Resolution 1873 is a Security Council act preserved through a Wikisource transcription of the record. Its paragraphs are numbered for a reason: each can be lifted out and cited on its own in later disputes. The entry keeps all of them together and in order, which is how the Council issued them.
un-sc-res-273: Holding number 273 in the Council series, this resolution carries a 1963 date in the library catalog. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-573:
Israel's bombing of the PLO headquarters in Tunis was condemned in October 1985. Tunisia's complaint letter of 1 October told of an air raid on Hamman-Plage, in the southern suburbs of Tunis. Israel claimed responsibility at once. The raid caused heavy loss of life and wide material damage. Tunisia's foreign minister addressed the Council.

The Council condemned vigorously the act of armed aggression against Tunisian territory. It was a flagrant breach of the Charter and of international law, the text said. Israel was told to refrain from such attacks and from threatening them. Member states were urged to take measures to dissuade Israel from striking at the sovereignty of any state. Tunisia was declared entitled to reparations for the loss of life and the damage done, for which Israel had claimed responsibility. The Secretary-General was asked to report on the text's working by 30 November 1985.
un-sc-res-673: In the sequence of Security Council decisions, Resolution 673 is the entry catalogued for 1990 in this library. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations.
un-sc-res-73:
Armistice agreements between Israel and its Arab neighbors changed the Palestine question in 1949. The agreements had been reached through talks led by the United Nations mediator. They grew out of Resolution 62 of 1948, which had called for an armistice. Resolution 73 was adopted on 11 August 1949. Later texts cite that date, although the file's own header gives 21 August.

The Council noted the agreements with satisfaction. It called them a major step toward lasting peace in Palestine. The armistice replaced the truce ordered in 1948, but one part of that order stayed in force. The call for an unconditional cease-fire, from Resolution 54, held until a final peaceful settlement was reached. The acting mediator, his work complete, was released from any further duties under the Council's earlier resolutions. The mixed armistice commissions would now watch over the agreements, with help from the truce observers on the ground.
un-sc-res-973:
Western Sahara's promised referendum still had no date in January 1995. On 13 January 1995 the Security Council restated its pledge to hold the vote without further delay. The vote would let the territory's people choose their future. The Settlement Plan accepted by both parties set the rules. Voter identification had begun, though it moved slowly. The Council praised MINURSO for the progress made so far.

Both parties had to work fully with the Secretary-General and the mission. The planned timetable in his December report set the pace. The Council stayed committed to a just and lasting solution. It asked him to keep it informed of every step. Identification of voters later bogged down in appeals, and the vote never came.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1073, adopted on 28 September 1996 by fourteen votes to none with the United States abstaining, answers a week of deadly clashes in Jerusalem and the West Bank. Israel had opened an entrance to an archaeological tunnel near the Al Aqsa Mosque. Fighting spread through Jerusalem, Nablus, Ramallah, Bethlehem, and Gaza, killing many Palestinian civilians and also costing lives in clashes between Israeli soldiers and Palestinian police.

The Council called for an instant halt to, and undoing of, every act that had sparked the crisis, including the tunnel opening. It urged both parties to honor their existing agreements and get the peace process moving again. Foreign ministers of several countries had joined the Council's debate, underlining the alarm.

Binding world rules against terrorism are laid down here on 28 September 2001, weeks after the September attacks. Passed under Chapter VII, the text orders every state to act, not just those directly attacked. Its target is the money and support networks that let terrorist groups operate.

States must block terrorist funding, freeze the assets of people involved in terrorism, and ban help or safe haven for them. They must also share intelligence, tighten border and document controls, and bring terrorists to justice. A new Counter-Terrorism Committee, made up of all Council members, would track how each country carried out these duties, with reports due within 90 days.

East Timor's support mission, UNMISET, has its drawdown adjusted on 4 April 2003. Timor-Leste had made real progress since independence with the mission's help. Yet security problems remained, and building a capable national police force was the top priority identified.

The cuts are slowed and reshaped. The police component gains an international formed unit for one year and more training capacity in key areas. On the military side, two battalions stay near the border line through December 2003, with supporting units, rather than leaving on the old schedule. Total military peacekeepers are to fall more gradually, reaching 1,750 later than first planned.

Timor-Leste's UN mission gets a final stretch in Resolution 1573, adopted unanimously on 16 November 2004. The Council praised Timorese leaders and citizens for the peace and stability they had built since independence, and credited UNMISET, the support mission, for progress during its consolidation phase. Partners helping with institutions and development were thanked as well.

Even so, the text is candid that Timor-Leste had not reached self-sufficiency, above all in public administration, law enforcement, and security. The Council extended UNMISET into May 2005 so its remaining tasks could be finished in an orderly wind-down. It also noted improving ties with neighbors and work toward settling border questions, and it commended the Serious Crimes Unit's efforts.

The committee that watches over resolution 1540, the text barring weapons of mass destruction from reaching non-state actors, is extended on 27 April 2006. The committee had reviewed the first round of national reports on how states were applying the rules. Not every state had yet reported.

The 1540 Committee's mandate is extended for two years, and it is told to step up its work promoting full implementation. States that had not filed a first report are called on to do so without delay. The committee is to keep helping states that ask for assistance with their laws and controls, and to report back on progress before its renewed mandate ends.

A Belgian-run trust land in central Africa became a kingdom in 1962. Burundi won its freedom on 1 July that year. King Mwambutsa IV took the throne of the new state. Its bid for a UN seat came weeks later. Resolution 173 passed with no dissent on 26 July 1962.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit the Kingdom of Burundi. The Assembly agreed that fall. Burundi came in beside its twin, Rwanda, freed the same day from the same trust. The two states shared much: hills, tongues, and a tense mix of Hutu and Tutsi. Their paths since have been marked by bloodshed. This calm one-line text holds none of that dread. It is a plain legal birth note.

Lebanon's force, UNIFIL, is extended until 31 August 2008 on 24 August 2007. The force had been greatly expanded after the 2006 war. Commitment to Lebanon's sovereignty and to full respect for the cessation of hostilities and the Blue Line is restated.

All parties are called on to respect the halt in fighting and cooperate fully with the United Nations and UNIFIL. Work on the causes of the conflict is pressed for, with a note that the abducted Israeli soldiers still had not been released. The Secretary-General is to keep reporting on the carrying out of the 2006 settlement, including progress toward a permanent ceasefire and a long-term settlement between Lebanon and Israel.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force, UNFICYP, is extended on 29 May 2009. Full settlement talks between the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders had been running since 2008, and the progress made and the leaders' joint statements are warmly welcomed. Finding a solution, it is echoed, rests first with the Cypriots themselves.

UNFICYP's mandate is extended for a further period, and the leaders are strongly urged to use the rare opening: faster talks, more trust, and a constructive spirit. More confidence-building steps are sought, including opening further crossing points. Both sides are also told to settle the demarcation of the buffer zone with the force. That is a matter of urgency, so the mission's work is not hampered by disputes over its lines.

UN Security Council Resolution 1973 — the historic 2011 resolution authorizing the no-fly zone over Libya. It permitted all necessary measures to protect civilians from Gaddafi’s forces. The 2011 Libya no-fly is the historic authorization: the Libyan civilians’ protection formally permitted.

Senegal complained to the Council about shelling from a Portuguese base in late 1969. Shells fired from Portuguese Guinea had hit the village of Samine in southern Senegal. One person was killed and eight were badly wounded on 25 November. More shelling followed on 7 December. Resolution 273 was adopted on 9 December 1969.

The Council strongly condemned the Portuguese authorities for the shelling. Houses were destroyed in the attacks, and a gendarmerie building was struck. Portugal was again called on to stop violating Senegal's sovereignty and territory at once. The Council warned that it would meet to consider other measures if Portugal failed to comply. It also kept the question on its agenda, so the matter stayed open for further action.

Sao Tome and Principe is recommended for United Nations membership in Resolution 373, adopted unanimously on 18 August 1975. The Council weighed the bid of Sao Tome and Principe, a two-island country in the Gulf of Guinea. It had gained independence from Portugal a month earlier, in July 1975.

The Assembly was asked to admit the new state, and it did so that September. Admission texts rarely run longer than this one; the real work is done by the recommendation itself, which the Charter makes a condition for membership. For one of Africa's smallest countries, the resolution marks the formal start of its presence in international politics.

Israel's bombing of Tunis is condemned in Resolution 573, adopted in October 1985 by fourteen votes to none with the United States abstaining. On 1 October, Israeli jets had struck a target in the southern suburb of Hammam-Plage, and Tunisia complained to the Council the same day. Its foreign minister told the Council the raid caused heavy loss of life and extensive material damage, and Israel claimed responsibility openly.

The Council condemned vigorously what it called armed aggression against Tunisia's soil, a flagrant breach of the Charter. It demanded that Israel refrain from such attacks and from threatening them. It also held that Tunisia was entitled to appropriate reparations for the lives lost and damage done.

Israel refused to receive a fact-finding mission to the occupied territories in October 1990, and the Council answered on 24 October. Resolution 672, passed on 12 October after deadly violence in Jerusalem, had ordered the mission. The Secretary-General briefed the Council on the refusal on 19 October. Resolution 673 is the reply.

The Council deplored Israel's refusal to receive the mission. The Israeli government was urged to reconsider its decision. The Council insisted that Israel comply fully with Resolution 672, so the mission could go ahead as planned. The Secretary-General was asked to send in the report that the earlier resolution required. The Council said it would give that report full and speedy consideration. The dispute over access became part of the wider record on the occupied territories.

Armistice deals between Israel and its neighbors drew the Council's blessing in 1949. On 11 August, it adopted Resolution 73. Nine members voted yes and none voted no. The Ukrainian and Soviet republics held back. The deals had grown out of talks held under the Council's 1948 truce calls.

The text hails the deals as a big step toward lasting peace. It declares that they replace the earlier truce. It restates the order for a full, lasting ceasefire. Mixed armistice panels, chaired by the UN truce chief, would watch the lines. The Council also frees the Acting Mediator from his duties. The lines blessed here shaped the region's map for eighteen years.

Resolution 973 was adopted unanimously by the UN Security Council on 13 January 1995, and it deals with Western Sahara. The Council was trying to move a long-delayed settlement plan toward a referendum that would let the people of the territory decide their own future. Progress on identifying who could vote had begun, but it was going slowly.

Acting on a December 1994 report from the Secretary-General, the Council approved a larger deployment for MINURSO, the UN mission running the referendum process. It repeated its pledge to hold a free and fair vote without further delay and pressed both parties to cooperate fully with the mission. The Secretary-General had to report back by the end of March 1995 on staffing, supplies, and final plans.
wheatley-poems-1773:
Phillis Wheatley published Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral in London in 1773. The title page names her as servant to Mr. John Wheatley of Boston in New England. Brought from Africa as a child and held in slavery, she had won rare fame as a young poet by then.

The contents list verses on virtue, on the works of God, and on the death of preacher George Whitefield. Elegies, hymns to morning and evening, and a poem on Goliath of Gath fill out the book. Her clear and poised verse forced a doubting world to face Black genius, and it fed early calls to end slavery.
zola-fat-and-thin-1873:
Vizetelly's English version calls Zola's 1873 novel The Fat and the Thin, or Le Ventre de Paris. A Shakespeare motto up front gives Cassius a lean and hungry look. Vizetelly's opening essay centers on the vast central markets of Paris, the Halles.

The markets form a world of their own, teeming with life at set hours. Zola loved subjects where vast crowds could be shown in motion, Vizetelly notes. Into that plenty steps Florent, an escaped political prisoner, thin and haunted among the fat and thriving. The clash of hunger and plenty becomes a strong parable of appetite in all its forms.
